stories.Headline: Getty Images v Stability AI – Court of Appeal hearing
stories.Summary:
The Court of Appeal held the second day of a landmark hearing on November 12, 2026. Getty Images brought this appeal against Stability AI, the developer of the Stable Diffusion AI image generator. This legal dispute focuses on intellectual property and how copyright law applies to generative AI models. The case follows a mixed High Court judgment delivered in November 2025 that largely favoured Stability AI. Getty won a small part of its trade mark claim, but its copyright claim failed.

The appeal examines section 27(3) of the Copyright, Designs, and Patents Act 1988 regarding infringing copies. Getty argues that making a model includes training it, even if the finished article contains no copies. Stability AI wants to overturn findings that an intangible model is an article and that it distributed it. The High Court previously ruled that Stable Diffusion was not an infringing copy because it stored no images. This specific model was trained outside the United Kingdom, which influenced the original trial's copyright claims.

Getty Images argues that the law does not require a finished model to contain copies of works. They claim that any article whose making in the UK would be infringing is an infringing copy. Stability AI says the court should focus on what was produced rather than how it was developed. Stability AI further argues that extending laws to overseas training is a matter for Parliament, not courts. They believe the High Court was correct in its original ruling regarding the nature of copies.

The British Recorded Music Industry Limited intervened to support Getty and warn of consequences for creative industries. BPI says the High Court approach could let developers train models offshore and bring them back. BPI also cited two Munich Court cases where AI models were found to have memorised copyright works. This intervention highlights that the outcome will affect a wide spectrum of various global creative industries. Rights holders and AI developers are both affected by how these legal protections are eventually applied.

Getty previously dropped primary copyright claims on June 25, 2025, to pursue secondary infringement and passing off. The High Court accepted that intangible models are articles but rejected the secondary infringement claim in 2025. This dispute is part of a wider wave of litigation, including a US lawsuit over 12 million images. The UK government is also considering its approach to copyright and AI after a March 2026 report. Parallel proceedings between Getty and Stability AI are currently ongoing within the United States legal system.

The Court of Appeal will now hand down a judgment that may influence how rights holders protect content. A Getty victory would allow copyright claims against models trained abroad on unlicensed works, regardless of storage. A Stability AI victory would keep the training location and storage of copies as the key factors. The articles leave open whether the court will overturn the findings on intangible articles and distribution. The final ruling will determine if AI models can be infringing copies without containing the original works.

stories.Headline: Lee Jae-yong Pledges 46 Trillion Won Investment to Transform Onyang Campus into HBM Hub
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong unveiled plans on Thursday to transform the company's Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province, into a major advanced packaging hub for high-bandwidth memory, a key semiconductor for artificial intelligence. Lee attended the groundbreaking ceremony for the Chungcheong Mega Project at the Onyang Campus alongside President Lee Jae-myung, government officials, local government representatives and business leaders. Samsung Electronics plans to invest a total of 46 trillion won in the campus in phases and build five HBM production lines. The existing semiconductor assembly and testing facility will become a state-of-the-art HBM packaging production base. The new facility launched with the groundbreaking ceremony is known as the fifth production line.

Samsung plans to invest 6 trillion won in construction and another 40 trillion won in advanced equipment as part of the 46 trillion won investment. The fifth production line will feature a cleanroom covering approximately 31,000 square meters in a three-story building, and Samsung aims to begin operations in June 2028. Once completed, the total floor area of the Onyang Campus will expand from the current 270,000 square meters to approximately 420,000 square meters, an increase of about 60%. The new facility is expected to create around 700 direct jobs. The Onyang Campus has served as one of Samsung Electronics' key semiconductor back-end manufacturing sites since late 1991.

Lee said in his welcoming remarks that with today's groundbreaking ceremony the company promises another leap forward. He added that the Onyang Campus would evolve from a facility primarily focused on semiconductor assembly and testing into a cutting-edge HBM hub, which he described as the heart of AI semiconductors. Lee recalled that about four decades ago the area consisted largely of barren land and unpaved roads, but has since developed into an advanced semiconductor facility specializing in assembly and testing. He stressed the importance of cooperation between the government, local authorities and businesses in carrying out the large-scale investment. Lee pledged that Samsung would take greater responsibility in strengthening the country's industrial competitiveness, saying the company will take on an even greater sense of responsibility.

President Lee Jae-myung praised Samsung's investment decision at the groundbreaking ceremony, noting that construction began roughly four months after Samsung announced its Chungcheong investment plan in July. He thanked Lee Jae-yong and Samsung employees for making bold investment decisions and implementing them quickly. The two leaders toured the site together following the ceremony, where Lee Jae-yong introduced the president to Samsung's Test & System Package, one of the main products manufactured at the Onyang Campus, and President Lee signed the product during the visit. The president later attended the fourth public-private joint inspection meeting for the Mega Project, where the government discussed measures to proactively address difficulties faced by companies at investment sites and accelerate the realization of investment outcomes. Industry observers say the competition in the HBM market is increasingly extending beyond memory production capacity to advanced packaging technology.

The Onyang Campus has accumulated more than three decades of experience in semiconductor assembly and testing at the site, and the shift toward HBM is aimed at leveraging that accumulated back-end manufacturing expertise to strengthen Samsung's competitiveness in advanced packaging. HBM consists of multiple DRAM chips vertically stacked to deliver high bandwidth and improved data-processing efficiency. As demand for AI accelerators and data centers grows, advanced packaging technologies for connecting, stacking and testing memory chips have become increasingly important to HBM competitiveness. The project is also part of Samsung's broader plan to strengthen the semiconductor ecosystem in the Chungcheong region, combining the existing semiconductor infrastructure in Cheonan and Asan with new HBM packaging capabilities in Onyang. Samsung's 46 trillion won investment is expected to serve as a key step in rebuilding its HBM competitiveness and strengthening its position in the rapidly growing AI semiconductor market.

Samsung expects the Onyang project to strengthen the semiconductor back-end ecosystem in the Chungcheong region and plans to add advanced HBM packaging capabilities to its existing assembly and testing operations. The company aims to further develop the Cheonan-Asan area into a major production hub for advanced semiconductor packaging. With Lee Jae-yong personally emphasizing the site's transformation into an HBM hub, Samsung is expected to accelerate its efforts to expand advanced packaging capabilities and establish the Chungcheong region as a major base for next-generation AI semiconductor production. stories.Headline: European shares log record close on Siemens, CoreWeave-fuelled AI optimism
stories.Summary:
European shares closed at a record on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, just short of their intraday high, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and CoreWeave lifted investor confidence in artificial intelligence. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 0.72 per cent to 663.05 points, a whisker below the intraday record of 663.41. Germany's DAX also rose 1.2 per cent and hovered near its own all-time high. Siemens Energy led the gains after its shares jumped 10.8 per cent.

The AI equipment maker raised its profit margin expectations for 2027 and said it planned to more than triple its dividend. Peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, while the broader tech sector added 2.5 per cent. Chip-related stocks also rose, with Soitec up 11.9 per cent and Aixtron up 8 per cent. Optimism was further boosted by CoreWeave, a neocloud company, which said it expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.

CoreWeave had been at the centre of AI bubble fears that triggered a global market selloff the previous week. Analysts quoted by Reuters questioned whether the large AI investment would prove profitable across the industry, noting that not all AI companies would succeed. Societe Generale analysts said the rally looked somewhat stretched given political and economic risks, and they saw limited further upside for the index by year-end. Investors also watched interest rates closely after hotter-than-expected US inflation data and hawkish Federal Reserve comments pointed to another rate hike next month.

Sectors less exposed to AI, including retail and food and beverage, lagged on the day. Czech ammunition and arms producer CSG fell 21.6 per cent after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast. A rebound in Brent crude after shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz added to inflation concerns in energy-importing Europe. Traders expect at least one quarter-point rate hike by the European Central Bank by February 2027.

stories.Headline: What California's new law means for legal teams using AI and whether other states could follow suit
stories.Summary:
California became the first state to regulate how attorneys use AI by statute, and the new law takes effect January 1, 2027. Senator Tom Umberg, chair of the state's Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced Senate Bill 574 in February 2025. After two rounds of amendments in the Senate and four in the Assembly, it passed both chambers on the last day of the session. On Sept. 30, 2026, Governor Gavin Newsom signed it. The State Bar first issued AI guidance for attorneys in 2023, and the Judicial Council followed in 2025 with rules for how judges and court staff use generative AI.

The law lets attorneys use generative AI to assist in the practice of law but not delegate the practice of law to it. SB 574 also sets limits for arbitrators and tightens citation rules for filings in California courts, whether or not AI was involved. Attorneys can't put confidential, personal identifying, or other nonpublic information into an AI system unless access is limited to them and the people they authorize, who also have to keep it confidential. The law's definition of personal identifying information covers dates of birth, witness addresses and phone numbers, and medical and financial details. Attorneys have to take reasonable steps to verify anything AI produces and fix errors or hallucinations before using it, contract review included.

Attorneys who use AI have to disclose it on documents they submit to a court, and for content shared with the public they only have to consider disclosing it. Every citation in a court filing has to be personally verified by an attorney responsible for it, whether it came from AI, a research database, or a colleague's old brief. Arbitrators can't hand off any part of their decision-making to AI, and if they want to rely on AI-generated information from outside the record they have to tell the parties first and, where practical, let them weigh in. Courts can sanction attorneys and their firms, and firms are generally on the hook for their lawyers' and staff's violations. Attorneys usually get 21 days to withdraw or fix a challenged filing first, and the bill doesn't spell out separate penalties for the other duties.

The law doesn't draw a firm line between assisting and delegating or even what type of AI tools need a disclosure, such as whether AI-powered grammar suggestions built into Word trigger disclosure. It also doesn't say what a disclosure should say or how hands-on personally verified has to be, and an earlier version required attorneys to read every cited source personally before lawmakers cut that. The law applies to every attorney licensed in California, including in-house counsel, and the citation rule also reaches anyone filing in a California court, wherever they're licensed. Firms are generally on the hook for violations by their lawyers and staff, and on large filings with many contributors the law doesn't say which attorney is responsible for the citations. In-house teams face the duties to protect sensitive information and check AI output beyond the courtroom, including when in-house lawyers use AI to review contracts or answer questions from the business.

When California passed its consumer privacy law in 2018, it stood alone, and currently roughly 20 states have their own. In most states the state supreme court regulates the practice of law, so the next round of AI rules is more likely to come from courts than legislatures. The New York state court system adopted a statewide rule on attorney AI use in June 2026, and lawmakers have also introduced bills that would require an AI-disclosure affidavit with court filings, though similar bills have stalled in committee. The Florida Supreme Court updated its practice rules so that signing a filing certifies its cited authorities exist and are cited accurately. The Illinois Supreme Court's AI policy lets lawyers use AI without disclosing it, as long as they review the output, and the court decided its existing rules were enough.

California's State Bar guidance says understanding an AI tool's capabilities and limits is part of a lawyer's duty of competence, and it is also proposed adding AI guidance to several professional conduct rules. The Bar's 2026 guidance already says the more autonomy a tool has, the more oversight the lawyer owes. Florida's Supreme Court already replaced a patchwork of local AI disclosure orders with one rule about whether citations are real. Citation verification is the most likely rule to spread, since California and Florida both landed on it, while disclosure is where states will probably keep disagreeing. For teams working across state lines, that means a patchwork for a while, and some may find it simpler to treat California's rules as their baseline everywhere.

stories.Headline: Google’s new AI ‘ultimatum’ sparks concern over tech giant’s power in California schools
stories.Summary:
Google announced this week that starting in January it plans to block K-12 students from using its search engine unless districts opt into the company's AI-generated version of it. The announcement came on Tuesday, according to the San Mateo Daily Journal, and Google's vice president and general manager of education, Chris Phillips, discussed it on Monday during a virtual briefing. Google said in a blog post on Tuesday that it will update its search function for schools. The company also clarified in a post on X on Tuesday that schools can turn off its separate AI products, Gemini and Gemini Notebook. The KXAN article, posted November 11, 2026, said Google told education leaders they must either accept some AI in classrooms or lose access to its search engine.

Google announced that early next year its Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will automatically be turned off for school districts, and administrators will have to choose to opt into the features. The company said Search and AI are "deeply integrated," and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI. Google is updating its Search feature so AI Overviews "will offer step-by-step guided learning" instead of instantly giving students the answers. About three-quarters of American teens and tweens use or interact with the AI summaries in search results, according to a recent report by Common Sense Media. In a series of 180 tests, Common Sense Media researchers found that Google's AI Mode completed students' homework for them every time, and the AI feature also invented fake questions and cited unreliable sources such as Reddit and Facebook.

Phillips said on Monday during a virtual briefing that if a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have Search on at all. Google said in a blog post on Tuesday that it will update its search function for schools so that students don't get quick answers, according to the San Mateo Daily Journal. The company said it will continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure it is giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning. Google said Search and AI are "deeply integrated," and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into public schools.

Lila Byock said that "educational value ,  not shareholder value ,  must determine" the technology used by students, and she said Google forced its AI products into classrooms and parents fought back. Byock said the company's hostile ultimatum is a desperate attempt to maintain its stranglehold on public education, and she said districts should "reclaim their authority from corporate interests and divest from Google." Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense Media, said Google search, Google Drive and other Google tools support student learning in a myriad of ways, and she said losing that option seems like a missed opportunity. Rory Mir, director of community tech engagement at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said "degoogling," or divesting from Google software, may be easier for individuals or smaller organizations than for school districts. Mir said the trick comes with real monetary costs as well as labor costs and disruption, and he said Google's new policy should involve a "big discussion about Google's role as a monopolist" with "undue power over" schools' decisions.

Los Angeles Unified, the state's largest district, has already placed restrictions on generative AI, and Google's decision could complicate such efforts, particularly because schools rely on the company's digital tools. L.A. Unified uses a statewide purchasing arrangement for Google Workspace, and a district spokesperson said the district is monitoring the situation and its potential implications for schools, educators and students. Some parents of Long Beach Unified students, who are part of a new tech policy group that also includes teachers, students, administrators and industry experts, will "have an opportunity to provide input" into the district's options, a district spokesperson said. The Long Beach Unified spokesperson said the district is in the middle of a student survey about AI use in school. Common Sense Media researchers have not reviewed Google's Guided Learning mode, and many school districts will have to decide to opt into Google's AI-integrated search or find a new search alternative in the middle of the school year.

Google has long been woven into California students' education, with Google search, Chromebooks and Gmail quietly in the background in students' daily lives. The decadeslong relationship between the search giant and education turned into the subject of a furor this week, according to the San Mateo Daily Journal. Google's announcement comes as districts across California debate restrictions on artificial intelligence and technology use in the classroom. Renteria of Common Sense Media said school districts with more robust technology departments are more likely to handle the change. Mir, with EFF, said Google's new policy should involve a "big discussion about Google's role as a monopolist" with "undue power over" schools' decisions.

District leaders say a fight would be a big undertaking, but some may be up to the challenge, especially as public outcry after the announcement grows. Mir said it is important for Google to do the right thing and offer more control over these tools to administrators and users, so they can choose the experience that is right for their students and not get swept up into these suites where it's all or nothing. Mir said he is hoping that following a higher bar for students. The articles do not say what districts will decide before the January start date. The articles do not say whether Google will change the policy in response to the outcry.

stories.Summary:
San Francisco based Charta Health secured 55 million dollars in Series B funding on November 10, 2026, to automate medical billing workflows. Insight Partners led this investment round, which was the third for the company in less than two years of total operation. Existing investors Madrona, Bain Capital Ventures, and South Park Commons participated in the round, along with the investment firm known as QuantumLight. This latest funding brings the total amount raised by the company to 85 million dollars for its AI powered tools. The company uses these funds to launch Charta for Providers and expand its Charta for Payers offering to new specialties.

The platform provides autonomous coding, revenue discovery, risk adjustment, automated feedback, and payer compliance tools for healthcare providers using the software. For payers, the company offers HEDIS and quality analytics, RADV and audit management, and a smart coding platform for projects. The new Charta for Payers launch includes six AI products designed to improve operational efficiencies and accuracy around medical billing workflows. Charta Health also announced an agreement earlier this year to provide its offerings in the digital app store called athenahealth Marketplace. This ecosystem serves healthcare providers who use athenahealth platforms for medical billing, practice management, and electronic health records for patients.

Jeff Horing is a cofounder and managing director at Insight Partners who stated that healthcare payments depend on the medical chart. He said that charting errors cause costly problems across the entire process and that the opportunity lies in getting records right. Horing believes that Charta pairs AI with customer specific coding expertise to serve both the payer and provider sides of market. He expressed excitement about partnering with Justin, Scott, and the team as they scale their operations to reach more healthcare clients. The company aims to establish the ground truth of a medical record before a claim is submitted to the payer.

Other companies in the revenue cycle management space include Candid Health, which secured 120 million dollars in Series D funding. Candid Health stated that this funding tripled its valuation from the Series C round that occurred in February of 2025. CodaMetrix is another AI medical coding company that raised 40 million dollars in 2024 after a 55 million dollar Series A. San Francisco based Arintra offers an enterprise AI platform and raised 25 million dollars in Series B funding earlier this year. Arintra previously raised 21 million dollars in Series A funding in 2025, bringing its total raise to 51 million dollars.

Charta Health raised 8.1 million dollars in seed funding and 22 million dollars in Series A funding during the last year. The company focuses on automating chart review, billing, and coding workflows using artificial intelligence to reduce errors in medical records. This market includes various AI platforms that focus on healthcare revenue assurance and financial platforms for providers and health plans. The company operates in a competitive landscape where multiple firms are raising significant capital to automate the healthcare revenue cycle. These tools are designed to help both health plans and providers manage the complexities of medical billing and coding.

The company will now use the new funds to support the launch of its Charta for Providers product for clients. It also plans to expand the Charta for Payers offering to include a wider range of medical specialties for users. stories.Headline: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive
stories.Summary:
EU leaders gathered in Dublin on Friday for the bloc's first-ever summit on artificial intelligence, held at the Convention Center where the European Political Community summit had met that same week. The meeting came at a critical moment as the EU sought a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology. French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," addressed the leaders. Mensch urged them to act now to keep pace with the United States and China in AI development.

The articles describe no new law, budget or rule adopted at the summit. Mensch said Europe needs speed, financing and strong coordination between member states to compete. Estonia and Finland wrote a letter before the summit calling for EU-level arrangements to respond to serious AI incidents. That letter also urged developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly. European Council President Antonio Costa said Europe must capture AI's benefits, from higher productivity to better public services, while managing its risks and changes.

Costa's office framed the summit's aim as helping set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI. Costa stated the summit's purpose in a post on X. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she was frustrated with the notion that Europe had somehow lost the AI race. She said the EU has world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI, and that ideas need financing to grow in Europe. Kaja Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, cited drones equipped with artificial intelligence being used to find and kill targets in Ukraine.

The summit came amid growing worries about a technology expected to transform industries, labor markets and societies. It followed a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign this week after it was revealed he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company. Leaders faced questions about how to unlock AI's potential, catch up with China and the United States, and protect individuals and businesses from its risks. The articles also note that weekend protests across Europe were warning of AI's environmental costs and demanding a halt to new data center expansion.

Mensch's company, Mistral, is considered Europe's leading AI model developer. The articles describe the summit as taking place as the bloc sought a common position on a technology it had not yet unified its policy on. Metsola's comments responded directly to the perception that Europe was trailing in the race. Concerns about the risks to individuals and businesses were raised alongside the push for competitiveness. The protests against data centers add the environmental dimension to the debate over AI's costs.

The articles do not say what policies, funding or coordination mechanisms, if any, the leaders agreed to pursue after the summit. They also do not state whether the EU-level incident response arrangements proposed by Estonia and Finland will be adopted. How Europe will catch up with the United States and China, and how it will balance AI ambitions against citizen protection, remain unresolved in the reporting. The articles leave open when, or whether, the bloc will act on Mensch's call to move now.

stories.Headline: Banks Face Agentic AI’s Twin Tests: Customer Authority and Internal Costs
stories.Summary:
Banks are facing two linked pressures as artificial intelligence agents move from answering questions to taking action. On one side, customers may delegate financial decisions to agents, raising legal questions about consent and accountability. On the other, banks deploying their own agents may face runaway computing costs that erode expected savings. A WilmerHale client alert and a Reuters report on McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review describe both problems.

The compliance issue starts with whose instructions a bank is carrying out. WilmerHale's analysis, focused on the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority framework, separates authenticating an agent from establishing its authority. Software may legitimately access an account yet make a transfer or investment beyond the limits the customer intended. Under the U.K. Payment Services Regulations, payment authorization depends on payer consent through an agreed procedure, and strong customer authentication is a separate requirement. Banks therefore need to consider how authority is established, restricted and withdrawn, and when customers must approve further action.

Those concerns help explain the caution across the industry. Reuters reported that most banks currently block external agents from authorizing transactions within their systems. Demand nevertheless appears substantial, since McKinsey surveyed 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide. Among AI users, 72% said they would allow a banking agent to perform one financial task, though they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. The consultancy expects widespread customer use of agents within three years.

Delegation also complicates financial crime monitoring and disputes. WilmerHale describes an agent choosing payment methods, currencies or intermediaries that individually seem reasonable but collectively produce unusual activity. Existing anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations still apply, so banks must separate legitimate automation from fraud or evasion. When a customer disputes a transaction, ordinary records may not show whether the agent followed its instructions, so WilmerHale suggests banks consider what evidence they need, including permissions and action histories.

Banks' own agents raise a separate cost problem. Reuters reported McKinsey's warning that token spending, the units underlying AI processing charges, could easily reach 20% of banks' total labor costs. Some banks have assigned oversight to teams called AI FinOps, and agent-to-agent communication makes earlier usage controls less effective. As a result, banks are becoming more selective, favoring applications with stronger expected returns and asking whether added revenue justifies higher AI spending. The two pressures could compound, since customer agents might shift deposits into higher-yielding alternatives while banks absorb the costs of their own automation.

stories.Headline: EU to mobilise billions of euro for AI Gigafactories, Europe's tech sovereignty
stories.Summary:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said seven AI Gigafactories are in the planning and about 30 billion euro is being mobilised for them, after EU leaders held their first-ever AI Summit on November 13, 2026. She spoke at a news conference after the informal European Council meeting, which took place in Dublin on Friday, November 13, 2026. The European Council said leaders gathered for their first dedicated summit discussion of artificial intelligence, putting European AI sovereignty, investment in advanced computing and enforcement of new technology rules at the centre. The meeting was scheduled to examine how AI can support productivity, industrial change and public services, while also addressing cybersecurity, market concentration, democratic integrity, fundamental rights and the effect on labour markets. On November 12, the European Parliament adopted by 405 votes to 133 with 60 abstentions a resolution calling for parliamentary scrutiny and regulation of AI's impact on EU democratic processes, institutional balance and fundamental rights.

Von der Leyen said the seven Gigafactories will provide the computing capacities startups need to build the most advanced AI models, and that more computing capacity will be key for Europe to play a role in frontier models and frontier AI. She said Europe's tech sovereignty requires massive investments, at least 500 billion euro according to the Commission's own estimates. She said Europe is creating more tech start-ups than the US but many fail to receive the necessary support to scale, and that the Scaleup Europe fund has been a great success from the outset, while what is missing now are large investments in chips, compute and frontier AI. She said the Savings and Investment Union must be completed, private investment attracted, and the next European budget must reflect this ambition, and that the meeting saw a shared will to put forward ideas for Tech sovereignty financing, with her to follow up with an ambitious proposal. She said Europe leads in AI adoption, with 37 per cent of EU businesses using AI on average in 2025, and Finland outstanding at 66 per cent, almost double the US.

Von der Leyen said she wants to move AI from the screen to the real world, and that earlier this year she appointed Jim Snabe as Special Envoy for Industrial Artificial Intelligence. She said work is focused on five sectors where AI can have the biggest value and impact, with a vision coupled with concrete actions in each sector, and the first part of this work to come out in two weeks. European Council President António Costa told the news conference that AI is the most important technology of our time, and that Europe must make the most of its benefits from higher productivity to better public services. Costa said risks must be managed effectively, global standards and responsible global governance set to make AI safe and human-centric, and Europe's skilled talent, world class research and dynamic start up scene translated into real advantages. He said this depends on how much public and private investment can be mobilised for competitive AI models, capacity to secure value chains and reduce dangerous dependencies, and access to affordable and clean energy.

Costa said effective adoption of AI in the economy is needed to reap productivity gains, and that initiatives like the Savings and Investments Union and the so called 28th regime will help. He said the volumes of funding needed to catch up with global peers require significant extra efforts, and the next European long-term Budget, in particular the new European Competitiveness Fund, will play a decisive role. Costa said clear oversight for managing AI's risks and challenges is a pre-condition for public trust, and without trust an AI strategy cannot succeed. He said the European Union is the first region in the world with an AI governance framework, and that the EU must be active in the G7, the G20, supporting the efforts of the upcoming UK presidency, and in the United Nations. Costa said AI's impact on labour markets and society, especially the sustainability of the social model, must be reflected on, and that AI and its impacts on societies will be the central theme of the Social Summit in 2027, marking 10 years of the European pillar of social rights together with social partners.

MEPs said AI can assist with evidence-based policymaking and the simplification and evaluation of EU law but must never replace human political responsibility or result in purely automated political decisions, and that European AI tools should be prioritised, particularly within EU institutions. The text says the EU should scale up European technology and ensure strategic autonomy across the AI value chain, and that technologies with global security and societal implications require an international agreement modelled on nuclear non-proliferation, with the EU taking a leading role. MEPs said safeguards must be built alongside AI without unnecessarily hampering innovation or competitiveness, and called for a systematic parliamentary assessment of AI's risks and opportunities and a reform of European electoral law. They said the Charter of Fundamental Rights should include new rights such as protection of personal identity and likeness and algorithmic transparency, and the report proposes a budget-neutral administrative unit, the European Parliament AI observatory, to support Parliament committees in ex post evaluation of AI-related legislation and analysis of AI's impact on institutional balance and democratic processes. The rapporteur on the resolution, Manolis Kefalogiannis, said AI does not progress linearly but advances in leaps, and Europe must take the lead in shaping it, paraphrasing Abraham Lincoln with the words by humans, for humans, with humans, so that AI does not become the last invention humans will ever need to create.

The European Commission has placed high-performance computing at the core of its industrial policy, and its AI programme says the InvestAI initiative is intended to mobilise 20 billion euro for up to five AI gigafactories. The facilities are planned to give researchers, start-ups, industry and public authorities access to large-scale computing resources for developing and training advanced models. In July, the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking opened a call for private-led AI gigafactories, and the Commission said the projects are designed to combine advanced processors, software, cloud capabilities, high-speed connectivity and data centres, and that the call could unlock more than 30 billion euro in investment. The initiative is separate from the AI Factories programme, which provides access to supercomputing resources for companies and researchers, and the Commission says 19 AI Factories are being rolled out across Europe, with 13 factory antennas intended to extend regional access. The Commission has set the broader goal of tripling the EU's data-centre capacity over the next five to seven years, and the new gigafactory programme is intended to add facilities capable of supporting the development of frontier models rather than only smaller-scale experimentation.

Costa convened the meeting after leaders had designated 2026 the Year of Competitiveness, and in an invitation letter issued this month he said a leaders-level discussion was needed because of the speed of AI development and its effects on economies and societies. The format was informal, so it was not designed to produce binding legislation or formal European Council conclusions, and its stated purpose was to guide the bloc's next strategic choices. At the first session, leaders were due to hear from Arthur Mensch, chief executive of the French AI company Mistral AI, on Europe's position in the global AI market and the steps needed to strengthen competitiveness and strategic autonomy. The Council's agenda lists investment, infrastructure, access to affordable clean energy, industrial adoption and reductions in critical dependencies as the main subjects for that discussion. The Council said the leaders would consider reducing critical dependencies across the AI value chain, expanding European capabilities and developing infrastructure backed by clean energy and public and private finance.

Von der Leyen said she will follow up with an ambitious proposal on Tech sovereignty financing, and the first part of the work on the five sectors is to come out in two weeks. The articles do not say when the seven Gigafactories will be built, where they will be located or who will fund them, and they do not give the date of the follow-up proposal. The articles do not say what the informal meeting concluded or whether the leaders reached any decision on the financing ideas. The articles do not say how the 30 billion euro being mobilised relates to the 20 billion euro InvestAI figure or the more than 30 billion euro the call could unlock. The articles do not say what the European Parliament AI observatory would cost or when it would be set up, and they do not say what the EU will propose at the G7, G20 or United Nations.

stories.Headline: AI Is Killing Autonomously. Time for New Rules.
stories.Summary:
Next week, leaders will gather at the United Nations in Geneva to decide whether to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons, according to León Castellanos-Jankiewicz, writing on November 13, 2026. He says machines of this kind have already killed soldiers in eastern Ukraine, and three civilians in Zaporizhzhia last July. The first such incident came two years ago, when a swarm of ten drones struck a field near Bakhmut and killed at least two combatants. In the July case, a Russian drone guided by experimental AI killed three Ukrainians after failing to clear a building and exploding near sheltering civilians. Separately, UVA Darden professors Mike Lenox and Alex Cowan have proposed that AI firms using unlicensed training material release their model weights to the public once a year.

The Geneva meeting is where officials will decide whether to start negotiating a binding treaty, and the report drafted by governmental experts is the latest text on the table. That report covers human control before and during deployment, but once a drone is jammed, only inputs made before launch remain relevant for liability. The Russian drone was programmed by human operators to destroy propane fuel tanks at a gas station, and forensic analysis showed it flew with no link to an operator. It steered itself with a commercially available Nvidia chip, and the writer notes that the operators selected a target category, not a victim. Under the Darden proposal, any firm training models on unlicensed material, or building on a model that did, would release those weights annually, while keeping a lead of six to 18 months, about a year on average.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz is a senior researcher in International Law at the University of Amsterdam Faculty of Law and a non-resident fellow at the UN Institute for Disarmament Research. He argues that the experts' report is a good start but fails to close the enforcement gap for weapons operating in unobserved environments. He says it assigns no responsibility to the tech companies building these systems, which fiercely protect their commercial secrets from public scrutiny. He calls for enforceable obligations on states that field unpredictable killing machines, and for liability on the companies that build them. On the other side, Lenox and Cowan say their annual release rule would advance safety, competition and fairness, and that the time to adopt it is before AI companies go public.

Ukrainian drone maker Alexander Kokhanovskyy said the Bakhmut targets were identified by AI, adding that they simply launch it and know everything in the selected area will be dead. The International Committee of the Red Cross has called for unpredictable autonomous systems to be prohibited outright. Some argue that drone commanders already carry liability under existing laws, but the writer says this is hard to sustain when drones fly in dark mode behind enemy lines with no pilot input. In electronically jammed missions, he says, it becomes impossible to verify what the drones saw or targeted, even after strikes happen. Civilians such as the three killed in Zaporizhzhia are among those affected, while the Darden authors point to a public that is worried, with 55% to 77% in five national polls saying AI is moving too fast or should slow down.

Castellanos-Jankiewicz says international humanitarian law assumes each attack flows from a discrete decision, whereas drone swarms are decentralized by definition. He adds that machine learning systems can show emergent behavior, so their choices cannot be fully predicted or explained ahead of time as the law requires. A 2019 US Army report identified neural, ocular and auditory enhancement as technically feasible by mid-century, which he says further blurs the line between operators and their platforms. The Darden authors note that on October 26 Anthropic filed to go public, with reports putting its valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion. Three days later, Alphabet lost nearly 13% of its value in a single day, about $500 billion, on worries about whether its AI spending will pay off.

The articles do not say whether the Geneva leaders will vote to open treaty negotiations, only that they meet next week to decide. Castellanos-Jankiewicz warns that if diplomats fail to negotiate a new treaty, ever more lives will hang by a line of code. The Darden authors say their proposal could be tried first, and that if it proves insufficient the public could ask for more regulation. They add that under Nasdaq's new fast-entry rules, a newly public company of significant size can join the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days. The articles leave open how states and companies would respond, and whether any treaty or release rule would reach weapons that operate while jammed.

stories.Headline: Model schools turn to premium AI models to teach students better
stories.Summary:
Government model schools in Chennai and a private school in Chicago adopted premium artificial intelligence tools to teach students better in 2026. Headmasters in Chennai spent up to 1 lakh rupees on annual subscriptions for platforms like Claude to improve student learning. In Chicago, Alpha Chicago uses AI powered software called 2 Hour Learning to teach core subjects like math and science. These initiatives aim to modernize education through technology, though they operate in very different public and private school settings. The Chennai pilot program took place at the Centre for Academic Excellence in Saidapet to test these new digital tools.

The Chennai system involves 38 model schools, one per district, which share platforms with other schools in their neighboring districts. Teachers use Claude to generate codes and Gemini for image generation, while developers use GitHub to create a data dashboard. Students at the Chengalpet model school use more than 30 tablets after class hours to take various online assessments. In Chicago, students spend two hours each morning on computers before learning life skills like sewing, cooking, and public transportation. Alpha Chicago currently has 50 students but can hold 500, with tuition costing nearly 55,000 dollars per student.

Senthilvalavan, the headmaster at the Centre for Academic Excellence, said the tools help analyze where students need more academic help. He noted that these tools are useful for entrance exams like JEE, which test problem solving speed and error avoidance. Manikandan, the JEE coordinator for TN Model Schools, explained that the dashboard categorizes test results to show student performance. Senthilvalavan added that this process can widen the pool of students who clear the cut off for these exams. He also mentioned that teachers were trained in data analysis to read trends and provide supporting worksheets to students.

Owen, a student at Alpha Chicago, said the software feels different from using an iPad because he feels he is learning. Carrington Haas, the lead guide at Alpha Chicago, stated that the magic of the school is teaching real world life skills. These life skills include leadership, teamwork, financial literacy, and public speaking, which are taught after the morning AI sessions. The students affected by these changes are those in the 50 Alpha campuses across the country with 1,500 students. In Chennai, the students benefiting are those in the model schools who struggle with specific topics and need re-teaching.

The Alpha Schools model replaces traditional teachers with guides, most of whom do not have a professional background in education. A February analysis by the University of Colorado's National Education Policy Center found only one third of guides have education degrees. In Tamil Nadu, the government model schools provide a specialized environment for students preparing for competitive entrance exams like the JEE. The Chennai schools use a system where data from answer sheets is used to identify specific student weaknesses. These background details show a shift toward data driven instruction and the use of non traditional educators in Chicago.

School education director P Naresh said the department could explore implementing these AI tools across all regular government schools. However, he noted that the volume of students is much larger in regular schools than in the model schools. Naresh believes the department will lean toward training teachers with data to help them tweak their teaching methodology. The articles leave open whether the high cost of Alpha Chicago tuition will limit its growth to wealthy families. They also do not state if the Chennai government will provide funding for subscriptions in all 38 model schools.

stories.Headline: Open-source AI without Jensen - by Nathan Lambert
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on November 14, 2026, according to a report by Nathan Lambert. This sudden departure is described as a decapitation that creates a major setback for the American open model ecosystem. Lambert notes that the timing of the announcement followed a midterm political swing in the United States. The resignation removes a powerful champion who had supported open source AI for about two years. This event leaves the open model movement without its most influential advocate and protector.

Nvidia must now stabilize its operations and deliver to customers over the next 24 months to prevent a total implosion. The company faces challenges including potential chip smuggling investigations and the loss of talent to poaching sharks. The open model economy is currently in its nascency and requires established revenue flows and clear use cases. Some Western models like Inkling 2 Small from Thinking Machines are far behind Kimi K3.1 Pro. Meanwhile, Mira is reportedly seeking a new funding round at a valuation of 40 billion dollars.

Nathan Lambert says that Jensen Huang was more than a cheerleader because he used his power to prevent crises. He argues that the open model economy has correctly focused on enterprise post training and the ownership of intelligence. Lambert believes that the movement is regressing in operational capability just as attacks and stakes are destined to rise. He suggests that open model believers must now engage in soul searching and build a new coalition. The author claims that the shoes Huang emptied will never be fully refilled.

Dylan Patel, the CEO of SemiAnalysis, says that talent is a bigger problem than money for the open model ecosystem. He notes that the most talented people work at OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Meta, leaving others split across startups. Inference startups are struggling to get chips because OpenAI and Anthropic are buying up most of the available capacity. Chris Hughes warns that blunt federal and state regulations could create a costly moat for the largest players. These regulatory changes would only benefit the biggest companies that can afford to navigate the complex rules.

The articles state that Nvidia's business operations are extremely dependent on Jensen Huang as an operator and a founder. Huang had flooded the open model zone with funding, but this financial support is very likely to dry up. The open model ecosystem has faced pressure from the AI safety community and Democratic government funding for regulation. There is a recurring concern that a popular Chinese open weight model could trigger a cybersecurity crisis. The media often drives narratives based on harm and risk rather than the availability of exact information.

The open model movement may now turn to hyperscalers like Satya Nadella, Andy Jassy, or Mark Zuckerberg for support. The industry must determine if a truly frontier open model player can be incubated within the United States. It remains unclear if Thinking Machines or other small labs can overcome their deficits in compute and deployment. The articles leave open whether the open model economy can become a meaningful engine without Huang's protection. Future success depends on whether the ecosystem can survive sloppy state level and national regulations.

stories.Headline: DUI suspect released after officer used AI in arrest report: Judge
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, an Arizona judge released Anthony Edward Rene Quidera, a DUI suspect, after the arresting officer used artificial intelligence in his arrest report. Maricopa Superior Court Judge Daniel Fenzel ordered the release during Quidera's initial court hearing. The police report about the October 29 arrest ended with a disclaimer that it was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. Quidera, 37, was accused of driving 100 miles per hour on Interstate 10 in Phoenix around 12:33 a.m. The unidentified Arizona Department of Public Safety trooper alleged he smelled an intoxicating beverage and found several open containers in the car.

Quidera was arrested on October 29, 2026, on charges of DUI, exceeding the posted speed limit by more than 20 mph, and possession of an open container in a vehicle. The arrest occurred on eastbound Interstate 10 after a trooper observed a vehicle traveling over 100 mph in a 65 mph zone near 79th Avenue. The trooper alleged Quidera's Dodge Charger failed to maintain its lane and drove on the left median shoulder. The trooper reported bloodshot, red, and watery eyes and six out of six cues on a Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus test. Quidera allegedly declined a preliminary breath test, and several open containers were found on the passenger floorboard.

Fenzel said the use of generative AI affected the case and that the court was unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations were authored in whole or in part by AI. Fenzel said the court was therefore unable to determine probable cause at this time. Fenzel added that his order did not mean the DUI case could not go forward in the future. Raul Garcia, who represents DPS, said the department uses Truleo to help draft reports. Garcia said AI tools may be used only as an aid, the trooper remains the author and is responsible for accuracy, and a supervisor must review reports before they become part of the official record.

Garcia said troopers must review drafts against body-worn camera footage and other evidence, verify times, names, locations, and actions, and correct errors. Garcia said troopers may not use the tool until they complete Department-approved training. Attorney information for Quidera wasn't available, and a spokesman for the Arizona DPS declined to comment. The case comes weeks after the Arizona Court of Appeals ordered Gabriel Paul Horcasitas to be resentenced for his manslaughter conviction. The September 30 appellate ruling found that the judge's consideration of an AI video so prejudiced Horcasitas as to render the sentencing procedure fundamentally unfair.

In October, ABC15 reported on Phoenix PD's trial program with Axon's Draft One AI report writing software. In September, an appeals court threw out a 10-year sentence in a road rage shooting after determining an AI victim impact statement influenced the sentence. The Arizona Supreme Court has declined to ban judges from using AI. The Court asked the Arizona Steering Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts to recommend rules or administrative orders for clear standards on responsible use of emerging AI technologies. The Court asked the Committee to send a status report by March 1, 2027.

An arraignment date was scheduled for Thursday, and Maricopa County Justice Court records show Quidera was eventually charged and scheduled to be arraigned on November 12th. The ruling raises new legal questions about how AI-generated or AI-assisted police reports may hold up in court. The articles do not say what happened at the arraignment or how the case was resolved. The articles do not give the outcome of any further probable cause review. The articles do not identify the trooper or provide Quidera's attorney information.

stories.Headline: New awards show celebrates AI music and its creators
stories.Summary:
Catalyst Performance, a personal training studio at Manulife Tower in Singapore, celebrated one year since it opened in November 2025, according to an article dated November 13, 2026. The studio was founded by Bervin Manoharan, Jeremy Soh and Dr Luqman Haris. In its first year the studio reached seven-figure sales and became the first fitness brand to win the SME AI Impact Awards. It was quoted twice by CNA Lifestyle as an expert source on training. Over 1,500 people completed the studio's free two-minute online Healthspan Audit.

The studio sits at 8 Cross Street, #05-03 Manulife Tower, Singapore 048424, in the Central Business District near Raffles Place. It won Adoption Excellence at the SME AI Impact Awards 2026, organised by IMDA and the Singapore Business Federation, and was the only fitness brand among the 2026 winners. Every personal training client trains on Catalyst Coach, the studio's own app on the App Store and Google Play. The Catalyst Healthspan Assessment is a four-pillar evaluation of body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, stability and strength, measured at intake and again every 16 weeks. Each bioelectrical impedance scan is read by the studio's own OCR software, which checks every value against 14 arithmetic rules.

Manoharan, co-founder and general manager, said the studio opened with a simple idea that people who train for the next thirty years should see whether it is working. He said many people arrive expecting a body transformation with an end date, and that what a transformation gym sells as the finish line is a pit stop for the studio. He said a seven-figure first year tells him professionals in the CBD want a coach, a number and a plan they can check. He said that with AI he built what a much bigger company would hire a software team for, using several AI models and giving each one the job it does best. He said that when a studio has paid five figures for a machine, a subscription to reach its own clients' data should not be part of the deal.

Dr Luqman Haris, MBBS, Head of Training Systems, said muscle strength and cardiorespiratory fitness are among the strongest predictors of healthy ageing. He said journalists ask about women's training and heart health because the studio measures strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in every client. In August 2026 CNA Lifestyle quoted Manoharan in a report on heart screening for people who train for endurance races such as HYROX and marathons. In September 2026 CNA Lifestyle quoted Dr Luqman Haris throughout a report on why women may need to train differently from men. SethLui ranked Catalyst Performance fifth in its guide to the best personal trainers in Singapore, and Little Big Red Dot published a hands-on review of the studio.

The studio built its own scan reader because InBody charges a paid subscription before a studio can reach its own clients' scans through its API. Catalyst Concierge, the studio's AI nutrition concierge on WhatsApp for its clients in Singapore, takes a photo of a meal, estimates calories, protein, carbohydrate and fat, logs the estimate against that client's daily targets and replies with what is left for the day. Behind the client app, Catalyst Operator, the studio's own back office, keeps one file for every client. The founders' coaching careers span more than 25 years combined. The studio offers one-to-one private personal training for working professionals from their 30s onward.

In its second year Catalyst Performance will move its body composition scanning to open-API equipment partners, extend Catalyst Coach and Catalyst Concierge, and keep publishing its Singapore healthspan statistics. The studio holds its personal trainers in Singapore to one method: every client is measured at intake and measured again every 16 weeks. The article does not say what the seven-figure sales figure was in dollars. It does not name the open-API equipment partners the studio is moving to. It does not give the date of the SME AI Impact Awards ceremony or the size of the 2026 winner list.

stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Announces Cutting Edge AI Company Aaru Will Expand in New York City, Creating Over 650 New Jobs | Empire State Development
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul announced that Aaru, a Manhattan-based AI company that helps businesses test new products and ideas before bringing them to market, will expand its operations in New York City. The expansion is expected to create more than 650 new jobs over the next five years, and the company plans to make New York the home of its research and development operations. The announcement was made on November 13, 2026. Aaru will lease and build out more than 27,000 square feet of office space near Union Square. The company currently employs about 60 people and expects its workforce to grow to more than 700.

Under the plan, Aaru will invest in the State as it grows, deepening its roots in the city where it was founded just two years ago. The company's workforce is set to grow tenfold, which Governor Hochul pointed to as evidence that New York has overtaken the San Francisco Bay Area as the nation's largest tech talent market. Hochul credited her investments in computing power, research and talent with drawing companies and jobs to the state. She said Aaru started in New York, is growing here, and is creating hundreds of well-paying jobs for New Yorkers. The governor's remarks framed the expansion as a sign that leading AI companies are choosing New York to grow.

Aaru Co-Founder and CEO Cameron Fink said the company deliberately chose to build in New York City. He pointed to the depth and diversity of local talent, the closeness to the world's largest enterprises, and the city's history of innovation as reasons for the decision. Fink also said being a New York company is central to Aaru's identity and thanked Hochul and Empire State Development for their support. Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said the company's growth shows what innovative firms can achieve when they have the talent, resources and support they need. Knight described the expansion as an important investment in Aaru's future and said the state is helping companies scale their operations and build lasting economic opportunities.

stories.Headline: Inside the algorithms: How artificial intelligence is enhancing traditional pathology practice
stories.Summary:
Lee Cooper, director of computational pathology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, said digital imaging methods are becoming more popular in pathology, as Medill Reports described on November 13, 2026. After a blood or tissue sample is placed on a glass slide, the slide goes into a scanner that produces a digital image that can be shared electronically. Cooper runs a lab where researchers develop artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms that review digitized samples. He said the algorithms will help pathologists make more accurate and detailed diagnoses and help researchers interpret how diseases progressed in past patients. The article said glass slides are often still carried between offices so multiple pathologists can look at them.

Cooper said a computer can analyze a sample in much greater detail than a human can, because each image could contain a million cells or more. Researcher Fattaneh Pourakpour, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, uses digitized tissue data from Northwestern’s Mesulam Institute for Cognitive Neurology and Alzheimer’s Disease brain bank, which accepts brain donations upon death from people who had dementia. Her tissue segmentation algorithms distinguish brain regions such as gray matter and white matter, and her cell classifier algorithms identify and categorize cell types within gray matter. Researcher Ramin Nateghi, a post-doctoral researcher with a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Shiraz University of Technology in Shiraz, Iran, applies machine learning to prostate cancer detection. Nateghi said biopsies taken over time might show few differences over 25 years, so detecting subtle changes in slides can help doctors make better decisions.

Cooper said digital pathology tools are meant to augment pathologists, not replace them, because the models he works with operate on the basis of correlation and have no causal understanding inside them. He said an algorithm is less helpful on a rare case it has never seen, and that he does not think the models should be trusted implicitly. Researcher Lawrence Chillrud, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, said the United States has a huge shortage of pathologists but heaps of patient biopsy data that needs to be inspected, analyzed and reviewed. Chillrud develops tools that conduct a preliminary screen of pathology data, sort out the most obvious cases and flag others for fast-tracked, specialized review. His models might also count items such as a certain kind of cell, direct a pathologist’s attention to important areas or review a pathologist’s report for potential errors.

Chillrud is also developing uncertainty tools that quantify the likely accuracy of a model’s prediction, because many models are overconfident and give a false picture of how well their predictions can be trusted. He said models inherit the biases of the data sets they are trained on, giving the example of training on mostly white, affluent patients living in a certain part of a city. Artificial intelligence pathology tools can also help address shortages of specialized pathologists, since a general pathologist might not have the training for a detailed read of a prostate cancer biopsy. Specialists are harder to find in smaller, more rural areas, while large, city-based medical systems might have them on staff. According to Cooper, the Northwestern Medicine health care system generates about 2 million glass slides per year.

Cooper is not sure how quickly digital pathology will become commonplace, because the tools must undergo FDA clearance and be validated on very high-quality data that can be hard to access. Not all medical systems have adopted the digitizing tools and technology Northwestern has access to. In the Cooper Lab, glass slides are digitized using the Aperio slide scanner, manufactured by Leica, which takes about 90 seconds per slide and can hold up to 450 glass slides at a time. Cooper said each image typically has several billion pixels, and pathology at Northwestern generates about 3 petabytes, or 3 million gigabytes, per year. Cooper said he is optimistic about adoption after seeing researchers use the tools to measure patterns in tissue and relate them to metrics such as treatment success.

Cooper said the tools are useful and easy to use, and that it is not just tool developers but scientists using them. The article said pathology data is by far the biggest source of data in the medical field. Whether models possess deep understandings of the subjects they are trained in, or only superficial ones, is an unanswered question, though Cooper said he thinks they can deliver accurate and efficient predictions regardless. Cooper said computers can consider many more properties of the samples than a doctor could, which can help generate a fuller prediction of that patient’s future. The article did not say when the algorithms might receive FDA clearance or reach routine clinical use.

Articles.Title: Inside the algorithms: How artificial intelligence is enhancing traditional pathology practice

stories.Headline: Akhilesh Yadav says phones can't be trusted in AI age amid Rahul Gandhi's phone-tapping allegation
stories.Summary:
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday backed Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's allegation that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was having his phone tapped. Yadav said phones and modern technology could not be trusted in the age of Artificial Intelligence. He spoke in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, on November 13, 2026, after arriving at the Samajwadi Party's state headquarters. He came to attend an election review meeting with assembly-level presidents of 86 reserved constituencies. Rahul Gandhi made his allegation the same Friday in a video posted by the Congress on X.

Yadav claimed 1.27 crore names had been removed from electoral rolls and that votes belonging to the Samajwadi Party were being deleted. He said the Chief Minister knows that 12.7 million, or 1 crore 27 lakh, voters have been removed from the rolls. He alleged the BJP was preparing to bring people from Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh to register them as voters in Uttar Pradesh. He also named Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand among the places from which people could be brought. He said the BJP was preparing a plan to replace votes deleted due to relocation and fraudulent registrations by bringing in people from outside the state.

Yadav said one should not trust the technology of today and that in the age of AI anything is possible. He added that a leader who was no longer alive had once spoken about their phones being tapped. He said that if it is true that 1.27 crore Hindu voters are missing, that is precisely why the BJP meeting is taking place. He alleged the BJP was preparing regarding those shifting votes, votes deleted due to people relocating to Delhi or elsewhere, and instances where fraudulent names had been added. He said the BJP was orchestrating a plan involving underground or unregistered elements to bring in individuals from Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and potentially other locations to get them registered as voters.

Gandhi said the Prime Minister is aware of the tapping because he has his phone tapped. Gandhi said that the day Modi agrees to a face-to-face debate, everyone will learn who is under the control of foreign powers, who is anti-national, and how long they have been involved in anti-national activities. Gandhi claimed proof of the Prime Minister being under the control of foreign powers was already available on his phone, adding that Modi was aware of the evidence. Congress MP Imran Masood said the PM is scared and the country is listening to Rahul Gandhi. Masood also reacted to the UP CM's claim of 1.27 crore Hindu voters missing, saying what can we say in this fight between the CM and the Deputy CM, and that we know there has been an about the SIR.

Yadav said the Samajwadi Party had raised the voter list issue in Pilibhit, following which action was taken against two Sub-Divisional Magistrates. He alleged a major scheme is underway to manipulate the voter list. He warned that voters might reach polling booths only to be told their votes were not registered there, forcing them to search for their names elsewhere. He called for a durable and secure card linked to Aadhaar and advocated biometric-based voting to ensure greater transparency. He said that if a Samajwadi Party government is formed, they will introduce biometric voter cards.

Yadav said he would say to announce the election dates, and that the very day they are announced, the BJP will be defeated. He made the remarks as the 2027 State Assembly election approaches, with both the BJP and the Samajwadi Party exchanging heated jibes. The articles do not say what the BJP said in response to Yadav's allegations. The articles do not say what action, if any, followed Gandhi's phone-tapping allegation. stories.Headline: 42Gears Achieves ISO/IEC3 Certification for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems
stories.Summary:
42Gears announced on Nov. 13, 2026, that it had achieved certification to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the international standard for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, according to a GlobeNewswire release datelined Bengaluru, KARNATAKA. The certification followed a rigorous independent audit conducted by the British Standards Institution, known as BSI, the release stated. 42Gears, described as a global leader in Unified Endpoint Management, issued the announcement through GlobeNewswire, and the Manila Times carried it on November 13, 2026. The company said it is now recognized for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving structured governance across its AI-enabled enterprise capabilities. The certification covers 42Gears' role as a producer, provider, and user of AI systems integrated within its flagship SureMDM platform.

The certification covers the utilization of third-party large language models to deliver AI-powered unified endpoint management services across key global sectors, including Banking & Financial Services, Healthcare & Life Sciences, Industrial & Supply Chain Operations, and Consumer & Commercial Services. Achieving ISO/IEC 42001:2023 demonstrates that 42Gears embeds accountability, transparency, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle, the release stated. It also establishes robust governance frameworks for the responsible development, deployment, and use of AI technologies, including the adoption and use of large language models. The release listed key benefits for customers and partners, beginning with independently audited AI governance, which provides verified assurance that SureMDM's AI management framework meets rigorous international compliance benchmarks. End-to-End Risk & Impact Assessment establishes a structured methodology for identifying, evaluating, and mitigating AI-related risks across the entire deployment lifecycle.

Transparency & Human Oversight enforces clear accountability mechanisms and human oversight controls over AI-assisted decision-making and workflows, according to the listed benefits. Governed Third-Party LLM Integration ensures strict security, privacy, and vendor oversight protocols when leveraging external large language models. Comprehensive Compliance Posture complements 42Gears' existing enterprise security and privacy portfolio, including ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, and HIPAA compliance programs. The release said this offers heightened confidence for organizations operating in heavily regulated industries. Mr. Onkar Singh, Co-founder & CEO, said enterprise IT teams want the efficiency and intelligence of AI, but not at the expense of security, transparency, or regulatory compliance.

Singh said achieving ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification validates the company's commitment to responsible AI innovation. He said customers in banking, healthcare, and mission-critical operations can deploy SureMDM's AI capabilities knowing they are backed by internationally audited governance and strict human oversight. The release described 42Gears as a trusted authority in Unified Endpoint Management and Security, delivering one strategy to manage, secure, and empower diverse, complex technology environments. It said 42Gears goes beyond traditional MDM and RMM, enabling IT teams and MSPs to start where they are and grow without switching. The release said this helps scale from endpoint management and Zero Trust security to identity and access management, automation, and self-healing technology.

The release said 42Gears products are available in cloud and on-premises deployments across all major mobile, desktop, and specialized operating systems. It said 42Gears products are used by 23,000+ customers across 170+ countries. It said the products are available through 1,000+ global partners. The release directed readers to https://www.42gears.com for more information. Press inquiries go to the 42Gears Marketing & Communications Team at press@42gears.com.

The release was issued through GlobeNewswire and appeared on itbusinessnet.com and manilatimes.net, both dated November 2026. The Manila Times version carried a byline of GlobeNewswire and a November 13, 2026 date. The release did not state when the BSI audit took place or how long the certification remains valid. It did not name the auditors, the audit scope boundaries, or any nonconformities found. It did not say what changes, if any, 42Gears made to SureMDM or its processes to earn the certification.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO in November 2026 after 33 years of leadership. He stepped down amid an alleged spy scandal and reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as the interim CEO. This abrupt departure occurred during a dizzying week for the AI industry. Huang had previously bankrolled the boom before his sudden exit.

Kress may rein in 120 billion dollars in equity investments and circular financing. She cut a 250 billion dollar guarantee for an OpenAI Ohio data center project in half. Nvidia planned to buy Hugging Face for 12.9 billion dollars in September 2026. The company also intended to invest 10 billion dollars in Anthropic through private placement. Kress previously checked Vice President Nico Caprez, who is the son-in-law of Huang.

Researcher Gary Marcus said Nvidia acted like a bank by backstopping the entire industry. He described Huang as a swashbuckler who made bets of arbitrary size. Marcus stated that Kress must now clean up a legal mess involving China. He questioned why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not intervene earlier in the matter. Lawmakers want to know what information Huang shared with Alice Huang.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and CoreWeave relied on Nvidia funding while struggling to turn a profit. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue called the situation deeply regrettable and a sad day. Cathy Logue said a CFO is the best choice to send stability to markets. Some analysts believe Kress will focus on managing risk rather than opening new businesses. Many employees want the board to bring Jensen Huang back to the company.

Huang previously made business decisions quickly and intuitively while taking reports directly from executives. The company has relied heavily on his financial backing to support the AI industry. Kress has spent 13 years at Nvidia and avoids the public spotlight. Harvey Jones has served on the Nvidia board for more than 25 years. He previously served as a mentor to Huang during his long tenure.

Harvey Jones will now fill the board chair position to supervise the CEO strategy. This new arrangement aims to reduce financial risk by checking the leader's decisions. The planned acquisitions of Hugging Face and Anthropic may now be subject to revision. It remains open if Kress and Jones can fully break from the past. An internal post urging Huang's return drew more than 1,600 comments from engineers.
