stories.Headline: China's $3 billion-plus pipeline of Nvidia-powered AI data centres
stories.Summary:
Reuters has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia's restricted processors, according to a report published on November 13, 2026. The findings came a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over a scandal. The review found projects ranging from China's wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces. Nvidia has said that US export controls have effectively shut it out of the Chinese AI data-centre market. The report stresses how deeply Nvidia's technology remains embedded in China's AI expansion.

A proposed 6.2 billion yuan, or $873 million, AI computing centre in Xianyou county, Fujian province, specifies Nvidia H100 chips and is seeking commercial partners. In Shaanxi province, Sinomach said a subsidiary won a contract for a 3 billion yuan computing centre specifying H100 and H200 processors. An April government prospectus in Jilin province describes a 2.26 billion yuan project combining H100 processors with Chinese-developed chips, with banks expected to finance about 80% of the investment. In Inner Mongolia, a 1.5 billion yuan development proposes installing 625 Nvidia H200 servers. In Gansu province, a 1.16 billion yuan contract awarded in July covers a centre planning about 3,072 Nvidia processors.

The report suggests these plans depend on US processors that are vulnerable to trade restrictions. Tighter curbs could cause construction delays, higher costs or redesigns around domestic alternatives. Nvidia's chief executive resigned, and Huang's departure could deepen vulnerabilities for Chinese companies exposed to potential delays and supply disruptions. The Reuters review did not establish whether the processors in the Gansu project have been delivered. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, had been a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions.

Other Chinese facilities already use restricted Nvidia hardware, according to the review. The Wuxi municipal government in Jiangsu province said in March 2025 that a computing cluster using H800 processors had entered operation. In June, Shanghai-listed Damingcheng disclosed that a computing venture in Fujian had built an H800 cluster under a computing-services agreement originally worth 759 million yuan, which ended early. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors in September, and US-blacklisted Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips the following month. Demand thus extends to research institutions.

A separate Global Times editorial published on November 8 argued that US technology companies could consider deploying some AI computing capacity in China. The editorial pointed to American constraints such as insufficient electricity supply, grid upgrade delays, high construction costs, lengthy approvals and local opposition to data centres after the midterm elections. It cited China's advantages in electricity, equipment manufacturing and infrastructure planning. Some estimates in a related commentary put US construction costs at $8 million to $12 million per megawatt, against $5.5 million to $6.5 million in China. The editorial acknowledged practical limits involving national security, data protection, latency and regulation.

The Global Times commentary described the idea of "American computing, Chinese data centre" as an online joke that is little more than a joke because of Washington's securitisation of technology. It blamed continued US export controls and investment restrictions for making cooperation harder. The editorial said the two countries should move away from zero-sum competition and expand practical cooperation while jointly advancing AI governance. It also urged the United States to recognise China's strengths rather than pursue technological decoupling. Commentary on the editorial said it should not be mistaken for an official policy proposal.

Background from the articles shows that Nvidia's restricted chips have been used in China despite US curbs, and that several projects and buyers, including state-owned and university entities, rely on them. The Reuters review noted that Nvidia has said export controls effectively shut it out of this market. The Global Times editorial framed the issue around US grid and construction bottlenecks, while the Reuters review focused on the exposure of Chinese projects to trade restrictions. The articles also reference earlier reporting on Chinese purchases of restricted Nvidia chips and on the chief executive's departure.

The articles leave open whether the Gansu processors were delivered and how the Xianyou, Shaanxi and Jilin projects will be financed or completed. They do not establish how tighter US curbs will affect the projects or whether Chinese companies will switch to domestic alternatives. It is unclear whether US companies will take up the offshore data-centre idea, and the Global Times editorial was not an official policy proposal. The articles also leave open how the APEC leaders' meeting may shape these positions, and whether any cooperation on AI governance will follow.

stories.Headline: Exclusive: US-sanctioned Jinan Supercomputing Center still gets Nvidia AI products
stories.Summary:
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed that sanctioned Chinese entities obtained restricted Nvidia AI chips despite existing United States export controls. This discovery occurred as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation on a Thursday in November 2026 amid a scandal. The resignation followed allegations of an extramarital affair that may have been a Chinese spy plot targeting the company leader. The United States government is investigating Huang's ties to Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore company Megaspeed. Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is suspected of collecting intelligence for Beijing and helping clients obtain restricted chips.

The National Supercomputing Center Jinan, also called Shandong Computing Center, won a bid for RTX 5090 cards and DGX Spark systems. On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network announced the winning bidder was Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd. The project, titled Edge Intelligent Computing Team AI Workstation and Graphics Card Procurement Project, cost RMB 148,500 or 22,000 US dollars. The RTX 5090 uses Blackwell architecture with 32GB GDDR7 memory, while the DGX Spark uses the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. These items were listed under the Yixin brand, which is operated by the winning bidder, Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology.

The United States Department of Commerce is responsible for the Entity List, which includes the Shandong Computing Center since April 2021. Commerce officials stated that seven Chinese institutions, including those in Jinan, Shenzhen, Wuxi, and Zhengzhou, supported military modernization and weapons programs. These activities were determined to be contrary to United States national security and foreign policy interests, requiring licenses for any transfers. Chris Tseng of the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said controls rely heavily on corporate self-compliance. He noted that licenses are required even if products are shipped to legitimate distributors before being transferred to controlled entities.

Sylvia Chen of DSET stated that third-party enterprises cannot legally purchase controlled products and then transfer them to the Jinan Center. She noted that enforcement is difficult because the Bureau of Industry and Security has only fifteen end-use verification officers worldwide. Only one such officer is stationed in Beijing to handle verification for the entire region, creating significant staffing constraints for enforcement. An industry commentator suggested that Qiyuan Jiasu might be a shell company for the previously sanctioned firm Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology. This potential shell company would allow sanctioned entities to continue acquiring high-end AI hardware through deceptive business registration and branding.

The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with the Qilu University of Technology in China. The National Supercomputing Center Jinan was established in 2011, and both entities now belong to the same institutional framework. Broad United States export restrictions on advanced computing chips to China began in 2022, following the 2021 Entity List additions. Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology was an Nvidia Elite Partner since 2015 before being placed on the Entity List on April 11, 2024. Bloomberg News reported that Nvidia underreported approximately 50,000 AI chips sold to Megaspeed, valued at billions of dollars in total.

Nvidia must now investigate the sales and ultimate flow of products if Qiyuan Jiasu inherited the operations of Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology. The company is obligated to conduct Know Your Customer procedures to verify the end-user and destination when red flags appear. It remains open whether the RTX 5090 cards purchased were the original versions or the China-specific RTX 5090 D models. There is currently no direct evidence proving that Qiyuan Jiasu and Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology belong to the same beneficial ownership system. The United States government continues to investigate the extent of the spy plot and the illicit leak of chips.

stories.Headline: Malaysia Probes Whether Megaspeed Unit Re-exported AI Chips
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's trade ministry announced on 13 November 2026 that it is probing a specific company. The ministry is checking if AI chips imported by Speedmatrix were later re-exported. Speedmatrix is the Malaysian unit of the Singapore-based firm known as Megaspeed. This investigation focuses on whether these shipments complied with the laws of Malaysia. The probe follows reports from news agencies including Reuters, AFP, and The Korea Times.

Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and imports servers and chips. Since July 2025, any entity exporting or transshipping high performance US AI chips needs a permit. Giving customs false information about these items is considered a serious offence by the ministry. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, or MITI, is working with the customs department. MITI is also coordinating closely with authorities located in Singapore and the United States.

MITI stated that Speedmatrix has never been cleared of any wrongdoing during this process. The ministry said official visits to the facilities were part of regular monitoring of the sector. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there is no indication that chips were shipped out of Malaysia. He added that Malaysia has received no request for assistance from Singapore or the US. Ibrahim stated that the government wants to make sure the rules are being followed.

Singapore is investigating Megaspeed because servers were suspected of being delivered to other destinations. A US senator alleged the firm may have been used to bypass US semiconductor controls. The US alleges Alice Huang spied for China, though the Chinese government denies this claim. Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her role. The Nvidia scandal reportedly wiped almost half a trillion dollars off the company's market capitalization.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny over ties between former executive Alice Huang and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang resigned over an affair with Alice Huang, who is a suspected Chinese spy. Megaspeed is accused of steering Nvidia AI chips to China despite existing US export rules. The reports describe the chips generally as advanced or high-performance AI chips linked to Nvidia. None of the reports state that a re-export from Malaysia has been established yet.

MITI is considering stronger controls and further measures to strengthen the current permit regime. The outcome of the customs check remains an open development that the public awaits. It is unknown if Singapore or the US will officially request assistance from Malaysia. Official text from the US Commerce department on remote access is also still pending. The investigation into whether Speedmatrix violated the law is currently still under way.

stories.Headline: Gemini Enhances Personal Finance Insights with Google Wallet Integration
stories.Summary:
Google launched a Gemini app feature connecting to Google Wallet, announced in a blog post, rolling out today for all Gemini users in the U.S. The feature lets users receive personalized financial insights drawn from their spending habits. It is initially rolling out to users in the US on Android, iOS, and the web. Small Business Trends published its report on Nov 13, 2026, by David Wilson. How-To Geek published its report on Nov 13, 2026, at 4:57 PM EST, by Jefferson Mangubat. Users can link Google Wallet via Gemini’s Connected Apps settings and mention @Google Wallet when asking questions about their finances.

Google also allows users to link bank accounts and credit cards to Wallet through Plaid, a financial technology company that helps connect financial institutions to third-party services. The integration is part of Google's Personal Intelligence initiative, which already connects Gemini with Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search. Google is also rolling out an update to its Memory Summary feature that will enable users to review, edit, and delete what Gemini remembers about their preferences and ongoing goals. Google says the integration is read-only, so Gemini can see linked account information but can’t move money, manage accounts, make purchases, or invest for you. Google says connecting Wallet is entirely optional, and users can revoke access at any time.

Google provides several practical suggestions for using the service, such as asking Gemini to look at spending over the last quarter and come up with a plan to save $1,000 over the next three months. Google says the integration is fully opt-in, so privacy-conscious users can keep it switched off. How-To Geek says it still takes a giant leap of faith to give an AI the keys to your transaction history, particularly when chatbots are still prone to the occasional math error and hallucination. Small Business Trends says business owners will need to dedicate time to learn how to fully leverage the capabilities of the Gemini app. Small Business Trends says they must also consider the security implications of linking financial accounts, as this might raise concerns about data privacy and vulnerability.

Small Business Trends says small business owners often face the dual challenge of limited resources and high competition, making financial efficiency crucial. Gemini has evolved from a general-purpose chatbot to a more personal AI assistant by integrating with services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search to give it more context about users’ lives. Many small business owners already use a range of Google services, such as Gmail and Google Search. The Gemini app leverages Personal Intelligence to provide tailored responses.

With Google Wallet in Gemini rolling out across both web and mobile platforms, small business owners now have access to a robust suite of tools, backed by the reliability of Google services. Users can ask the app specific questions like, “Can we review my spending from last quarter so I can save $1,000 over the next three months?” With this request, Gemini generates dynamic charts that illustrate cash flow, asset allocation, and budget outlines directly within the chat interface. The question, “What subscriptions am I still paying for, and did any of them go up in price this year?”

can prompt Gemini to search through linked accounts, highlighting recurring charges and alerting users to any price hikes. Users can ask “How much did I spend on gifts and travel last year? Use that to help me set a holiday budget for this year.” Gemini will sift through past transactions and suggest budgets customized to individual spending behavior.

stories.Headline: AI-generated lesson plans save teachers time. Just don’t let the kids know.
stories.Summary:
The AI Hub for Education, part of Stanford University’s SCALE Initiative, released a review of 52 studies on artificial intelligence in educational settings on Tuesday, November 13, 2026, Chalkbeat reported. The review found that most AI tools do not help students learn and that education-specific AI tools are not necessarily better than general purpose chatbots. It also found that even tools that help teachers save time can have unintended consequences for students. The report’s authors said they are not throwing in the towel on AI in education. The review is the AI Hub’s second AI research review and incorporates 32 new studies.

The included studies were selected from hundreds in the field and are either randomized controlled trials or have a quasi-experimental design providing strong causal evidence. The goal is eventually to have a robust research repository that teachers and districts can use to inform decisions about whether and how to use AI. The review is a synthesis of findings from high-quality studies, not a meta-analysis. AI in education is not just one thing, with too many different tools used in too many different ways to pile studies together and reach strong conclusions. Many of the studies come from other countries or involve college students, and there is still very little research on AI in K-12 settings in the United States.

Susanna Loeb, faculty director at the SCALE Initiative and an author of the report, said AI tools can be quite powerful to differentiate lessons for students at different levels or support students learning a new language. She said you just have to use them thoughtfully and track how they are doing and whether they are really benefiting students. Loeb said that if a district does not want to think about it and does not want to design its classwork, homework and school day to leverage these tools well, she would not use them. She said that on their own without thought, the tools have some negative effects on learning. She said teachers and district leaders need to proceed thoughtfully and that if they do not have the capacity to do so, it is better not to use AI at all.

Collectively, the studies suggest students do not learn much when they use AI to produce essays or solve problems, and when those students later do work without AI, they do worse than other students. AI shows more promise when students use it to explain concepts and help them practice, but even then the results are mixed or do not show much benefit over traditional study methods. AI tools that provide interactive formats and adaptive practice questions may improve student learning more than static digital textbooks, and students sometimes experience AI-generated feedback as clearer and more motivating than feedback from teachers, but even where students reported positive experiences the evidence of learning gains was mixed. Teachers who used an AI tool to do the first pass on grading assignments provided more and more detailed feedback in one study, and teachers who used AI progress-tracking tools saw students complete more assignments, though students’ grades on those assignments were not necessarily better.

Studies found teachers could save time using AI to generate lesson plans without reducing the quality of those lessons, but students who believed a lesson was AI-generated reported being less motivated, and in one study from Turkey students did worse when teachers who already were lower-performing used AI to generate lesson plans. The review comes as school districts are navigating competing pressures to adopt AI rapidly and to limit technology in the classroom. Google caused an uproar this month when it said that school districts that ban AI will not be able to use Google Search. The American Federation of Teachers has embraced training teachers to use AI while pressing major tech companies to agree to guardrails.

A forensic audit found serious flaws in a number of previous meta-analyses that found positive outcomes for AI in education, such as hallucinated references and statistics that did not make sense, according to The Hechinger Report. Another challenge with studying AI in education, particularly with younger students, is that they often do not want to use the tools. The report’s authors said the technology has potential to provide personalized assistance for students and remove some of the tedium from teachers’ jobs, and Loeb said that potential is worth developing. The articles do not say what specific steps districts or the AI Hub will take next.

The articles do not say how the 52 studies break down by country or age group. The articles do not name the other authors of the report. The articles do not say when the AI Hub’s research repository will be complete. The articles do not say how Google’s statement will affect districts that ban AI.

Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named the interim chief executive to fill the vacancy. Huang had previously built a circular financing network worth over 500 billion U.S. dollars for AI. This network used equity investments and credit guarantees to provide capital to the cash burning industry. The founder left in disgrace while the company now faces a major leadership reshuffle.

Kress previously cut the Ohio data center guarantee for OpenAI from 2.5 trillion to 1.05 trillion U.S. dollars. NVIDIA's July 26 filing showed contingent liabilities of 5.305 trillion U.S. dollars, excluding some new transactions. Huang announced a 5 trillion U.S. dollar financing platform in August with a 25 percent backstop. Supply commitments surged from 58 billion to 279 billion U.S. dollars in three months. The Ohio project involves 1.5 million GPUs and potential revenue of 200 billion U.S. dollars.

Jensen Huang stated that NVIDIA was in trouble because many companies could not pay for chips. He called Colette Kress a startled deer and a reporting CFO who lacked strategic decision power. Kress questioned the pricing logic and return measurements of the company's rapid financing guarantee expansion. She launched braking actions and required the board to review all new revenue sharing credit transactions. Kress emailed employees on the 12th, stating NVIDIA remains a central pillar of the AI revolution.

James Schneider of Goldman Sachs said existing commitments will likely be honored but future investments will be harder. Tim Arcuri of UBS estimated a pause could siphon 50 billion U.S. dollars from the AI ecosystem. Sebastien Naji of William Blair warned that competitors like AMD and Broadcom may gain more market space. Sunaina Sinha Haldea told CNBC that participants may now demand higher returns due to the uncertainty. AI companies counting on future NVIDIA checks now face deeper uncertainty regarding their operational financing.

Alice Huang allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang and links to China's Ministry of State Security. This chip team, under Minister Chen Yixin, aims to neutralize export controls and penetrate global supply chains. Alice Huang reportedly tried to extract information from Jensen Huang to influence AI chip sales to China. A firm run by Alice Huang and her husband bought a 27 percent stake in a data center. The FBI and Justice Department are investigating these links and allegations involving companies like Megaspeed.

NVIDIA will hold a companywide meeting on December 18, following a quarterly earnings release on the 17th. Legally binding investments in Safe Superintelligence and Thinking Machines Lab are expected to proceed as scheduled. The 10 billion U.S. dollar investment in Anthropic's IPO and 5 billion for Nscale remain uncertain. Congress may pass the AI Overwatch, Chip Security, and MATCH Acts into the 2027 defense bill. It remains open who will become permanent CEO among Kress, Ian Buck, Rene Haas, or Chris Malachowsky.

stories.Headline: AI Job Interviews Lead to Better Outcomes - The University of Chicago Booth School of Business
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon’s Brian Jabarian, a former principal researcher at Chicago Booth, and his coauthor partnered with a recruiting firm hiring for customer service positions, and 70,000 candidates were randomly assigned to interview with an AI agent or a human recruiter. Candidates knew when they were speaking with AI, and final hiring decisions were always made by human recruiters reviewing the interview transcripts and audio. The researchers found that candidates who got a job interview with an AI were more likely to receive a job offer, more likely to start the job, and more likely to stay in the position after 30 days and up to four months. The retention rate was much better for the AI-interviewed group, and this retention did not come at the cost of productivity loss. Comparing employees interviewed by an AI and employees interviewed by a human, the researchers saw no difference in productivity metrics and no difference in separation after 30 days.

Both human and AI recruiters were required to cover 14 interview topics, but humans naturally vary in how consistently they conduct interviews, and fatigue, time pressure, and conversational drift can all change how questions are asked. AI is more consistent than human recruiters at covering more topics, with less variation in follow-ups and in the flow of the interview, and it more consistently applies a higher language across interviews. In response to this consistency, candidates are more likely to reveal their true type in a job interview conducted by an AI than in one conducted by a human. Candidates who got a job interview with an AI are more likely to display interactivity as a signal during a job interview and less likely to display other cues. Forty percent of people left voluntarily in both cases, and the researchers saw no deterioration in productivity downstream.

Jabarian said the overall takeaway of the research is not that you should replace all the time humans by AI, calling it more subtle and more complicated. He said AI adoption shouldn’t be seen as a task-by-task decision but more about organizational design as a whole, and about thinking how to combine AI agents working together with human agents in the workplace. He said AI is not so magic, and that it is an interesting tool to more consistently perform different interviewing tasks, such as covering a certain set of topics, having a certain order, and having a certain language. He said that when you are a human interviewer, sometimes you start the job interview in the morning and perform really well at your task, but for reasons of fatigue you might be less consistent. He said that if we were in a world where AI was artificially inflating your value during a job interview, you would see deterioration in terms of productivity downstream, but we don’t see this here.

Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company, said human eyes may not be the first to look at a job application these days. He said most of the companies he deals with run applications through that, and then they have also a human or HR professional. He said the practice picked up in the last two years, with technology scanning resumes for buzzwords pulled from the posted job description. He cautioned against copying a posting outright, saying you want to tailor it to the job description when you are applying, but you don’t want it to read word for word, which indicates a red flag to an employer. He recommends people use AI to help organize and format a resume, and not use it to embellish skills they do not have, and he said Microsoft and Claude work well.

Pasola said he “absolutely” believes some qualified candidates are slipping through the cracks or not getting hired because they are not using AI tools. He said this is because they have skills that they can put to the forefront in front of the employer that they are not showing. As Texas prepares for its first new governor in 12 years, Gina Hinojosa is searching for her team using a digital portal rather than a stack of paper resumes. That mirrors a hiring shift playing out across the job market, according to Pasola. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these accounts.

The articles leave open what happens next, and they do not give further background beyond the experiment and the staffing company’s observations. The Chicago Booth article was published November 13, 2026, and the KSAT article was published November 11, 2026. The KSAT article was reported by Olivia Dague, who joined KSAT 12 in July 2026 after spending three years reporting in Knoxville, Tennessee, at WBIR. Dague is from Arlington, Texas, and is a graduate of the University of Oklahoma. The articles do not state any additional plans or follow-up studies.

stories.Headline: Vertiv launches global ecosystem for AI liquid cooling
stories.Summary:
Vertiv launched a global ecosystem initiative to help data centre operators manage and optimise liquid cooling infrastructure for artificial intelligence workloads, the company announced on November 12, 2026. The offering combines an expanded collaboration with materials science company Dow and a new partnership with specialty chemicals and water treatment solutions provider Solenis. Together the partnerships will deliver end-to-end thermal and fluid management services, Vertiv said. The announcement comes as rapid growth of AI workloads drives higher computing densities in data centres, increasing the need for advanced liquid cooling systems. Vertiv said the ecosystem brings together its infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities with expertise in coolant technologies, fluid chemistry and water treatment.

The ecosystem integrates infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities, according to Vertiv. Dipti Singh's sponsored DataCenterDynamics piece, dated November 13, 2026, says the primary facility water system serves as the heat-rejection backbone for the coolant distribution units that protect the racks. A heat exchanger inside the CDU sits between the technology cooling system and the facility water system, so facility water never enters the servers. Singh puts the heat-transfer relation as Q = UAΔT, where heat moved equals how readily heat crosses the exchanger surface times the surface area times the temperature difference. ASHRAE's integrated design guidance, part of its AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework, says rack densities have climbed from roughly 120 kW to several hundred kilowatts, with megawatt-class racks expected in the near term.

Ron Bednar, Senior Vice President of Global and Americas Services at Vertiv, said AI is changing liquid cooling from an equipment decision into a system-management imperative. He added that operators need to manage thermal infrastructure, fluid health, monitoring and lifecycle service as one interconnected discipline. Bednar believes managing these complex interdependencies and fluid chemistry together will help operators improve system efficiency and uptime, reduce risk and extend equipment life. Singh argues that operators should stop treating the system as a building utility inspected on a schedule and should manage it continuously as an engineered thermal system. She writes that primary-side fouling, low flow, unstable temperature, biological growth and corrosion debris each eat into the CDU's thermal margin.

Singh says the facility and technology loops need separate chemistry specifications, and the parameters monitored on the facility side should look much like those on the technology loop. Her list includes pH and conductivity, chloride, hardness, alkalinity and silica, dissolved oxygen where relevant, inhibitor residual and glycol concentration, suspended solids and corrosion metals, and microbial indicators. She tells engineers to drop the assumption that deionized water is safe by default, because without buffering and inhibitors it can aggressively pick up ions from the metals and other materials it touches. Steven Lucente, a business development manager for Xylem's Applied Water business who leads its data center business development, wrote in an October 5, 2026 article in Data Center Knowledge sponsored by Xylem's Bell & Gossett that the power a data center draws can bring a water footprint of its own. Manfreid Chua, ZutaCore's VP of Business Development, AI and Sustainability, cites IEA figures in an Enterprise Viewpoint piece and argues the challenge of supporting much higher computational density while using energy and resources responsibly starts at the chip.

Singh says specifications should spell out capped storage for pipe, clean methods of assembly and the use of temporary strainers, and should set flushing velocity, turnover volume, passivation criteria, acceptance limits for differential pressure across filters, endpoints for particles or turbidity, and rules for preserving branches that stay idle until a later phase. She recommends checking headers, branches and CDU connections against both the initial and the expanded loads, and says design reviews should map which racks lose cooling in each failure. Commissioning should record clean-system performance at representative loads and test how controls respond to failures, she says. She also covers the tradeoff behind every choice of heat rejection: evaporative systems use more water but less power, a closed loop recirculates its coolant and uses little water itself but isn't zero-water, and dry cooling avoids evaporation but runs more compressor and fan power, which pushes power usage effectiveness up. Her rule of thumb is that water-stressed sites with plenty of power may accept that penalty, while power-constrained sites with plenty of water may favor evaporative cooling.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2025 update says data centers could account for 9.5 to 15.3% of US electricity by 2030, and the IEA estimates data centers worldwide consumed about 415 TWh in 2024 and projects use could reach about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI a major driver. ASHRAE says integrated liquid-cooled facilities can achieve a PUE of about 1.10 versus about 1.4 to 1.6 for traditional designs, and its framework says warm-water, chiller-less cooling enables near-zero water use in many climates. Singh notes that water usage effectiveness counts water per kWh of IT energy and leaves out the water used to generate the electricity. Lucente suggests project teams begin with the full water cycle: the source of the water, the quality it needs, how it is treated and moved, how much can be reused, how heat is rejected and what happens before discharge. ASHRAE says that when integrated design is not applied effectively, facilities risk stranded capacity, operational instability and costly retrofits.

stories.Headline: ReNew pledges ₹80,000 crore for green data centre, clean energy in Andhra Pradesh
stories.Summary:
ReNew Energy Global announced in November 2026 that it plans to invest about ₹80,000 crore in Andhra Pradesh for data centre infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing. The plan includes a 1 GW green hyperscale data centre in Anakapalli that is designed to run on renewable energy. The company has allocated ₹67,000 crore for the data centre and ₹11,000 crore for polysilicon and metallurgical silicon facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore. It also plans to invest ₹1,500 crore in a permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli, with commissioning expected by March 2029.

Separately, ReNew will set up the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence in Visakhapatnam under the PM SETU Scheme. The centre will develop a cluster of five industrial training institutes in Gajuwaka. ReNew already makes solar cells and modules and is developing a 6.5 GW ingot and wafer facility in Anakapalli, expected to be commissioned by March 2028. The new facilities will add polysilicon and metallurgical silicon production to its existing operations.

The investment comes as India expands its data centre capacity to support artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Installed capacity grew from about 375 MW in 2020 to 1.57 GW by August 2026 and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030. The articles say power availability, water consumption and project approval timelines remain challenges for the sector. Google announced in October 2025 that it would invest about $15 billion, or ₹1.3 lakh crore, in an AI infrastructure hub in Visakhapatnam between 2026 and 2030.

Clean Max Enviro Energy Solutions also signed a preliminary agreement with the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board for an investment of about ₹50,000 crore. Its proposal includes 3 GW of combined wind and solar capacity and 1 GW of pumped hydro storage. These would supply a 2 GW green compute factory in Kurnool, developed with Neysa. Neysa, an AI cloud provider, will anchor 1 GW of the facility's IT load.

stories.Headline: Applied Materials Q3 CY2026 deep dive: AI demand and advanced packaging drive outlook
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials reported results for its calendar third quarter of 2026, which is its fiscal fourth quarter, on November 12, 2026. Sales rose 53.1% from a year earlier to $10.41 billion, above the $10.33 billion analysts expected. Non-GAAP profit was $4.16 per share, 2.6% above the $4.05 consensus. Adjusted operating income was $3.68 billion, a 35.3% margin, and operating margin was 35.1%, up from 25.2% a year earlier. Inventory days outstanding fell to 122 from 132 in the prior quarter, and market capitalization stood at $302.3 billion.

For the next quarter, the company guided revenue to $11.1 billion at the midpoint, above the $10.87 billion analysts estimated, and adjusted earnings per share to $4.35 at the midpoint, above the $4.23 consensus. Advanced packaging revenue grew about 90% for the year, and the eBeam and optical process control businesses grew more than 50%. The connected installed base passed 37,000 chambers, with service and spares revenue up 26% year over year. Customer roadmaps now extend through 2030, and more than 10 new major fab projects were recently added to its tracker.

CEO Gary Dickerson credited leadership in foundry logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, where he said customer demand was strong because of AI computing investments. Management said record revenue and profitability came from operational execution and supply chain collaboration. CFO Brice Hill said the company is investing so it can double systems output by 2028, and he described AI-driven demand as a multi-year opportunity for revenue and margins. The company also cited rolling eight-quarter customer forecasts and earlier orders.

Applied Materials plans to more than double manufacturing and lab capacity by 2030. Management said growth depends on scaling the whole semiconductor ecosystem, including clean room availability and supplier capacity, and that delays there could be headwinds. The stock traded at $383.72, roughly in line with $380.96 just before the earnings. Analysts will watch whether advanced packaging and process control momentum holds, how fast capacity expands, and progress on doubling output and growing service revenue.

stories.Headline: Uber Data Breach Exposes Thousands of Drivers Through AI Firm
stories.Summary:
Hackers stole the personal information of thousands of Uber drivers through an AI startup. The ride-hailing company filed security breach notices with several state attorneys general this month. A third-party provider notified Uber of the incident on October 9. Uber determined on October 13 that hackers had accessed its driver data. The breach involved the theft of internal credentials to access the account.

The breach affected 1,873 Rhode Island residents and 3,430 South Carolina residents. TechCrunch reports that 2,567 people in Massachusetts also had their information stolen. The stolen data included driver's license information from the Fireworks AI startup. Notion also lost data, including AI chat transcripts for fewer than 1% of workspaces. Fireworks AI reported that hackers accessed billing information and incomplete AI models.

Fireworks AI said the attack was carried out by a financially motivated cybercriminal group. The company described the practice as LLMJacking, where hackers steal credentials to use or sell AI models. Fireworks AI stated it notified law enforcement and worked with Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. Uber said it immediately cut off all data connections with Fireworks AI. Uber stated it has not identified any misuse of the stolen information.

Affected drivers are encouraged to monitor credit reports and review account statements for suspicious activity. Uber is offering these drivers free fraud assistance and credit monitoring through Cyberscout. Drivers have 90 days from their notification letter date to sign up. Notion customers were affected by the exposure of anonymized chat transcripts. Uber operates a fleet of over 10 million drivers and couriers.

Fireworks AI disclosed that hackers accessed development machines through a separate cloud provider security incident. Uber previously dealt with a security incident in August involving its logistics subsidiary, Uber Freight. A hacking group claimed to have stolen nearly 1 million files from that subsidiary. Uber Freight confirmed unauthorized access to some systems but did not verify the file claims. Uber requires drivers to upload residency, insurance, and bank statements.

Uber will notify all affected workers, though the total nationwide number remains undisclosed. The company recently expanded policies for banning drivers based on public records and background checks. The articles do not state if the cybercriminal group has been identified. It is unclear if any other Fireworks AI clients were compromised. The reports leave the final count of affected drivers open.

stories.Headline: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping the Legal Profession
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved into courtrooms, law offices and legal research departments across the country, according to TechSpective on November 14, 2026. The article says the technology is no longer confined to science fiction or Silicon Valley boardrooms. It describes the rise of AI as both an opportunity and a genuine shift in how legal work gets done. It says attorneys, paralegals and clients alike face this change. It adds that understanding these changes is essential for anyone navigating today’s legal landscape.

AI-driven platforms scan thousands of case files, statutes and legal precedents in minutes, work that once took junior associates hours or full days. The tools retrieve information and also analyze patterns and surface insights a human researcher might overlook under time pressure. AI tools help lawyers identify problematic clauses, inconsistencies and missing provisions faster than manual review, and can be trained to flag language deviating from standard agreements or posing legal risks. Predictive analytics tools evaluate how courts have ruled on similar cases, and AI-driven e-discovery platforms streamline document review during discovery. A probate litigation attorney in California may use AI-assisted research and case analysis in complex matters like estate disputes involving contested wills or trust administration.

Former President Ram Nath Kovind said human judgment and oversight must remain indispensable to protect the credibility of courts and the rights of litigants, the Deccan Chronicle reported on November 14, 2026. Speaking at the Justice K. Ramaswamy Endowment Lecture at Dr B.R. Ambedkar College of Law, Andhra University, in Visakhapatnam on Saturday, he cautioned young advocates against blindly relying on AI-generated case laws and judicial precedents. He said, in the article’s words, that professional credibility cannot be transferred to a software provider. He urged advocates to personally verify legal assertions from authentic sources, including original judgments, rather than rely on software to validate its own output. He said technology should democratise access to justice instead of widening the gap between metropolitan law firms and lawyers practising in district courts.

Kovind cited the US case of Mata vs Avianca Inc., in which lawyers were penalised for submitting fictitious case citations generated by AI. He also referred to the Supreme Court case of Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd., where orders based on fabricated citations were set aside. He noted that more than 83,000 Supreme Court judgments were available in 18 Indian languages and said AI could accelerate translations while human supervision preserved the nuances and precision of legal terminology.

He urged law schools to adapt teaching methods to the digital era by emphasising critical thinking, legal research and oral advocacy, and to train future lawyers to examine electronic evidence and identify deepfakes. He said the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and the Bharatiya Nararik Suraksha Sanhita showed India’s legal framework had recognised the growing importance of electronic records and digital proceedings. TechSpective says questions around data privacy, attorney-client privilege and the accuracy of AI-generated outputs are at the forefront of ongoing legal and ethical debates. It says bar associations and regulatory bodies are actively working to establish guidelines keeping AI use within appropriate ethical boundaries.

It warns that over-reliance on automated tools could lead to critical errors if attorneys accept AI outputs without proper scrutiny, and that the most effective approach treats AI as a powerful assistant rather than a substitute for genuine professional legal judgment. It says legal fees may decrease as efficiency improves and turnaround times on documents and case updates can be significantly faster, while AI-powered client portals and chatbots make basic legal information easier to access and let people communicate with legal teams outside traditional office hours. It says the overall client experience is becoming more transparent, more responsive and far more service-oriented. Kovind paid tribute to Justice K. Ramaswamy, recalling his contribution to the landmark S.R. Bommai judgment and the constitutional principle of secularism.

He concluded by urging young lawyers to combine technological skills with constitutional values and a commitment to justice, saying technology provides powerful tools but will never possess a conscience. TechSpective says the human element of law, including empathy, ethical reasoning and nuanced judgment, remains irreplaceable, and that attorneys who thrive will embrace AI as a tool while prioritising the personal and professional skills that define excellent legal practice. It says the future of law is both human and machine working together toward better outcomes. The articles leave open which guidelines bar associations and regulatory bodies will adopt and when.

stories.Headline: Nonprofit advocacy groups cite dangers, sue to stop development of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A coalition of five nonprofit online safety and advocacy groups filed suit in the San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, alleging that artificial intelligence systems are already autonomously breaking the law and causing harm. The suit demands an immediate injunction to halt all further development of AI, particularly ChatGPT, Grok, Muse, Gemini, and Claude. The plaintiffs allege that several Big Tech companies violated the Business and Professions Code of California's Unfair Competition Law, specifically the section prohibiting unlawful business practices. The plaintiffs allege that under the code AI is a public nuisance, defined as anything injurious to health or an obstruction to the free use of property that interferes with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by an entire community or neighborhood. The suit was filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and Future Tech Insights, doing business as The Alliance For Secure AI, and names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX.

The complaint quotes Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX and has invested heavily in AI, as saying AI has the potential of civilization destruction. The complaint also quotes Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, as saying AI developers do not understand how their own AI creations work. Amodei also said AI could enable a group to carry out a large-scale biological attack, which he called a grave threat to U.S. national security in a hearing before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee. In June, the mother of a Canadian child who died by suicide filed a suit against OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT encouraged the girl's suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in the same month, alleging ChatGPT harmed children by providing information to school shooters, advising children on self-harm, and intentionally addicting children.

Attorney Matthew Platkin, who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs, said in a press release from Public Citizen that it is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race. Platkin said they are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm. The plaintiffs wrote that no other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products, much less ones that could kill us all, as inevitable. A group of state attorneys general filed a similar suit in October. In July, Illinois passed legislation holding AI developers responsible for safety risks, including a requirement for audits of safety issues by independent third parties, with publication of the results.

The University of Missouri's Career Center directs students looking for work to Handshake, which describes itself as the career network for the AI economy and which Mizzou partnered with in 2017, guaranteeing students an account and access to the platform's job network. Handshake AI pays around $60 million monthly to students from over 1,600 institutions and connects other AI companies to Mizzou students for remote projects usually lasting between two weeks and six months. Handshake AI's entry-level positions offer hourly rates of $17 to $30, while positions requiring years of extensive experience can offer over $100 hourly, and last academic year Handshake AI paid out $117,174 to Mizzou students. According to Cynthia Singleton-Diaz, student coordinator I at the Career Center, 1,623 Mizzou students have submitted 2,710 applications to jobs posted by Handshake AI. Mizzou junior Prajit Rayaprolu was an AI trainer for seven months last school year, attracted by the work's simplicity, flexible hours and a friend's recommendation, and while he felt fairly compensated he eventually stopped seeing the job as sustainable for his well-being.

Amanda Nell, senior student services coordinator at the Career Center, said there are lots of networking opportunities and skill-building opportunities and that they invest and innovate the platform on a pretty regular basis. During his time as an AI trainer, Rayaprolu sorted online photos and evaluated AI-created images and videos for realism, and he was also tasked with writing lengthy prompts and having conversations with AI assistants to complete tasks. Researchers investigating this digital labor use the term human computation to describe human labor in tasks AI struggles with, including sorting data, labeling pictures and letting AI know when it makes a faulty or unfair association, and this labor was extensively used in the early development of AI models such as ChatGPT, Llama, Claude and Gemini. In the early development of AI models much of this training was done by workers paid below their local minimum wages, often contracted through middlemen who assigned digital labor as gig work, and the most popular subcontracting platform for human computation, Amazon Mechanical Turk, was discontinued Sept. 30, 2026, with workers paid per task as independent contractors at rates as low as 1 cent. Peter Mueser, an emeritus professor and specialist in labor markets, said this work was valuable to outsourced workers, as in any growing industry workers are attracted only when jobs pay higher wages than their alternatives.

Elizabeth Lucas, an AI fellow at the Missouri School of Journalism, said these are all things that are part of bigger systems that have really broad impacts and that it is incumbent upon us as humans to think about that and recognize that and see ourselves as one small piece of a very large system. Hayden Hawkins, an undergraduate student representative on the AI standing committee, said in an email that it is imperative that artificial intelligence companies ensure their workers receive fair pay, maintain worker safety and consider data privacy when sourcing their labor. The median wage on MTurk was significantly above the World Bank's $3-per-day international poverty line, though The Journal of Collaborative Computing and Work Practices reported that other crowdsourcing platforms pay around or below this line. Companies hoping to employ students at Mizzou for human computation are vetted by the Career Center before they can be connected with students, and the Career Center works with Mizzou's standing AI committee and UM System Associate Director of AI Justin Palozola to ensure operations on Handshake align with system policy. MU Career Services notifies potential users of Handshake that users are responsible for evaluating the safety, wages, working conditions and other aspects of job listings.

Rayaprolu said he stopped working for Handshake AI after it created a large Slack channel where it frequently posted new guidelines, limited the hours employees could work per day and started to require employees to complete quizzes before they could start working for the day. On Oct. 1, AI trainers working on Project Hedgehog, the project Rayaprolu had spent the majority of his time working on, were required to pass an assessment, and if they did not pass they risked being removed from the project. Rayaprolu also mentioned a four-level rating system for every output he submitted, with scores matching bad, acceptable, good or excellent outputs, and he said that if your scores dropped below two you weren't allowed to access any assessments. The process some social scientists call human computation was first used on a large scale by a Stanford professor, Fei-Fei Li, and as generative AI development progressed companies used this process to test their models and create training data, often sharing methodologies and employees. The extent to which human computation is currently being used in the training of AI systems is unclear, as many tech companies view pre-training strategy as a trade secret that provides them with a competitive advantage, and the future of human computation is unpredictable as AI is increasingly used to evaluate and learn from its own inputs.

stories.Headline: Doc: Amazon, wary of AI agents favoring sites with better data, plans to gather data on nearly every product sold anywhere, including by crawling rivals' sites (Greg Bensinger/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Amazon plans to gather data on nearly every product sold anywhere, including by crawling rivals' sites, according to a document reported by Greg Bensinger of Reuters on November 13, 2026. Amazon is wary of AI agents favoring sites with better data, the document says. Techmeme posted the report at 9:40 PM on November 13, 2026. The document describes Amazon's plan to collect product data beyond its own marketplace. The report was attributed to Greg Bensinger of Reuters.

The plan covers nearly every product sold anywhere, including products sold by rivals, and includes crawling rivals' sites, according to the document. The document says Amazon is wary of AI agents favoring sites with better data. The report was posted by Techmeme on November 13, 2026, at 9:40 PM. stories.Headline: White House Urges Easing Liability to Encourage AI Disclosure
stories.Summary:
A White House AI task force issued a recommendation on Thursday, November 13, 2026. The group urged federal agencies to stop using regulatory penalties against companies that report cybersecurity incidents in good faith. This proposal aims to encourage firms to disclose vulnerabilities rather than hide them. The task force believes that current enforcement standards may be outdated.

The plan suggests a liability relief window of at least 12 months, which could be extended later. This relief applies only to cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents, not to general AI failures or bad advice. For the plan to work, agencies must write it into formal guidance. Additionally, Congress must renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015.

The task force includes National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, Pentagon research chief Emil Michael, and OPM Director Scott Kupor. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also attended the meeting. These officials argued that strict penalties create a chilling effect on information sharing. They noted that organizations are now more vulnerable because attackers use AI tools.

The recommendation is currently voluntary and is not an executive order or a law. Agencies can choose to ignore the advice, and none have promised to follow it yet. The government is also discussing a voluntary process to analyze reports and share defensive data. Future success depends on whether regulators actually offer the promised relief.

stories.Headline: MeitY reviews house help platforms' AI training data collection
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology sought details from home services platforms about their collection of first-person video and sensor data from gig workers. The ministry asked Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp for information on data used to train physical AI models. A meeting chaired by MeitY secretary S Krishnan brought together senior executives from quick home services platforms and other technology and robotics companies. The meeting discussed concerns around workers' consent, consumer privacy and data sovereignty, according to a report by ET. Officials are concerned that recordings of everyday household activities could infringe workers' rights, compromise consumer privacy and pose risks to national data security.

The ministry sought details on the standard operating procedures companies follow for collecting, processing and storing such data. It also sought information on safeguards for obtaining workers' consent and protecting the privacy of other individuals captured in the recordings. MeitY further sought clarity on whether companies were selling, sharing or transferring the collected data to physical AI developers outside India. It asked Pronto to submit details of its data collection practices and the SOPs it follows, ET reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. Pronto confirmed it was running an opt-in pilot involving first-person video recordings of household chores, initially available only to customers who actively opted in during booking and limited to less than 0.01% of its users.

Pronto said it participated in the meeting as part of a broader industry consultation involving home services platforms, robotics companies and other stakeholders. A spokesperson said the consultation gave the ministry and industry participants an opportunity to exchange perspectives, share existing practices and discuss opportunities and challenges emerging from the evolving AI landscape. The spokesperson said Pronto shared its current practices as part of this exchange and looks forward to continued engagement with MeitY and other industry stakeholders. Pronto stated that raw footage was deleted immediately after work completion, while an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording remained accessible only to customers for 48 hours. Pronto said this anonymised footage was subsequently used for AI training, as outlined in its terms.

Snabbit clarified that it had conducted a limited assessment of the technology in a controlled training-centre environment but decided against proceeding with the proposal. Urban Company founder Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the company neither records inside customers' homes nor plans to do so. Inc42 has reached out to Snabbit and Urban Company for their comments on the development, and the story will be updated upon receiving responses. Concerns were also reportedly raised about India becoming a source of cheap training data for foreign AI companies. Executives suggested that the country should focus on developing its own physical AI capabilities rather than merely supplying data to overseas developers.

The development comes shortly after Pronto faced scrutiny over a pilot programme to record household chores using cameras worn by service professionals to generate training data for robotics systems. The controversy also brought Snabbit and Urban Company under scrutiny over their potential involvement in this. In July, Pronto formalised its data collection experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which professionals wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. Last month, Pronto founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based physical AI venture that will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. Provision Labs also announced the acquisition of Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a startup focused on perception technologies, and Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision's hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models.

The relationship between Pronto's household data collection and Provision Labs' operations remains unclear. Inc42 said the story will be updated upon receiving responses from Snabbit and Urban Company. The articles do not say what action MeitY will take after reviewing the details submitted by the platforms. The articles do not say whether the ministry set any deadline for the companies to respond. The articles do not say whether other home services platforms beyond Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp were asked for details.

stories.Summary:
Cerebras Systems shares rose more than 14 per cent in early trading on Friday, after the chipmaker raised its annual sales forecast and posted a surprise profit. The company said it now expects 2026 adjusted revenue of $940 million to $960 million, up from its previous forecast of $880 million to $890 million. Analysts had expected sales of $887.04 million for the period, according to LSEG data. If the gains hold, they would add over $3 billion to Cerebras' market value.

The results come as Cerebras challenges Nvidia in the AI chip market. Adjusted cloud and services revenue, which reflects its OpenAI deal, more than tripled to $144.9 million for the third quarter. Adjusted profit was $29.82 million, compared with an adjusted loss of $10.86 million a year earlier, while analysts had expected an adjusted loss of $38.4 million. As of Thursday's close, Cerebras shares were down 47.2 per cent from their May IPO price of $185 apiece.

CEO Andrew Feldman said on the earnings call that delivery delays under Cerebras' $20 billion multi-year OpenAI deal came from industry-wide shortages of land and power, not chip manufacturing constraints. The chipmaker reiterated plans to triple revenue in 2027. It also said it has signed a cloud deal with Microsoft, with details to be shared next year. The upbeat forecast helped offset concerns over heavy AI spending and uncertainty triggered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence policy implemented by Kansas Board of Education
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education created an instructional technology policy earlier this week, the Kansas State Department of Education announced in a press release on Nov. 13, 2026, from Topeka. The policy requires Kansas public school districts and accredited nonpublic schools to develop policies outlining how technology is used in classrooms. The policy establishes statewide minimum requirements for instructional technology use while allowing local school boards to decide how those expectations will be implemented. Kansas Education Commissioner Dr. Jake Steel said the policy is intended to ensure technology strengthens teaching and learning rather than replaces meaningful interactions between teachers and students. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners.

Every district and accredited nonpublic school must adopt both an instructional technology policy and an implementation plan, and both must be approved by local school boards and reviewed annually. The plans must address the purpose and intended use of classroom technology, student access to school-issued devices, whether students can take school-issued devices home, digital citizenship and student well-being, the use of artificial intelligence by teachers and students, student privacy and cybersecurity protections, and technology expectations and violations. Schools will also be required to establish guidelines for how artificial intelligence tools, including chatbots and generative AI, are used. Districts and accredited nonpublic schools must make their policies and plans publicly available on their websites and submit their adopted plans to the Kansas State Department of Education by July 1, 2027. Beginning in the 2028-29 school year, parents or guardians must receive access to their school's technology-use plan and acknowledge it before students receive access to school-issued devices, and the policy will remain in effect until July 1, 2030 unless it is reauthorized, amended or extended.

Steel said the State Board has sent a clear message that technology only belongs in the classroom when it strengthens teaching and learning. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners. KSDE officials said it encourages schools to involve families and caregivers in developing their technology-use plans. It also recognizes that some students may need additional or different access to technology because of disabilities, medical needs, language needs or other educational requirements. The Kansas State Board of Education created the policy earlier this week, according to the KSDE press release.

Princeton University recently decided to offer access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro to its students and faculty through a new one-year pilot program, The Daily Princetonian wrote on Oct. 30. The Daily Princetonian later published an editorial about the program on Nov. 6, questioning how the implementation of AI in an academic environment will affect students' ability to learn and how it reflects on the university's fundamental mission of education. The Daily Princetonian's Editorial Board said it was not convinced that a sweeping ChatGPT pilot will suit the distinct learning methods across disciplines. Students at the College have had the ability to use several different AI tools at their full capacity for about a year now, after Vice President for Operations Sharon Blanton announced in an email to the College on Oct. 2 that students and faculty were granted secure access to Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Google NotebookLM, The Signal reported in 2025. Students can find an instructional article on the College's website titled "Getting Started with Gemini: Your AI Assistant for Campus Life."

Artificial intelligence has been developing at an exponential rate since ChatGPT was first introduced to the internet in 2022, and after about four years it has become an integral part of every app, including search engines like Google. The Daily Princetonian wrote that students will be able to request access to ChatGPT Plus before the start of next semester, and faculty and staff could request access beginning Wednesday. The tech giant Google recently announced that if schools ban use of their AI features, students will no longer be able to use Google Search, according to The Guardian. Students at the College were encouraged to use the tools responsibly and to follow course guidelines, which can differ for each instructor. Princeton's implementation of ChatGPT Plus and Pro, which one typically has to pay for, also brings up the question of how much money is being spent to give access to all students and faculty who request it.

stories.Headline: FAA Ground Stop and Microsoft Outage: Did AI Play a Role?
stories.Summary:
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and it described the information as preliminary. The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific, and more than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. AP reported that European departures for the United States were suspended at the FAA's request from November 13, 22:00 UTC (5:00 p.m. EST), until November 14, 05:00 UTC (midnight EST). Duffy said aging switches and routers in the agency's telecom network got overloaded with data and began producing inconsistent information, adding that the FAA still relies on 1980s little copper lines.

He said newer equipment held up, stating that the new IP switches did not go down and that it was the old hardware that went down. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said. Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing, and that as the agency put patches into the system and added new equipment and new technology, it was overwhelming the older system. Neither official said exactly what that equipment was. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself and said there is no connection between this and Microsoft.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement from a company spokesperson that it had no indication that the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption. Duffy ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA's new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it is not connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights and that there was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today. Asked whether a cyberattack or rogue AI could be ruled out, Mullin said there was nothing completely certain right now, that it appears this was mechanically driven, and that officials were still looking and would not rule that out. Asked whether officials had seen any evidence of a cyberattack, he said they had seen zero evidence. At an afternoon news conference, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

Air Space Intelligence denied any connection in a post on X, saying the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or its integration with FAA and ATC. The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers. The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes, and FAA specialists review its recommendations while local facilities decide whether to act on them. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence. It is the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA's Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon. The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network, and AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028. In justifying the award, the FAA said its current telecom network can no longer adequately support air traffic operations, MeriTalk reported. Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system, and Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency. The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported, and Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Duffy said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning. The FAA's November 13 statement said technicians were investigating, and a ground stop holds affected departures on the ground. Travelers should check their airline and airport for flight-specific information, since a national advisory alone does not tell an individual passenger when their flight will leave. Alaska Airlines' advisory describes the affected U.S. departures as excluding Alaska and Hawaii and offers a flexible change-or-cancel policy.

stories.Headline: Tech companies want AI to shop for you. Most Americans aren't buying it.
stories.Summary:
A Bank of America survey released in November 2026 found that 72% of Americans do not plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025. The 23-percentage-point jump was reported by Fortune on November 14, 2026, in a story by Tatiana Sataua. Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop, and Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart, Meta's Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. The survey suggests a gap between the industry's ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it.

Among those who do not plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they do not trust AI recommendations. The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year. It also found that 63% said they base their spending strictly on their own budgets rather than what friends or family spend. The survey found that 17% plan to use AI to compare prices or deals, 14% for gift ideas or inspiration, and 7% to write messages or cards, and respondents could select more than one use. Bank of America said it asked the AI shopping question the same way in both years, though the survey only measures intentions, and the bank does not have data showing whether shoppers are actually using AI less.

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America, said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending. She told Fortune that some of last year's curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and that we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue. She said gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they are giving. She said that same budget-focused approach may be shaping how consumers use AI and social media to shop. Monfared's comments were reported by Fortune in its November 14, 2026 story.

Colleen Kirk, a professor of marketing and management at New York Institute of Technology, told Fortune that the hesitation may have less to do with what AI can do than what shoppers feel they lose by using it. She said gift giving is a very personal act, and gifts, especially to close family and friends, are given from the heart. In her research studying consumer psychology, she has found that consumers can feel guilty when they use AI to write heartfelt messages because the words no longer feel entirely their own. She said that effort creates what researchers call psychological ownership, or the feeling of having a personal stake in something, and that using AI can take away this sense of ownership. Kirk said AI may have a more natural place in the less personal parts of shopping, such as finding coupons, comparing prices, or buying groceries and household supplies, and she suggested consumers come up with their own ideas first, then turn to AI to help narrow their options.

Amazon.com Inc. is considering building a global product database to minimize buyers' use of Google and other websites, according to a Reuters-reviewed internal document reported by GuruFocus on November 13, 2026. The initiative, called World Product Graph, gathers data on internet-sold products, including items Amazon does not sell, so shoppers can compare goods, find newer models, and buy without leaving Amazon. The project would merge manufacturer and retail website data, Coke and Bayer are sharing product information, and Amazon is considering a Procter & Gamble experiment. Amazon's Alexa for Shopping, formerly Rufus, may benefit from the project, though the assistant's replies were wrong or partial and the service was pricey, according to an internal paper. Amazon refuted the paper, stating that its shopping assistant is 97% accurate worldwide, and the concept included an October 2027 start date that Amazon has not verified.

Amazon said the paper is preliminary and may not reflect its current goals, and retail sales and advertising income depend on Amazon's shopping traffic. The Reuters-reviewed document reflects competition from AI shopping bots that can compare and buy across sites. Fortune reported that it is an awkward moment for tech companies betting that shoppers will eventually trust AI to do more than recommend products, including making purchases on their behalf. Kirk said research has found that people feel more ownership over an outcome when they generate their own ideas before using AI. She said some consumers may decide that letting AI handle the less personal tasks is a worthwhile trade-off, and that consumers might just decide it is worth it to give up a little bit of ownership of the process in exchange for getting more time for those special emotional connections with the humans they love.
