stories.Headline: Anthropic Says AI Safety Scores Can Mislead, Urges Overhaul of Model Testing
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published recommendations for building more reliable AI safety evaluations in a research post on Friday, November 13, 2026. The company warned that safety scores can be misleading when tests are easy to game, poorly documented or measure the wrong behavior. Anthropic is a leading developer of large language models. The recommendations cover evaluation design, testing environments, grading and the reporting of results. Anthropic said decisions about whether a system is ready to ship, what guardrails it needs and where future safety work should focus all rest on the quality of the evaluations behind them.

Anthropic said evaluations should assess whether responses raise or lower the likelihood of harm rather than what a model can do. It argued that refusal rates alone are a poor gauge, since declining to engage with a user in crisis is itself a failure. The company called for multidisciplinary evaluation teams, sandboxed testing without internet access, multi-turn conversation tests, human validation of AI graders and published statistical uncertainty. It said it had hardened its own testing environments after incidents, temporarily halted many evaluations that grant models internet access and added real-time monitoring for web-search tests that still need connectivity. Anthropic narrowed its advice to three priorities: define what is being measured before testing begins, validate AI-based grading against human expert judgment, and report statistical uncertainty so readers can tell a real improvement from noise.

Anthropic wrote that when it says a model is safer than its predecessor, it means the model scored better on a set of evals someone built. The company wrote that a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. It wrote that when a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure. Anthropic wrote that in recent months, in response to its own incidents, it had hardened its evaluation environments. It wrote that humans extract harmful information from a model through gradual escalation, so a model that handles the first message well may respond inappropriately by the fifth.

Anthropic said an appropriate response in biology and cybersecurity is rarely a flat refusal, and models should engage with legitimate requests while withholding operational details that could enable misuse. The company said evaluations need to capture both a model's willingness to comply with harmful requests and its tendency to reject harmless ones. It said results can shift on seemingly minor design choices, such as whether a question is multiple-choice or open-ended, or how the answer options are ordered. Anthropic said it runs multi-turn evaluations that grade an entire conversation against rubrics written by domain experts, with a single failure sinking the whole interaction. The recommendations arrive as regulators and enterprise buyers increasingly ask vendors to substantiate safety claims, and as model releases are marketed partly on benchmark performance.

Anthropic distinguished observational designs, suited to understanding how a model behaves, from causal designs, needed to test whether a specific intervention changes outcomes. It called for measurement specialists to decide how responses are sampled and scored, and subject-matter experts to identify realistic risks and define what a sound answer looks like. The company likened the state of the field to psychology a decade ago, when similar problems with measurement were addressed through reforms such as preregistration and better methodology. Anthropic said some evaluations run with standard safeguards switched off so that a model's baseline behavior can be observed, which can let a system reach beyond its intended testing environment. It urged developers to document testing configurations so that independent teams can reproduce results.

Anthropic said that if scores can move with the format of a question, comparisons across models and versions become difficult to defend, weakening the case for evaluation results as a procurement or compliance signal. For AI developers, the practical burden is heavier than running a standard benchmark, since expert-designed rubrics, human validation of automated graders, longer conversational tests and published uncertainty ranges all add cost and time to the release cycle. Anthropic's own account suggests the payoff is a clearer picture of what a model will actually do once deployed, rather than a number that may not mean what it appears to. The articles do not say when Anthropic will publish further recommendations or whether regulators will adopt them. The articles do not say how many incidents prompted Anthropic to harden its testing environments.

stories.Headline: How Nvidia became the backbone of the global artificial intelligence industry
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on November 13, 2026, following allegations of misconduct. He was accused of facilitating access to restricted computing chips for a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. These events occurred as governments imposed semiconductor export restrictions and technology firms sought to reduce their Nvidia dependence. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, was appointed as the interim chief executive of the company. Nvidia has now begun searching for a permanent successor to lead the global artificial intelligence hardware supplier.

The controversy involves Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials suspect of being a spy for China. She allegedly told Chinese investors she could secure Nvidia GPUs and proposed a deal for 240,000 restricted chips. US restrictions on advanced computing chip exports to China were introduced in 2022 to limit military applications. Researcher Will DePue found numerical patterns in six Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek and Ant Group, matching Blackwell hardware. Other models showing these traces include those from MiniMax and Moonshot AI, though export violations are not proven.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and directed its transformation from a gaming manufacturer into an AI backbone. He insisted that the CUDA software platform be included in every GPU, despite increasing production costs for gamers. Huang personally delivered the first DGX-1 deep learning supercomputer, containing eight GPUs, to the non-profit organization OpenAI. He has not confirmed reports from the New York Times regarding a second affair with an Nvidia executive. China has dismissed the allegations involving Alice Huang, who is not related to the former chief executive.

Investors and businesses whose AI operations depend on Nvidia hardware and software are affected by the leadership change. The company's valuation reached 4.5 trillion dollars, making it the most valuable company in the world before this. Initial allegations wiped almost 500 billion dollars from its market value, with further declines following the resignation. Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are affected as they develop their own specialized chips to compete with Nvidia. DeepMind used 176 GPUs for AlphaGo in January 2016 before switching to 48 Google tensor processing units.

Nvidia originally manufactured graphics processing units for computer games to perform intensive calculations for three-dimensional images. The company introduced the CUDA software platform in 2007 to translate algorithms into instructions for these GPUs. In 2012, researchers adopted CUDA for artificial intelligence, and the AlexNet neural network demonstrated superior image-recognition performance. This combination of hardware and software revived neural network research and accelerated the development of the deep learning field. Nvidia's competitive advantage grew from combining its processors with a software ecosystem that is difficult for competitors to displace.

Nvidia must now identify a new chief executive to replace the man who led its massive industrial transformation. The company faces growing competition from other technology firms that are developing alternative artificial intelligence processors. Colette Kress continues to serve as the interim leader while the search for a permanent successor remains ongoing. The articles leave open whether the traces of Blackwell chips in Chinese models prove any actual export law violations. It remains unclear if Alice Huang will publicly respond to the allegations regarding her suspected role as a spy.

stories.Headline: Uganda: Will Uganda's Youth Power the Ai Economy, or Be Left Behind By It?
stories.Summary:
Uganda faces a choice over whether its young people will benefit from artificial intelligence or be left behind by it, according to a new Commonwealth study unveiled at the leaders' summit in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda, held from November 1 to 4. The inaugural 2026 Commonwealth Youth AI Readiness Index, produced by the Ayre Think Tank, was presented on the sidelines of that gathering. The study found that AI could raise Uganda's GDP by an estimated US$899 million over the next decade, provided the country creates the conditions for young people to benefit. Uganda has one of the most youthful populations in the world and a sizeable entrepreneurial base, but its ability to turn that advantage into productive jobs remains constrained. The article was reported by Ronald Musoke and published on November 13, 2026.

Uganda ranks 23rd among 56 Commonwealth countries, scoring 47.0 out of 100, below the study's readiness benchmark of 53. The country is marginally behind Kenya, which ranks 22nd with 48.7 points, and ahead of Tanzania at 25th with 45.5 and Rwanda at 47th with 38.1. Uganda has 13.4 million people aged 15 to 29, according to the data used in the study. Uganda Bureau of Statistics figures from its 2025 Labour Market Survey put youth unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 at 17.9%, against a national rate of 12.2%. Young women face a 21% unemployment rate compared with 15.2% for young men, and the survey found 89.2% of employment was informal.

The index was produced by the Ayre Think Tank, whose founder, Calvin Ayre, said that AI will change how people work, do business and create wealth. He argued that the race is not one only the biggest or richest countries can win, and that giving young people skills and chances matters most. Ayre said governments now have to decide what they will do about the gaps the index reveals. The study measures the conditions that let young people benefit from the technology rather than directly measuring AI competence or adoption. Uganda's score is based on usable information for 61 of the 102 indicators, and its Data Gap Index is 50.0, which indicates substantial missing evidence.

Young people in Uganda are also affected by the infrastructure gaps the study identifies. Electricity reaches just 55.3% of the population, according to the figures cited, and fewer than half of young people report using the internet. The study found that 41.9% of people aged 18 to 29 were starting or running a new business, while another 20.6% owned an established business. Joshua Pi'Rwot, a consultant at the AVODA Institute of Entrepreneurship in Kampala, said businesses lack a date for when the national AI policy will be completed. The Ministry of ICT is leading the drafting of that policy after a national stakeholders' consultation in May 2026.

Uganda's readiness challenges were identified in a 2025 national AI landscape assessment by the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance, working with the International Telecommunication Union. That assessment highlighted inadequate AI infrastructure, shortages of specialised skills, limited collaboration between academia and technology companies, and the absence of a comprehensive AI policy and regulatory framework. A national task force set up in 2018 developed the Uganda National Fourth Industrial Revolution Strategy, which targets creating 300,000 new earning opportunities by 2040. The strategy also seeks to raise agricultural GDP output by 2% annually.

The Ayre Index places Singapore first with 77.6 points, while Mauritius leads Africa in eighth place with 64.4 points. The articles leave open when Uganda's national AI policy will be finalised and whether the country can close its infrastructure and skills gaps in time. They do not say how the 300,000 earning opportunities target is progressing toward its 2040 deadline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Pentagon rebrands principle AI shop as 'Super Intelligence Office'
stories.Summary:
The Defense Department announced that its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, known as the CDAO, has been redesignated as the Super Intelligence Office, or SIO. The change was reported on November 13, 2026, by Breaking Defense. The department said the new name does not alter the office's mission. It said the change instead lines the office up with a broader push across the federal government to replace references to artificial intelligence with the term "super intelligence."

The department said the transition will roll out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters over the coming weeks. Existing operational programs, industry solicitations and defense partnerships will continue without interruption under the new name. The department has also launched SI.mil, which will serve as the renamed office's main digital domain. The office's portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central data hub formerly known as Advana.

Cameron Stanley, the department's top AI official who also leads the office, said in a statement that the rebrand reflects the Pentagon's priorities going forward. He said the department has moved beyond experimental prototypes. Stanley said the office's mission is to harness the full power of sovereign super intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain. The redesignation follows an announcement by President Donald Trump in September that federal agencies should replace AI references with the term super intelligence, which he argued made the technology sound fake.

The article notes that the terminology has drawn questions in the tech community, where superintelligence has traditionally described a hypothetical form of general artificial intelligence that exceeds overall human intelligence. The Pentagon has been among the federal government's most aggressive adopters of AI, with the CDAO leading efforts to expand its use across military operations. Those efforts include making generative AI tools more widely available to personnel through GenAI.mil, an enterprise platform providing access to commercial generative AI models. The article does not say what the rebrand will cost or whether it will affect the office's budget.

stories.Headline: ChemInsight: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating and Diagnosing Chemistry Understanding and Reasoning in Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Changyu Hu and nine other authors introduced a benchmark called ChemInsight on November 14, 2026, to evaluate large language models on chemistry tasks. This new tool assesses whether these models can handle multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding through a specific set of challenging questions. The researchers designed the system to diagnose the reasoning capabilities of various models by using a two-dimensional scoring method for evaluation. This benchmark consists of 203 chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles to support the scope and depth scoring evaluation scheme. The team evaluated ten representative large language models and found that their performance was consistently low across all the tested metrics.

The ChemInsight system requires scope scores and depth scores, which were below 30 percent and 11 percent for the ten tested models. The research paper spans 16 pages and includes 6 figures, with Changyu Hu, Yiming Zou, and Xin Tang contributing equally to work. Zhenduo Zhang, Wang Ren, and Xiao Li served as the corresponding authors for the study on chemistry understanding and reasoning in models. In Taiwan, the AI Evaluation Center began ranking models in September based on language proficiency, Taiwanese society, and specific Taiwanese values. These rankings include the GSAT university entrance exam, while the startup APMIC rose from 15th to 1st place between September and October.

The authors of the chemistry study asked if statistically driven training methods are effective at modeling symbolic language like the SMILES chemical notation. They also questioned if intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora could improve performance or what factors limit current advancement in chemistry. Ling-Jyh Chen, chief executive of Taiwan AI Academy, stated that proficiency in Chinese does not translate to an awareness of local context. Chen argued that models from U.S. companies like Google and OpenAI often fail to understand the culture and values of Taiwan. The Ministry of Digital Affairs stated that Taiwan must control its own data and perspectives to ensure democratic views are understood.

The AI Evaluation Center says it measures understanding of democratic institutions and historical experiences, though it does not prescribe politically correct answers. Alice Yang, a research fellow, questioned if Taiwanese values can be defined objectively and suggested the government fears Chinese influence. Audrey Tang, an ambassador at large, noted that Taiwan has 20 national languages, 16 recognized Indigenous peoples, and 42 language variations. Tang argued that gathering everyone's data for one national model is misguided and that sovereignty should be implemented at the local level. The Ministry of Digital Affairs believes authoritarian regimes use artificial intelligence to rewrite the past and dominate the future of human society.

The chemistry researchers noted that the performance of the ten large language models was substantially lower than the performance of human experts. Earlier versions of ChatGPT were trained on 190 million Chinese words, most of which were simplified Chinese originating from mainland China. This training caused the chatbot to fail a question about beef soup noodles, which do not contain chunks of meat. APMIC improved its GSAT score by nearly 17 percentage points because it was fine-tuned using data provided by the Taiwanese government. U.S. models perform well on language and society metrics but fall behind Taiwanese models on the specific Taiwanese values metric.

The chemistry study leaves open whether domain-specific training can fix the low depth scores and the failure to model symbolic chemical language. The AI Evaluation Center remains vague about the exact methods used to measure the third metric regarding specific Taiwanese values. It is unclear if a single national model can truly represent the diverse voices of the many different Taiwanese indigenous groups. The researchers continue to investigate what specific factors limit the advancement of current large language models when performing complex chemistry tasks. Future developments may determine if sovereign AI is the key to securing democracy or if it is fundamentally an anti-democratic approach.

stories.Headline: Labels required for AI-made dramas
stories.Summary:
China's top broadcast regulator introduced landmark rules for the digital entertainment market to bring AI generated short dramas under unified national oversight. The National Radio and Television Administration enacted these new policy measures on September 1 to manage the booming micro short drama sector. This regulatory crackdown followed an explosive surge in production volume and widespread viewer backlash regarding a market plagued by disorder. These rules now subject AI titles to mandatory pre release filings and strict tiered administrative reviews to improve overall output quality. The move formalizes an ecosystem that previously existed in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full scale series.

The rules require episode by episode AI labels and a three tiered system based on budgets and themes for all productions. High budget works of 800,000 yuan or more, or those covering politics, national security, military, or religion, need NRTA licenses. Mid tier productions between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan are subject to review and registration by provincial level broadcast authorities in China. Low cost productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. This differs from live action dramas, which typically require budgets of 2 million to 3 million yuan to trigger top level licensing.

He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, stated in early November that standardized governance is essential for quality. He argued that regulating AI short dramas means stabilizing volume and improving quality while holding the copyright and ethical bottom lines. Lin Qiwen, vice president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI dramas identity. Lin noted that clear labeling protects the right of viewers to know and reduces risks of being misled by false content. He added that these rules provide a foundation for the industry to move toward a more quality driven development model.

Viewers complained of repetitive tropes like domineering executive romances, time travel themes, instant revenge stories, clickbait, copyright theft, and digital clones. Model Qi Hai found the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app used her likeness without consent, gaining 40 million views. Actor Luo Yunxi had his legal team object to a near identical digital replica of his likeness in another AI production. DataEye reported the user base for AI assisted series grew from 120 million in 2025 to 600 million in 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI series were published in early 2026, but only 1,055 exceeded 100 million views per series.

Micro short dramas are ultra concise serials with episodes typically lasting one to two minutes that dominate mobile screens across China. The China Network Audiovisual Association found that platforms released over 367,000 micro short drama series in the first half of 2026. AI generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, with over 1,500 new AI series published daily. Professor Zhang Lanshan of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications said AI makes narratives more industrialized and standardized for creators. She believes humans must remain responsible for guarding the soul of narrative, including creation values, story themes, and character emotions.

The NRTA launched a two month enforcement campaign on November 6 targeting low brow themes, copyright violations, and various technical loopholes. Regulators are currently working to eliminate the practice of smaller studios shrinking disclaimers into screen corners to maintain viewer immersion. Officials are still refining operational definitions, such as the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers the mandatory labeling requirement. They are also determining how self review standards should be unified across the different competing streaming platforms operating within the market. The articles leave open how these unified standards will be finalized and how the enforcement campaign will specifically penalize violators.

stories.Headline: Shufti Launches Patented On-Device AI Age Verification, Taking User Privacy Concerns Out of the Equation
stories.Summary:
Shufti launched its Privacy-Preserving Age Verification Solution, incorporating patented on-device AI technology, on Nov. 13, 2026, in London, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The company described itself as a Glocal identity verification, Anti-Money Laundering and fraud prevention platform. The solution lets businesses confirm users' age eligibility without the facial image or any other higher-assurance proof of age leaving the user's device. The technology is protected by US Patent No. 12,749,342 B1, titled AGE VERIFICATION, issued by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The patent covers an AI-based system combining on-device facial analysis, split inference and encrypted One-Time Age Tokens.

The solution uses patented split-inference technology to divide AI processing between the user's device and a secure verification server. AI models analyse facial characteristics to estimate age and assess liveness locally, helping identify spoofing attempts involving photographs, masks, screen replays and manipulated images. The device generates an encrypted One-Time Age Token containing intermediate AI outputs rather than transmitting the original facial image. The verification server validates the token, completes the remaining AI processing and determines whether the user meets the required threshold, such as 18 or 21. Tokens are time-limited, can be marked as used after verification and may be restricted to a specific merchant to prevent unauthorised reuse or sharing across platforms.

Shufti's wider Age Verification Solution lets businesses select the level of assurance appropriate to their risk exposure, users and regulatory requirements while minimising collection and exposure of personally identifiable information. It offers docless age checks through facial age estimation or eIDV, configurable age thresholds and confidence-based escalation, risk-based verification, document verification or authoritative database checks, and biometric liveness detection supported by iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance. Shahid Hanif, CEO of Shufti, said a business should not have to collect someone's full identity simply to confirm whether they are old enough to access a service. He said the company developed the solution to help businesses prevent underage access without requiring every legitimate user to provide higher-assurance proof of age. He said the patented on-device approach keeps facial information on the user's device while securely confirming age eligibility, and called the US patent an important milestone.

The articles said a self-declared "I am over 18" click offers little assurance, while an ID upload and selfie can provide stronger evidence but many users are reluctant to share such personal information, particularly for sensitive services. Businesses collecting these records must also manage their security, retention and deletion. In the UK, Ofcom does not recognise self-declaration as a highly effective age assurance method under the UK Online Safety Act. The European Commission is advancing privacy-preserving proof-of-age tools that allow users to establish age eligibility without revealing their identity. The solution supports adult entertainment platforms checking age before content access, social media services applying minimum-age policies, gaming and gambling operators verifying eligibility at registration, and e-commerce businesses checking age before restricted purchases.

Shufti said dividing the final AI model between the device and server reduces exposure of the complete model, making it harder to reverse-engineer the verification process or manipulate locally generated results. The articles said an adult entertainment platform may need to confirm a visitor is over 18, while a regulated gambling operator may also require documentary proof of identity. Shufti's Glocal Trust OS unifies KYC, KYB, eIDV, age assurance, AML screening, agentic transaction monitoring, Know Your Agent and fraud prevention. Shufti's biometric liveness technology holds iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance under ISO/IEC 30107-3. Shufti is recognised as a Leading vendor in Liminal's 2026 Age Verification and Age Estimation Indexes, receiving the highest-tier Exceptional rating for Market Presence in both categories.

Shufti invited businesses to book a personalised demo of the patented Age Verification Solution. The articles listed Aroosa Virk, Brand and Communications Manager at Shufti, as media contact at partnership@shuftipro.com. A photo accompanying the announcement was available at a GlobeNewswire attachment link. The articles did not say when the solution would become generally available or how it would be priced. The articles did not name any business that has adopted the solution.

stories.Headline: [INTERVIEW] Ex-vice minister brings Shakespeare to life with AI music
stories.Summary:
Yong Ho-seong, former vice minister of culture, sports and tourism, released his debut full-length album “Fragile Beauty” on Nov. 10 under the stage name Dr. Dragon. The album sets 15 of William Shakespeare’s sonnets to AI-assisted music and vocals. It is the first installment of “DiVerse,” a project to set all 154 of Shakespeare’s sonnets to modern music. Yong gave an interview to The Korea Times at a cafe in Seoul on Thursday, published Nov. 13, 2026. The idea was sparked by a hardcover edition of Shakespeare’s complete sonnets that a British friend gifted him while he was director of the Korean Cultural Centre UK.

The album leans into late-1960s avant-garde folk and chamber folk, using nylon-string guitars, upright contrabass, cellos, violas, flutes, harmoniums and bass clarinets. It features the contralto tones of his AI vocal persona NikkiD. Yong adapted the sonnets’ themes for modern listeners, recasting a verse about passing down family lineage as a message about artists sharing their talents with the world. He said the name DiVerse reflects Shakespeare’s original verse, the newly written lyrics and the diverse genres used to reimagine the classics. In July, Yong won the AI.LOVE.JAZZ.

composition competition in Montreux, Switzerland, with “Frozen Edge,” a vocal jazz piece inspired by Sonnet 97. Yong said he uses AI as a creative assistant rather than a replacement for human artistry. He writes detailed prompts spanning a full page to specify rhythm, instrumentation and musical references, and sometimes regenerates a track 30 or 40 times before editing individual tracks himself. He compared AI to the introduction of digital sampling in popular music in the 1980s, saying it broadens the pool of people who can create music. He said students could turn personal stories and daily emotions into original songs, calling music a powerful tool for self-expression.

He said happiness is not about the high intensity of achievements but the frequency of joyful moments. Yong plans to issue a new sonnet-inspired album every month, spanning jazz, blues, hip-hop, rap-metal and K-pop. He has reached out to Shakespeare-related societies, associations and academic institutions around the world to explore educational and cultural collaborations. He is developing progressive rock operas based on Shakespeare’s tragedies “Hamlet” and “Macbeth,” and a project reinterpreting the poetry of Joseon Dynasty poet Yi Mae-chang (1573-1610).

Before retiring last year, he studied classical music and jazz, collected more than 10,000 records, debuted as a music critic in 1993 and played drums in jazz and rock bands. He composes up to six hours a day and practices drums for two hours, and he recently earned his first musician revenue by composing a theme song for T&C Foundation. In fall 2026, Concord Academy presented Shakespeare’s “Macbeth” in the Hammett Ory Theater, directed by Shelley Bolman P’27. The production used AI-inspired staging to explore the tension between power and technology, with intricate dance and fight choreography.

Bolman said greed for power and artificial intelligence both resonate strongly with the current time. William Jiang-Fogel ’27 played Macbeth, who is consumed by prophecies of his ascent and murders the king to seize the throne. The production retained Shakespeare’s original language and immersed audiences in a world where technology and human behavior are intertwined. Audiences sat on either side of a spare central stage, where a staircase and gate with camouflage paint were entwined with wires and cable extending across archways and pillars.

Live feeds displayed the opposite side of the audience, while screens featured “Heck 8.0,” an AI system that generated prophetic outputs. The production opened in darkness with a flash of lightning illuminating an ensemble in Guy Fawkes masks, and the Weird Sisters were reimagined as analogues for predictive AI. Lady Macbeth, played by Aslan Liu ’27, and Fleance, played by Ren Lipman ’29, were depicted as frequently attached to their phones. Bolman said the play offered an excellent opportunity to bring an over 400-year-old text from the classroom to the stage.

stories.Headline: Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures
stories.Summary:
Google open-sourced its Ambient Quality Agent, known as AQuA, a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. Google did this, and TechGig published its report on Nov 14, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST, while InfoQ published Leela Kumili's report on Nov 13, 2026. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters and tracking issues.

Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics, and AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand. For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment, and its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs or retrieved data, but AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically. Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, and the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation, and after developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13.

The Google blog post states that an insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score, and that findings link to supporting traces, with proposed root causes required to reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation, and AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code. Google's open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows, according to the articles. The Google blog post describes the citations as the insight rather than a self-reported confidence score.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote that agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early. AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces, and cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. The articles state that these results came from controlled replay, not production traffic, and that sampling can miss rare failures while replay may not reproduce external state. The tool is affected by these constraints, and teams integrating production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows are the users the open-source implementation serves. The articles do not name further individuals beyond Dmytro Aprelenko of Redcore and author Leela Kumili of InfoQ.

The articles give as background that AQuA is a reference implementation designed to analyze production AI agent sessions, verify recurring failure patterns and investigate root causes against deployed source revisions. They state that the tool targets silent quality regressions conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. They describe AQuA operating alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, drawing telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. They note that Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, with six issues confirmed after verification. They add that the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster.

The articles state that AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand, and that developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria using a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. They say AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and that Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. They note that Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. They state that AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically, and that its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows. stories.Headline: Will the Senate's BAAJA Bill Let AI Giants Outmuscle Utilities?
stories.Summary:
The United States Senate approved a preliminary version of the BAAJA bill on November 12, 2026. This legislation is formally known as the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act. A large Senate majority supported the measure during a procedural vote on November 9. The bill creates a legislative roadmap for new power generation at data centers. It also introduces various other changes for the American electric power industry.

The bill requires a rapid build-out of gas pipelines and electric power transmission. It limits the ability of tribal authorities and state attorneys general to stop these lines. The act allows the industry to ignore existing environmental regulations regarding water and air pollution. It aims to increase transmission, improve grid capacity, and increase the overall generation supply. It also seeks to facilitate the connection of consumers to cheaper sources of generation.

Analysts Leonard Hyman and William Tilles are responsible for the report on this bill. They argue that the legislation allows AI giants to build power facilities regardless of legal constraints. These authors describe the large AI companies as apex predators or T-Rexes due to their influence. They claim the bill provides a roadmap for these giants to outmuscle the utility industry. The authors believe this allows a grab for gas to power new data centers.

Critics warn that the permitting bill is a massive giveaway to the AI data center industry. These critics believe the rules are being rewritten to favor big tech companies. Electric utilities are affected because they may be stomped on by the rapid data center build-out. Power consumers in Texas might gain access to cheaper electricity through these new generation sources. However, this shift will likely occur at the expense of future utility company profitability.

The authors previously reported that AI facilities often use inefficient and polluting gas combustion turbines. Anthropic recently announced a multi-billion-dollar purchase of these turbines for a new facility in Texas. In September, ERCOT listed 158 gigawatts of solar and 166 gigawatts of batteries for interconnection. Additionally, 49 gigawatts of wind power requested grid interconnection according to the ERCOT update. Currently, there are only 38 gigawatts of installed utility-scale solar power in the region.

A final vote on the BAAJA bill could occur during the week of November 16. The early draft will likely be revised several times before it reaches a final version. It may still die in a newly reconstituted House of Representatives after the November election. The overall grid impact remains uncertain because gas turbines produce power at uncompetitive prices. The articles leave open whether these massive interconnection requests will actually be funded and built.

stories.Headline: Court allows news publishers' copyright lawsuit against OpenAI to go ahead
stories.Summary:
The Ontario Court of Appeal allowed a copyright lawsuit against OpenAI to proceed on Friday, November 13, 2026, after dismissing a company appeal. A coalition of Canadian news publishers filed this legal action two years ago to address the use of their content for AI. The publishers claim that OpenAI used their news articles to train ChatGPT, which they argue is a breach of copyright laws. These news organizations allege that the company is profiting from their intellectual property without providing any permission or financial compensation. This specific legal battle is the first Canadian case to address the practice of using copyrighted content to train generative AI.

The case involves a coalition including The Canadian Press, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, Postmedia, and the public broadcaster CBC/Radio-Canada. OpenAI argued that the case should be heard in a United States courtroom instead of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. The court rejected this jurisdictional challenge, ruling that the legal proceedings will remain in the province of Ontario for now. The decision noted that OpenAI failed to provide evidence that a Canadian judgment would conflict with any existing laws in America. The court also stated that the efficient working of the Canadian legal system favors authors bringing claims against foreign companies.

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice is responsible for hearing the case after the higher court dismissed the appeal from OpenAI. The court stated that allowing Canadian authors to sue foreign companies for breaches of Canadian laws supports the fair legal system. Judges found that there was no evidence that enforcement of a Canadian ruling would be complicated by laws in the United States. The court determined that it does have the proper jurisdiction to hear the claims brought by the news publishers. These legal rulings ensure that the merits of the copyright claims can be argued within the Canadian judicial system.

The news publishers are affected by the alleged scraping of their articles from the internet to train the generative AI system. Other publishers, including Condé Nast and McClatchy, are involved in a separate United States case against the Canadian AI company Cohere. News and cultural industry groups have called on the federal government to take a stand on how AI uses copyrighted content. These groups want the government to clarify the rules regarding the use of intellectual property by artificial intelligence companies. The publishers argue that the current practice of using their content without payment is an unfair use of their work.

The lawsuit against OpenAI has dragged on since 2024, following the rise of generative AI systems like the one powering ChatGPT. Earlier this year, Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, and The Canadian Press launched another separate lawsuit against the company Anthropic. Multiple lawsuits dealing with AI systems and copyright have been underway in the United States since as early as 2023. These cases highlight a growing global conflict between traditional media publishers and the developers of new artificial intelligence technologies. The legal landscape is evolving as courts decide if training AI on existing data constitutes a copyright violation.

The lawsuit will now move forward in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to determine if OpenAI breached Canadian copyright laws. The articles leave open whether the federal government will ever update the Copyright Act to address these specific AI concerns. It remains unclear if Ottawa will eventually take a formal stand on how AI systems should use copyrighted news content. The outcome of the case against OpenAI may influence other pending legal battles involving AI companies and media publishers. Future rulings will likely define the boundaries of fair use for training generative AI systems within the Canadian legal framework.

stories.Headline: ISMG Security Report: Can Banks Trust AI?
stories.Summary:
Mathew J. Schwartz released the ISMG Security Report on November 13, 2026, to examine AI risks in financial services. This report explores how banks can safely adopt artificial intelligence while maintaining necessary accountability and control over their systems. The journalist focuses on the transition from shadow AI to autonomous agents within the banking and finance industry. He investigates the balance between embracing new technology and protecting critical operations from unpredictable and costly AI actions. The report specifically addresses the governance challenges that financial institutions must overcome to trust these next generation technologies.

Safe adoption requires extending identity and access management to autonomous agents to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive financial data. Banks must implement strict controls on what AI can do and limit the specific systems it can access. The report highlights the danger of shadow AI and the need for human oversight for high impact financial decisions. These measures are necessary when AI touches customer databases, payment systems, and other critical financial infrastructure in the bank. Every human must remain accountable for the actions taken by AI to avoid the risks of hallucinations and errors.

Executive Editor Mathew Schwartz led the examination of these risks based on his two decades of experience in security journalism. He stated that banks cannot afford to blindly trust AI because unpredictable actions can lead to very costly consequences. Schwartz suggested that the solution is not to avoid AI but to enforce controls and maintain strict human oversight. He emphasized that maintaining accountability is the only way for banks to embrace AI without putting their operations at risk. The editor believes that limiting AI access is a key component of a secure and governed financial environment.

Security experts discussed the specific dangers posed by shadow AI and the necessity of extending identity management to autonomous agents. These experts noted that human oversight remains essential for decisions that have a high impact on the financial system. Customers and bank operations are the primary entities affected by the potential for AI hallucinations and unpredictable system actions. The experts argued that the current governance gap must be closed to ensure the safety of critical financial systems. They believe that the risk of failure is too high to allow AI to operate without strict human control.

Artificial intelligence promises to transform banking by accelerating credit decisions and automating various labor intensive processes to improve overall productivity. However, the integration of AI into payments and customer databases introduces new vulnerabilities that could lead to significant financial losses. The report is part of a broader discussion on securing AI adoption across the enterprise for various chief information officers. It follows a trend of examining how agentic AI is reshaping the modern security operations center and data policies. This background highlights the tension between the productivity gains of AI and the inherent risks of autonomous agents.

Banks must now determine how to implement these controls while continuing to scale their use of artificial intelligence and agents. The report suggests that the industry must move toward continuous control to bridge the existing governance gap in banking. It remains open whether banks can successfully balance the speed of AI credit decisions with the need for oversight. The articles do not specify the exact technical tools banks should use to enforce these identity and access management rules. There is no mention of specific regulatory deadlines that banks must meet to satisfy these new AI governance requirements.

stories.Headline: AI-Assisted Imaging Method Advances 150-Year-Old Technique for Studying Tissue
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Harvard Medical School have developed NoR-AI, a tissue-imaging pipeline that pairs a custom microscopy method with AI-powered image analysis. The team reported the work in a study published Nov. 5 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and the Harvard Medical School announcement appeared on Nov. 13, 2026. The system is meant to capture fine tissue details that current histopathology methods miss, including lipids, which conventional tissue preparation usually removes. The pipeline builds on normalized Raman imaging, or NoRI, which uses stimulated Raman scattering to measure how light changes as it passes through different tissues. NoRI then corrects computationally for light-scattering effects, producing clear, quantitative images that include lipids alongside proteins and water content.

A convolutional neural network then analyzes these images, and the researchers say it needed only two or three NoRI images of mouse kidneys to identify three distinct tubule types, classify anatomical regions, and determine the sex of the mouse. The technique requires little to no pre-processing and can be completed in 30 minutes, compared with several days for traditional biopsy analysis. The senior author, Marc Kirschner, the John Franklin Enders University Professor of Systems Biology at HMS, said the method lets scientists see into cells and tissue in ways that were not previously possible. Co-first author William Trim, a research fellow in the Kirschner Lab, said the neural network can pick out fine-scale distinctions because NoRI images contain little noise. Working with Joseph Bonventre of Brigham and Women's Hospital, the team used NoR-AI on a mouse model of acute kidney injury and tracked changes over 25 days after injury.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, and Kirschner and Seungeun Oh hold a patent for NoRI. The researchers are already applying NoR-AI to preclinical models of colon, liver, and prostate cancers and plan to extend it to diabetic kidney disease and other areas. The tool can also distinguish between cholesterol, saturated fats, and unsaturated fats, which may help clarify their roles in inflammation and immune response. Kirschner described lipids as the terra incognita of histology, and said the team's early results suggest lipid amounts and distribution change significantly in the cases studied. The article notes that the work could eventually support faster, more detailed clinical evaluation of tissues, though it remains a research tool at this stage.

stories.Headline: Generative AI uses more energy on non-English text
stories.Summary:
Researchers from University of Michigan Engineering discovered that generative AI consumes significantly more energy when processing non-English text. This study was presented at the Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing conference of the Association for Computational Linguistics. The team analyzed three open-source models, including Meta's Llama 3.1, Google's Gemma 3, and Alibaba's Qwen 3. They found that these models often produce lower-quality output while using more power.

The energy cost for non-English text ranges from 1.4 to 180 times that of English. Bengali requires 15.3 times more energy, while Hindi needs 7.9 times more. Most Western European languages use twice as much energy or less. These disparities affect roughly 5.2 billion people who must pay more or switch languages. This occurs because non-Latin scripts require more tokens, which consumes more memory and power.

Naihao Deng, a doctoral student and first author, stated that the most energy-intensive languages often have lower accuracy. He warned that this double penalty could price some people out of using AI. Rada Mihalcea, the U-M AI Lab director, urged developers to create more resources for these languages. She suggested using crowdsourced native speakers to improve training data and efficiency.

The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation and DARPA, with support from OpenAI and Ford. To fix these issues, the team recommends that companies use translation pipelines or models tailored to specific languages. They also suggest routing queries to specialized models to reduce costs. These changes would help prevent global inequalities in AI access.

stories.Headline: Knots, quantum computing and AI: $6m grant supports exploration of the surprising connections
stories.Summary:
The Simons Foundation renewed a $6 million grant for an international research collaboration led by Aaron Lauda, a mathematician and divisional dean at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. The collaboration, called the Simons Collaboration on New Structures in Low-Dimensional Topology, was established in 2023 and brings together 11 institutions worldwide. The new award raises the foundation's total investment in the project to $14 million, and USC will receive more than $2 million of the new funding. The renewal supports the work for another three years.

The research explores connections between knot mathematics, quantum computing and artificial intelligence. One focus is anyons, particle-like phenomena first observed in 2020, whose movements form braids that could help quantum computers keep information nearly error-free. In a 2025 Nature Communications paper, Lauda and collaborators Filippo Iulianelli, Sung Kim and Joshua Sussan added a new type of anyon, called a "neglecton," to an expanded model and showed the full range of quantum computations could be done through braiding alone. The breakthrough remains theoretical, and researchers still need to find a physical system to put it into practice.

Lauda said the team began with fundamental questions about knots and the possible shapes of three- and four-dimensional spaces, including those used to describe spacetime. He said following those questions led to new ways of thinking about quantum computation and machine learning. Cris Negron, an associate professor of mathematics at USC Dornsife, said the team wants to turn insights from physics into precise mathematical tools that offer new methods for analyzing and distinguishing knots and spaces. Negron also said working with people who approach problems differently helps young researchers refine their questions and can have a lasting positive impact on their careers.

The collaboration also studied how AI learns through trial and error when rewards are rare, using the Andrews, Curtis conjecture, a puzzle that has stymied researchers for more than 60 years. Caltech collaborator Sergei Gukov and colleagues showed that several suspected exceptions to the conjecture were not exceptions after all, and the work points toward ways to improve AI's search methods. Researchers Qiuyu Ren of Stanford University and Michael Willis of Texas A&M University used knot mathematics to distinguish some four-dimensional spaces beyond spacetime. In June, Negron co-organized a workshop at the American Institute of Mathematics in Pasadena, California, for graduate students and recent PhD recipients. With the renewed funding, Lauda said the team can develop ideas from the first phase together, giving the mathematics time to mature while pursuing connections to quantum computing and AI.

stories.Headline: FSU Participants to Share Work on AI, Library Services and Information Well-being at ASIS&T 2026
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the Florida State University School of Information presented their work at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Association for Information Science and Technology (ASIS&T), held in Bangkok, Thailand, from November 6 through November 10. The conference brings together information science researchers and practitioners from around the world to exchange ideas about questions shaping the field. This year's theme, "Crossing Boundaries: Advancing Global Dialogue and Well-being through Information Research and Practice," reflects how interconnected information has become in society. The FSU work featured at the event covers human interaction with artificial intelligence, information well-being and the changing role of libraries in their communities.

A team of six FSU researchers, Shuyuan Mary Ho, Sumra Anis, Akerke Kuanysh, Subhasree Sengupta, Ghazal Hussain and Rasleen Kaur, presented a paper on generative AI as a cognitive partner in collaborative information practice. The paper examines how generative AI, collaborative information practices and information well-being relate to one another. Its authors treat these AI tools as participants in how people process, interpret and use information, not simply as sources of answers. Margaret A. Sullivan, working with Sein Oh of Louisiana State University, also presented research comparing frontline and leadership perspectives in libraries responding to the opioid crisis. That project focuses on how the experiences of library staff and the priorities of organizational leaders shape library responses to complex community problems.

Sullivan and Isis Malcolm are listed as coauthors of a poster on library social workers responding to sexual and reproductive health needs in their communities. The poster points to the role libraries can play beyond traditional information services as community institutions address sensitive and evolving social needs. FSU also took part in an alternative event titled "Talking About How We Use AI: Ethical Reflection, Research Practice, and Boundary-Setting Across Information Science," which gathered researchers to discuss ethical questions and professional considerations around AI use in research. The articles present these contributions as part of a common theme: information research covers the people, communities and institutions that interact with technology, not only the systems themselves. The School of Information describes the conference as an important platform for sharing its work, building international connections and contributing to the future of the field.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit casts shadow over Wall Street’s $500 billion AI financing bet
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, chief executive and board member, the company's board said on Thursday. Nvidia has never named a successor to Huang, who had led the chipmaker since it was founded in 1993. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, has been named interim chief executive. Shares in the company initially fell more than 13% after the resignation, before paring those losses. The resignation followed revelations that Huang had two extramarital affairs, one with an employee and another with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy.

In August, Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding with six major financial firms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. The firms are Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The arrangements seek to tap institutional investors and private capital to finance computing infrastructure, including data centers and chip factories. The funding would run through specialized financing vehicles, with Nvidia's AI chips serving as underlying collateral, in structures comparable to real estate or toll road securitizations. The financing arrangements remain preliminary and are subject to final agreements.

Huang's departure raises the question of whether his successor can carry forward a strategy meant to turn GPUs from rapidly depreciating hardware into bankable infrastructure assets. Nvidia's $4.2 trillion market value and industry dominance, with Huang at the front, allowed it to secure those memorandums. The company has been described as the "central bank" of the AI build-out, with Huang seen as the sector's "hypeman" and its chips considered the industry's gold standard. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress following his resignation, according to CNBC's live coverage. Nvidia's board chair is Harvey Jones, who wrote to employees along with Kress.

Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said a leadership change gives every firm involved a natural moment to pause and review the terms. She said a new chief executive would be wise to leave these partnerships alone in the first months and focus on signing the final agreements. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said a successor would need to reassure lenders that Nvidia's technology roadmap, customer relationships and strategic vision remain intact. Chanana warned that a leadership shake-up could make Wall Street more cautious, potentially slowing commitments or tightening financing terms. BlackRock and Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the resignation, and the other firms were not immediately available.

Chanana said the bigger risk is a ripple effect across AI financing, given that rising debt, circular financing and uncertain investment returns were already under scrutiny. Haldea said she expects more discipline among investors after the scandal, with lenders asking harder questions about who really carries the risk in these structures. A separate CNBC analysis said Huang's exit raises critical questions about the future of AI. Those affected include lenders and the financial firms party to the memorandums, along with the AI infrastructure deal market more broadly. Analysts said the financing could come under heightened scrutiny in the aftermath of Huang's departure.

Early in November, a Motley Fool podcast recorded on October 30, 2026 discussed a market shift in which investors were questioning how big technology companies would finance AI spending. Alphabet's stock fell about 13% after earnings, even though its Cloud business reported 100% growth. Microsoft's Cloud growth was 48%, and its free cash flow was roughly double analyst estimates. Alphabet took on another $29 billion in debt and issued about $12 billion in new stock in the quarter, with another $28 billion already approved for issuance. Oracle said at its investor day that it would turn free cash flow positive sooner than expected, which investors welcomed.

Analysts disagree on how long the financing strain will last, and the articles give no clear answer. The articles do not say whether Nvidia will name a permanent chief executive, or when the preliminary financing agreements will be finalized. It remains unclear whether the six financial firms will proceed, slow commitments or seek higher pay for the added uncertainty. Huang's testimony before Congress is also not yet scheduled in the articles. Whether the scrutiny spreads into a broader repricing of AI risk, as Chanana suggested, is not settled.

stories.Headline: ASEAN AI Regulation: 49th Summit Puts AI Center Stage
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is set to take center stage at the 49th ASEAN Summit, which leaders will hold in the Philippines this November. ABS-CBN News reported on November 11, 2026, that AI is expected near the top of the summit agenda. The same report said leaders are expected to sign the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, known as DEFA, at the meeting. ABS-CBN News also carried an August report in which a commission warned that unauthorized AI deepfakes of real people may violate data privacy. A trending post also claimed a tech expert urged greater ASEAN action on AI regulation, but the verified ABS-CBN report does not name any such expert.

The verified reporting describes a trade-style framework agreement and a growth-oriented statement, not a binding AI law. Leaders are expected to consider a statement on AI-powered growth for micro, small, and medium enterprises, known as MSMEs. The talks also cover AI in healthcare, including health services and medical diagnosis, and AI's potential role in addressing climate change. The report does not describe a licensing regime for frontier models or a numeric safety threshold. DEFA is the agreement most likely to define the summit's legacy, and the verified reporting says AI cooperation was a negotiation priority.

Dominic Xavier Imperial, Executive Director of the DFA ASEAN Office, described AI as very prominently involved in the ASEAN discussions during the Philippine chairship this year. Imperial also said ASEAN is now more responsive to whatever crisis or emerging threat arises. The Philippines holds the chairship this year and shapes what gets drafted for the summit. ASEAN works by consultation and consensus, so the chair sets the agenda but cannot impose outcomes on member states. Member states will weigh the draft texts before leaders sign anything.

The ASEAN Secretary-General, Kao Kim Hourn, said in 2024 that the bloc had identified cooperation on emerging technologies, including AI, as a key priority in the DEFA negotiations. He also said the bloc was committed to concluding DEFA by 2025 and that it could unlock up to USD2 trillion in digital economic value by 2030. That 2025 target has slipped, since signing is now expected in November 2026. Kao described ASEAN's guidance instruments as proof of the bloc's leadership in setting norms, and those instruments affect organizations across the region's digital economy and its MSMEs.

ASEAN adopted its Guide on AI Governance and Ethics in 2024 as a voluntary baseline for responsible AI governance across the bloc. In 2025 ASEAN approved an expanded guide focused on generative AI risks, along with a Responsible AI Roadmap for member states. At the 47th ASEAN Summit in October 2025, leaders adopted the declaration establishing the ASEAN AI Safety Network, called AI SAFE. The network is described as reflecting a commitment to a human-centered approach to AI development and safety. ASEAN Secretariat materials say officials were developing a Leaders' Declaration on AI-powered growth for MSMEs together with an action plan.

The verified reporting does not say whether the summit will adopt a binding AI law, and no outlet reviewed names one. The articles also leave open whether the final DEFA text contains model-level obligations, since no clause list has been published. It is unclear how far member states will translate the shared principles into domestic rules. The articles do not say whether the MSME statement and action plan will be adopted at the summit. They also do not confirm the identity or remarks of the tech expert named in the trending post.

stories.Headline: A Practical Blueprint for an AI-Ready Enterprise
stories.Summary:
Braiin Limited announced on November 11, 2026 that its Agentic Real Estate Intelligence and Automation platform, ARIA, won the 2026 Best Enterprise-Ready AI Platform Award from the Polirian Awards, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 11, 2026. Braiin Limited trades on NASDAQ under the ticker BRAI and describes itself as a global AI platform company delivering automation and predictive analytics across precision agriculture, customer experience and property technology. ARIA is described as an AI-native workforce designed for the global real estate industry. The Polirian Awards recognize comprehensive AI platforms built for organizational use, evaluating enterprise readiness, measurable business value, AI relevance, usability and market differentiation. Polirian selected Braiin for ARIA's agentic AI based approach to planning and coordinating multi-step operational workflows across connected systems while maintaining human review for consequential legal, financial and operational decisions.

ARIA is designed to understand an operational objective, plan the steps needed to complete it, and coordinate execution across property and customer systems, while escalating material decisions and exceptions for human review. The platform combines agent orchestration, natural-language interaction, document generation and data analysis with human-in-the-loop controls, and is designed to maintain auditable records of actions, approvals and exceptions. Its intended workflows include preparing tenancy documents, identifying potential lease compliance issues, producing comparative market reports, supporting rent reconciliation, managing routine tenant and landlord communications, analyzing rent rolls to flag risks and opportunities, coordinating e-signature workflows, and building customized workflows from plain-language instructions. The platform's design also connects property workflows with residential services such as utility activation, broadband and insurance. It draws on Braiin's broader capabilities across artificial intelligence, customer experience automation and property technology.

Natraj Balasubramanian, Braiin Founder and CEO, said real estate teams spend considerable time moving information between systems, following up on documents and coordinating the services people need when they move into a property. He said the company designed ARIA to help bring that work together, with agentic AI planning and coordinating the steps and professionals retaining control over important decisions. He said the recognition reflects the direction the company is building toward. The award announcement was issued as a GlobeNewswire release from New York, NY, on Nov. 11, 2026. The Manila Times published the item on November 11, 2026.

ARIA is positioned as moving beyond conventional generative AI assistants that primarily answer questions or produce content. The approach supports Braiin's broader strategy of connecting property technology with the services residents need throughout the tenancy and when moving between homes. The Polirian Awards evaluated platforms on enterprise readiness, measurable business value, AI relevance, usability and market differentiation. The award recognizes comprehensive AI platforms built for organizational use. Braiin's platform is intended for the global real estate industry.

Adobe's 2026 State of AI Readiness Report found that around 59% of organisations in the region are stuck in the "Frozen Middle", where they are piloting or deploying AI but lack the coordination needed to scale it, and for agentic AI the figure stands at 40%. Neo-cloud provider Neysa observed that enterprise leaders are increasingly comfortable adopting AI but remain significantly less comfortable relinquishing control, with the dominant preference being enterprise-controlled AI rather than vendor-controlled AI. Neysa proposed a shared AI Platform that helps enterprises move from experiments to everyday use, giving teams a common foundation for running applications, monitoring performance and tracking costs while still choosing different models and tools for different tasks. Neysa describes a walled garden for AI, a controlled environment in which an enterprise manages the infrastructure supporting its AI applications, including the models, tools and frameworks it uses. Neysa's proposed architecture divides this environment into three broad areas: an experimentation environment for innovation teams, a tightly controlled environment for workloads with strict requirements around data privacy, security and compliance, and a general deployment environment for AI applications that do not require the same level of regulatory oversight or data protection.

Adopt AI uses TrueFoundry's AI Gateway to connect applications to models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock and Groq. Adopt AI's co-founder and CTO Rahul Bhattacharya explains that applications no longer communicate directly with individual model providers, and requests pass through a central gateway, which allows the company to switch models and manage traffic without changing application code. Neysa's approach allows enterprises to retain existing investments, for example continuing to use Azure AI Foundry to select and develop an AI solution while directing the computing workloads required to run that solution to infrastructure provided by Neysa. Before an AI application moves into everyday use, it needs a named business owner, approved data access, measurable quality targets, a support plan and an operating budget. The articles state that governance determines how AI systems can be used across the organisation, and that enterprises need to establish which teams can access particular models and data, what restrictions apply to sensitive workloads and how security and compliance policies are enforced.

The articles state that the cost of running AI depends on factors such as the models selected, computing capacity, workload volumes and the infrastructure required to support applications in production. They state that organisations must also account for the cost of operating and, at that point, the first article's text ends. The second article's text ends mid-sentence with the word "Braii". stories.Headline: Cisco forecasts $9 billion in AI infrastructure revenue in FY27
stories.Summary:
Cisco reported record quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended October 24, up 24% year over year, and record non-GAAP earnings per share of $1.40, up 40% year over year. CEO Chuck Robbins said on the vendor's quarterly financial call that these were Cisco's strongest top and bottom-line growth rates in over 15 years. Networking product orders grew 28% in Q1, Cisco's ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, with double-digit growth across every product family. Robbins said the results support Cisco's view that it is in the early stages of a multiyear, multibillion-dollar networking supercycle. Cisco said its AI infrastructure revenue is projected to grow to $9 billion in fiscal year 2027, more than double fiscal year 2026 levels.

Enterprise product orders were up 15% year-over-year, on top of 4% growth a year ago, with double-digit growth across all geographies and in networking and security. Campus networking product orders grew 14% year-over-year, and Robbins said the transition is less than 10% along. Product orders from service provider and cloud customers grew 47% year-over-year. Cisco had 18 AI design wins in the last 5 quarters, and Robbins said hyperscalers are deploying its scale-across networking architecture as they extend coordinated AI workloads across data centers. Core security products aside from Splunk grew 15%, the best in three years, firewall orders grew more than 30% for the third consecutive quarter, and the zero-trust secure access portfolio has 5,400 customers after almost 800 were added in Q1.

Robbins attributed the growth to five technology drivers: hyperscale success, campus refresh, the post-Mythos opportunity, sovereignty, and the hybrid data center. He said Cisco announced Sovereign Critical Infrastructure for Europe a year ago, expanded and launched it for Canada, and recently preannounced it in India. He said work with sovereign cloud providers such as Humai and G42 continues to grow. He said enterprise data center networking orders have seen double-digit growth in 9 of the last 11 quarters as customers run open weight and open-source models and train on their own data in their own data centers. He said Cisco is protecting 2 trillion tokens per month at the AI Defense layer and approaching 500 customers for AI Defense.

Robbins said customers in Europe are attributing orders to early Mythos implications, including service providers upgrading managed services CPE for their customers. He said customers want to move fast but are taking time to plan and design the right architecture. He said Cisco earlier this week announced it is integrating Anthropic's Claude Mythos cybersecurity model into Cisco AI Defense for adaptive AI red teaming, providing automated, continuous testing across enterprise systems. He said Cisco is using Splunk as a platform for AI security and that customers are buying into security and networking coming together on monitoring workloads and east-west traffic segmentation with technologies such as Hypershield and Live Protect. The articles name no other affected parties beyond Cisco, its hyperscaler, service provider, cloud and enterprise customers, and Anthropic.

The article, by Network World senior editor Michael Cooney and dated November 13, 2026, describes Cisco as continuing to benefit from a networking supercycle driven by demand for AI infrastructure, security, and campus refreshes from hyperscalers and enterprise customers. It cites the five drivers Robbins listed as fueling what he called a multiyear, multi-billion-dollar market opportunity. It notes that Cisco's zero-trust secure access portfolio, which includes Duo, Secure Access and Identity Services Engine, did not exist three years ago. It also lists related Network World coverage, including Cisco boosting its AI Defense platform with Anthropic's Claude Mythos on November 11, 2026, and Arista posting record growth as the AI networking supercycle accelerates on November 4, 2026.

The articles do not say when Cisco will report fiscal year 2027 results or how the $9 billion projection compares with any figure other than fiscal year 2026 levels. They do not give the size of Cisco's fiscal year 2026 AI infrastructure revenue, the terms of the Anthropic integration, or the names of the 18 AI design wins. They do not identify the customers behind the 5,400 secure access customers or the roughly 500 AI Defense customers. They do not say which countries beyond Europe, Canada and India will receive Sovereign Critical Infrastructure. They do not give a date for the full rollout of the sovereign offering or further detail on the Mythos orders heard in Europe.
