stories.Headline: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?
stories.Summary:
A federal district judge in Texas, Mark Pittman, criticized attorneys he believed used AI to draft briefs and labeled them lazy, calling their arguments tortured, all before holding a hearing, according to an article published by Above the Law on November 13, 2026. The article also reports that a judge in the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky denied a motion to dismiss by a police officer who allegedly relied on AI facial recognition, and only AI, to make an arrest. The article says the Kentucky case involved a Black man who entered a bank in Florence, Kentucky, and attempted to cash what appeared to be a fraudulent check. The article states the bank refused to cash the check and the man left, and a security camera captured an unobstructed view of his face. The article reports that a local police department detective named Kilmer allegedly took a screenshot of the man's face from the footage and used AI facial recognition technology to match it with a booking photo on file.

The article says Kilmer took the booking photo and a Facebook profile image he found and compared them to the screenshot, concluded they all matched, and identified a man named Osorio as the culprit. The article reports that Kilmer signed a criminal complaint stating he had used "investigatory tools" to determine Osorio's identity and did not mention he used AI. The article states an arrest warrant was issued and served on Osorio, a Nebraska resident, in Florida, and Osorio was extradited to Kentucky, charged, and indicted even though he claimed the suspect in the footage looked nothing like him. The article reports Kentucky prosecutors eventually dismissed the indictment against Osorio with prejudice because Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the fraudulent check was presented to the bank. The article says police department policy in that Kentucky jurisdiction stated that AI facial recognition technology was only advisory and did not "establish probable cause without further investigation."

The article reports that Osorio filed suit in federal district court against the cop, asserting claims for false arrest and imprisonment under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments of the Constitution and Kentucky law, malicious prosecution, and assault and battery. The article states the cop filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that qualified immunity shielded him from liability, among other things, and that the court was required to take all Osorio's allegations as true for purposes of deciding the motion. The article says Judge S. Chad Meredith was presented with the issue of whether AI facial recognition technology alone could support a finding of probable cause and justify issuing a warrant. The article reports Meredith noted that qualified immunity could shield an officer from liability but not if he violated a federal statutory or constitutional right and the unlawfulness of his conduct was clearly established at the time of the violation. The article states Meredith found that under the Fourth Amendment neither probable cause nor a warrant can stand when based on materially false or misleading statements made knowingly or in reckless disregard for the truth.

The article reports Meredith found that the facts that the cop delegated the entire task of determining probable cause to AI facial recognition technology without using any independent judgment and made misstatements or omissions in his affidavit were sufficient, at this stage, to support the denial of the motion to dismiss. The article says Meredith posed a hypothetical in which Detective Doe uses a Magic 8 Ball to determine whether each pedestrian passerby is a potential suspect in a bank theft. The article reports that in the hypothetical Detective Doe shakes the Magic 8 Ball about Plaintiff Peter, gets the answer "You may rely on it," applies for a warrant stating he used "investigative tools," and the charges are dropped when Peter's alibi checks out. The article states the court noted that just because Plaintiff Peter couldn't cite a case that using the Magic 8 Ball is a constitutional violation doesn't mean relying on it was OK, and Meredith wrote that "a Magic 8 Ball alone will not cut it." The article reports Meredith concluded that while AI facial recognition technology has developed rapidly and is likely more reliable than the Magic 8 Ball, placing unquestioning reliance on it is still not much different, and wrote that no reasonable officer would think Kilmer's allegedly exclusive reliance on AI is lawful, especially given how Osorio's booking photograph looks nothing like the suspect from the security camera footage.

The article says the author recently wrote about Pittman, who excoriated some attorneys because he thought they used AI to draft briefs and because he didn't like the arguments they made. The article states the author's view was that this was the wrong way to look at AI and those who use it. The article reports the author's view that Meredith's opinion represents the right and studied way for courts to view AI and its use. The article says the cases are factually different, one involving lawyers using AI and the other a cop, but both turn on the same question of how a court should think about AI and its use by those appearing before it. The article states the author's view that Meredith kept AI in its rightful place and confirmed the need to keep the proverbial human in the loop, and that the difference between how the Texas judge and the Kentucky judge looked at AI could not be more stark.

The article reports that Meredith's denial of the motion to dismiss allows a civil action to proceed where a person had been deprived of his liberty, even if only briefly, based on the law, not pique. The article states the author's view that this is a right and appropriate view of AI, not a knee-jerk reaction, and that he hopes more judges treat AI-related issues like Meredith and fewer like Pittman. The article does not state what further proceedings will follow in Osorio's suit or what rulings, if any, followed Pittman's criticism of the attorneys. The article does not state the outcome of the criminal case against Osorio beyond the dismissal of the indictment with prejudice. The article does not state whether Kilmer faced any discipline or whether Osorio's suit has been scheduled for trial.

Articles.Title: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?

stories.Headline: Oracle's $125 billion debt raises a major AI warning
stories.Summary:
Oracle Corp. is under growing financial pressure as its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure keeps running ahead of the cash it generates, according to a November 13, 2026 report on Yahoo Finance that first appeared on GuruFocus. In the last quarter, the company spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures, more than its quarterly revenue of $19.3 billion. Free cash flow came in at negative $5.4 billion, and total borrowings stood near $125 billion at the end of August. Oracle's shares have fallen roughly 34% this year as investors weigh its growth prospects against borrowing costs and execution risks.

Demand for Oracle's cloud infrastructure remains strong despite those concerns. Revenue from that business rose 121% to $7.4 billion, supported by rising demand for AI computing capacity. Oracle's remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, and management expects about half of that to convert into revenue within 36 months. The company forecasts capital spending of $90 billion to $95 billion for the fiscal year.

Management expects free cash flow to turn positive during the second half of fiscal 2028 and to exceed $30 billion in fiscal 2029. The article does not attribute these projections to a specific individual beyond the company's management team. Wall Street maintains a Strong Buy consensus on the stock, with an average price target of $241.83. The report notes that investors will be watching whether Oracle can bring new data center capacity online while meeting its cash flow targets.

Articles.Title: Oracle's $125 billion debt raises a major AI warning

stories.Headline: For insurers, the AI bill gets bigger after the pilot
stories.Summary:
Insurers are raising their AI budgets and becoming more selective about which projects they take beyond the pilot stage, according to an article published November 13, 2026, by Insurance Business. The piece reports that once a tool enters daily use, the cost of protecting customer data and monitoring its output can determine whether it is worth rolling out across the company. Chris Raimondo, EY's global and US insurance consulting leader, is the main source for this reporting. Coverage draws on several surveys to show that spending is rising across the sector.

KPMG's US insurance practice reported this year that 90% of the insurance executives it surveyed said their companies had increased AI budgets from the prior year. A separate Celent survey of 44 North American property and casualty insurers found that the average respondent expected overall IT funding to rise nearly 10% in 2026, with AI and supporting data among the priorities. Deloitte's 2027 insurance outlook, published November 12, found that only seven of 35 insurance technology leaders rated the returns on their AI investments as high or very high. Deloitte also said operating costs could become more variable as insurers use different models and as usage grows.

Raimondo said the conversations he has with carriers have shifted past early trials, with clients now asking how to run AI securely at scale and what return they will get. He said insurers see the opportunity but recognize that the path is more complex and likely requires more investment, so they will be more selective about which opportunities get funding. He also said that moving a tool into regular use forces an insurer to decide who can access the data and how to reconstruct what happened if an output is questioned. In his view, the industry needs proper investment in governance, safety and security while also needing to operate at a more profitable baseline.

The article adds that adoption has moved faster for employee productivity tools and AI features built into software staff already use, such as claims systems, while custom agents remain more often the subject of experiments. Raimondo expects agents to act more independently in internal IT, but he expects people to keep working alongside them in underwriting, pricing and claims servicing, where errors can affect what a customer pays. A 2026 WTW survey of 59 P&C insurers in the US and Canada found that 16% were using AI to support human underwriters, and 60% planned to prioritize that use by 2028. Raimondo also said that the closer the technology gets to the core insurance value chain, the higher the bar for automating it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: For insurers, the AI bill gets bigger after the pilot

stories.Headline: Samsung Eyes U.S. Cooling Maker Modine to Court Big Tech AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics is pursuing the acquisition of Modine, a cooling equipment maker based in the United States. This strategic move occurred around November 2026 to target artificial intelligence data centers. Samsung wants to pair European technology with North American production and customer networks. The company aims to expand its climate control business into high value cooling solutions. This strategy targets Big Tech clients in the world's largest data center market.

The deal involves Modine, which operates a 63,400 square meter plant in Grand Prairie, Texas. Samsung previously spent 1.5 billion euros to acquire Germany's Flakt Group last year. A 240 billion won Gwangju plant production line should start operating in early 2028. Modine plans to increase chiller production lines from 13 to 20 by March 2027. The estimated purchase price for a 100 percent stake is 7.5 to 8 billion dollars.

An industry official stated that stable supply and maintenance are critical for AI data centers. This person noted that Modine's local facilities would help win large North American projects. The official added that the deal provides a base in North America and Europe. Samsung may sign a merger agreement or launch a tender offer for shares. The company previously used shareholder approval to acquire Harman in 2017 for 112 dollars per share.

Big Tech firms like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are affected by the need for server heat handling. These companies adopt high performance AI chips in large volumes, increasing demand for cooling. Modine's third quarter data center revenue rose 95 percent to 439.7 million dollars. One customer signed a contract for over 4 billion dollars of equipment from 2027 to 2029. This customer provided an advance payment of 165 million dollars in May.

The Americas hold 50 percent of global data center capacity, with 90 percent in the United States. Samsung secured coolant distribution units and fan wall units through the Flakt Group acquisition. Modine uses the Airedale brand for chillers and precision air conditioning units. It also employs free cooling technology that uses cold outside air to reduce power. Modine forecast revenue of up to 3.2 billion dollars for fiscal 2027.

Samsung must secure approval from 66.7 percent of voting rights, or 35.41 million votes. Major shareholders include BlackRock at 5.4 percent, Vanguard Capital at 4.5 percent, and Vanguard Portfolio at 4.1 percent. Competition is fierce with LG Electronics building a chiller plant in Virginia for early 2027. Daikin and Vertiv are also expanding through acquisitions of related companies. The articles leave the final acquisition price and shareholder consent results open.

Articles.Title: Samsung Eyes U.S. Cooling Maker Modine to Court Big Tech AI Data Centers - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Nscale Has a $100 Billion AI Dream and a Very Expensive Funding Problem
stories.Summary:
Nscale said in an amended IPO filing that preliminary revenue reached $307.5 million in the nine months through September, up 1,344% from $21.3 million a year earlier. Its expected net loss widened to roughly $1.7 billion from $433 million. The London-based company builds AI computing infrastructure, including data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs. It has marketed more than $100 billion of contracted revenue to major AI customers, with the largest prize a deal with Anthropic that could generate as much as $44.6 billion.

Nscale plans to deploy Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin systems at its Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia, but its filing says it has not yet secured binding commitments for the financing required to fund that project. Nscale says it has raised more than $13.4 billion through equity, project financing and credit facilities. It nevertheless warned that bigger 2027 commitments mean more financing will be needed, reversing the message in its September filing that existing resources were sufficient for at least 12 months. Nscale has considered delaying the listing until next year and has been targeting a valuation around $30 billion to $35 billion, while Bloomberg reported that some investors think something closer to $16 billion to $19 billion would be easier to sell.

Nscale itself warns that there is no guarantee the required financing will be available on acceptable terms. That risk matters because the company expects about $5.5 billion of debt while its current revenue base is still relatively small. It has also suffered customer changes, including Microsoft declining to expand one Texas arrangement and a separate London project being delayed by grid constraints. The filing says management believes it can lock down financing for the Anthropic buildout, but binding commitments are not yet in place.

Investors will watch whether the IPO proceeds this year and where the valuation lands. A successful listing near $30 billion to $35 billion would show public markets are still willing to finance aggressive AI infrastructure expansion despite huge losses. A delay or sharply lower valuation would send the opposite message. Nscale has no shortage of customers wanting compute, and its challenge is proving that demand can be turned into profitable capacity before the bill for building it arrives.

Articles.Title: Nscale Has a $100 Billion AI Dream and a Very Expensive Funding Problem - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
stories.Summary:
Researchers Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli have introduced MACaQ, a post-training quantization method for neural networks, described in a paper posted to arXiv and listed on doi.org on November 13, 2026. The method compresses both the weights and the activations of a network to MXFP4 precision, a 4-bit format, which the authors say can cut the memory and compute cost of inference. Unlike many recent approaches, MACaQ treats each linear layer independently, so it does not need costly optimization or transforms that must be propagated across layers. The paper describes it as a model-agnostic method, meaning it can be applied without architecture-specific changes.

MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform to each layer's activations during inference, while folding the matching inverse transforms into the layer's weights. Because these transforms stay online, the process can be streamed so that only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve on standard round-to-nearest quantization, the authors add Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. According to the paper, the activation transforms add only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B when run in vLLM. The authors report lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and say MACaQ matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time.

The authors also report applying MACaQ, without architecture-specific modifications, to an image diffusion model, which they present as evidence of the method's generality. They state that quantizing a 122B parameter model took 64 minutes using only 32.5GB of GPU RAM. The code is said to be publicly available, though the article gives only a link placeholder. The source material does not describe any further peer review or deployment, and it does not say what comes next for the project beyond the released code.

Articles.Title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

stories.Headline: If AI Cut the Hours, What Are Clients Actually Paying For?
stories.Summary:
The article reports on a question facing accounting firms as AI shortens tax preparation: what clients should pay for when the hours drop. It centers on IRS Office of Professional Responsibility Alert 2026-19, dated June 24, 2026, which says practitioners cannot rely solely on AI, must treat AI-generated text as a draft, and remain responsible for final decisions. The alert ties this to Circular 230 § 10.22, which requires due diligence, and § 10.27(a), which bars unconscionable fees before the IRS. It warns that billing for time not actually spent, or double billing for an AI-assisted task, may violate § 10.27 depending on the facts, and it says cost savings should be passed on openly with AI activities disclosed.

Firms are already changing how they charge. An AICPA and CIMA news release dated September 10, 2025, describes a slow rise in value and fixed pricing alongside a decline in hourly billing. The 2025 MAP executive summary, from the AICPA Private Companies Practice Section and CPA.com, surveyed firms in May through July 2025, with 1,073 completing the survey, and found hourly billing used by 63% of responding firms, per-tax-form fees by 40%, value billing by 30%, up five points since 2022, and fixed pricing by 29%, up four points. Forty percent said they had not worked out how to track efficiencies from technology, and 61% said they had raised fees to cover technology investment. The article notes these figures describe accounting firms surveyed, not law firms, agencies, or design practices.

The article attributes the warnings to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility through its alert and frames the pricing guidance around the Circular 230 provisions it cites. It also addresses contingent fees under ET § 1.510.001 of the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, which bars preparing an original or amended return, or a refund claim, for a contingent fee, and notes that a fee tied to the tax result falls within that restriction even if labeled value pricing. The author, Steven de la Fe, CPA, a co-founder of Precision AI OS with 20 years of experience including seven at PwC, offers practical steps such as recording existing billing methods, keeping the signer on drafts, removing minutes the file did not take, and keeping stated return prices separate from tax results. The article does not describe any enforcement action or follow-up beyond the alert itself.

Articles.Title: If AI Cut the Hours, What Are Clients Actually Paying For?

stories.Headline: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers, Sota Ogawa, Shojiro Yamabe, Daiki Nishiyama and Jun Sakuma, has published a paper describing a method for reconstructing the family tree of fine-tuned large language models, with the paper appearing on doi.org on November 13, 2026. The authors note that fine-tuned derivatives of these models are now released in large numbers, but their provenance depends on self-reports that cannot be checked. The paper argues that misattributed lineage prevents a verifier from auditing outsourced fine-tuning, confirming that derived models comply with licenses, or tracing vulnerabilities passed from a parent model to its children. Because each of these tasks depends on knowing the direction of derivation, the authors treat direction as essential rather than just the existence of a relationship. Earlier output-only methods could only test whether two models are related or estimate undirected lineage, and recovering a directed tree was thought to require access to the model weights.

The authors formalize the problem of rebuilding a directed model tree, including intermediate nodes, under what they call gray-box access, in which only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Their approach rests on the observation that fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and that a child model inherits this increase from its parent. Using this property, they define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it a weight for each ordered pair of models. They propose an algorithm called TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these weights, and the authors say it needs no hyperparameters and no imposed tree-structure constraints. The method was tested on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks.

According to the paper, TRACE-Edge reached a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples. The authors report that on average it also outperformed an output-similarity baseline even when the probes were held out and drawn from the same distribution as the training data. The article does not say whether the method has been adopted by any organization, released as software, or tested on models beyond the 25 trees described. It also does not indicate how the approach would perform against models whose fine-tuning data is unknown to the verifier. The work is presented as a formal and empirical contribution to verifying the provenance of language models under limited access.

Articles.Title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference

stories.Headline: Banks need sovereign AI, but not as expected
stories.Summary:
Vikram Bharwani, CTO for Banking and Financial Services at NTT DATA in the UK and Ireland, published an article on November 13, 2026, arguing that every major bank will need sovereign AI. He defined sovereign AI not as a bank-owned frontier model or a warehouse full of GPUs, but as the ability to use powerful AI while retaining control of knowledge, actions and decisions. The article appeared on nttdata.com at 06:00:00Z on 2026-11-13, and a second version appeared on 2026-11-14 at 06:00:00Z. Bharwani wrote that banking has spent half a century digitalizing how money moves and how financial services operate. He said AI is now beginning to digitalize something far more complex, namely the judgment behind banking decisions.

Bharwani cited a 2024 survey by the Bank of England and the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, which found that 75% of responding firms were using AI, up from 58% in 2022. He described the reverse information paradox as framed by Satya Nadella, who said that in the AI age the buyer risks giving away knowledge just to use what they bought. Bharwani said a bank's knowledge includes the credit officer's correction, the fraud analyst's rejected lead and the exception an experienced underwriter accepted, with the reasons for those decisions. He said the knowledge layer is more valuable than the model itself, and that a bank can use external models while owning its private evaluations, approved knowledge, feedback and orchestration. He said data residency is important, but a model can run in a bank's own building and still leave the bank unable to explain a decision or switch suppliers.

Bharwani said sovereignty comes down to whether a bank controls its data, can explain decisions, retains what the system learns and can keep operating when something fails. He said an agent's permissions, network access and spending limits need to sit outside the model, and critical actions need approval and an effective way to stop them without it. He said these controls can exist in a public cloud and can also be missing from a private deployment. He said the FCA expects firms to apply existing duties and governance to AI, including consumer outcomes and senior accountability. He said a decision passport should capture inputs, permissions, policy and model versions, tool actions, human interventions and the final explanation, and a bank must recreate that record after changing models.

Bharwani said a mortgage application from someone with irregular income shows what the architecture must do, with AI reconciling payslips and bank statements, finding policy, flagging conflicting evidence and preparing an affordability recommendation. He said the underwriter should see conflicts and assumptions rather than a confident paragraph that hides them, and a declined customer deserves a clear reason and a way to correct the record or seek review. He said an upheld appeal may expose a faulty interpretation, arrears may show whether affordability assumptions reflected risk, and a complaint may reveal that the explanation failed the customer. He said learning should stay in a sandbox, tested against unseen cases, before release under control, and historical lending data can reflect past exclusions while declined applicants create gaps in outcome data. He said the same principle applies to fraud, customer service and operational resilience, and the test is fewer avoidable referrals, lower false positives, faster resolution, sounder decisions and better customer experiences.

Bharwani said banks do not need to own every part of the AI stack but must control their data, knowledge and evaluations, with freedom to change models without losing context. He said banks need clear controls over what agents can do, decision records that survive each technology change and, for critical services, a tested fallback. He said some tasks warrant private inference while others are better served by a smaller model or a clear deterministic rule. He said a bank should start with one material process, establish what a good decision costs today, how long it takes, where it goes wrong and what customers experience, then measure whether AI improves those outcomes. He said cost per token means little if the result is a faster, cheaper mistake.

Bharwani said banks should consider what happens to human judgment as work is automated, asking how junior underwriters learn to challenge AI in five years if it builds every first-pass credit pack. He said they should be given supervised exceptions, simulated cases and access to model traces, and human oversight is meaningless if a person clicks approve without the chance to investigate the evidence. He said powerful AI will be available to everyone, and the real difference will be whether banks turn it into a governed extension of institutional judgment without giving up control. He said a bank can rent a model but cannot rent accountability, and he expects sovereign AI to become part of core banking infrastructure. The articles leave open which specific process a bank should choose first and what the IDC InfoBrief sponsored by NTT DATA concludes.

Articles.Title: Banks need sovereign AI, but not as expected

stories.Headline: Backdoor subsidy for AI data centers? Cato analyst says let CHIPS Act tax credit expire
stories.Summary:
Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, published an analysis this week calling on Congress to let the CHIPS and Science Act's advanced manufacturing investment tax credit expire at the end of the year. The CHIPS Act was signed into law in 2022 and subsidizes domestic semiconductor manufacturing, which Michel called the central components of artificial intelligence data centers. He argued the credit amounts to a backdoor subsidy for AI at a time when some in Congress want a moratorium on data center construction. Michel said he is not against data centers and called them good for America, but said the government should not be actively subsidizing their inputs.

Without congressional action, the credit expires at the end of this year, though projects already under construction can be placed in service up to 10 years from now and still claim it. Michel said the credit's official cost has almost tripled since it became law four years ago, and that a permanent extension could cost between $125 billion and $325 billion in total. He said he does not believe the subsidy moved the needle much on domestic manufacturing, arguing most investments would have happened anyway and that the credit amounts to a windfall profit for the companies receiving it. He pointed to TSMC, Texas Instruments, Samsung and Intel, which he said announced or broke ground on domestic fabrication facilities in the year or two before the credit existed.

The two top members of the Senate Finance Committee have advocated for extending the credit, calling it a critical tool for strengthening domestic semiconductor supply chains, creating good-paying jobs and advancing national security interests. One of them, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, is also pushing for increased tax burdens on data centers, and Michel said an extension would be quite counter to the anti-data center sentiment running through the public. Mark Muro, a Brookings Metro senior fellow and digital economy expert, shared Michel's view that letting the credit expire alone would be a weak tool for slowing data center construction, and said fabrication and data center construction should see a lot of investment with or without it. Muro said policymakers should instead focus on siting rules, utility rate design and helping communities drive tougher, more advantageous deals.

Articles.Title: Backdoor subsidy for AI data centers? Cato analyst says let CHIPS Act tax credit expire

stories.Headline: Could AI reduce shipping costs and grocery bills?
stories.Summary:
EAIGLE says its AI-powered camera technology can cut truck check-ins at distribution centers from roughly 10 minutes to under 30 seconds, Fox News reported on Nov. 13, 2026. The company's Automated Vehicle Access Control system, known as AVAC, uses artificial intelligence and existing security cameras to automate manual gate checks. The system identifies arriving vehicles and compares the information against facility records. EAIGLE says its computer vision technology can capture more than 25 truck and trailer data points in under 30 seconds. Those data points include license plate numbers and other identifying details that help determine whether a vehicle should enter the property.

According to the most recent update from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the national average diesel price was $6.13 per gallon for the week of Nov. 9. A USDA-supported study examined how diesel prices and truck-driver availability affect food transportation. The researchers found that higher transportation costs generally increased food prices in the scenarios they studied. Potatoes were especially sensitive to changes in transportation expenses, partly because they are often shipped long distances from growing regions to major markets. When the information matches, an automated gate can allow the driver to proceed, and if something looks suspicious, the system can flag the vehicle for additional review.

EAIGLE says the system reduces a process that typically takes around 10 minutes to less than 30 seconds. The company says its technology could save trucking companies money, and if those savings spread across supply chains, they could potentially help reduce some of the cost pressures behind grocery bills. EAIGLE describes AVAC as bringing an E-ZPass-like experience to warehouse gates. At many distribution centers, truck drivers still go through manual check-ins, and security personnel may need to review shipping documents and verify that the right truck has arrived for the right load. During busy periods, those checks can create long lines, and drivers who leave their engines running consume fuel before reaching the loading dock.

The article says there is currently no evidence that EAIGLE's technology has directly lowered grocery prices or delivery fees for shoppers. Retailers could use the savings to offset other expenses or improve their profits. Because freight-yard check-ins account for only a small part of overall transportation costs, any savings would need to add up across many facilities to have a noticeable impact on what families pay. A major distribution center processing hundreds of trucks every day could use less fuel and avoid unnecessary operating expenses by reducing repeated delays.

Shoppers are affected through grocery bills and delivery fees, and retailers and transportation companies are affected through operating costs. The article says part of what shoppers pay for everyday products can be tied to delivery trucks sitting in long lines outside warehouses. Those trucks can burn expensive diesel while drivers wait to check in, and transportation companies face higher operating expenses that can eventually find their way into retail prices. When diesel prices rise, transportation companies often add fuel surcharges or increase shipping rates to cover the additional expense.

Those costs can eventually reach the companies selling products to shoppers. Fresh produce often travels hundreds of miles before reaching a neighborhood supermarket, and many grocery products also move through distribution centers where trucks unload incoming merchandise before stores receive their deliveries. If trucks spend less time waiting at warehouse gates, facilities may be able to process incoming shipments more efficiently, which could help retailers keep merchandise moving through their networks. The article says it is worth watching whether savings from faster shipping could reach shoppers.

The article leaves open whether EAIGLE's technology has directly lowered grocery prices or delivery fees, and it gives no evidence that it has. The article also leaves open how much of any savings retailers would pass on rather than use to offset other expenses or improve profits. It does not say how widely AVAC is deployed or how many facilities use it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Could AI reduce shipping costs and grocery bills?

stories.Headline: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
stories.Summary:
Researchers Liting Huang, Huizhi Liang, Yi Lei, Xingjun Ma and Varun Ojha have published a paper describing a new method for attacking large language models so that they make wrong judgments when checking facts. The paper, posted to arXiv and dated November 13, 2026, introduces a framework called Debate-to-Deceive, or D2D. The authors say that earlier attacks, which relied on adversarial suffixes, template injection or a single agent reflecting on its own output, were either not robust across different defenses or prone to confirmation bias and costly trial and error. The D2D framework is built on the structure and rhetorical style of human debate, with several AI agents arguing against one another. The authors model the process as an evolutionary game in which agents adjust their rhetorical strategies, drawing on the classical appeals of Logos, Pathos and Ethos, through competition.

To keep the search manageable, the work splits each agent into a strategic layer, which picks a rhetorical action from a compact set, and a generation layer, where the language model writes a concrete passage based on that choice and the debate context. The passages are meant to be semantically coherent, rhetorically effective and resistant to early confirmation bias. The paper reports tests on four fact-checking benchmarks: FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER and SciFact. According to the authors, D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks on these benchmarks and evades most of the defenses they were tested against.

The abstract frames the work as a demonstration of risk, since manipulated fact-checking judgments pose significant threats to the reliability of AI systems. The article does not describe any specific responses from the developers of the models tested or from the benchmark maintainers. The source is a research preprint rather than a peer-reviewed publication, and the abstract does not say whether the authors plan to release code or propose specific defenses. The available material does not describe any follow-up steps beyond the paper itself.

Articles.Title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate

stories.Headline: NYC Council bans ‘surveillance pricing’ that has customers’ data used against them
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council passed a bill on Thursday, November 12, 2026, to ban surveillance pricing, which stops companies from using browsing data to charge different customers different prices for the same product. The bill passed in a 44-5 vote in the Democrat-dominated council. It was one of several pieces of legislation lawmakers took up at the meeting. The council also opted into a state program exempting disabled veterans from property taxes and discussed a proposal on vacant rent-stabilized units. The law bars companies from setting different prices for the same product at the same time based on demographics, web browsing history, shopping habits, or social media activity.

Larger companies face an immediate $1,000 fine for violating it, while small businesses can first present an action plan to fix any missteps. The council also approved a bill sponsored by Republican Councilman Frank Morano to opt the city into a state law exempting permanently and totally disabled veterans from property taxes, which passed 48-1 one day after Veterans Day. A separate bill from Brooklyn Council Member Farah Louis would require the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to analyze and develop a plan over 60 days to bring vacant rent-stabilized units online, with about 57,000 reported vacant citywide and nearly 279,000 rent-stabilized apartments in Brooklyn alone. City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who sponsored the surveillance pricing bill, said many factors drive up costs, some obvious to consumers, but she called surveillance pricing a more subtle and predatory corporate practice. She said companies set different prices for the same product for different consumers shopping at the exact same time, using their demographics, browsing history, shopping habits, and social media activity to make New Yorkers pay more.

Morano said the state bill required an opt-in and that the city was opting in, calling it a powerful statement about how the council values its veterans. Louis said a clearer understanding is needed of why these homes remain unavailable and what it will take to return them to the rental market. The surveillance pricing law has the support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Critics of the bill were concerned the regulations would harm small businesses, but the final language allows wiggle room for smaller companies. The vacant units bill addresses the city's over 50,000 vacant rent-stabilized apartments despite a vacancy rate of only 1.4%, with critics saying landlords are warehousing units by intentionally keeping them empty.

Articles.Title: NYC Council bans ‘surveillance pricing’ that has customers’ data used against them - New York Post

stories.Headline: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team and reassigned the researchers working there to other parts of the company. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision. The spokesperson portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week.

OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen. The applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, but when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen. OpenAI rebuilt a stand-alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI.

OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots. The company said that at the start of the year, its researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown they can be directly applied to robotics.

Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, told Fortune he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark, compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence through other methods. OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text, the approach that eventually yielded ChatGPT in late 2022. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts, including Sora, to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses, which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter. OpenAI is seeking to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. Shi said large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection. Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former OpenAI robotics team members still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. One of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots

stories.Headline: China-nexus actor uses AI tool in campaign targeting US defense, semiconductor industries
stories.Summary:
A suspected China-nexus threat group ran a campaign against key U.S. sectors, including advanced semiconductors, the defense industry and civil-society organizations, according to a report Palo Alto Networks released on a Thursday in mid-November 2026. The attackers paired an AI pen-testing framework called Cairn with two Chinese open-source models, DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM, to target at least 19 organizations. Researchers say they gained access to or pulled data from 10 of them. The attackers obtained dozens of valid credentials, created administrator accounts inside a production system and exposed more than a million personal records at one organization.

Researchers say the combination let the hackers scale their attacks well beyond what a person working by hand could manage. Andy Piazza, senior director of threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, said tools like Cairn let attackers hit more targets faster. He added that such tooling lets them carry out technical tasks without learning the underlying technologies. Researchers are tracking the group as CL-STA-1238, which they describe as part of a China-nexus intelligence-collection effort. The report presents the activity as the latest in a growing wave of attacks built on AI pen-testing frameworks.

The article places the campaign within a broader pattern. Over the past two months, threat groups used a testing framework called Artex to attack hundreds of companies worldwide, and the same tool was linked to a campaign against South Korean banks and Japanese companies. In a separate matter, Arctic Wolf researchers reported on a Tuesday that attackers used the AntiFox pen-testing framework, hosted on Alibaba, to steal Amazon Web Services credentials. At least two organizations were confirmed compromised, and researchers suspect six more were affected. Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, said that activity appears opportunistic rather than aimed at a specific industry.

An Amazon spokesperson said AWS services were not specifically compromised and operated as designed, while the attackers used credentials taken from compromised applications to reach customers' accounts. The spokesperson urged AWS users to follow security best practices, including least-privilege permissions, requiring Instance Metadata Service on EC2 instances, and keeping long-term access keys out of application configurations. The articles do not say whether any government agency has responded to the Palo Alto Networks findings. They also do not describe the specific defense or semiconductor companies that were affected. The reporting ends with the findings themselves and the warnings from researchers and Amazon.

Articles.Title: China-nexus actor uses AI tool in campaign targeting US defense, semiconductor industries

stories.Headline: AI's impact on math is a preview of what AI will do to AI research, with AI matching top human researchers potentially just a couple of years away (Dwarkesh Patel/Dwarkesh Podcast)
stories.Summary:
Dwarkesh Patel wrote in a blog post on November 13, 2026, that AI's impact on math previews what AI will do to AI research. He said he had updated his views a ton over the last three months. He now believes we are only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs as good as the best humans at AI research. He also believes automating AI research will compress so much progress into a single year that we will soon have AIs at least as good as the best human experts in every field. He said this could come by 2030, but plausibly as early as next year.

He credited Max Farrens, Gabe Fried and Thomas Larsen for pairing with him through significant parts of writing and researching the essay. He said METR, an independent evaluation organization, concluded after three months embedded inside Anthropic that Anthropic's overall rate of progress on well-scoped tasks is 2x what it was a year ago. He said METR found a majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic's extensive use of AI to do R&D. He said OpenAI published a blog post in September showing the heaviest 10% of AI users among OpenAI's researchers went from around $1,000 a day of internal coding agents at the beginning of the summer to over $7,000 a day by the end of August. He said Anthropic reported in September that, as of August, Claude leads more than 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D work, up from under 1% as recently as February.

He said current AIs are slicing through well-scoped problems in mathematics like a hot knife through butter. He traced the progress from 2023, when a model could not reliably add four-digit numbers, to 2024, when a model could barely solve any problems in a high school math competition. He said in 2025 a model could win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad, and earlier this year models were solving open Erdős problems. He said about a month ago a model solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.

He quoted Toby Ord's essay saying current AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proof but there is very little evidence they can ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical enquiry. He said AI research is surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress current AIs are disproportionately good at. He said his friend Sholto Douglas has a perennially half-finished blog post explaining how the transformer could have been invented two years earlier than it was. He said the transformer paper was published in 2017, and quoted Chris Olah saying the transformer architecture was a natural combination of many ideas, attention and residual networks, which had independently been effective. He said AlexNet kicked off the deep learning revolution in 2012.

He said he would guess 2028 as his median year for when automated researchers will be as good as the very best human AI researchers, assuming the labs don't intentionally slow down. He said there is a 25% chance it doesn't happen until after 2032, and that we could hit the milestone in 2027. He said some of the most well-informed researchers he knows expect AI to beat the best humans at AI research as early as next year. He said 2027 is the straightforward implication of plugging METR's finding that Anthropic's rate of AI progress has doubled in a year into a takeoff model. He quoted former guest Ajeya Cotra saying that if AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and acceleration is smooth, this naively implies reaching extreme superintelligence within a year.

He said today's AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed, and automated researchers would work around the clock, nights and weekends included. He said each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week. He said OpenAI has not fired all of its researchers despite having a model that can autonomously solve Millennium Prize problems, because some parts of AI research are less verifiable than math. He said he saved the technical details of how AI research works for the Appendix. He said he did not believe his own claim even a couple of months ago.

Articles.Title: AI's impact on math is a preview of what AI will do to AI research, with AI matching top human researchers potentially just a couple of years away (Dwarkesh Patel/Dwarkesh Podcast)

stories.Headline: AI Creditable Hours Programs Let Lawyers Experiment With Tech on Billable Time
stories.Summary:
A growing number of law firms have recently introduced programs that allow associates to use billable time for AI training. These initiatives were reported on November 13, 2026, by Jon Campisi. The programs allow junior lawyers to experiment with new technology during their workday. Associates have expressed that they enjoy the chance to get their hands dirty with these tools.

These programs change how firms track the recorded time of their associates, who are typically the primary workhorses of the industry. By permitting a substantial amount of billable hours to be dedicated to AI, firms are shifting their traditional productivity requirements. This change allows lawyers to focus on enhanced training rather than only client work. The articles do not list specific hourly quotas or dates for the rollout of these individual programs.

Law firm leaders and associates are responsible for the implementation and success of these efforts. Firm leaders have expressed satisfaction with the outcomes of the training. Experts suggest that this shift shows that firms believe these tools are truly transformative. They believe success can be measured by the positive feedback from both the associates and the leadership.

The context of these changes is a broader industry trend toward AI fluency in legal practice. Other firms are also updating their training playbooks to accommodate associates who are increasingly knowledgeable about technology. Some firms are even hiring specialized C-suite members to lead AI and knowledge efforts. These shifts indicate a long-term move toward integrating artificial intelligence into the core of legal work.

Articles.Title: AI Creditable Hours Programs Let Lawyers Experiment With Tech on Billable Time

stories.Headline: Audit Reveals AI Disclosure Mandates Miss Chinese Agricultural Livestreaming Sellers
stories.Summary:
Researchers Tianxing Tang and Zhihua Hu conducted an external audit of the Douyin livestreaming platform. They studied the site between June 9 and June 13, 2026, to check for AI labels. The team looked for mandatory disclosures among agricultural producers selling their own harvests. They found that these statutory labeling requirements were entirely invisible for these specific sellers. No produce growers openly disclosed using artificial intelligence tools in the evaluated videos.

The audit followed the January 2023 Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis in Internet Information Services. It also tracked interim generative AI measures and the September 1, 2025, Measures for the Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content. These rules include the national standard GB 45438, 2025 for developers, platforms, and end users. The researchers searched for ten product categories, including navel oranges, apples, peaches, honey, and mountain goods. They also searched for tea, sweet potatoes, rice, and mangoes across 575 videos.

The authors stated that public transparency mechanisms fail to show if genuine farmers operate digital storefronts. They explained that growers face an authenticity penalty because AI disclosures reduce a consumer's willingness to purchase. This makes voluntary compliance incentive-incompatible for smallholders whose goods sell at a premium based on presence. Conversely, software vendors and commercial intermediaries use AI tools as attractive credentials for their business models. The researchers noted that platform governance cannot depend on public label-reading alone to ensure compliance.

The study affected 455 unique authors and 19 specific accounts retrieved through technical keywords. Commercial intermediaries represented 68.4 percent of the supply layer, while media organizations made up 31.6 percent. Consumers rely on indexical cues, like weathered faces and regional dialects, to verify the quality of credence goods. These visual and vocal cues are costly to counterfeit but can now be fabricated by generative tools. Such technology allows third parties to manufacture simulated grower identities without having any real agricultural ties.

The background involves a three-layer algorithm audit of policy documents, technical keywords, and commodity queries. Policy screening showed only 3.2 percent of 189 mechanism-level texts named authenticity as a farmer asset. The transaction layer used a text-rule detector with a 94.7 percent recall rate on synthetic accounts. Metadata analysis of 575 records showed no platform-side AI labels in the show_ai_corner or video_labels fields. Inspections of 472 cover images revealed no visible watermarks or mandatory notices for synthetic content.

Future policy frameworks may need to pair synthetic transparency with other tools to be effective. The researchers cannot determine if smallholders reject AI tools or deploy them without providing mandatory disclosures. Disentangling these two possibilities would require access to private sales metrics or internal platform upload histories. The articles leave open whether internal platform data would reveal hidden synthetic watermark scans. It remains unclear how regulators will resolve the tension between rural AI adoption and transparency mandates.

Articles.Title: Audit Reveals AI Disclosure Mandates Miss Chinese Agricultural Livestreaming Sellers

stories.Headline: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA published an article on November 12, 2026, written by Ralf Malter, Managing Director for Global Automotive, Business Consulting and AI at NTT DATA DACH, titled around the shift from software-defined vehicles to an AI-native operating model. The piece draws on the company's 2026 Global AI Report, which argues that most automakers and suppliers have moved past pilot projects and proofs of concept. It says the real question now is whether leaders are using AI in ways that change how the business actually runs. The article describes AI as becoming the operating model itself rather than a complement to it.

The report's data shows a widening gap between leaders and laggards. Of leaders, 38.6 percent are already rebuilding applications with embedded AI, compared with 12 percent of laggards. Leaders focus on redesigning high-value workflows end to end, including engineering, change management, quality escalation, warranty triage and procurement exceptions. The article contends that the main constraint is no longer model quality but workflow design. It also says 93.2 percent of leaders apply AI in core operational workflows, against 68.8 percent of laggards.

The author argues that the rise of software-defined vehicles points to a broader change, since AI in engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and in-vehicle experiences makes the whole value chain driven by data-based decisions. He describes agentic AI as able to carry out and adjust workflows as conditions change, with examples such as coordinating over-the-air updates, simulating test conditions and adapting in-vehicle experiences to usage. The article notes that many organizations still treat AI mainly as a tool for efficiency, which it attributes to viewing AI as "better automation." Governance is presented as essential in a sector where safety and compliance are non-negotiable, and 67.6 percent of leaders have adopted centralized AI governance compared with 38.4 percent of laggards.

The article is promotional in nature and is written by an NTT DATA executive, so its figures come from the company's own research and have not been independently verified. It describes the report as offering a playbook for automotive AI leaders and invites readers to download it. The piece does not describe any regulatory action or external deadlines. It concludes that competitive advantage will come from how well organizations align their operating models with AI, and it frames the future of automotive as both software-defined and AI-native.

Articles.Title: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model - NTT Data

stories.Headline: AI Code Surges 30% But Actual Delivery Hits Zero? SoduWork Sets Rules for Runaway Agents
stories.Summary:
SoduWork, an open-source enterprise-level AI-native engine built by the Anhui Digital Intelligence Building Materials Research Institute, sets rules for runaway Agents, according to a CSDN article published on 2026-11-12 at 19:41. The article reports that AI code production has surged while actual business delivery has hit zero growth. Researchers from Harvard University, working with an engineering data platform, tracked more than 700 software enterprises and 720,000 developers over multiple years. The article states that after AI tools were introduced, monthly lines of code rose 30% and code merge requests rose 23%. The number of business demands that passed testing and went online successfully showed almost zero growth statistically.

SoduWork requires that requirements have standards, code has tests, merges have reviews, and deliveries have evidence. The system supports full self-deployment and is built by the Anhui Digital Intelligence Building Materials Research Institute. It sets a "work start access control" at the front end, so a task cannot start unless "what counts as a good completion" is clearly defined first. The initiator must write the acceptance line before work begins, for example that test logs for empty boundaries must be included and no empty assertions are allowed. The base that executes tasks and the base that reviews are not affiliated to each other, and an independent review node checks real logs and operation evidence against the acceptance line.

The article says humans set standards, Agents do the work, acceptance is based on evidence, and correct methods are precipitated into reusable plugins. It says the AI that does the work cannot get the right to tick the pass for itself. Any inspection not actually executed is not marked as passed, and results that fail acceptance are returned for rework directly in the original conversation. The article describes the design as a defensive system made by engineers tortured by AI delivery on the front line. It says the design forces you to spend time thinking about the standards before you start working.

Surveys cited in the article show that the time from code submission to merge increased by 49% exactly, and the proportion of rework requests almost doubled. Many technical teams must transfer more than 10% of their core backbones to act all day as full-time quality inspectors for AI. Public system data from mainstream laboratories shows that under fatigue the proportion of humans clicking "Agree" on Agent pop-ups is as high as 93%. Experiments show that human recognition of AI dangerous operations and logical loopholes drops from 17% in the early stage to less than 5% later. The article says the human engineer who clicked to pass still takes the blame when a production failure occurs.

The article says that by the end of 2026 the fanaticism had spread to deeper daily scenarios, with Meta launching Muse, a personal agent residing permanently in the cloud, and OpenAI bringing Dots, which emphasizes "always on". It says terminal-based CLI Agents are emerging endlessly, and non-technical staff such as operations and product managers now command Agents in dialog boxes to process complex cross-system businesses in batches. It says a term has been coined in the technical community, "Testslop", for test spammer. The article says AI assistants generate large numbers of meaningless tests with empty assertions and even fabricate assertion logic backwards from existing bugs. It says most high-value usages are locked in individual employees' temporary conversation windows, so methods disappear with the person and model iteration clears previous results.

The article says the industry has diverged into two paths, one pinning hopes on the next major model version self-correcting and the other depriving AI of the right to make self-judgment. It says expecting Agents never to slack off or hallucinate without external constraints is an unrealistic fantasy. The article says SoduWork does not focus on making AI write faster. It says the article leaves open whether this defensive approach will be adopted widely. The article does not state what happens next for SoduWork or the teams it describes.

Articles.Title: AI Code Surges 30% But Actual Delivery Hits Zero? SoduWork Sets Rules for Runaway Agents - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Secure, Scalable AI for Manufacturers
stories.Summary:

The InfoBrief is offered as IDC guidance for the manufacturing and automotive sectors, with a chapter for each industry.
