stories.Headline: ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI
stories.Summary:
Zimperium researchers reported on November 13, 2026 that the ArcticRAT cybercrime gang had turned its Android malware from a cryptocurrency stealer into a full remote access Trojan. The operators added large language model services to sift stolen text messages for financial data worth exploiting. Zimperium called the change a dangerous escalation in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions let attackers interact with infected devices in real time instead of relying on hardcoded actions. The gang used malvertising, smishing and third-party forums to send visitors to malicious websites carrying the malware.

Early ArcticRAT versions targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications to harvest data for access to crypto accounts. The new versions add remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and theft of SMS messages, contacts and call logs. Attackers can also steal or change lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices. Since July, Zimperium identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads and 21 IP addresses used for command-and-control communications. The researchers also found 129 distinct commands for remotely controlling infected devices, stealing information, monitoring activity and manipulating device functions.

Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, said ArcticRAT uses AI to read user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used to perform fraud. He said one particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay, with attackers abusing legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off. He said defending against such threats requires AI-powered on-device threat detection, controls over application installation and permissions, and runtime application protection to spot suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays. Zimperium said the primary attack vector relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application. The researchers observed attackers in some instances using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Zimperium found the malware features an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency and trading platforms. The AI capabilities let ArcticRAT process stolen SMS messages and separate routine and promotional messages from one-time authentication codes, account balance changes and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium. The firm said this automates much of the work of sorting large volumes of stolen information rather than manually examining the data. Zimperium said that as mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints.

Once installed, the latest version abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity and currently active applications. It sends that information to the attackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. The malware uses a completely black, un-dismissible screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Analysts noted the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating mobile devices as secondary security concerns and to apply the same threat monitoring, access controls and protections as for traditional endpoints.

The article was written by Illinois-based Jai Vijayan, a veteran technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. Zimperium is tracking the malware and described the evolution as an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make malware more capable and dangerous. The article gives no indication of how many victims have been infected or where they are located. It does not say whether law enforcement or Google has taken any action against the gang or its infrastructure. It also does not say what the attackers do with the financial intelligence after it reaches their command-and-control servers.

Articles.Title: ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Why is Nvidia king of the AI chip hill and how soon can rivals catch up?
stories.Summary:
Chief executive Jensen Huang resigned from US chipmaker Nvidia on November 13, 2026. His departure followed revelations of extramarital affairs with several women. One woman was a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. This scandal has triggered intense scrutiny of the company. It has also led to investigations into the firm Megaspeed.

US authorities are examining if Singapore-based Megaspeed aided in bypassing export controls. They are checking if chips were unlawfully rerouted or smuggled into China. The US has banned Blackwell and Rubin GPUs from being exported to China. In September, Nvidia released the RTX Spark Superchip for the personal computer market. These chips power AI chatbots, autonomous vehicles, and delivery robots.

Omdia analyst Su Lian Jye said Nvidia's dominance stems from its comprehensive chipset portfolio. Su noted that the proprietary CUDA platform removes the need to code complex functions. Proxima vice-president Chris Hampden expects continuity rather than disruption after the leadership transition. He stated that innovation is the work of large engineering teams and partnerships. Su believes the board is unlikely to fix what is not broken.

Data centre operators in South-east Asia may face stricter checks on advanced chip purchases. Singtel stated there is no impact on chip supply or partnerships amid the resignation. Hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services, Google, and Microsoft are developing their own in-house chipsets. Google released new tensor processing units in November to encrypt sensitive data. These competitors offer better inference speed, larger memory, and ultra-low latency.

Nvidia holds around 80% of the global market for high-end data centre chips. In Singapore, Singtel, HTX, and Equinix use these chips for AI training. The Aspire 2B supercomputer at Nanyang Technological University uses 1,500 Nvidia H200 GPUs. This national research supercomputer provides power for more than 9,000 public researchers. It has more computing power than 120,000 high-end AI laptops combined.

Huawei plans to debut next-generation chips in 2027 to compete on a global stage. DeepSeek plans to deploy 160,000 950DT chips at a data centre in Inner Mongolia. Huawei is also exploring foreign markets in Egypt and Malaysia with its Ascend chips. IDC manager Galen Zeng says any catch-up by rivals will take several years. The US administration will decide the future availability of advanced H200 models.

Articles.Title: Why is Nvidia king of the AI chip hill and how soon can rivals catch up?

stories.Headline: Uranium price hits record as AI demand prompts nuclear comeback
stories.Summary:
Uranium prices reached record highs on November 14, 2026, due to a global revival of nuclear energy. This surge was driven by the rapid growth of artificial intelligence data centers and ongoing crises in the Middle East. These factors combined to create a very tight global electricity supply. The increased demand for power has pushed the cost of fuel to unprecedented levels.

The shift toward nuclear power is evident as the number of reactors under construction globally has risen to 79. In Japan, Kansai Electric Power has already restarted seven of its nuclear power reactors to meet energy needs. This movement is part of a broader effort to secure stable fuel sources for the future. The industry is now adapting to the massive power requirements of the AI boom.

Market analysts and energy officials are responsible for monitoring these supply constraints. They suggest that the thirst for data center power is a primary driver of the current price spike. These experts believe that nuclear energy is becoming essential for maintaining grid stability. They note that the transition is necessary to support new technological infrastructure.

The broader context involves a global race for energy security amidst geopolitical tensions. Japan is specifically looking into next-generation fast breeder reactors to keep pace with China and Russia. The country is also exploring nuclear reprocessing technology to salvage rare earth elements. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Uranium price hits record as AI demand prompts nuclear comeback

stories.Headline: Growth beyond AI puts corporate Japan on track for 20% profit gain
stories.Summary:
Major Japanese companies are expected to see their total net profits rise by 20% during the current fiscal year. This growth would mark the sixth consecutive year that these firms have reached a record high. The increase follows a series of upgraded earnings forecasts for various large corporations. These gains are happening even for businesses that are not part of the artificial intelligence boom.

The financial improvements are driven by better capital efficiency and price hikes. A weak yen has also helped manufacturers increase their profit outlooks. Specific companies like Astellas and Mitsubishi have upgraded their forecasts to record levels. Other firms, such as Komatsu, are seeing higher demand for construction and mining in the Americas.

Kazuki Kawahara reported that these trends are benefiting a wide range of industries. He noted that drugmakers are among the sectors seeing success without relying on AI. The report suggests that corporate Japan is finding growth through diverse operational improvements. These changes allow companies to maintain a strong upward trajectory in their earnings.

The current economic environment is supporting these record-breaking profit projections across the country. Many manufacturers are leveraging global demand and currency fluctuations to boost their bottom lines. The reports indicate a broad recovery and expansion within the Japanese corporate sector. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Growth beyond AI puts corporate Japan on track for 20% profit gain

stories.Headline: AI is helping agents sound more knowledgeable than they are
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, Realtor and instructor Nathan White wrote in Real Estate News that AI is helping real estate agents sound more knowledgeable than they are. White said he has used AI to run comps and watched it deliver wrong information in the same confident voice it uses when it is right. He said that because he has sold more than 500 homes, he can tell when the tool is wrong, while many agents leaning on AI the hardest do not have that experience. He wrote that AI is obscuring knowledge gaps rather than erasing them.

White described a proposal that NAR's board took up in June. It would have required Realtors to disclose when they lack the knowledge, information, or skills about a property type or geographical area to protect and promote their clients' interests. The Executive Committee recommended defeating it, and the board voted 497 to 356 to send it back to the Professional Standards Committee, which had already worked on it for two years. White cited NAR's latest technology report saying 23% of Realtors use AI daily, and he said other surveys suggest usage may be much higher. He also said NAR's AI policy kit for brokers states that agents and staff are fully accountable for the AI content they use.

White wrote that AI does not hold a license and agents do. He said he serves on the Ohio Realtors grievance and mediation panels, where every name on a complaint belongs to a person. He recalled that during the board meeting a director from Florida said that once an agent discloses a knowledge gap, trust with the consumer is lost. White disagreed, saying clients lose faith after finding out an agent never had the knowledge or skills to promote their interests. He said the standard should be to use AI as a tool, check its outputs against a reliable source, and tell the client first if you cannot explain the answer yourself.

White noted that NAR's directors met again in New Orleans the previous week. One session focused on the risks of using AI and the importance of maintaining consumer trust and compliance, but the knowledge gap proposal was not discussed. White wrote that he hopes that changes. He said he does not know if the proposal's wording is right and would want it fixed before panels like his had to apply it, but he argued that requiring agents to be honest about what they do not know is not what puts consumer trust at risk.

Articles.Title: AI is helping agents sound more knowledgeable than they are

stories.Headline: As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up
stories.Summary:
Test takers are turning to artificial intelligence to answer questions on IT certification exams, Dark Reading reported on November 11, 2026. Marielle Carlos, a data forensics scientist at Caveon, said AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certification. Caveon added a new category to its testing security threats taxonomy called unknown. Casey Marks, chief operating officer at ISC2, said widespread irregular exam results and verified cheating attempts were found during the nonprofit's online proctoring pilots. ISC2 then required in-person testing for its exams.

ISC2 implemented what Marks called the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities, including biometric and identity verification. ISC2 is exclusively test-center based for all exams, which Marks said ensures no access to outside resources or technology during exam administration. The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professions such as doctors. Certifications range from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge and cover Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services updates. In industries like government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current on compliance regulations.

Carlos said it is hard to know if an exam is measuring actual competence or someone's ability to use AI to answer the question. She said this challenges the usefulness of that exam. Marks said the candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process. Carlos urged programs to have conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process, including secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to security concerns. She said a layered approach is crucial because tools can indicate possible AI use but it is hard to pinpoint exactly.

Carlos pointed to research by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, who conducted an experiment comparing AI and human test taking based on test results and response patterns. Carlos said Toton has seen distinct differences in response timing, with someone using AI often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker. Carlos said AI can get some things wrong, particularly questions that involve some realm of human judgment. Marks said certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions. Carlos noted a huge boom of people testing fast and receiving high scores, though no concrete data exists that says it is all due to AI.

Carlos said traditional threats like harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, or collusion proxy testing have evolved as people use AI as an unauthorized aid. She said the problem is still in its infancy stage. Exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor, from Meta Glasses to AI browsers and deepfakes. The industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols to keep certifications credible. Carlos said she and her team will look more at the trend of fast testing and high scores because of organizational interest and concern over its growth.

Marks said many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional, have and continue to evolve to address how AI is impacting security best practices. He said new AI-specific security certifications are also entering the market. The Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations. Marks said that as certifications evolve, especially with AI playing a key role in so many facets of work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing. Carlos said cheating is a risk that has existed for as long as testing has.

Articles.Title: As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
stories.Summary:
Ransomware and data extortion attacks have risen sharply in recent months, according to researchers who track the field, as reported by WIRED on November 14, 2026. Some researchers put the number of alleged attacks posted on leak sites, where groups name supposed victims, at nearly 3,000 over the summer. By some estimates that is a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring. Researchers say the volume always moves up and down somewhat, but attacks have stayed consistently and worryingly high in recent years.

Cynthia Kaiser, a former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research at the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon, said most of the recent increase came from international attacks, while the United States was steadier but still high. She said the international rise is the really new part and is partly fueled by AI. Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, said AI is being used more heavily in parts of the attack chain, such as writing better phishing emails and handling negotiations, but successful groups are still largely run by humans. He said the heavy experimentation with AI means this could change, and change quickly.

Halcyon's analysis says around 111 ransomware groups claimed attacks between July and September this year. The Gentlemen, Qilin and Akira have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations, with smaller groups and new actors in their shadow. ReliaQuest's analysis found one new group, Global Secret Group, claimed 48 victims, more than half listed on the same day, while another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest, said the growth happened because AI has accelerated these actors, essentially letting them go out and start their own groups. Tirado said his team identified the person behind one new group as an inexperienced teenager who made more than $800,000 in under two weeks, and he declined to name the teen publicly.

Researchers told Kernel Panic they have seen more lone-wolf operators instead of people tied to traditional ransomware-as-a-service providers. Kaiser said more actors are using AI to try to strike out on their own, with abilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code and even compromise other groups' remote-access tools for backup access to a victim. She suspects many of these upstarts may surge and then burn out, because they lack the knowledge and resources of established groups. Liska said the number of attacks Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total for 2025, but the number involving encryption may actually fall year over year.

Articles.Title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom

stories.Headline: Korea's AI windfall comes with risks: Rogoff
stories.Summary:
Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff warned on Thursday that a burst of the AI bubble could hit South Korea especially hard. He spoke at a panel discussion after a lecture on secular stagnation at the Bank of Korea in central Seoul. Rogoff is a Harvard University economics professor and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund. He said the bursting of the AI bubble is clearly going to happen at some point and will be very painful, and very painful in Korea.

Rogoff cautioned the Korean government against expanding spending commitments too aggressively during economic upswings. He warned that the AI-driven boom could expose the economy to greater volatility and said Korea starts from a very favorable position, which will make demands very big. He also warned that rapidly expanding AI could push up living costs and resource prices, including land and minerals, saying AI will devour many resources. He acknowledged that Korea has majorly benefited from the AI boom and is in a more favorable position than economies that missed the expansion, describing it as being like a suburb of Silicon Valley.

Rogoff also highlighted growing generational tensions as a major challenge for Korea. He noted that older generations hold a disproportionate share of wealth and housing assets, while younger workers face greater exposure to AI-driven labor market disruption. He said this will involve reshaping how money is spent and how things are done across many societies, and called it the biggest pressure on budgets and fiscal policy. He framed the task as cutting a deal between the elderly, who worked very hard and created a great country, and young people who need to have hope.

On monetary policy, Rogoff welcomed the Bank of Korea's efforts to internationalize the Korean won. He said wider use of the currency in cross-border transactions could reduce costs and strengthen the economy's resilience. He said the won obviously is not going to be a global currency, but Korea can still get a lot of benefits by internationalizing it. He said he gathers the Bank of Korea is moving to do that and called it very smart, saving a lot of costs and protecting Korea to some extent, and said modern technology makes this possible in a way that was not much cheaper before.

Articles.Title: Korea's AI windfall comes with risks: Rogoff

stories.Headline: CI Guarantee marks 30th anniversary with AI-driven innovation push
stories.Summary:
CI Guarantee, South Korea's leading construction guarantee provider, marked its 30th anniversary on Thursday with a ceremony at the Westin Josun Seoul. The event brought together about 250 guests, including Kim Sung-hwan, director of the construction industry division at the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, and Nam Young-hee, Incheon's deputy mayor for balanced development. Former chairmen and executives of member companies also attended. At the ceremony, the organization announced plans to speed up AI-driven innovation and expand digital financial services.

CI Guarantee unveiled a new long-term vision called "A Leap Forward in Trust: Building the Next 100 Years through AI Innovation." Under this vision, the organization aims to improve the safety and efficiency of its asset management and to upgrade digital financial services for members. The article says the organization was established in May 1966 with government approval and 3,221 member companies. By the end of 2025, membership had grown to 10,054, and total assets reached 1.55 trillion won, or about 1.16 billion dollars. It began with guarantees for construction-related transactions and later expanded into lending and mutual aid, offering eight mutual aid products.

Choi Un-gu, acting chairman of CI Guarantee, said the organization's 30-year history was one of partnership built on the trust and solidarity of its members through difficult times. He said it would build on that trust and embrace AI and digital innovation to become a more accessible and reliable financial partner for members. He added that this would help shape the next 100 years of the mechanical construction industry. The article also says the organization has recently lowered guarantee and mutual aid fees and expanded digital services, including self-serve guarantees and Kakao-based guarantee services, to cut costs and improve accessibility for members.

Articles.Title: CI Guarantee marks 30th anniversary with AI-driven innovation push

stories.Headline: Caixin Summit: China’s AI Push Needs More Than Better Model Rankings
stories.Summary:
Tony Chan spoke via video on November 13 during the 17th Caixin Summit. He is a former president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and a member of the U.S. National Academy of Engineering. Chan addressed the current state of the artificial intelligence industry in China. He urged the nation to prioritize genuine innovation over simple model rankings.

The speaker suggested that China should leverage its supply chains, traditional industries, and culture. He argued against merely increasing parameter counts for large models or trying to avoid export sanctions. Chan noted that Chinese models reach 90 to 95 percent of benchmark performance compared to U.S. versions. He estimated that the gap between the two countries is less than six months.

Chan stated that China currently leads in AI applications, mature-process chips, and renewable energy. However, he acknowledged that the U.S. maintains an advantage in capital markets, advanced chips, and top scholars. He expressed doubt that increasing computing power alone would lead to artificial general intelligence. He believes the industry must earn respect through original approaches.

The context of these remarks involves a competitive landscape where open-source models and lower costs pressure U.S. firms. Chan believes that focusing on these strengths will better position China in the global market. He emphasized that the goal should be creating value rather than chasing rankings. The summit provided a platform to discuss these strategic shifts for the future.

Articles.Title: Caixin Summit: China’s AI Push Needs More Than Better Model Rankings - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Man who used AI to fake 900 million won balance and fool judge gets 7 years
stories.Summary:
A South Korean man was sentenced to seven years in prison on Thursday for fraud and forgery. He used artificial intelligence to create fake documents to deceive victims and a judge. These crimes took place between July 2025 and January of this year. The man posed as a businessman and a doctor to carry out his schemes.

The defendant swindled two victims out of 377 million won, which is about 283,000 dollars. He used AI to forge a medical license certificate and cryptocurrency trade records. He also faked a prosecution notice and bank statements. One forged certificate claimed he had over 900 million won, though the account only held 23 won.

The Busan District Court’s Eastern Branch handed down the sentence. The judge stated that the man's indiscriminate forgery of public and private documents was extremely dangerous. The court noted that the victims were not compensated and had not forgiven him. Because of these factors, the judge gave a longer sentence than the six years requested by prosecutors.

The man initially avoided jail when he used the fake balance certificate to convince a judge to reject an arrest warrant. He claimed through his lawyer that he could use those funds to pay back his victims. Prosecutors later discovered the document was a fraud and secured a second warrant. The man was then taken into custody for his crimes.

Articles.Title: Man who used AI to fake 900 million won balance and fool judge gets 7 years

stories.Headline: US uses French supermarket cyberattacks to smear Chinese AI, fueling broader tech containment push: analyst
stories.Summary:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed on Thursday that a Chinese AI model caused cyberattacks on French supermarkets. These attacks targeted refrigeration systems and occurred in October, causing food to spoil. Bessent spoke at the Heritage Foundation and alleged that Chinese AI tools lack necessary guardrails. He stated that these models are dangerous to global security.

The attacks affected 150 grocery stores across France by exploiting remote management interfaces. Hackers activated forced-defrost functions and raised temperatures to 50 C, destroying vast amounts of food. These actions caused losses that could reach millions of euros. China's Ministry of State Security highlighted these events on October 28 to warn about threats to physical infrastructure.

Professor Hu Qimu of Huaqiao University criticized the US for making these claims without public technical evidence. He argued that Washington is using the incident to smear Chinese technology and justify containment. Hu stated that cybersecurity should rely on objective analysis rather than political accusations. He noted that the US frequently restricts Chinese firms based on national security.

French authorities previously accused Iran's Revolutionary Guard of responsibility for the October attacks. They warned that there would be consequences for the Iranian group. Meanwhile, China promoted its 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan to encourage international cooperation. Hu suggested that nations should work together to prevent the misuse of technology.

Articles.Title: US uses French supermarket cyberattacks to smear Chinese AI, fueling broader tech containment push: analyst - Global Times

stories.Headline: From human-guided learning to self-evolution: How AI is learning to drive itself
stories.Summary:
At the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, a new stage of autonomous driving was presented. Xu Shanquan, who leads government affairs at Pony.ai, explained that artificial intelligence has evolved beyond the need for human tutoring. This shift allows AI to manage difficult driving scenarios with greater stability and efficiency. The technology now focuses on self-evolution to improve its own performance.

This transition requires AI to move toward a system of self-diagnosis and targeted evolution. By removing the reliance on human guidance, the software can identify its own errors and correct them. These changes ensure that the vehicles operate with higher safety standards. The goal is to create a system that learns independently to handle complex road conditions.

Xu Shanquan is the official responsible for sharing these updates from Pony.ai. He stated that the technology has moved past the phase of being taught by humans. According to Xu, the AI is now capable of evolving on its own to solve tough cases. He emphasized that this process increases the overall safety and reliability of the driving system.

Articles.Title: From human-guided learning to self-evolution: How AI is learning to drive itself - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Chinese medical team explores AI solutions for radiology in Tanzania
stories.Summary:
Ji Yugang, a radiologist with the 36th Chinese medical team, began exploring AI solutions for radiology in Zanzibar, Tanzania. This effort started after he noticed that Mnazi Mmoja Hospital lacked the AI tools he used in China. He found it difficult to manually review hundreds of images per patient without software assistance. The team arrived in Zanzibar on September 16 with 24 members. These specialists are divided between Unguja Island and Pemba Island.

The initiative focuses on introducing AI-assisted imaging for pulmonary nodule detection to improve diagnostic efficiency. Ji noted that his hospital in China adopted this technology eight to 10 years ago. The process requires training local doctors on AI principles, practical applications, and the necessity of professional verification. The team is also considering a system to send anonymized data to China for expert review. This would help local doctors overcome the current lack of software.

Team leader Wang Wei stated that the group provides clinical services, technical support, and professional training. He explained that the doctors also conduct free consultations in rural areas and mobile outreach programs. Local radiologist Saria Awesu Omar said the training is very important because it reduces workloads. She believes the technology will help doctors identify tiny lesions in the abdomen and chest. Omar added that the cooperation improves patient care and strengthens the friendship between the two nations.

The team currently uses real-time remote consultations to connect Zanzibar doctors with specialists in Chinese hospitals. They are working to resolve challenges regarding network connectivity and the anonymization of patient data. These steps are necessary before the AI analysis system can be used on a larger scale. The project aims to integrate mature Chinese medical experiences into the Tanzanian healthcare system. This collaboration allows local medical professionals to gain new skills.

Articles.Title: Chinese medical team explores AI solutions for radiology in Tanzania - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Meta left AI videos of athlete abuse up after user reports — until journalists stepped in
stories.Summary:
Meta failed to remove AI-generated videos showing the abuse of young female athletes until journalists intervened. Reporter Maggie Harrison Dupré and her team at Futurism discovered the content during an investigation. They used a personal Facebook account to flag the material for review. The company initially ignored these reports and kept the accounts active.

The team flagged 10 pages that showed older male coaches inappropriately touching athletes who appeared to be teenagers. Meta initially cleared eight of these accounts, claiming they did not violate community standards. Two other accounts disappeared for unknown reasons. After Futurism provided the list of accounts directly to the company, Meta finally deactivated the remaining pages.

Meta is responsible for the moderation failures and later admitted that mistakes were made. The company claimed that it moderates content proactively and that abuse has no place on its platform. However, Harrison Dupré argued that deleting specific accounts flagged by journalists is not true moderation. She expressed disappointment that the platform failed to be proactive against abusive AI material.

The reporter noted that new pages sharing similar videos appeared daily during her investigation. Facebook even recommended this abusive content to her account. Harrison Dupré warned that account-by-account enforcement cannot keep up with the speed of AI generation. She continues to see similar pages in her recommendations despite the deletions.

Articles.Title: Meta left AI videos of athlete abuse up after user reports — until journalists stepped in

stories.Headline: Microsoft vs. Meta: enterprise AI distribution against monetization speed
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Corporation and Meta Platforms Inc are competing for dominance in the artificial intelligence sector as of November 13, 2026. Microsoft is focusing on enterprise distribution, while Meta is prioritizing the speed of monetization. Both companies have invested heavily in infrastructure to secure their positions. This competition highlights a struggle between building a broad business ecosystem and achieving immediate financial returns.

Microsoft reported FY2026 revenue of $331.84B with 17.8% growth, while Meta reported FY2025 revenue of $200.97B with 22.2% growth. Both firms spent roughly 35% of their revenue on capital expenditures, specifically 34.9% for Microsoft and 34.7% for Meta. As of September 30, 2026, Microsoft had a P/E of 27.2x and Meta had a P/E of 21.5x. Microsoft's annualized AI revenue exceeded $37B by June 2026, and it generated $66.99B in levered free cash flow by June 30, 2026.

Analysts suggest that Microsoft leads in distribution through Azure, GitHub, and Copilot, but must prove its massive spending can create profitable workloads. Meta is seen as leading in efficiency because it applies AI directly to content ranking and advertising. Meta's revenue reached $64.60B as of October 21, 2026, though its shares dropped 6.54% following that release. Experts note that the market is now demanding clear proof of returns from both tech giants.

The current landscape is a race between distribution and monetization speed rather than a battle of specific models. Microsoft offers more options for enterprises, but Meta converts AI improvements into advertising revenue more quickly. Investors remain tense as they weigh these different strategies. The market will continue to penalize uncertain payback periods while rewarding clear financial returns.

Articles.Title: Microsoft vs. Meta: enterprise AI distribution against monetization speed

stories.Headline: Microsoft says service is returning to normal, AI not to blame for ‘historic’ outage
stories.Summary:
Microsoft said its services were returning to normal after a global outage that disrupted work for millions of customers, and it said artificial intelligence was not to blame. The disruption began around midday Thursday and affected Outlook email, Teams messaging and the Copilot AI assistant. The company said the underlying issue was resolved and that the cause was a technical issue not related to cyber activity or AI. Microsoft said it saw broad recovery and stability across its services.

The outage hit government workers, hospital employees, business owners and students. Hospitals in the UK temporarily relied on paper records, according to the BBC, and pharmacies there were concerned about filling prescriptions. US congressional staffers told Politico that the outage derailed policy negotiations. Microsoft said it restored services gradually and validated stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration. The company promised a post mortem later.

Microsoft said initial information showed the outage was not the result of a malicious attack. Cybersecurity expert and former Microsoft employee Katie Moussouris told The Post that the global scale and the duration made the incident historic. She noted that Microsoft’s alert system appeared not to work and said something really bad must have happened for the cascade to last so long and for the company to be unable to recover. The company is a major partner with OpenAI and Anthropic, and both saw technical failures with their products during the outage, according to reports.

The disruption came during a challenging time for Microsoft, which recently offered buyouts to more than a quarter of its workforce, 60,000 employees, as it looked to cut costs and restructure staff for AI. Last year the company laid off 9,000 employees. Industry experts and users on social media conjectured that the cost cutting brought on the outage, though they offered no evidence. Microsoft has been doubling down on building AI infrastructure and securing partnerships with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Articles.Title: Microsoft says service is returning to normal, AI not to blame for ‘historic’ outage

stories.Headline: "No path to real use": a veteran Microsoft AI scientist quits, says research that could halve AI costs wasn't even seriously considered
stories.Summary:
John Langford, a veteran researcher, left Microsoft in November 2026. He co-founded the AI Frontiers lab and worked there for over 14 years. His group of roughly 50 people was absorbed into Microsoft AI in September. Langford claims the company ignored research that could halve AI costs. He believes the current leadership only cares about scaling models.

Microsoft AI was formed in March 2024 by Mustafa Suleyman and Karén Simonyan. AI Frontiers was reorganized into this division in early September 2026. Langford previously joined the New York City lab in May 2012. He developed Vowpal Wabbit and served as ICML president from 2019 to 2021. His Full Bandwidth Transformer research was published in August.

Langford stated that Microsoft AI has a philosophy of scaling and aggressively not research. He said he was not comfortable at a company where his work had no path to use. He believes the deal to do good work for good results is broken. He described the current situation as a bit of a train wreck. He noted that his team was non-consensually reorganized.

An anonymous commenter moving into Microsoft AI expressed similar feelings to Langford. ByteDance's Seed team published Recycler on October 25, which uses similar methods. Langford says this proves his research could match models of twice the size. This affects an industry with investments approaching a trillion dollars. Microsoft is also offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees.

Langford created AI Frontiers in 2023 after the release of ChatGPT. The group developed the AutoGen framework and the Fara-7B computer use model. Microsoft Research previously produced Phi small language models for the Edge browser. Satya Nadella has discussed 20 million AI agents doing work. Microsoft is scaling back Copilot features in Windows 11.

AI Frontiers is over and will not offer internships next year. Microsoft's AI Frontiers page says the lab continues to pursue frontier research. The company is building a superintelligence lab announced at Build 2026. Langford believes Microsoft could become attractive for research if leaders develop more wisdom. The articles leave open if Microsoft will respond publicly.

Articles.Title: "No path to real use": a veteran Microsoft AI scientist quits, says research that could halve AI costs wasn't even seriously considered

stories.Headline: AI-enabled motors power robotic arms
stories.Summary:
Metanergy Inc. has developed robotic arms that are powered by AI-enabled motors. This technology was highlighted in a report published on November 11, 2026. These motors allow the robotic systems to operate with greater intelligence. The integration of AI enables the arms to move independently.

The system requires specific motor and posture control to function. These AI-enabled components change how industrial machinery operates by increasing overall efficiency. The technology allows the robotic arms to manage their own movements. No other specific dates or numbers were provided regarding the requirements.

Wang Lei, who serves as the board secretary and special assistant to the general manager at Metanergy Inc., is responsible for these details. He stated that artificial intelligence is becoming more prominent in industrial settings. According to Wang, these specialized motors make the entire system smarter. He believes the technology significantly improves operational efficiency.

The context of this development is the growing role of AI within industrial scenarios. The robotic arms use these motors to achieve autonomous movement. The provided text does not mention what will happen next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI-enabled motors power robotic arms - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: As Microsoft services return online, company says outage wasn't caused by AI or cyberattack
stories.Summary:
Microsoft services including Outlook, Teams and its Copilot AI tool went down starting Thursday, and the outage lasted more than 24 hours as of Friday morning, affecting millions of customers worldwide. Microsoft said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. The company said it had addressed the underlying issue and was continuing to restore service to remaining customers and regions. It is estimated the outage could have cost billions of dollars in lost productivity.

Microsoft said there was no indication the outage was the result of malicious or cyber activity, and it also said the disruption was not caused by artificial intelligence. The company's statements appeared to be an attempt to push back on rumors circulating online that linked the outage to Microsoft laying off experienced workers or increasingly relying on AI in its workflows. Despite the disruptions, many people took to social media to celebrate what became an impromptu work holiday. The outage was reported by KUOW, which covers artificial intelligence, tech and the local economy in the Pacific Northwest.

Microsoft, based in Redmond, Washington, is responsible for the services and issued the statements about the cause. The company said the incident came from an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. It said it had addressed the underlying issue and was restoring service to remaining customers and regions. Microsoft also confirmed there was no indication of malicious or cyber activity.

The outage hit Outlook, Teams and Copilot starting Thursday and was still affecting customers more than 24 hours later on Friday morning. Microsoft said service was being restored to remaining customers and regions after the underlying issue was addressed. The company's update came as rumors spread online about the cause, including claims tied to layoffs and AI use. Many customers celebrated the forced break on social media.

Articles.Title: As Microsoft services return online, company says outage wasn't caused by AI or cyberattack

stories.Headline: Huang's exit puts Nvidia leadership, AI policy in focus
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as the president, chief executive, and board member of Nvidia on Thursday, November 13, 2026. His immediate departure followed his admission of an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman and reports of two other affairs with company employees. This sudden leadership change caused Nvidia shares to drop as much as 14 percent, eventually closing at $166.19. The company ended the day with a market value of $4.01 trillion.

The company now requires a permanent replacement for Huang, while Colette Kress, the chief financial officer and executive vice-president, will serve as the interim chief executive. The board is currently reviewing both internal and external candidates for the role. This transition occurs as the stock has fallen about 30 percent from its peak in October. Meanwhile, the company faces intense scrutiny from Congress and the FBI regarding national security and chip sales.

House Speaker Mike Johnson stated that there is a growing consensus in Congress to limit the export of semiconductor chips to China. Analysts from SemiAnalysis, including founder Dylan Patel, suggested that restrictions on China will likely accelerate now that Huang, a primary defender of market access, is gone. Ker Gibbs, a former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, noted that Nvidia lost its most effective advocate for the Chinese market. He believes the company will become more cautious and spend less time lobbying against export controls.

The situation may shift the balance of influence in Washington, as Huang had unique access to the White House. Lawmakers are considering whether Huang should provide congressional testimony this month to determine if national security was compromised. Observers will now monitor next week's earnings and forward guidance for signs of customer hesitation. Future developments depend on the selection of a permanent leader and the results of ongoing government investigations.

Articles.Title: Huang's exit puts Nvidia leadership, AI policy in focus - China Daily

stories.Headline: Nvidia continues to be ‘connective tissue’ of AI trade, investment strategist says
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a television segment rather than a news event. The segment aired on Fox Business on November 13, 2026, as part of the program Claman’s Power Players. It featured Eric Freedman, chief investment officer at Northern Trust Wealth Management, and Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management. The two discussed market trends and the artificial intelligence trade, and the segment was titled around the idea that Nvidia remains the connective tissue of the AI trade.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond those already listed. They do not describe any requirement, rule or change resulting from the discussion. The only timing detail is the air date of November 13, 2026, and the video’s listed date of November 14, 2026. No specific figures on Nvidia, the AI trade or the market are provided.

Freedman and Arone are identified by their firms and titles, and the segment is attributed to the Claman’s Power Players show. The articles do not paraphrase any further remarks from either guest beyond the framing about Nvidia. No other person is named as responsible for anything described. The material is presented as a video clip and carries a standard copyright notice from Fox News Network.

The context given is limited to market trends and the artificial intelligence trade as a topic of discussion. The articles do not say what happens next, and they include no follow-up plans or announcements. They also note that all market data is delayed by 20 minutes. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia continues to be ‘connective tissue’ of AI trade, investment strategist says

stories.Headline: Osaic in talks with Anthropic as AI reshapes advisor workforce
stories.Summary:
Osaic, one of the largest independent broker-dealer networks in the U.S., is in talks with Anthropic, the maker of Claude, an executive told InvestmentNews. Cindy Hamel, Osaic's head of business operations and execution, confirmed the talks during an interview at ConnectED 2026, the firm's flagship conference held November 8 to 11 in Atlanta. She said Osaic has had active conversations with Anthropic on a number of different topics and that those will continue. The talks come after Stifel Financial announced on November 10 that it is working with Anthropic to rebuild its advisor dashboard platform with Claude.

Osaic has about 10,000 advisors in its network and over $800 billion in assets under administration. Charles Schwab in September became the first RIA custodian to integrate Claude for Financial Advisors, and LPL Financial in February added Anthropic's AI plug-ins for its more than 30,000 advisors. Hamel said any AI partnership for Osaic would put client data security first, including keeping client information secure within a private ecosystem the firm wants to create. In August, Osaic named Sayee Bellamkonda its first chief AI and technology officer, a newly created role covering advisor and client-facing technology, including AI and cybersecurity.

Shannon Reid, Osaic's president and head of advisor growth and engagement, said being non self-clearing lets the firm plug in vetted third-party tools faster and unplug them faster if something better comes along. CEO Jamie Price described a plug and play ecosystem where advisors can choose from tools such as Jump, Zocks, GReminders, Vanilla and Redtail CRM. He said note takers Jump and Zocks reached 35% uptake among Osaic advisors in six months, a pace he said he had never seen for a tool. Price said the firm's job is to stay agnostic to any tool and move data bidirectionally so advisors get the most efficiency and capabilities.

McKinsey & Co. projects a shortfall of 90,000 to 110,000 advisors by 2034 at current productivity levels. Price said AI may let Osaic's existing workforce fill that gap by freeing its 9,000 registered assistants, who support 10,000 advisors, to face clients more often. He said most of those assistants won't do the same work as today because much of the administration is being automated, and they are already licensed. Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry also said earlier this year that AI will help solve the industry's talent shortage, and in 2025 Schwab said the RIA industry would need 70,000 new hires by 2030 to keep up with current growth trends.

Articles.Title: Osaic in talks with Anthropic as AI reshapes advisor workforce

stories.Headline: Thailand expects AI industry to reach 12.2 bln USD by 2030 - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The National Board of Digital Economy and Society Office announced on Friday, November 13, 2026, that Thailand's artificial intelligence industry is poised for significant growth. The agency expects the sector to reach a value of 412 billion baht, or roughly 12.2 billion U.S. dollars, by 2030. This represents a substantial increase from the 187 billion baht, or 5.5 billion dollars, estimated for the current year. The growth is fueled by government support, foreign data center investments, and the nation's role as a global exporter of AI hardware.

This expansion requires a compound annual growth rate of 20.5 percent between 2025 and 2030, starting from an estimated 162 billion baht in 2025. Currently, hardware and infrastructure account for 72 percent of the industry's value and 86.6 percent of the 31.1 billion baht, or 921 million dollars, invested last year. Data from the National Electronics and Computer Technology Center shows that 53.7 percent of Thai organizations use AI this year, compared to 17.8 percent in 2024. Meanwhile, software and data services are growing the fastest at 26.3 percent annually.

The BDE is responsible for these projections and clarified that the figures measure the AI value chain rather than the gross domestic product. The agency noted that while demand for high-performance computing will drive investment, several risks exist. These challenges include a lack of AI talent, a dependence on imported graphics processing units, and energy supply issues for data centers. The agency believes that as AI spreads to the broader economy, more investment will flow into software, data platforms, and model development.

Articles.Title: Thailand expects AI industry to reach 12.2 bln USD by 2030 - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Do U.S. air traffic control and email blackouts after China AI espionage have a common answer?
stories.Summary:
The United States suffered two major infrastructure blackouts on November 12 and 13, 2026. Microsoft services failed first, followed by a nationwide grounding of all departing flights. These events occurred shortly after a major espionage scandal involving China. The disruptions caused massive economic losses and widespread travel chaos. The FAA grounded flights at 3:54 p.m.

ET on November 13 across 22 centers. Microsoft services failed at 11:17 a.m. ET on November 12 in 74 countries. The flight stop delayed 10,243 flights and cancelled 3,234 within four hours. Microsoft 365 outages affected 19 services and millions of its 450 million paid seats.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the aviation crisis a communication issue under investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin provided no clear answers or timeline for a fix. Microsoft initially denied malicious activity before blaming a network capacity upgrade flaw. They first cited elevated load and then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out.

The outages incapacitated the U.S. House of Representatives and a federal appeals court. Britain's Parliament and National Health Service, plus Australia's spy agency and police, were affected. One risk adviser estimates Microsoft's bill in the billions for Australia alone. Many travelers were sent home as airports warned that cancellations would persist for days.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. This happened as lawmakers demanded tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China. The FBI lost 1,500 special agents and CISA lost nearly 1,000 staffers since Trump returned. Aviation infrastructure upgrades would have cost 40 billion dollars despite trillion dollar Pentagon spending.

Experts warn that AI enabled hacking is spreading and targeting unknown flaws. China's Volt Typhoon hackers have reportedly burrowed into American energy, water, and transportation networks. Some researchers suggest these blackouts may not be coincidental given Beijing's history of diverting attention. The articles leave open whether these events were malicious attacks or infrastructure degradation.

Articles.Title: Do U.S. air traffic control and email blackouts after China AI espionage have a common answer?

stories.Headline: Chinese company unveils AI-powered laser mosquito zapper - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A Chinese company recently launched a new laser device designed to kill mosquitoes. This technology uses artificial intelligence to track the insects while they are flying. Once a target is identified, the machine burns the wings of the mosquito. The product was unveiled on November 13, 2026.

The system relies on autonomous technology to operate effectively. This specific design ensures that the laser remains safe for humans. It also prevents the device from harming pets in the home. The company intends for this to be a modern solution for pest control.

The developers of the device are responsible for its safety features. They claim the AI can distinguish between pests and other objects. This allows the laser to fire only at the intended targets. They believe this represents the future of eliminating insects.

The company introduced this tool as a high-tech alternative to traditional zappers. It aims to provide a more precise way to handle infestations. The device is now available for use in various environments. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Chinese company unveils AI-powered laser mosquito zapper - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Jasmin Lau on pushing harder on flexible work, ‘hot seat’ portfolio of manpower and AI
stories.Summary:
Acting Manpower Minister Jasmin Lau gave her first interview to local media since taking the role at the Ministry of Manpower in July's Cabinet reshuffle. In the interview, published on 13 November 2026, she said the ministry must do a lot more to push flexible work arrangements. She suggested shining a light on good employers and workplace culture as one way to do this. She also said her own experience as a working mother has been sometimes a bit painful and a bit of a struggle.

Lau said parents have told her that policies such as childcare leave exist but can be hard to ask for or apply for. The hesitation is not that they are not allowed to take the leave, but that they are committed to their work and find it hard to get colleagues to take over, she said. Guidelines on flexible work arrangements were put in place in 2024 and set out a process for workers to request changes like different locations or timings. An MOM report released in May said 84.5% of employees who needed a flexible work arrangement received one, but the rate at which workers request such arrangements is low.

Lau, who is 43 and a mother of two boys, said policies alone are not enough and that she feels she really needs to do something for working parents. She entered politics at the 2025 general election and is also Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information. She said her portfolio covering workforce transformation and artificial intelligence strategy is extremely hot and very relevant to what people want to understand. She said many firms here use AI in areas like digital marketing but have not used it deeply in business processes such as inventory management, warehousing and just-in-time delivery, which is partly why workers here have not been so affected yet.

She said she is conflicted daily about what deeper AI use would mean for affected workers, which is why firms need to do things like job redesign. The recent retrenchments at GovTech, where she is minister-in-charge, provided learning points, including that a long transition period can weigh on workers every single day. She said retrenchment experiences are highly personal and emotional, and some workers may need time to process the news before seeking career support. She said life is exhausting on all days for her and that the idea of work-life balance that keeps a working mother happy and healthy is very hard to achieve.

Articles.Title: Jasmin Lau on pushing harder on flexible work, ‘hot seat’ portfolio of manpower and AI - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: How China gets the Nvidia chips it needs to develop AI
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a Chinese executive at a Singapore company. This company is suspected by the United States of smuggling artificial intelligence microchips into China. The scandal occurred around November 2026 and highlighted how China obtains cutting edge chips. China remains a major AI power despite strict US export restrictions on advanced hardware. These events have focused global attention on the methods used to bypass trade controls.

Washington bans the export of top end Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China for security reasons. In 2026, the US eased controls on the less powerful H200 chip for sales. The United States takes a 25 percent cut of those H200 sales under the new policy. These restrictions aim to keep top US AI labs in the lead and limit military applications. The policy affects shipments to China and involves the US government and Nvidia.

Jensen Huang lobbied the US government to allow sales, warning that restrictions fuel competitive home grown alternatives. Nvidia told The Information that reports of chip smuggling seem far fetched and lack evidence. White House adviser Michael Kratsios said Moonshot AI accessed high end Nvidia chips in Thailand. Stephen Wu stated that export controls restrict where a chip is shipped, not who uses it. Lian Jye Su said Chinese vendors still use cutting edge Nvidia chips to train models.

Chinese start ups including Moonshot AI, Z.ai and DeepSeek have launched high performing models using these chips. DeepSeek reportedly used thousands of chips dismantled overseas and brought into China in December 2025. Customers in Shenzhen can log in to GPUs located in Malaysia's Johor region to bypass rules. Washington has accused Chinese AI labs of training systems to mimic the capabilities of US models. These activities allow Chinese firms to maintain AI development despite the official American trade bans.

Nvidia GPUs were originally created for 3D visuals in video games but now train colossal digital data. The 2022 launch of ChatGPT sparked an investment gold rush among tech giants and various governments. Nvidia's market valuation soared to 4.5 trillion US dollars, making it as valuable as Apple. Chinese electricity is cheap and chips are state subsidised, which helps offset higher engineering costs. Training on Chinese chips usually takes more time and more engineering than using Nvidia hardware.

Huawei is the top competitor in China and will reportedly provide chips for the next DeepSeek model. Huawei said in September that its next generation AI chip will be ready by early 2027. This release is three quarters earlier than planned to help China match the power of Nvidia. The articles leave open whether the US will implement tighter curbs due to the smuggling. It remains unclear if Beijing will increase purchases of the approved H200 chips from Nvidia.

stories.Headline: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race
stories.Summary:
China's Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive, has been at the centre of a controversy over an alleged extra-marital affair and claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. Commentators and social media have turned the saga into widespread entertainment, with memes and influencer gags spreading online. The matter has also prompted questions about its effect on the frontier artificial intelligence race between the United States and China. Analysts see the episode as a potential shift in that contest, one that could influence how the two countries compete in AI development. The coverage gives the story a central place in the wider debate over AI leadership.

Huang has long been seen as a villain by many US hawks because he has argued for relaxing restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. The latest allegations have added to hawkish views about him, and the scrutiny extends to concerns over alleged corporate espionage. An HT analysis of trade data shows China has rising import dependence on commodities that are likely GPUs or related products. The United States has tried to restrict China's access to cutting-edge chips and GPUs, while China has limited rare earth mineral supplies to the US. The Pax Silica alliance, launched by the US in December 2025, is designed to ease American access to rare earth minerals.

China has denied the allegations of spying and has downplayed the controversy, as expected. The Straits Times writer argues that some pain for Nvidia could help secure the West's AI lead over China in the long run. Commentators disagree on how much China needs Nvidia's chips, and the actual evidence on that question is not clear. The HT analysis notes that the disclosure of Huang's affair is certain to add paranoia in the US AI ecosystem about a Chinese catch-up. The writer's view is that Nvidia's weakening might also spur competition and innovation.

China's trade surplus is expected to exceed a trillion dollars for a second consecutive year in 2026, according to the HT report. China released the open-source reasoning model DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025, bringing it within striking distance of leading frontier AI developers, all based in the US. A Lowy Institute report shows Chinese models are catching up fast with American models, although the US leads China in every AI field except human resources. A Carnegie China report, cited by HT, indicates China is catching up quickly with the US in skilled AI workforce. Huawei announced a new chip-design approach in May 2026 that could limit the effect of US export controls.

The articles leave open whether the constraints on chips and rare earths will matter in the long term, and whether either side will crack its challenge before those constraints become redundant. The Lowy Institute report says Huawei could design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to TSMC's 2028 chips, but whether this succeeds is not yet known. Beijing countered the Pax Silica alliance with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization earlier in 2026. The articles do not say how the allegations against Huang will ultimately be resolved or how Nvidia's position will change.

stories.Headline: What’s Working: What happens when AI bots take over landscaping? An Aspen company finds out
stories.Summary:
Jeff Margulies, owner of Good Earth landscaping and maintenance in Aspen, began using Claude AI about a year before the article, around late 2025, to streamline his business. The bots work inside AI add-ons he built to enhance his company software, Aspire. His brother, who once ran a custom software development business with around 30 offshore developers, helped him find where AI could apply. Margulies bought into Good Earth after a career in finance, and in 2018 the company had just a handful of employees. Good Earth has grown by a factor of six under Margulies, who is 41 and a father of two, and now employs 60 to 70 people.

The company does weekly maintenance and mowing, garden care, native plant management, restoration, irrigation and full landscape installations. Employees must use camera phones or tablets to snap pictures and clock in and out of each project, and project managers update the clock-in information daily to gauge efficiency against labor estimates. Margulies says he is exploring around a dozen different AI initiatives, including some for daily use, such as creating renderings for clients and handling back-end processes and analysis. Margulies said that at a smaller scale you can get away with a lot by keeping your eye on everything, but with 60 or 70 people you need everyone aligned and aware of issues early enough to correct them. He said the company needs clear processes so everyone knows what to do and can plan to deliver on promises to clients.

He said real time job cost information lets the company see labor and material costs immediately and compare them to budget, so it can intervene quickly instead of redoing a whole project. He said Good Earth has historically under-leveraged data on worker output, which limited its ability to manage crews and make good labor-management decisions. Margulies said the deeper the company goes with the AI he is building, the more encouraged they are that they can remove the paperwork, reporting and data crunching that tend to be weaker skill sets in the industry. He said there is still lots to figure out to use the technology to its full potential, but he is reaping benefits. He said the bots are going to help Good Earth keep growing.

Articles.Title: What’s Working: What happens when AI bots take over landscaping? An Aspen company finds out

stories.Headline: Opinion | America’s AI bubble is a Ponzi scheme
stories.Summary:
Independent economist Andy Xie published an opinion piece on November 13, 2026, regarding the American artificial intelligence market. He argues that the current AI bubble is beginning to resemble a Ponzi scheme. These companies have relied heavily on a boom in data centers to secure more funding from debt markets. This circular financing system allows firms to maintain valuations reaching trillions of dollars.

The situation changes because recent midterm elections brought in state governments that doubt the mass buildout of data centers. This political shift threatens the ability of AI companies to raise necessary debt. If these centers are not built, chip shipments will likely stop. Such a disruption could cause the entire financing loop among AI firms to short circuit.

Dr. Andy Xie is the person responsible for these claims and specializes in global economics and financial markets. He suggests that many investors may be misled by excessive optimism. He questions whether informed market insiders actually believe the trillion-dollar valuations of these firms. He believes this optimism can accelerate technology but often leads to significant waste.

The context of this issue is the growth of market bubbles driven by investor hope. These bubbles can create a large pool of people who do not understand the risks. The author warns that the current financial structure is unstable. He believes the reliance on debt and infrastructure makes the industry vulnerable.

stories.Headline: 2028 — A pit dug by the US midterm election for the AI upstream supply chain
stories.Summary:
In November 2026 the US midterm election results were released, and the Democratic Party secured control of both chambers of Congress and won gubernatorial seats in Texas and Ohio. Morgan Stanley's report Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the US Midterms concluded that about 5GW of US data center construction capacity would be postponed from 2028 to 2029. That figure equals 20% of the country's new capacity that year and 10% of global new capacity. The delay would cut year-on-year growth of new GW-scale US data center capacity by 4% in 2028, before a 38% rebound in 2029. Globally, year-on-year growth would hit 9% in 2028 and 20% in 2029.

The report said Texas and Ohio had a combined data center capacity exposure of about 4.9GW on IT metrics for 2028, and those projects would be pushed back by new approval processes. Interconnection applications with ERCOT, the Texas power grid, reached about 474GW, more than five times its historical peak electricity demand, with data centers making up about 90% of new power requests. Morgan Stanley kept hyperscale capital expenditure forecasts unchanged: Google/Alphabet at US$375 billion for 2027 and US$400 billion for 2028, Meta at US$225 billion and US$250 billion, Amazon at US$355 billion and US$365 billion, and Microsoft at US$238 billion and US$298 billion. It said some projects may shift from Texas and Ohio to states such as Tennessee and Louisiana, and that 20GW of potential spillover demand may flow to Asia and the EMEA region. Meta states a goal of a 10x improvement in computing power efficiency by 2027, while Google's TPU 8t and 8i deliver up to 2.7x higher training performance and 80% better inference cost-performance ratio respectively than the previous generation.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's campaign platform includes suspending approval for new data centers until stronger protection measures are enacted in the Texas state legislature. Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton has proposed a conditional suspension of new data centers and new permits, requiring projects to pay 100% of natural gas, water and electricity costs and to use union labor. Morgan Stanley said the postponed projects "may create an 'air pocket' in the tech supply chain in 2028", with weakened pricing power or inventory accumulation, and possibly order slowdowns, margin normalization and earnings downgrades even if AI demand remains intact. Analysts judged that projects under construction in 2027 would basically not be affected, as newly elected governors are unlikely to disrupt projects already under construction. The report said the impact is more about postponement than cancellation.

Analysts sharply cut target prices for Asian cloud semiconductor supplier Aspeed, citing the risk of US project delays in the next 2-4 quarters. Aspeed's target price was lowered from NT$24,000 to NT$14,417, a drop of approximately 40%, and Montage's from HK$432 to HK$207, a drop of approximately 52%. Morgan Stanley's legacy memory team downgraded Winbond, GigaDevice, Powerchip and Macronix from Overweight to Neutral and Phison to Underweight, covering only DDR3/4, SLC/MLC NAND and NOR and not mainstream DDR5 or TLC/QLC NAND. The report said the 2026 EPS of these companies is still being raised and the downgrade is about "cycle inflection point management" rather than earnings collapse. Investor Puru Saxena, founder of AlphaTarget, posted that the Democratic landslide "has indeed raised reasonable questions" but that reality is more complex, that 2027 capacity is "basically intact", and that "The AI infrastructure cycle is being extended, not ended".

The report said the direct trigger for the delays comes from the US midterm elections, and that power bottlenecks have long existed, with the election result only adding policy uncertainty. It said the scarcity of completed data center assets with guaranteed power supply will rise, financing quality divergence will deepen, and neoclouds and new projects will face stricter scrutiny while large cloud vendors consolidate advantages. Morgan Stanley said financing is still available but the midterm elections should deepen quality divergence. The report said electricity, not chips, is becoming the new bottleneck in the AI race. It advised investors to focus on large cloud vendors, selected data center supply chain targets, and software enablers and AI application adopters.

The report said the market has overreacted and that the partial shift of projects from 2028 to 2029 will not undermine the overall logic of capital expenditure. It said large cloud vendors will still "build as much capacity as possible" because new large language model-powered products target billions of users and still deliver a return on capital of over 30%. It said "how much to spend" and "when the construction is completed" are two different things. The article was published by 36Kr with authorization from the WeChat Official Account Wall Street CN, authored by Long Yue. The article states it does not constitute personal investment advice and does not represent the platform's position.

stories.Headline: Claude Launches Full Office Suite AI Integration: Why Netizens Say Skipping Excel Learning Was the Right Call
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released a full suite of office features for Claude on November 12, 2026. This launch followed the recent debut of Fable 5.2. The company introduced tools for spreadsheets, whiteboards, and data analysis. Claude will also soon participate in video conferences. These updates aim to keep entire work processes within Claude.

Claude Sheets supports 100,000 cells and integrates with Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet. Whiteboards can export to Lucid, Miro, and Zoho Vani. Interactive Connectors link to Notion, Confluence, Box, HubSpot, and Adobe. Supported tools include Canva, Carta, Dropbox, Vercel, and Webflow. Figma, Harvey, and Shopify are currently building their own integrations.

Nicholas Lin, the Head of Product at Anthropic, spoke to the media. He stated that Claude Sheets is currently fairly basic. Lin noted it is not designed for complex financial modeling. He suggested using Claude for Excel or Google Workspace for professional features. The company wants Claude to participate in turning answers into deliverables.

Microsoft investors worried if people will still need to open Excel. Microsoft stock fell more than 3 percent intraday and closed down 2.2 percent. Netizens created memes about Claude taking down Microsoft's decades old Office business. Some users joked that skipping Excel learning was the right call. These tools affect teams using traditional office software and data warehouses.

Users previously had to copy Claude's generated content into other software for editing. Claude Data, formerly Claude Dashboards, moved out of beta to become officially available. It uses SQL to generate dashboards, data stories, or short explanatory videos. The system supports importing CSV, Google Sheets, and Excel files. Whiteboards support Simplified Chinese voice dictation for unformed thinking.

Claude Meetings will join video calls to draft plans and tasks in real time. It will save notes and action items on clauda.ai after meetings end. The articles do not state when Claude Meetings will be released. They leave open if Sheets can eventually replace core financial models. It remains unclear when Anthropic will ring its IPO bell.
