stories.Headline: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Artificial Intelligence Overcounts Pulmonary B-Lines Compared to Clinical Experts
stories.Summary:
A prospective clinical investigation at Skåne University Hospital in Sweden found that an automated artificial intelligence tool in a commercial point-of-care ultrasound system substantially overcounts pulmonary B-lines compared with visual reviews by expert physicians. The single-center evaluation covered fifty-five hospitalized patients with acute respiratory symptoms, primarily acutely decompensated heart failure. Investigators found poor statistical agreement between the algorithm and experienced human evaluators, driven largely by overestimation across multiple anatomical thoracic zones. The software tested was the automated B-line application embedded in the Venue GO point-of-care ultrasound platform made by General Electric Healthcare. The tool highlights and quantifies B-lines in real time across captured video loops and logs the frame with the maximum artifact count to assign a score for each scanned lung zone.

Examinations were done at the bedside by an internal medicine resident in point-of-care ultrasound training, using a curved low-frequency transducer at a standard depth of sixteen centimeters. A standardized twelve-zone thoracic protocol was used: four anterolateral zones on each side with the patient supine at forty-five degrees, then two dorsal zones on each side with the patient sitting upright. Each sector was captured for four to five seconds in the sagittal plane between adjacent ribs, and a single operator acquired every video loop across all fifty-five subjects. The tool assigned each zone a category of zero, one, two, three, four, or greater than five B-lines, recording 672 thoracic zone clips. Two independent physician experts, a cardiologist and an internal medicine consultant who directs a regional point-of-care ultrasound training academy, classified B-lines into brackets of zero, one to two, three to four, and five or more while blinded to the software.

Of the 672 clips, 574, or eighty-five percent, were eligible for statistical analysis. Ninety-eight clips were excluded: eleven for insufficient image quality, twenty-six for no identifiable pleural line, and fifty-one for pleural effusions. Twenty-two of the twenty-six clips lacking a clear pleural reflection occurred in the second left anterior zone, where cardiac motion obscured the pulmonary field. Pleural effusions were found mostly in the dependent posterior inferior zones, sixty-three percent of effusion findings, with twenty-nine percent in the lateral chest regions. The median B-line count by the artificial intelligence platform was 23.5 per patient versus 2.8 per patient by visual reviewers, a statistically significant difference.

The automated platform classified thirty-eight percent of assessed zones into the highest category of more than five B-lines, while experts assigned only four percent to that category. The software showed a bimodal distribution, with forty-eight percent of readings at zero and thirty-eight percent at greater than five, and only thirteen percent between one and four B-lines. The intraclass correlation coefficient between software and experts reached only 0.28 for the total patient B-line sum and 0.37 zone by zone, while interrater reliability between the two human experts was excellent at 0.92 and 0.91. Bland-Altman analysis showed a systematic positive bias of 1.86 with a standard deviation of 2.15 and ninety-five percent limits of agreement from negative 2.35 to positive 6.07. Among the 574 analyzed zones, fourteen percent of algorithmic errors came from the software tracking acoustic data in adjacent rib spaces rather than the central intercostal target.

In one percent of zones the software mistook subpleural consolidations with irregular acoustic shred lines, also called C-lines, for true vertical B-lines, and in another one percent it counted normal rib shadowing as pathologic vertical artifacts. Correlation was poorest in anterior zone two and posterior superior zone five, where overcounting was most pronounced, and better in the lateral and posterior inferior sectors. Reviewers recorded significantly higher total B-line sums in hypervolemic patients than in euvolemic individuals, averaging 4.6 versus 0.75 artifacts. The authors noted recruitment from a single medical center, reliance on a single image operator, and software capping granular counting at five artifacts per sector. To align categorization schemes, researchers assigned software values of one or two to 1.5 and values of three or four to 3.5 to mirror expert score ranges.

An initial evaluation by Short and colleagues cited in platform marketing materials documented an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.79 using the same software, but that study evaluated only four patients. Later assessments found lower concordance, such as an evaluation by Russell and colleagues reporting 0.56 between automated scoring and expert review. An investigation by Damodaran and colleagues in patients with viral respiratory infections recorded intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.52 to 0.53, borderline moderate agreement closer to the Swedish cohort. The Swedish study used an upright twelve-zone method including dorsal regions, whereas recent heart failure research suggests a simplified two-zone anterior-superior protocol can yield comparable diagnostic utility to an eight-zone exam. Current commercial point-of-care tools rely mainly on prespecified image-processing rules that struggle with rib margins or tissue consolidations.

The researchers concluded that automated B-line quantification in current commercial point-of-care hardware requires further algorithmic refinement before it can be safely relied upon for autonomous clinical decision-making. They noted that future improvements likely depend on deep-learning neural networks trained on extensive imaging datasets coupled with expert human visual validation. True cardiogenic B-lines generate smooth pleural reflections in a diffuse pattern, whereas comet-tail artifacts from other pulmonary disorders feature irregular, fragmented pleural reflections with narrow heads and wide tails, and the platform may struggle to differentiate these presentations. The articles do not state whether the software's manufacturer has responded to the findings or whether regulatory action followed. They also do not say whether a follow-up study or software update is planned.

Articles.Title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Artificial Intelligence Overcounts Pulmonary B-Lines Compared to Clinical Experts

stories.Headline: Google Releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x Faster Than Gemini 3.8 Flash
stories.Summary:
Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 13, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. It is a proprietary model from Google DeepMind built for coding and everyday agent loops. Google calls it its daily driver for agentic workflows, and it sits below the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon. The model card says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon, and the knowledge cutoff is March 2026.

Hydrogen has a 1,048,576-token unified window shared by input, thinking and output tokens. It runs only on Google's hosted API, with no weights and no self-hosting, and serving hardware is not disclosed. Input covers text, images, audio, video, PDFs, tables and charts, while output is text. Developers set thinking_level in generation_config to low, medium, high or a new xhigh, and the default is high rather than medium as on 3.8 Flash.

The API price is $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens, flat across the full window, with output pricing including thinking tokens. Implicit caching cuts input to $0.075 per 1M for prompts of 4,096 tokens or more, and explicit caching is not supported. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs $0.75/$3.75 until December 31, 2026, then rises to $1.50/$7.50 on January 1, 2027, matching Hydrogen. Argon costs $2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20.

Google reports that Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash at the default high level, and partner tests showed 2x to 2.8x faster runs with 12% to 23% fewer tokens. It scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at high and 54 at xhigh, above Argon's 50. It reaches 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 versus 18.2% for 3.8 Flash, and it ranks only #5 on Agent Arena. Google also reports more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash and 2.3x more resilience to indirect prompt injection on Gray Swan's benchmark.

In Google Antigravity, an Orchestrator option switches models inside one task, with Carbon exploring, planning and resolving ambiguity while Hydrogen edits files, updates packages and runs tests. When Hydrogen hits friction, it hands control back to Carbon, and this pairing reached near-Carbon task success rates on Terminal-Bench 4.1 while using 24% less quota and finishing 19% faster than Carbon alone. The model ID is gemini-4-hydrogen, and it is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio on all tiers, Android Studio, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search and Sheets. Antigravity access requires Google AI Pro or Ultra, and Vertex AI is not mentioned in the launch posts.

stories.Headline: Utah Invites Public to Vote for Nine Pro-Human AI Finalists
stories.Summary:
Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce announced nine finalists for the inaugural Pro-Human AI Elevation Awards and opened public voting to Utah residents, according to a November 13, 2026 announcement reported by TechBuzz News. Voting runs through November 20. Winners will be announced December 8 at the 2026 Utah Pro-Human AI Summit at the Grand America. The awards recognize Utah-connected companies using artificial intelligence to empower workers, strengthen communities, and build human-centered principles into technology.

The nine finalists are grouped into three categories. Workforce Elevation, for companies using AI to help employees do more, learn faster, and develop new skills, includes ARUP Laboratories, Techcyte, Inc., and XL PR. Community Advancement, for companies using AI to address needs in areas such as healthcare, education, public safety, and government, includes Leland Makombo, Skill Struck, and Pro-Human Breakthrough, which covers companies building AI products with accountability as part of their design, includes Autonomous Solutions Inc. (ASI), Elnora, and Glacis Technologies, Inc. Each Utah resident must affirm residency and may submit only one ballot, selecting one finalist per category and separately nominating one of the nine for the overall grand prize. The public vote determines the winners in all three categories and contributes to selection of the grand prize recipient.

Gov. Spencer J. Cox said artificial intelligence should make people's lives better and help workers succeed, and that the companies are showing what that can look like in practice. He said the state wants to recognize their work and challenge more businesses to put people at the center of how they build and use the technology. Jefferson Moss, commissioner of the Governor's Office of Economic Development, said Utah has built a strong innovation economy and that a wave of companies are developing and using AI in ways that put people first. He said the awards recognize those companies, share what they are doing, and encourage more of this kind of innovation, and that the state wants an economic environment and a Summit that make clear human-centric AI is how Utah does business.

The awards are organized by Utah's Pro-Human AI Taskforce and spotlight companies that emphasize human agency, dignity, and accountability rather than simply automating tasks or replacing people. The effort builds on the 2025 Utah AI Summit at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City, which advanced the state's push to shape AI around human agency, workforce empowerment, and responsible innovation. Residents can review the finalists through their videos and cast ballots through the official online voting form. Winners will be recognized at the December 8 summit, and more information is available at aisummit.utah.gov.

Articles.Title: Utah Invites Public to Vote for Nine Pro-Human AI Finalists

stories.Headline: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
stories.Summary:
Perplexity released the open-weight decision models pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3 on November 13, 2026. These models return probabilities for answers instead of generating text for the user. They can answer multiple-choice, score, and yes or no questions about images or text. The latest version introduces Locate to extract exact text spans based on instructions. These models succeed the previous v1.2 and Flash v1.2 versions.

The v1.3 model uses Qwen3.8-27B with 27B parameters, while Flash uses Qwen3.5-4B with 4B parameters. Hugging Face lists them as 26B and 5B parameters, shipping under Apache 2.0. Local defaults are 32,768 tokens, but the API supports under 256K tokens. v1.3 requires a CUDA GPU with 49 GiB of BF16 weights, while Flash needs 8.5 GiB. Both models are available on OpenRouter and the Perplexity Decisions API.

Perplexity stated that the models adapt a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. They used a linear decision head and bidirectional full-attention layers to improve performance. The company explained that Flash v1.3 was distilled from the larger model using KL divergence. They noted that the new attention system prevents answers from shifting between different questions. Perplexity also added a LoRA adapter and a span head for the Locate feature.

The models are inspired by Jev from TypeSafe, which was described as a System One model. These decision models affect tasks like PII detection, NER, and extractive QA. They outperform Jev 1.14 on most self-reported evaluations, including a 91.6 percent mean accuracy. They also beat Qwen3-Reranker-8B on retrieval tasks with an 83.99 mean nDCG@10. The models show a low answer-flip rate of 0.27 percent on real-world requests.

Decision models differ from traditional classifiers because their output classes are not baked into the head. They avoid the computational overhead and schema errors common when LLMs generate JSON objects. Traditional classifiers require retraining to add new labels, but decision models evaluate predefined primitives. Zero-shot classification allows candidate labels to change from one request to another at inference. This approach replaces autoregressive decoding when an application only needs to choose between options.

The models will be used for domain classification, where v1.3 leads Jev 1.14 in seven domains. They will also handle multilingual tasks across eight languages with 88.16 percent accuracy for v1.3. Production requests cost 26.47 dollars per 1M requests according to the company. The articles leave open whether these self-reported figures are accurate since no external audits are mentioned. It remains unclear how the models perform on tasks outside the provided benchmarks.

Articles.Title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Geodesign Methods While Facing Interpretability And Data Challenges
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a review in Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning on November 13, 2026, regarding spatial planning methodologies. They determined that integrating artificial intelligence into geodesign improves environmental modeling and territorial data analysis. This integration also introduces critical challenges regarding ethical governance, interpretability, and data reliability. The authors establish that these computational tools augment human expertise rather than replacing professional judgment. The study examines the evolution of geospatial design from early systems into modern computational frameworks.

The process utilizes a framework by Steinitz based on six interconnected models including representation, process, evaluation, change, impact, and decision. These models answer six core questions divided into understanding existing systems and designing future changes. The first three questions investigate how a study area is described, how it operates, and if it works well. The final three questions evaluate how areas might be altered, what impacts modifications cause, and how to implement decisions. This system builds on the 1960s Canada Geographic Information System by Tomlinson and the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics.

The authors of the review state that traditional overlay mapping is static and struggles with dynamic social and ecological systems. They note that conventional site suitability assessments are labor intensive and often neglect broader regional implications. The researchers explain that environmental impact assessments frequently overlook cumulative impacts, which risks underestimating true environmental degradation. They argue that physical models and manual sketches are time consuming and lack precision for large scale quantitative evaluation. The authors further claim that participatory planning often faces disputes and allows vocal groups to overshadow others.

Planners and non technical stakeholders are affected by the shift from manual sketches to generative artificial intelligence. Zhang and colleagues used convolutional neural networks in Wuhan, China, to achieve superior land cover classification performance. Chen and colleagues used hierarchical convolutional recurrent neural networks to monitor forest cover. Johannsen and Oh developed deep learning models to improve predictions of urban heat island patterns. Aslam and Satarzadeh used hybrid models to enhance hazard predictions for landslides and floods, respectively.

Geodesign roots trace back to the 1960s and the work of Tomlinson on digital infrastructure for geographically referenced datasets. McHarg established an ecological planning paradigm in Design with Nature using layered mapping of soil, vegetation, and hydrology. Modern tools now include convolutional neural networks for imagery and recurrent neural networks for predicting urban growth trajectories. Transformer architectures and generative adversarial networks now synthesize urban layouts and simulate potential environmental impacts. Diffusion models and variational autoencoders are used to visualize flood patterns and explore alternative landscape configurations.

Future applications include using the non dominated sorting genetic algorithm to balance infrastructure cost efficiency and environmental sustainability. Planners may use ridge, multiple linear, and logistic regression to handle spatial variables and categorize development suitability. However, the articles leave open how to address the lack of spatial data in less developed regions. They do not resolve the black box problem where model complexity obscures the rationale behind design decisions. The text leaves unresolved the risks of algorithmic bias and covert privacy breaches in large training datasets.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Geodesign Methods While Facing Interpretability And Data Challenges

stories.Headline: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights
stories.Summary:
MarkTechPost published a report on November 13, 2026, regarding the top AI video generation models. The analysis used blind human preference votes from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena to rank the tools. These rankings focused on text-to-video and image-to-video quality. The report also examined API costs and the availability of open weights.

The top model is Wan 3.0 by Alibaba, which has a text-to-video Elo of 1175 and costs $0.20 per second. It can create 30-second 1080p clips from text, PDFs, and slide decks. Utopai X from Utopai Studios ranks second with 1170 Elo and is accessed via the PAI platform. MiniMax H3 follows in third place with 1161 Elo and offers restricted open weights.

Artificial Analysis provided the data, using Kling 3.0 as a fixed anchor at 1000 Elo. They explained that models within 25 points of each other are statistically similar. The evaluators used blind pairwise votes to compare two clips from the same prompt. This method ensures the quality signal remains objective.

The current landscape shows that native audio and clips lasting 15 to 30 seconds are now standard. Alibaba launched Wan 3.0 on August 24, 2026, to differentiate itself with document-to-video inputs. Utopai Studios built its model by post-training MiniMax H3 for filmmakers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights

stories.Headline: VA plans further VA.gov updates as it looks to expand AI integration
stories.Summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs announced a refreshed VA.gov on Nov. 11, 2026, with updates meant to simplify how veterans reach health care and benefits information. The changes include new CLEAR and Passkey sign-in options, which join existing Login.gov and ID.me credentials. The site also gained a search function that lets veterans ask questions in plain language. The department said the upgrades responded to nearly 90,000 veteran survey responses from March through May 2026, and veterans tested the updates before release. The refresh also added a way for veterans to check application status through links sent by text message, which Zach Schwartz called magic links and which do not require signing in.

The VA streamlined its QuickSubmit document tool so veterans can upload documents in three steps instead of 11. Schwartz, principal deputy assistant secretary for the Office of Information and Technology, said Friday that more releases are coming around January. He described the work as a cadence of regular incremental wins rather than a one-time overhaul. Schwartz said the VA is working closely with the newly launched America.gov to support AI tools on VA.gov, and he said the department is refocusing its solutions to be friendly to what the Trump administration calls SI, or super intelligence. He said the VA needs the most help in that area, particularly from industry.

He added that VA.gov is a beast and that the department wants to make it easier and more secure and meet veterans where they are. He also said the VA wants to serve as an example for other federal agencies adopting AI. Schwartz said he was meeting Friday with new Federal Chief Information Officer Carter Farmer, who he said wants to understand how the VA is pushing out so much in the SI space. He said Farmer wants the department to continue to be a representative example for many other agencies. The article does not say what specific updates are planned for the January releases.

Articles.Title: VA plans further VA.gov updates as it looks to expand AI integration

stories.Headline: Nobel Prize laureates gather in Stockholm to discuss artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Nobel Prize laureates and other leading thinkers will meet in Stockholm on 9 December 2026 for the Nobel Week Dialogue, an event organized by Nobel Prize Outreach to discuss artificial intelligence. The gathering will run from 10:00 to 15:30 at House of People in Stockholm. The speakers include Philippe Aghion, who won the economic sciences prize in 2025, Steven Chu, physics 1997, John Jumper, chemistry 2024, and David MacMillan, chemistry 2021. The announcement was made in a press release dated 13 November 2026.

The event will examine the opportunities, risks and choices that come with life in the age of AI, according to the release. It says AI tools are rapidly becoming more powerful, with advocates highlighting potential benefits for humanity and major scientific advances, while others warn of risks to society, work, education and democracy. The release asks why experts are so divided and how the path to living with AI should be mapped so its benefits are shared as fully as possible. The event is fully booked, but media can apply to take part using a registration form, and all interviews must be booked in advance.

The release states that the Nobel Week Dialogue is held in Stockholm every other year and in Gothenburg every other year. It is organized by Nobel Prize Outreach in collaboration with Carl Bennet AB, the City of Gothenburg, Royalty Pharma and Volvo Group. The release describes the event as an annual conference on 9 December in Nobel Week that brings together scientists, policy-makers and thinkers for sessions and working groups on a topical science-related theme. It says the aim is to deepen dialogue between the scientific community and the rest of society on issues connected with the Nobel Prize and important to the world.

The release notes that this year marks the 125th anniversary of the Nobel Prize. In September, the Nobel Foundation announced that the Nobel Prize amount would rise to SEK 12 million per prize category, an increase of SEK 1 million from the previous year. This year's laureates were announced from 5 to 12 October. The release does not say what will follow the dialogue.

Articles.Title: Nobel Prize laureates gather in Stockholm to discuss artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Six Studies Show Artificial Intelligence Can Augment Obstetric and Pediatric Clinical Decisions
stories.Summary:
Researchers Jeffrey S. Barrett, Catherine M. Sherwin, and Samuel L. Seward Jr. wrote an editorial on November 14, 2026. They synthesized six original research studies about artificial intelligence in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology. These studies show how digital tools can augment clinical decision making. The researchers focused on integrating routinely gathered patient data with pharmacological principles. This work appeared in the journal Frontiers in Pharmacology.

Zhang and colleagues used a hybrid model for linezolid dosing in critically ill children. Westvik and colleagues analyzed blood gas, anthropometric, and nutritional data for preterm infants. Li and colleagues tested a consumer smartwatch for hypotension during cesarean delivery. Wang and He used XGBoost for labor analgesia efficacy among 137 parturients. He and colleagues studied nalbuphine-ropivacaine infiltration in 473 women.

Wu and colleagues built China's first Pediatric Rational Medication Intelligent Decision System. This platform contains 400,000 database entries and 1,030 medications. The authors stated that AI should augment rather than replace clinical judgment. They noted that clinical utility depends on population-specific evidence. They emphasized that human clinical oversight must be preserved during therapeutic interventions.

The studies affected critically ill children, preterm infants, and women undergoing cesarean delivery. Li and colleagues found the smartwatch had 79.2 percent sensitivity and 82.0 percent specificity. Wang and He saw performance drop from 0.875 to 0.759 during validation. He and colleagues noted that SHAP values reflect statistical associations, not biological mechanisms. The system by Wu and colleagues decreased high-severity prescription warnings.

Obstetric and pediatric pharmacology are historically evidence-poor areas of clinical practice. Dynamic physiological changes during pregnancy and childhood alter how drugs work. Providers often relied on weight-based dosing that ignored biological variability. Clinical trials in these populations have remained limited. Machine learning and predictive analytics now address these historical data gaps.

AI applications must move from retrospective single-center analyses to prospective multicenter evaluations. Future priorities include assessing calibration and transportability across diverse health systems. Researchers must establish leakage-free validation protocols before deploying hybrid dosing models. The articles leave open the direct effects of these tools on outcomes. Controlled clinical trials are still required to confirm therapeutic comparisons.

Articles.Title: Six Studies Show Artificial Intelligence Can Augment Obstetric and Pediatric Clinical Decisions

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Review Highlights Efficiency Gains and Operational Challenges in Photovoltaic Systems
stories.Summary:
Gaurav Kansal published a comprehensive review article in Discover Applied Sciences on November 14, 2026. The paper evaluates how artificial intelligence can be integrated into solar photovoltaic systems to improve reliability and forecasting. This research characterizes the use of machine learning as a breakthrough for solar energy generation. The author used systematic queries of ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Scopus to gather data.

The integration requires advanced computational frameworks to optimize energy conversion efficiency and system operation. Specifically, the review focuses on power generation forecasting, operational fault diagnosis, image-based inspection, and cybersecurity. It highlights the use of genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization to improve maximum power point tracking. However, the author notes that these changes require significant data management, high computational power, and constant model maintenance.

Gaurav Kansal is responsible for the synthesis, which identifies current research gaps and practical hurdles. He explained that while AI offers technical advantages, the complexity of real-world deployment remains a serious challenge for operators. He suggested that these tools can eventually reduce the global reliance on traditional energy sources. The author also pointed to emerging solutions such as edge computing, few-shot learning, and transfer learning.

This work provides a foundation for more intelligent system operations by analyzing existing literature. The review suggests that continuing advancements in hardware and algorithms will facilitate the integration of renewable energy. Future research directions will likely focus on the emerging solutions mentioned in the paper. These developments aim to overcome the current operational challenges facing solar installations.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Review Highlights Efficiency Gains and Operational Challenges in Photovoltaic Systems

stories.Headline: FedRAMP pushes new cyber vulnerability rules to keep pace with AI
stories.Summary:
FedRAMP, the General Services Administration's cloud security program, issued a notice on Nov. 10, 2026 requiring certified cloud services to adopt new vulnerability detection and response rules, along with new vulnerability evaluation and reporting rules, by Dec. 7. The rules respond to how artificial intelligence is helping hackers speed up attacks on unpatched software bugs. They align with a July binding operational directive from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on prioritizing security updates based on risk. FedRAMP said vendors can submit corrective action plans for any requirement they cannot meet by that date.

The program is giving vendors a three-month grace period through March 7, 2027 to meet the requirements. On March 8, any cloud service that has not fully migrated or is not working under an approved corrective action plan will have its FedRAMP certification revoked and be banned from FedRAMP for one year. The new rules will require more than 550 certified providers to move from legacy vulnerability scanning to an exposure and threat-based approach. Providers must weigh factors such as whether a vulnerability is likely reachable over the internet and how far it can be exploited. In early December, FedRAMP plans to start a quarterly security inbox emergency test to collect progress reports, and a service that fails to respond goes into remediation status on the FedRAMP marketplace for at least 30 days.

FedRAMP officials wrote that the primary concern of the U.S. government is that certified providers migrate to the new approach swiftly, safely and appropriately. They said the program will not take unnecessary administrative action against services that work safely and in good faith to adopt the rules. They also wrote that the urgency of the threat has only increased since then, pointing to the recent Black October incidents across the global information security community. Matt Bruggeman, director of GTM Federal at A-LIGN, told Federal News Network that the change is drastic compared with how vendors worked before and that it has been a pretty big uplift, with many providers looking for new third-party tools.

The July CISA directive was developed in reaction to the quickly evolving cyber capabilities of models like Anthropic's Claude Mythos. FedRAMP officials wrote that the mandatory migration is only the first of many migrations providers will need to make over the coming years and that yearly paperwork exercises are no longer appropriate or sufficient. FedRAMP Director Pete Waterman said earlier this year, after a Hugging Face hack by OpenAI agents, that vendors who only equate FedRAMP with compliance are cooked. Under the FedRAMP 20X initiative, the program is shifting to more automated, real-time security monitoring rather than large authorization document packages.

Articles.Title: FedRAMP pushes new cyber vulnerability rules to keep pace with AI

stories.Headline: Coming Tomorrow: Teach Yourself AI
stories.Summary:
Doug Levin announced on November 14, 2026, that the next day's post in his newsletter Lessons from a Startup Life would answer a question many readers had asked, which is how to learn AI on your own. He wrote that self-learners who progress fastest work in a loop of trying, observing, and adjusting. In his view, thinking probabilistically about what a model will produce is what turns that loop into real skill. The announcement appeared on his Substack site, douglevin.substack.com.

The post was set to offer a practical path that readers could start that week. Levin listed four steps, which were building a daily habit with two AI tools, running controlled experiments that change one variable at a time, building something small and then deliberately breaking it, and teaching what you learn to someone else. He said explaining an idea is the fastest way to find the gaps in it. The announcement gave no other numbers or dates beyond the November 14, 2026 date and the reference to the next day.

Levin is the author of the newsletter and wrote the announcement himself. He described his view that the fastest self-learners work in a loop of trying, observing, and adjusting. He also said that thinking probabilistically about what a model will produce turns that loop into real skill. He said explaining an idea to someone else is the fastest way to find the gaps in it.

The announcement was published on Levin's Substack, which describes itself as the home for writing, podcasting, and media founders. The site noted that it requires JavaScript to run correctly and asked visitors to turn on JavaScript or unblock scripts. The announcement did not say what the full post would contain beyond the steps Levin listed. It also did not say how long the post would be or whether it would be free or paid.

Articles.Title: Coming Tomorrow: Teach Yourself AI

stories.Headline: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Agentic AI And Infrastructure Are Still On A Roll
stories.Summary:
Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI for research and development, led the week's largest U.S. funding rounds with a $1 billion Series A, Crunchbase News reported for the period of Nov. 7 to 13, 2026. Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the San Francisco-based startup. Mercor came next with $750 million in Series D funding, a round backed by a long list of venture investors that set a $20 billion valuation for the San Francisco company, which was founded less than four years ago. Torus, based in Salt Lake City, announced $500 million in growth financing led by Magnetar Capital and also introduced a product called Foundry, described as modular AI infrastructure for inference compute.

Path Robotics and LangChain tied for fourth with $300 million each. Path Robotics, based in Columbus, Ohio, picked up Series E financing led by Georgian at a $2.45 billion valuation, while LangChain closed a Series C led by CapitalG at a $3 billion valuation. Nominal raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation, with Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners leading the round for the Austin-based startup. Imprint and Mavria tied at $130 million each, with Khosla Ventures leading the financing for New York-based Imprint at a $1.9 billion valuation and Paradigm leading the latest round for Mavria at a $1 billion valuation. Delix Therapeutics, Rox and Databento tied at $100 million each, led respectively by Johnson & Johnson Innovation and SV Health Investors' Dementia Discovery Fund, General Catalyst and March Capital, and Fifth Down Capital.

The vast majority of the week's largest rounds were AI-related, though biotech, fintech and enterprise software also appeared in the mix. The Crunchbase list covers the largest announced rounds raised by U.S.-based companies during the period. Crunchbase noted that most announced rounds are in its database, but there may be a small time lag because some rounds are reported late in the week. The article did not include further comment from the companies or investors beyond the details of each round.

Articles.Title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Agentic AI And Infrastructure Are Still On A Roll - Crunchbase News

stories.Headline: How Philip K. Dick Predicted the Future of Artificial Intelligence in literature
stories.Summary:
A 2026 article in The Guardsman describes how the writer came to Philip K. Dick's 1965 novel "The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch" after failing to find a book about the punk band Social Distortion. The Amazon algorithm then recommended a book called "Social Distortion: Biography," which reviewers rated one star and described as AI-generated. One comment said the book repeatedly called lead singer Mike Ness "her" instead of "him." The writer links this to reporting by Alexandra Alter in The New York Times last June, which found 2,168 self-published Amazon books with more than 50% AI-generated content, including 970 novels with more than 90% AI-written pages.

In October 2026, the Spanish newspaper El País published an analysis by journalist Kiko Llaneras finding that one in three best-selling self-published books were generated by AI. Both journalists used the software Pangram to detect AI content, which the article calls the most accurate and reliable tool for the job. Pangram was also the official tool in two recent literary scandals. Haitian-Canadian author Thélyson Orélien was removed from the Prix Goncourt, awarded by the Académie Goncourt, over AI use and plagiarism. Peruvian writer David Silva Rojas, winner of the Almadía-Ventosa Arrufat prize for short novels, was accused by El País of using 99% AI, according to a Pangram diagnostic, and while his prize was not withdrawn, presentations of the novel in Spain were canceled pending an investigation.

The writer says Dick understood the risks of technology's evolution, including AI and addiction to it, and to creating content from pre-standardized patterns. People ask large language models like ChatGPT for everything from math problems to book analyses and accept the first answer, which the writer says could distort reality. The article notes that in the novel's final pages human and AI realities collide, and the only way to survive is through pleasure, which fewer humans can feel. It ends by asking whether AI can describe the experience of seeing Social Distortion live.

Articles.Title: How Philip K. Dick Predicted the Future of Artificial Intelligence in literature

stories.Headline: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
The llama.cpp project released version 1.0.0 of its libraries on November 13, 2026, according to a post on Hugging Face by Daniel Bevenius, Georgi Gerganov and merve of ggml-org. The project began 3.5 years earlier and has grown into a platform for running multi-modal large language models on hardware ranging from consumer machines to enterprise servers. It uses quantization, optimized backends and a portable C and C++ implementation to make inference widely accessible. Many downstream applications already depend on the project's work.

The release marks a commitment to developers who rely on the library interfaces. From now on, both llama.cpp and ggml will signal API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps, and the team said it will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers. The project currently supports more than 150 architecture variants and all mainstream speculative decoding methods. Its ggml engine runs on virtually any hardware through dedicated backends, each of which can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

The team said a flexible but stable API is paramount as local AI and privacy become more important. It credited an open-source community of highly skilled contributors and said maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding implementation details will remain top priorities. The team also said it is investing more resources in CI infrastructure, using Hugging Face technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs to scale capacity and check every change landing on the master branches. It thanked hardware partners NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel for support in enrolling self-hosted runners across major platforms.

The post described the release as a significant milestone that would not have been possible without joint efforts, and it thanked long-time maintainers and all contributors. It said the team looks forward to expanding how ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users, and pointed readers to a discussion on adding the projects to packaging and release pipelines. It also noted that the team continues to adapt and integrate LLMs into its development cycle in a thoughtful and reasonable manner. The post mentioned Llama desktop apps for MacOS and Windows, shipped by the team behind llama.cpp and Hugging Face.

Articles.Title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

stories.Headline: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
stories.Summary:
Researchers released XYBench on November 13, 2026, to test how AI assistants handle misguided user questions. This benchmark evaluates if models can identify misconceptions when users ask for help with the wrong approach. The project was developed by researchers at Allen Institute for AI, Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins. It focuses on the XY problem, where a person asks for help with a mistaken solution. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at the EMNLP 2026 conference.

The benchmark uses 8,115 real-world questions about programming, cooking, and home repair to measure model performance. It includes 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 curated examples, and 6,272 from WikiHow. The system tests Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro. It measures pragmatic solution, pragmatic emphasis, and misconception identification to see if models prioritize the actual goal. Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge for these specific evaluations.

The developers stated that useful AI assistants must help users who ask misguided questions based on misconceptions. They explained that LLMs have a critical gap in recognizing implicit misconceptions and redirecting users toward effective solutions. The team hopes this tool helps researchers measure if model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions. They noted that models often suggest solutions to the stated request while ignoring the underlying goal. The researchers believe models must act on inferred intent when it diverges from the literal request.

The evaluated models were less likely than humans to steer users away from mistaken approaches toward actual goals. On Stack Overflow, models focused on the underlying goal in only 35 to 41 percent of responses. In contrast, they focused on the stated request in 47 to 57 percent of their answers. An experiment including GPT-4.1 showed models are better at recognizing useful advice than producing it themselves. This gap affects users who lack the knowledge to ask the right questions to solve their problems.

The benchmark draws on pragmatics, a branch of linguistics concerning how context and intent shape meaning. To create the WikiHow questions, researchers used Sonnet 4.5 to generate plausible misconceptions in procedural guides. Human reviewers validated the automated judge by assessing 500 responses with agreement rates between 74.2 and 100 percent. An oracle experiment showed that providing the intended request increased solution rates but decreased misconception identification. The dataset was filtered to remove cases where answering the literal request was sufficient.

Researchers can now use XYBench to test if changes to prompting or training improve how models identify misconceptions. Future work may investigate which training methods help models act on what users need rather than literal requests. The current benchmark only covers procedural problems and queries written in the English language. Extending the tool to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction for research. The project aims to build models that offer useful advice despite a user's mistaken assumptions.

Articles.Title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

stories.Headline: Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Shield, an IT services provider, announced on November 13, 2026 that its Forge platform now uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to let AI agents navigate legacy portals that technicians previously had to log into and finish by hand. The work is assigned by Forge's AI Engineer to a computer-use agent, and technicians decide which actions it can take on its own and where they need to review or approve. Shield says these browser workflows are live, with thousands of runs each month across its IT providers. Phone calls, on-site work and remote-desktop tasks still need human involvement.

Shield says GPT-6 Astra was 35-40% faster on average than the legacy models it had used for computer-use tasks. The company reports faster execution, fewer failures and fewer timeouts, and says its teams spend less time writing detailed instructions to an agent or helping it through a task. Jain also says customer satisfaction is higher on tickets where AI is used, with speed of resolution being a critical factor. Shield is testing remote-desktop workflows that would let agents perform more complex actions directly on a computer's desktop.

Mayank Jain, Head of Technology at Shield, said the only time a human technician should be needed is for their judgment, not because work is blocked on access. He said that before GPT-6 Astra, Forge's agents could get stuck at systems they could not access, and customers had to wait for a technician to complete that step. Shield tried computer use with earlier models, but Jain said they were not reliable or fast enough. He said GPT-6 Astra was natural with computer use, and that watching it feels like watching a human click around.

Jain said many portals that manage tickets, devices and software licenses lack APIs, so an agent needs to navigate the screen much as a person would. He said a system without an API is usually an old-school system that is hard to use, even by a human. He said GPT-6 Astra lets Shield's agents log into portals and legacy websites and perform tasks that only a human could six months ago. Jain said that with GPT-6 Astra, Forge is now truly an extension of Shield's human technicians.

Articles.Title: Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI

stories.Headline: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation
stories.Summary:
Yuxuan Wang and ten other authors introduced a new multi-agent system called DoGNAVY-Exploit on November 13, 2026. This tool uses open-weight models to turn known software vulnerabilities into working exploits. The researchers developed this system to overcome the high costs and access restrictions associated with frontier large language model agents. It aims to help open-weight models maintain progress across long exploitation chains.

The system requires a hierarchical architecture that separates strategic planning from parallel execution. It uses stage-aware decomposition to break long tasks into short, verifiable milestones, providing only the relevant expert knowledge for each step. Using GLM-5.2, the tool achieved a 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and a 100% one-day and 97.5% zero-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, GLM-5.3 solved 157 tasks, while GLM-5.2 solved 79, both outperforming Claude Code baselines.

The authors are responsible for the design, which includes a controller that accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. They stated that a shared structured memory allows agents to consolidate verified facts and failed routes across different branches. This design ensures that validated knowledge is carried into subsequent milestones. The researchers noted that these specific memory and orchestration designs substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.

Articles.Title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation

stories.Headline: Etiquette for the machine age: BVDW's 17-part code for AI at work
stories.Summary:
Germany's Bundesverband Digitale Wirtschaft (BVDW) published its first "KI-Knigge" on November 5, 2026, a 25-page etiquette guide for artificial intelligence at work. The document tells employees when to skip the chatbot altogether and how to behave when software summarises a meeting. It also says who should own an AI agent before the agent is allowed to act. The full title is "Der BVDW-KI-Knigge: Verhaltenskodex für den nachhaltigen, sozialen und verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit KI in der Arbeitswelt." The guide borrows its structure from the environmental, social and governance framework companies already use for sustainability reporting.

The guide is 25 pages long and was published on November 5, 2026. It has seventeen numbered sections: four under Environmental, five under Social and eight under Governance. By PPC Land's count those sections contain 94 orientation points, 23 environmental, 26 social and 45 governance. The final section on agentic AI systems, with ten points, is the longest single list in the document. The guide takes its name from Adolph Freiherr Knigge, whose 1788 book "Über den Umgang mit Menschen" made his surname German shorthand for a manual of good manners.

The guide was written inside BVDW's Lab Responsible AI for Business, a unit of the association's Working Group Digital Responsibility. Its lead author is Maike Scholz of Deutsche Telekom, who heads the lab. Scholz said AI can take work off our hands but not the responsibility for its use. She said the guide shows how responsible AI use in everyday working life can succeed, and that resources, human interaction and clear responsibilities must be thought about together. BVDW, which represents more than 600 member companies, presents the document as practical recommendations for companies that want to integrate AI deliberately along the three sustainability dimensions.

The authors write that they are convinced enabling users should come before bans. They say the guide is meant not as a set of rules but as guidance from practice for practice. Readers are addressed with the informal German "Du," and each chapter ends with orientation points rather than obligations. The guide reaches anyone in a company who drafts social posts, summarises meetings, generates images or hands tasks to AI agents. Several of its points mirror labelling duties that the EU AI Act has applied since August 2, 2026.

The environmental chapter opens with the premise that AI systems require considerable computing power and therefore energy. It says selecting AI tools and checking their environmental impact is primarily the responsibility of companies. Section E2 states that a search query consumes only about a tenth of the resources of a generative AI query, with no source given. The guide says uniform standards for measuring and reporting the energy consumption of AI workloads have yet to be created. Section E3 recommends capping iterations with a fixed upper limit of prompt runs per task, for example a maximum of three attempts.

Nothing in the guide is binding, so what changes depends on whether employers turn its pointers into house rules on approved tools, human sign-off and documentation. BVDW says the guide will be adapted as needed to new findings, requirements and practical experience. The guide's closing outlook repeats that technological, regulatory, commercial and ethical conditions around AI keep shifting. The imprint on the last page states that the paper was produced using artificial intelligence, without saying which tools were used or for which parts.

Articles.Title: Etiquette for the machine age: BVDW's 17-part code for AI at work - PPC Land

stories.Headline: AI penetration testing cannot replace independent cybersecurity assurance
stories.Summary:
The suspension of the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Phase 2 third-party assessment requirements has reignited the question of whether automated, artificial intelligence-based penetration testing could replace independent assessment, Terrence J. McGraw wrote in a November 13, 2026 commentary for Federal News Network. McGraw is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and chief executive officer of Cape Endeavors. The July 2026 CMMC reform effort called for discussion of the existing state of commercial cybersecurity and self-attestation. McGraw said that should be taken as a policy question, not as an indication that AI penetration testing will become a federal requirement. The underlying obligations of safeguarding covered defense information under Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement 252.204-7012 and National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171 remain in force for contractors.

McGraw wrote that a test continually probing a system is far more relevant than one that happens only every three years, but the two approaches answer very different questions. He said the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified vulnerability exploitation as a leading initial access path. He cited a Cape Endeavors analysis, published in a recent white paper using a hypothetical scenario of 500 hosts and 20 web apps, suggesting a model token cost of around $395 for a single on-demand test cycle versus around $4,200 per month for a high frequency continuous design. He said those are illustrative compute costs only, not actual market quotes or all-in contractor prices, and do not include vendor margins, infrastructure, human review or the engineering effort to fix issues found. He said a requirement to test continuously would turn a one-off assessment cost into a perpetual operating cost for small and midsize businesses in the defense industrial base.

McGraw said a penetration test is not in any way a complete analysis of how controlled unclassified information is protected, because many breaches result from stolen credentials, compromised third parties or misuse of legitimate access. He said independent assessments look at documented controls, interview people and examine evidence of implementation, but can only assess a particular point in time. He said a contractor can have a sophisticated test platform and still control which systems are tested, how it is configured and what results are reported. He cited a law firm Arnold & Porter example of a contractor who reported a perfect score in stark contrast to a later Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center evaluation. He said the gap between self-reported cybersecurity scores and government-assigned scores has been a factor in False Claims Act enforcement.

McGraw said the better approach is layered assurance: independently confirm required controls and the stated CUI boundary, test exposed technical controls continuously or after significant change, and run detection and response exercises. He said discovery finding CUI outside the approved boundary should modify the assessment scope, and a response exercise showing malicious activity went undetected means a clean vulnerability scan should not be taken as evidence of readiness. He said AI can speed up technical validation and make it more frequent but cannot on its own prove all appropriate safeguards are in place, all CUI is in the right place or the organization will deal with compromise appropriately. He said the point is to stop treating either human assessment or machine testing as the complete answer. He said contractors should keep an accurate inventory of CUI and the systems that process it, maintain system security plans and plans of action, minimize unnecessary exposure and document changes and remediation.

McGraw wrote that attackers do not wait for an assessment window and exploit exposed devices, misconfigurations and unpatched vulnerabilities when an opening appears. He said automated penetration testing can help close that timing gap by repeatedly checking reachable assets, attempting exploitation within allowed bounds and retesting the fix. He said for some technical controls, evidence that an attack actually failed may be more convincing than a policy stating the control should be in place. He said a tool probing the network perimeter will not see sensitive data copied to an unauthorized collaboration site, sent via normal email or left on an unmanaged device. He said a successful exploit does not tell whether defenders would detect and contain a skilled attacker already inside.

McGraw said there should not be any assumption today of a universal Level 2 AI testing mandate, and contractors can still make good decisions at this stage. He said better scoping will lead to lower security risk and fewer systems to test, and fewer recurring misconfigurations will mean fewer alerts to investigate and fewer issues to retest. He said federal policymakers should define the assurance outcome first and then pick the tool, asking whether an approach will verify implementation, find CUI outside authorized boundaries, find exploitable weaknesses and measure detection and response. He said credible evidence and clear accountability for exclusions and outstanding findings are needed, along with a look at the ongoing cost to the contractor base. He said if government policy eventually defines the scope, frequency or class of service providers that can carry out testing, contractors would have very little flexibility in managing that obligation.

Articles.Title: AI penetration testing cannot replace independent cybersecurity assurance - Federal News Network

stories.Headline: How I rehumanize the college classroom for the AI-augmented age
stories.Summary:
A millennial college professor implemented a new classroom framework to rehumanize education for students. This change occurred during a semester starting in late 2025. The educator focused on social interactions to prepare students for an AI-augmented workforce. This approach aims to counter the devaluation of college caused by artificial intelligence. The professor believes AI risks stripping humanity from daily lives.

The framework applies to an English 101 Writing Composition class with 20 students. It requires students to engage in small social interactions and five minute homework planning sessions. Students must give short presentations lasting five to ten minutes on their work. These presentations cover topics like factory farming practices and the impact of fast fashion. The original article was published on December 12, 2025.

Sean Cho Ayres is the professor responsible for these changes in the classroom. He stated that he teaches the skills he wishes he had been taught. Ayres believes the classroom should not be an intermediary between two computers. He argues that students must be able to articulate ideas to a group. He views the classroom as a place for students to battle exams together.

Gen Z students are affected by this shift toward interpersonal social skills. They are often described as having their faces glued to their screens. Some students use ChatGPT to help with commas or write entire conclusions. Ayres believes it is fine if AI helps students reach their final ideas. What matters is if the ideas originate from the person behind the words.

Generative AI looms widely in higher education and threatens the value of degrees. Many young adults are aware that an AI-infused workplace awaits them after graduation. Students often enter class listening to AI DJs or scrolling through AI-selected ads. This creates a tension between who these young adults are and who they must become. The professor identifies as a millennial who also struggles with some social cues.

Students now engage in small-group discussions about adapting AI practices into daily life. They talk to peers about challenging homework questions and their weekend activities. The professor uses Snapchat notification sounds to get the attention of the talking students. The articles do not state if other professors have adopted this specific framework. They leave open whether these social skills will guarantee success in the workforce.

Articles.Title: How I rehumanize the college classroom for the AI-augmented age

stories.Headline: Ukraine’s Health Ministry prepares rules for medical AI as 80.5% of surveyed clinicians use it
stories.Summary:
The Health Ministry of Ukraine began preparing new rules for medical artificial intelligence on November 13, 2026. This action follows a survey showing that 80.5% of clinicians in the country already use these tools. The government wants to create a formal legal framework for these systems. This will ensure that technology is used safely across the healthcare sector.

The new bill will require the classification of AI tools based on their specific risk levels. It will establish strict requirements for the transparency and safety of all medical systems. The rules will also define the accountability of both the providers and the users. These measures follow a survey of 7,000 healthcare professionals, 300 patients, and 39 industry representatives.

Minister of Health Viktor Liashko is responsible for the development of this legislation. He stated that the ministry is working on a bill to set clear rules for the development of these systems. Liashko emphasized that medical professionals must supervise all decisions suggested by AI. He also noted that the personal medical data of patients must be protected.

One example of current technology is CheckEye, which analyzes retinal images in 30 seconds. This tool was tested on 873 patients in the Chernihiv and Odesa regions. The ministry intends to present the proposed bill for public discussion in the near future. This will allow stakeholders to review the safety and accountability standards.

stories.Headline: How companies can support emerging AI data center policies
stories.Summary:
AI data center measures played a prominent role in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, and the electoral results pointed toward tighter restrictions and regulation of these facilities. Trellis, a sustainability news outlet, published an analysis on November 13, 2026, arguing that companies need to prepare for an evolving policy landscape. The piece was framed around how businesses can respond to these shifts rather than reporting a single discrete event. The articles provided describe the broader political trend, not a specific enacted measure with a named date or vote. The guidance centers on two main actions for companies.

First, they can make sure their trade associations advocate for responsible data center buildouts. Second, they can align their own policy agendas with legislation that responds to public concerns. The articles also suggest that companies and policymakers follow guidelines that serve the public interest, including roadmaps for data centers powered by cleaner energy. No specific dollar figures, deadlines, or bill numbers appear in the material provided. The author of the commentary is Deborah McNamara, executive director of ClimateVoice, who has spent more than 20 years in sustainability activism and advocacy with social change, environmental, and climate justice-focused nonprofits.

Her position, as described, is that companies should support policies that respond to public concern. The articles do not include direct statements from elected officials or industry groups on the midterm outcomes. The broader context is that data centers serving artificial intelligence are drawing growing scrutiny from voters and regulators. The articles indicate that sustainability executives and business leaders should prepare for further regulatory and policy changes. Beyond that general expectation, the material does not specify which rules will follow or on what timeline.

stories.Headline: Five-Tier K-12 Framework Proposes Age-Gated Limits for Classroom Generative Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A perspective study published in AI, Brain and Child on November 14, 2026, introduces a five-tiered framework for generative artificial intelligence exposure for students aged 3 through 18. The study was authored by researcher Sisi Tao. The model links specific artificial intelligence permissions, quantitative cut-off times, and mandatory independence ratios to neurodevelopmental and cognitive milestones. It moves past polarized debates between absolute classroom prohibition and unrestricted adoption. The blueprint establishes an evidence-based continuum grounded in developmental psychology.

Tier 0 covers ages 3 to 5 and mandates zero direct student interaction, with all technology use adult-mediated and back-stage. Tier 1 covers ages 6 to 7 with a cap of 15 minutes per day and an independent work ratio of at least 95 percent. Tier 2 covers ages 8 to 10 at approximately 30 minutes daily with an independence ratio of 90 percent or higher. Tier 3 spans ages 11 to 13 with a daily limit of 60 minutes and an 80 percent independence threshold. Tier 4 governs ages 14 to 18 with a daily ceiling of 120 minutes and a minimum 70 percent independence ratio, requiring a formal Artificial Intelligence Usage Statement with each assignment.

Educational policymakers must enforce regulation by design, requiring software vendors to incorporate age-gated usage locks matching tiered daily exposure limits as a prerequisite for procurement in public school districts. Technology developers are urged to end direct preschool engagement tools and instead engineer transparent, privacy-preserving teacher resources that operate across varied network bandwidths. Educators are tasked with developing process-oriented curricula emphasizing explicit bias detection checklists, student agency, and oral evaluations. Parents serve as home gatekeepers by aligning domestic device habits with school cut-offs, monitoring family conversational assistants, and curbing uncritical trust or personal disclosure patterns. The author emphasizes that the proposed quantitative thresholds represent theory-driven hypotheses and testable heuristic baselines rather than definitive physiological constants.

In the United States, a presidential executive order promotes system-wide artificial intelligence integration in K-12 schooling despite an absence of age-specific bans. Approximately 40 percent of national education systems restricted smartphone use in schools by 2024, while UNESCO guidance recommends a minimum age threshold of 13 for classroom artificial intelligence tools. An electroencephalography study showed declining neural functional connectivity and post-exposure cognitive debt when individuals write with continuous artificial intelligence assistance. Generative models frequently present factual inaccuracies, fabricated scholarly citations, and systemic societal stereotypes as authoritative output. The framework synthesizes five classical developmental psychology frameworks: Piaget's cognitive stage theory, Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, Erikson's psychosocial theory, Kohlberg's stages of moral reasoning, and Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory.

The author utilized an adapted best-fit framework synthesis methodology, integrating empirical literature from PsycINFO and ERIC using targeted Boolean strings covering generative technology, digital media, and developmental neuroscience in cohorts aged 3 to 18. Four evidence streams were triangulated to set boundaries: Piagetian representational transitions, longitudinal magnetic resonance neuroimaging showing cortical volume peaks and synaptic pruning in frontal and parietal regions, empirical attention spans and executive function trajectories, and practical K-12 grade bands. A four-tier model was rejected because it would artificially collapse the transition around ages 6 to 7 from preoperational to concrete operational thought. A six-tier structure would introduce artificial breaks within adolescence that lack neuroscientific warrant, given that longitudinal neuroimaging demonstrates executive function development follows a protracted, continuous trajectory from age 13 to 18. Historical parallels include the introduction of portable electronic calculators and internet search engines, when observers feared the erosion of fundamental arithmetic and inquiry skills.

Key limitations include the framework's foundation in Western developmental psychology, necessitating future cross-cultural research to explore adaptations within non-Western and collectivist educational settings. Because the model reflects current text-based systems, rapid transitions toward autonomous agentic and multimodal platforms will require regular recalibration. Long-term empirical studies remain essential to test the ecological validity of the suggested cut-off values, track cross-device exposure, and design inherently artificial-intelligence-resistant pedagogies such as collaborative problem solving, embodied physical experiments, and process portfolios. The article states that students must retain intellectual agency as educational technology evolves. The articles do not state any implementation date or adopting institution for the framework.

Articles.Title: Five-Tier K-12 Framework Proposes Age-Gated Limits for Classroom Generative Artificial Intelligence - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: Does the Trump Administration’s Campaign to Rebrand AI as ‘Super Intelligence’ Matter?
stories.Summary:
Secretary Markwayne Mullin promoted the term Super Intelligence during a press briefing on Friday, November 13, 2026. This occurred while a nationwide ground stop for all flights was in effect across the United States. Mullin corrected a reporter who used the term artificial intelligence when asking about a telecommunications failure. The Homeland Security secretary indicated that the cause of the coast to coast travel disruption was not yet ascertained. He used the moment to push President Donald Trump's campaign to rename the technology as SI.

The change requires the federal government to use Super Intelligence and not acknowledge artificial intelligence in official contexts. This policy was established by an executive order signed on September 29 titled Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence. Trump first expressed dislike for the word artificial in July 2025 during his AI Action Plan launch. He later floated supreme intelligence in December and polled options on Truth Social on September 19. He officially chose Super Intelligence during a United Nations General Assembly speech on September 22.

President Trump stated that the term artificial implies a defect and that the technology is actually pure genius. He believes the new name is more accurate and reflects the transformative capabilities and limitless opportunities of the technology. Trump said that whoever wins Super Intelligence wins, and he wants to maintain global technological dominance over China. A State Department official instructed diplomats to change all references in documents, positions, and press elements. Michael Kratsios of the OSTP adopted the term in his remarks at the UN the next day.

Social media users and technology writer Charlie Warzel called the focus on branding during an aviation crisis absurd. Harvard political scientist Ryan Enos noted that prioritizing regime approved rhetoric during an emergency is a sign of authoritarianism. Emily Tucker of Georgetown Law suggested the renaming might preempt arguments or make it harder to resist power abuses. Dave Karpf of George Washington University said the insistence on the term shows Trump is out of his depth. Jenna Ruddock of Free Press said industry leaders play along for lucrative contracts and regulatory fast tracks.

Trump has a history of renaming things, including the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on day one. In September 2025, he ordered the Department of Defense to be called the Department of War. He also renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America and suggested calling the Strait of Hormuz the Trump Strait. Industry leaders like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang have adopted the SI branding in their companies. Musk planned to rename the SpaceXAI unit to SpaceXSI, and Zuckerberg used the term in earnings calls.

The federal government will continue to use the term Super Intelligence to the maximum extent permitted by law. The administration aims to achieve and maintain unquestioned and unchallenged global technological dominance through this technology. Trump mentioned America.gov as a new website used to query government information. The articles leave open whether the telecommunications failure that stopped all flights was actually related to SI. The cause of the Friday air travel crisis remains unclear as of the time of publication.

Articles.Title: Does the Trump Administration’s Campaign to Rebrand AI as ‘Super Intelligence’ Matter? - Tech Policy Press

stories.Headline: Does state-and-local AI need a rebrand?
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in September mandating that artificial intelligence be known as “super intelligence,” arguing that AI makes the technology sound fake. Trump said so-called “SI” better reflects the technology’s immense capabilities, according to Route Fifty. The executive order applies only to federal agencies and departments, and some have already adopted the term. The effort has some state and local leaders wondering if they should follow the federal government’s lead. That is especially true as they reckon with AI’s impacts on the government workforce, the future of work, service delivery and the backlash against data centers.

Speakers at the Public Technology Institute’s GOVIT Leadership Summit and Symposium in Minneapolis this week said deemphasizing AI as a term might be an interesting path forward. But they also said government leaders should spend more time selling the technology and its benefits to the public, regardless of what it’s called. John Matelski, chief information officer at the National Association of Counties, said during a panel discussion that AI was here 50 years ago and was just called machine learning or something else. Matelski said he has looked at this not as artificial intelligence but more as augmented intelligence. He said he has never liked the term “artificial intelligence.”

Matelski asked how to leverage the varying types of technologies or services and recognize that it is here to stay. He asked how to embrace it carefully and with boundaries on it. PTI Senior Fellow Alan Shark suggested on stage that leaders instead be “talking about office automation.” Shark said leaders should “talk about solutions and leave out the word ‘AI’ because that’s a variable.” Shark said there are two universes, one internal where we have to use a language that our people understand.

Shark said the external universe is where he is seeing AI as a negative term. He said people have a right to be fearful, citing AI escaping, destroying systems, apologizing that it destroyed a system, and admitting that it actually failed to follow its own instructions. Shark said people have every right to be concerned and that we have got to be scared about what our public is seeing. He said we should be using it very carefully. Williamsburg, Virginia CIO Mark Barham said the government there has taken to calling data centers “co-location facilities.”

Barham said he knows that if leaders disclose they are meeting with data center vendors, “alarm bells go off” in the community. Amy Cheney, Bloomington, Minnesota’s CIO, said her city has seen a dramatic uptick in people using AI to submit requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Cheney said that use has positive potential but can also produce complex requests requiring much more staff time and resources. Cheney said a lot of work lies ahead there. She said FOIA requesters are using AI against them basically to create really complicated requests that staff quite frankly cannot keep up with.

Cheney said they are looking at how to automate that process, which does not necessarily involve AI and might be something simpler. She said automation is the key and getting staff to recognize AI isn’t going away, but we have to figure out ways of being smarter and how we’re addressing the demands we’re seeing now. For some time, government leaders at the state and local level have argued that the messaging around AI should focus on how it helps make employees’ work easier and more efficient and allows them to focus on more complex tasks. Those who work for small and rural governments have said previously that the technology has given them “breathing room,” and others argued that focusing on AI’s benefits will help sell it more to the public. Ben Bowen, vice president of U.S. sales at software company Claro Enterprise Solutions, said you can call it AI, super intelligence or whatever you like, but it’s efficiency that it’s going to help create.
