stories.Headline: Rules Governing Human Oversight of AI in Health Care Could Shape Public Trust — The Monitor
stories.Summary:
State lawmakers and professional organizations are developing new approaches to responsible AI use, often focusing on human oversight and accountability for these tools. A new report from the Transparency Coalition, an AI-policy advocacy organization, identified 115 AI-related measures that legislatures in 30 states passed this year. As of mid-October, 108 had been signed into law and seven were awaiting a governor's signature. The report ranked human oversight of AI in health care and AI disclosure requirements among the most common issues states addressed.

Eight states, for example, enacted laws limiting health insurers' ability to rely solely on AI or automated systems to deny or reduce coverage, including prior authorization for health insurance claims. At least five states have enacted laws this year restricting AI in mental health care, generally requiring therapy to be provided by a licensed human professional. California also enacted a law requiring health facilities to ensure clinicians retain independent judgment when using clinical AI tools. Most of these mental health laws are already in effect, while Rhode Island's and California's take effect in January 2027.

In October, the American Medical Association released a governance framework for agentic AI outlining questions for AI systems that take on clinical functions, including what evidence supports their use, what oversight is appropriate, and who is accountable for their risks and outcomes. The AMA says these questions will guide its work on liability, licensure, and regulation. The framework does not set requirements for physicians or AI developers. Separately, the Federation of State Medical Boards convened a workgroup in Washington in early October to begin developing recommendations for state medical boards overseeing the use of clinical AI tools.

The FSMB group is focusing on systems that perform clinical functions, such as diagnosis and prescribing, with limited or no direct physician supervision. FSMB's leadership has argued in the past that AI should be governed through existing medical accountability structures, with physicians remaining accountable for their use of AI. Draft recommendations are expected in the coming weeks or months and will be open for feedback before adoption. Once adopted, they will not be binding, though state boards and legislators could use them to shape policy.

In October, the health policy journal Health Affairs issued a policy for AI use that reflects standards many academic journals have put in place since 2023. The policy prohibits authors who publish in the journal from listing AI as an author or using it in place of human judgment. It also requires authors to review AI-assisted work, remain responsible for its content, and disclose all AI use. The journal also recommends against using AI tools to manage citations and references, citing the tendency of some AI systems to generate inaccurate or nonexistent references.

The results of the 2026 midterm elections could further influence state efforts to regulate AI and how they interact with federal policy. The Trump administration has previously urged Congress to adopt a national framework for AI regulation that would preempt existing state laws it considers unduly burdensome, but broad preemption may be less likely given Democratic control of Congress beginning in January. Many congressional Democrats have previously opposed overriding state AI laws without federal regulations in place. Some Democrats in the incoming Congress have indicated they will pursue new legislation related to AI, including requiring experts to evaluate AI safety and clarifying when technology companies can be held liable for harmful AI outputs.

Articles.Title: Rules Governing Human Oversight of AI in Health Care Could Shape Public Trust — The Monitor - KFF

stories.Headline: Georgia AI Playbook Is a Starting Point for Cities, Counties
stories.Summary:
Georgia’s new Local Government AI Playbook was created by tech leaders and state lawmakers, according to an article by Ashley Silver published November 13, 2026, on govtech.com. The idea took shape during a Google-hosted roundtable in Atlanta earlier in 2026, when state Rep. Dar’Shun Kendrick heard local officials asking for help navigating AI. Kendrick, a member of the Georgia Technology Authority’s Oversight Committee, asked GTA to turn its state agency guidance into a downloadable resource for cities and counties. Chief Digital and AI Officer Nikhil Deshpande, who helped develop the guide, joined state AI leadership while its program was still taking shape. The 56-page guide offers practical advice on setting AI policies, reviewing potential projects, training employees and putting safeguards in place before using new tools.

The playbook gives local governments a framework for deciding whether AI is the right solution, how to assess potential risks and when projects need additional review and human oversight. It lays out an eight-step project process that begins with defining the problem and considering alternatives, then moves to assessing risks, selecting or building a solution, testing it and deciding whether to expand. It recommends four risk categories: low, moderate, high and prohibited, and proposes a phased 90-day starting plan whose 30-, 60- and 90-day marks are not strict deadlines. The guide includes templates and references such as an AI use case intake form, vendor review questions, policy examples and training recommendations. It also encourages local governments to create a public register of significant AI uses so residents can understand where the technology is involved in government services.

Kendrick said smaller communities shouldn’t feel they have to become AI experts or use the technology for everything, and advised: “Take what you can and start.” State CIO Shawnzia Thomas wrote in the playbook that AI should support public employees, not replace the judgment, accountability and community knowledge that effective government requires. Deshpande said policies alone are not enough, because organizations need visibility into actual use, not just an assumption that employees are following the rules. Kendrick said residents should know when they are interacting with AI and have a way to reach a person, adding that there should always be a human making part of the AI decision. Kendrick sees the playbook as a resource that can evolve, not a mandate for local governments to adopt AI, and she doesn’t want communities to feel pressured to move faster than they’re ready.

The playbook recommends that local governments resist buying AI simply because a vendor is selling it or another community is using it. It recommends creating an inventory of AI tools, including chatbots, meeting transcription software, cybersecurity products, document management systems, permitting applications and AI features added to existing software, as well as tools employees may have started using on their own. It identifies situations that should automatically receive high-risk review, including systems involving law enforcement, surveillance, public safety, sensitive information at scale or decisions affecting people’s rights and access to services. It calls for extra scrutiny when an AI system can take action, such as modifying records, sending official messages or spending money, and says AI should not be the sole decision-maker on matters involving benefits, employment, enforcement, safety or access to government services. Cities and counties, including smaller communities with few technology employees or no dedicated AI staff, are affected.

The playbook’s practical guidance comes with a reminder that AI adoption must keep people at the center. Low-risk uses, such as drafting or summarizing approved information with employee review, can follow simpler controls, while moderate-risk projects should receive review from a cross-functional AI committee. High-risk projects should get a more extensive assessment and executive approval, and prohibited uses should not move forward unless the governing body formally changes the policy after legal and public review. During the first phase of the 90-day plan, governments should name a leader responsible for AI, appoint a coordinator, form a review committee, issue interim employee guidance and begin the inventory. The next phase focuses on creating repeatable review processes, setting risk levels, establishing vendor requirements and providing basic training.

The final phase calls for launching a small number of pilots, publishing an initial AI webpage and setting up incident response and reporting. GTA hopes, Deshpande said, to offer office hours where local officials can ask questions and get help adapting its recommendations. Deshpande measures success by whether technology makes workflows easier, speeds up services and prepares employees for what’s ahead, and he hopes AI will help governments rethink how they deliver services and reduce friction for residents and employees. The playbook recommends that local governments adopt basic controls such as approved accounts, clear rules about what information can be entered, employee training and a way to report problems, along with reviewing vendors, including where their tools are hosted, what models they use and how data moves through their systems. The articles leave open which local governments will adopt the playbook and when.

Articles.Title: Georgia AI Playbook Is a Starting Point for Cities, Counties

stories.Headline: Used AI? Speak up or risk an F, Seoul school tells students.
stories.Summary:
A high school in the Yangcheon District of western Seoul recently ordered students to retake a graded assignment. This decision followed suspicions that many students used artificial intelligence to complete the work. The school took this action after a teacher used a detection program to check submissions. The assignment focused on the ideas of Harvard professor Michael Sandel and his 2009 book, Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?

The detection software flagged about 170 out of roughly 240 students for using AI. The school initially asked those who cheated to confess by October 30 or face a failing grade. More than 10 students admitted to the act, which led the school to require the entire class to redo the test. Some students complained that this is unfair to those who studied hard and worked honestly.

The Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and the Ministry of Education are managing these academic integrity issues. Ministry officials stated they will increase oversight to stop cheating with digital devices. They plan to send warnings to students before second semester final exams in the third week of November. Other officials from the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation will also discuss ways to prevent such cheating.

The Ministry of Education found four schools where students used AI smart glasses to cheat on exams. These students received zeroes and faced penalties like community service or suspensions of up to five days. Because of these trends, many teachers are returning to handwritten tests in the classroom. Experts like Professor Ham Eun-hye of Kongju National University say society must now decide how to balance AI skills with fair testing.

Articles.Title: Used AI? Speak up or risk an F, Seoul school tells students. - Korea JoongAng Daily

stories.Headline: US workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and winning
stories.Summary:
Public workers in Oakland, California, took a strike vote on 22 October 2026 to press for protections against AI, and 94.1% voted in favor. Their union, the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21, feared that AI tools could increase surveillance and inaccurately rate their performance. The city and the union then reached a tentative three-year agreement, and the strike set for 5 November was put on hold. The deal requires the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI instead of firing them. The agreement also includes other AI-related protections for city workers.

Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and union member, said the city should be deliberate about how it engages with AI products. He argued that new tools can cost more, be harder to implement, and produce poorer results. John Samuelsen, president of the Transport Workers Union and a New York City subway track inspector, said automation is the ultimate threat to jobs. Liz Shuler, AFL-CIO president, said unions are using contract talks to set guardrails that policymakers have not. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, said AI does not belong on big-rig trucks, in hospitals or in schools.

A survey by Ernst and Young, conducted from July to August 2026, found that nearly 70% of state and local government agencies have adopted or are implementing generative AI. Researchers call the monitoring tools bossware, and an October report co-authored by Kung Feng describes them. Such tools rank and evaluate workers, track location and activity, monitor productivity, and scan biometrics for timekeeping. Gonzalez said Amazon used algorithms to push warehouse workers to dangerous speeds, and that strategy is now reaching the public sector. The tools also use cameras, wearable devices and sensors, and some predict employees' emotions.

Steve Catanese, president of Service Employees International Union Local 668, which represents more than 10,000 statewide public-sector workers, said Pennsylvania's 2025 pilot with OpenAI gave workers no guarantees. The union then pressed Governor Josh Shapiro to adopt a policy requiring employee input and supervision of state AI use. In Columbus, Ohio, the Transport Workers Union won contracts in 2024 giving it veto power over any Central Ohio Transit Authority plan to deploy autonomous vehicles. In New York, a law effective December 2025 protects state agency workers from AI displacement. Keith Brown of the Alameda Labor Council said workers have faced AI harms for a long time.

Public workers in Florida and New York are trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles, calling them unsafe and a threat to jobs. Samuelsen said his union supports systems that aid collision avoidance and bus and train timing, but he worries about safety. He said some airlines are experimenting with drones to inspect aircraft instead of human mechanics. In California, Governor Gavin Newsom signed the No Robo Bosses bill and a second bill banning workplace AI surveillance tools on 30 September. The No Robo Bosses bill bars employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers.

The articles leave open how the Oakland agreement will be finalized, since it is only tentative. They do not say whether the Pennsylvania union's expected 2027 contract negotiations will produce new AI terms. The articles also do not state how the Florida and New York efforts against autonomous vehicles will end. Whether the California bills will be enforced in practice is not addressed. Unions say more fights are coming, and Feng said the contest over technology in the workplace is ongoing.

Articles.Title: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning - The Guardian

stories.Headline: Humain raises $667m for AI buildout in Saudi Arabia
stories.Summary:
Humain and the National Infrastructure Fund, known as Infra, signed two financing agreements totaling SAR 2.5 billion, or $667 million, to support Humain's AI buildout in Saudi Arabia. The deals were announced on November 14, 2026, and are Infra's first transactions under its AI Data Center Financing Program. The first facility, of up to SAR 1.1 billion ($293.3 million), will support the procurement and deployment of GPUs with about 25MW of IT load. The second, of up to SAR 1.4 billion ($373.3 million), will finance substations, transmission infrastructure and grid connections for Humain's Saudi data centers.

Humain, which is owned by the Public Investment Fund, is ultimately targeting 1GW of IT capacity. The two parties previously partnered in January 2026, when they signed an agreement for non-binding financing terms of up to SAR 4.5 billion ($1.2 billion) for AI and digital infrastructure projects in the Kingdom. Earlier in November 2026, Saudi Aramco acquired a 49 percent stake in Humain, with PIF holding the remaining 51 percent. Humain is set to take capacity at the Oxagon data center under development in Neom's industrial district, and it has previously said it has more than 200 plots of land for potential data centers.

Esmail Bin Mohammed Alsallom, CEO of Infra, said the agreements aim to unlock investment well beyond Infra's own commitment. He said supporting Humain's computing deployment alongside essential power infrastructure helps prepare a broader pipeline of data center projects for investment. He said Infra's role is to strengthen project readiness and bankability, with commercial viability and economic value guiding how it deploys capital. He said the partnership connects Infra's priorities with commercial discipline and helps build a financing market that can attract a broader pool of private and institutional capital and sustain local AI infrastructure growth.

Articles.Title: Humain raises $667m for AI buildout in Saudi Arabia

stories.Headline: The unit-type publicly offered investment trust "Goldman Sachs Corporate Bonds / ROBOPRO Strategy Fund 2026-12," which uses the AI operation strategy of "ROBOPRO," is born
stories.Summary:
FOLIO, a subsidiary of FOLIO Holdings in the SBI group, announced on November 13, 2026, that a new publicly offered unit-type investment trust called "Goldman Sachs Corporate Bonds / ROBOPRO Strategy Fund 2026-12" will be set up by SBI Okasan Asset Management. FOLIO will provide investment advice on asset allocation ratios to Goldman Sachs International for the index linked to the fund. A securities registration statement was filed with the Kanto Local Finance Bureau on Friday, November 13, 2026, and subscription opens on Tuesday, December 1, 2026. The fund is nicknamed "Robotto Plus 5."

The fund invests in yen-denominated bonds issued by Luminis II Limited, backed by bonds issued or guaranteed by The Goldman Sachs Group, and aims for a redemption value about six years after launch that exceeds the principal. Its performance has two parts: a stable portion that invests heavily in the Goldman Sachs bonds to aim to preserve principal in yen terms, and an aggressive portion that aims for performance-linked returns tied to the ROBOPRO Strategy VT5 Index. That index uses asset allocations calculated by FOLIO with AI predictions, with risk control applied by Goldman Sachs International to keep annual risk at around 5 percent, and it covers seven assets: global stocks, bonds, REITs and gold, with investment ratios of up to about 150 percent. It follows the existing series of funds dated 2025-12, 2026-03, 2026-06 and 2026-10.

FOLIO says it has built a track record in AI-based asset management services since starting with its AI investing service ROBOPRO, and that AI use in publicly offered investment trusts is growing. It says it provides investment advice based on AI strategies, together with its group company AlpacaTech, for funds including the ROBOPRO Fund and the SBI Okasan NASDAQ AI Active Fund, both set up by SBI Okasan Asset Management. FOLIO says it will keep expanding and improving AI-based asset management and offer financial solutions through various approaches to help more people build assets. ROBOPRO is a registered trademark of FOLIO.

FOLIO is registered as a financial instruments business operator with the Kanto Local Finance Bureau under number 2983 and belongs to the Japan Securities Dealers Association and the Investment Management Association of Japan. Its securities account opening and management fees are free, but investing in its products may involve set fees and necessary expenses per product, and losses can occur, including below the invested principal, due to changes in share prices, exchange rates, interest rates and other indicators. FOLIO Holdings, led by President and CEO Shinichiro Kai and established on April 1, 2019, is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market and is part of the SBI Holdings group. FOLIO, led by President Masafumi Yotsumoto and established on December 10, 2015, is based in Chiyoda Ward, Tokyo.

stories.Headline: Luminal, which provides an inference cloud and develops inference compiler software to test running AI models on different chips, raised a $25M Series A (Chris Metinko/Axios)
stories.Summary:
Luminal, a company that provides an inference cloud and develops inference compiler software, raised a $25 million Series A round. The round was led by Standard Capital, according to CEO Joe Fioti, who spoke to Axios Pro exclusively. The funding was reported by Chris Metinko of Axios in a story dated Nov 12, 2026. The company's software is used to test running AI models on different chips.

Luminal's technology lets customers use different chips rather than relying on Nvidia, the article says. The company describes itself as a search compiler and inference cloud provider. The $25 million is a Series A round, and Standard Capital led it. The article gives no other funding figures, dates or names beyond those.

Fioti, the CEO, told Axios Pro about the round and the lead investor. The article attributes the details of the raise to him. It does not include further comments from him or from Standard Capital. No other executives or investors are named in the article.

The article frames the technology as a way for customers to avoid depending on Nvidia for chips. It does not say what Luminal plans to do with the money or what happens next. No timeline for future steps is given. The piece is an exclusive report from Axios Pro.

Articles.Title: Luminal, which provides an inference cloud and develops inference compiler software to test running AI models on different chips, raised a $25M Series A (Chris Metinko/Axios)

stories.Headline: Operand, which offers AI-powered due diligence tools for PE firms, raised $31M across a seed and a Series A led by Khosla Ventures at a $220M valuation (Lucinda Shen/Axios)
stories.Summary:
Operand, a startup that offers AI-powered due diligence tools for private equity firms, raised $31 million across a seed round and a Series A, CEO Ram Gorthi told Axios Pro exclusively. The funding was led by Khosla Ventures at a $220 million valuation. Lucinda Shen of Axios reported the news on November 10, 2026. The company focuses on using non-traditional data sources to help firms get an edge. It also uses AI to process a higher volume of data.

The $31 million covers both the seed and Series A rounds, and Khosla Ventures led the funding. The round values Operand at $220 million. The tools are aimed at private equity firms doing due diligence. Operand's approach combines non-traditional data sources with AI to handle more data than traditional methods.

Gorthi, the CEO, spoke to Axios Pro about the raise. The articles do not include further comment from him or from Khosla Ventures. Responsibility for the tools and the company rests with Operand and its CEO. The reporting comes from Lucinda Shen at Axios.

The articles do not say what happens next for Operand or how it plans to use the money. They give no further context beyond the funding details and the company's focus. No timeline for future steps is provided. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
stories.Summary:
A Wall Street Journal report alleges that Nvidia engineered a GPU and memory shortage. Former CEO Jensen Huang allegedly funded AI startups to buy these components. This activity reportedly took place before his official resignation on November 12, 2026. The goal was to maintain a perception of high demand. This strategy helped move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The plan involved investing in AI startups to build data centers. This included a 250 billion dollar deal with OpenAI. An August meeting occurred between Huang and his senior finance team. Colette Kress, the CFO and acting CEO, attended this meeting. She pushed to reduce circular financing agreements during the discussion.

Jensen Huang allegedly reacted angrily to the suggestions from Colette Kress. He reportedly called her a deer in the headlights during the meeting. Kress argued that small cloud providers could not afford the GPUs. She believed these investments could become a financial dead end. Huang pushed for more investment into these small scale providers.

AI hyperscalers are affected because they are moving toward custom solutions. These large companies are moving away from using off the shelf components. Some forum users believe Huang's business tactics were monopolistic and anti consumer. Others suggest that big money cares more about profit than the economy. Some users worry that retirement savings will evaporate due to this.

Nvidia was facing an avalanche of GPUs from TSMC without immediate buyers. The company used circular financing to avoid having unsold semiconductor inventory. This occurred as the AI industry demand drove prices for high end cards. Leaks had predicted 5000 dollar RTX 5090 GPUs earlier in 2026. The company also faced a changing tide in the hyperscaler market.

The articles do not state if legal action will be taken. Some observers wonder if this constitutes an antitrust violation or racketeering. It remains unclear if other companies like AMD will be investigated. The report leaves the full extent of the circular investments open. No official response from Nvidia regarding the WSJ report is provided.

Articles.Title: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs

stories.Headline: A secret transit hub for Nvidia AI chips? Minister says Malaysian police on the case since April
stories.Summary:
The Royal Malaysia Police opened an investigation in April 2025 into allegations from the United States. The US claims Malaysia is a transit point for illicitly diverted advanced chips. These chips are produced by Nvidia and power much of the world's artificial intelligence development. Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail confirmed the probe during a press conference in Sitiawan. The police began investigating immediately after the allegations regarding the chips first surfaced.

The probe is carried out under the Strategic Trade Act 2010 to find proxy companies. It involves Bank Negara Malaysia, the Inland Revenue Board, the Customs Department, and the police. The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission is also involved, with the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry leading. Since July 2025, anyone exporting or transshipping high-performance US AI chips must obtain a Miti permit. This rule applies to those exporting, re-exporting, transshipping, or transiting these chips through the country.

Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the investigation covers whether Malaysia has become a transit hub. He stated that gathering evidence on illicit procurement involves layered inquiries that are highly complex. The minister noted that updates on the progress of the investigation have been conveyed to Miti. He explained that Miti is responsible for passing feedback to the complaining party in the United States. He did not say if the police had found evidence supporting the US allegations.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim stated there was no indication that Nvidia-Megaspeed chips were exported from Malaysia. He added that Malaysia had received no formal request from the US or Singapore on the matter. Miti said it never cleared Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte Ltd or its affiliate, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd. The Prime Minister said Malaysia would cooperate with all agencies involved in the chip investigation. These agencies are looking into whether illicit procurement or diversion of the AI chips occurred.

The US raised its complaint through the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry regarding the diverted chips. Miti previously stated that no permit is needed to bring AI chips into the country. The investigation focuses on whether proxy companies in Malaysia were used for illicit procurement of chips. The case involves the diversion of advanced technology used for artificial intelligence development globally. The Royal Malaysia Police have been working on the case since the April 2025 start.

Miti is currently working with the Customs Department to determine if any chips had been re-exported. The articles do not state if any specific suspects have been identified in the probe. It remains open whether the police will find evidence that supports the original US allegations. The timeline for the completion of the layered inquiries has not been provided by officials. The final results of the investigation have not yet been relayed to the complaining party.

Articles.Title: A secret transit hub for Nvidia AI chips? Minister says Malaysian police on the case since April

stories.Headline: Using AI to accelerate neuroscience research
stories.Summary:
Researchers are integrating artificial intelligence into neuroscience, and the results will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience. The human brain contains approximately 86 billion nerve cells that form trillions of connections. To understand this complex system, neuroscientists are turning to AI tools that can process vast amounts of data and simulate brain processes. Insights into the brain also inspire improvements to computational models, and the applications show potential to advance research and affect people's lives. The work includes several specific projects and tools.

Studying artificial neural networks and fruit flies revealed a shared learning principle for forming flexible, robust memories, according to Guanglong Sun of Tsinghua University. A new free, open-source AI tool lets neuroscientists with no programming experience analyze complex genomic data by asking questions in plain English, according to Vivek Swarup of the University of California, Irvine. The neuroscience community is also developing data standards collaboratively to break down data silos and streamline workflows, according to Oliver Ruebel of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Satrajit Ghosh, a computational neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the event moderator, said the bidirectional connections between neuroscience and AI go back a long time. He uses neuroimaging and machine learning to create predictive models for human health.

He said the findings show how AI can help researchers understand the relationships between brain structure and function. He also said the work helps appreciate the complex connections between genes, environments, learning, and behavior across species. The articles describe the research as showing transformative potential, and they present the work as a summary of findings ahead of the meeting. They do not say what happens after the presentations or announce further steps. The material is provided for information purposes only and is subject to copyright.

Articles.Title: Using AI to accelerate neuroscience research

stories.Headline: The China Shock in the AI Era
stories.Summary:
Americans voted in midterm elections to slow the expansion of artificial intelligence. Forty local ballot measures in 10 states promised to tighten restrictions on data center construction. These measures won more than 70 percent of the vote in 30 contests. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on a Thursday. He may have been compromised in a potential espionage scandal.

The 2026 Pew Research Center survey found 52 percent of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI. Only 9 percent were more excited than concerned, while 37 percent felt this way in 2021. Roughly six in ten people wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives. China makes more than 80 percent of the world's solar panels. Its battery manufacturing capacity is already more than double the current global demand.

Yasheng Huang is a professor of global economics and management at MIT Sloan School of Management. He wrote that the China Shock and AI Productivity Shock could produce a glut of output. He stated that gains tend to flow to owners of capital and the government. Huang noted that China's imports consist largely of minerals, energy products, and agricultural products. He argued that one sided trade eventually backfires on the country that benefits.

Economists Shoumitro Chatterjee and Arvind Subramanian said low and middle income countries are the real casualties. These people in Southeast Asia and Latin America depend on manufacturing for jobs and upward mobility. Workers are affected when local companies close or cut jobs due to cheap Chinese imports. Ordinary citizens may not see income rises if AI increases output without employing more people. Many Chinese families face heavy burdens paying for healthcare and retirement.

Economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson coined the term China Shock two decades ago. This described the increase in Chinese exports to the U.S. in the early 2000s. That surge caused the loss of more than two million jobs in certain American regions. Urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 had a record 18.9 percent unemployment rate in August 2025. The national minimum basic pension was raised to 143 yuan a month in 2025.

China could produce more batteries than the whole world will use by 2030. China has roughly 35 percent of world manufacturing capacity but only 11 percent of global consumption. Household consumption in China is 39 percent of GDP, compared with 68 percent in America. Labor compensation in agriculture, industry, and utilities dropped from 21 percent in 1987 to 15 percent in 2023. The ratio of minimum wage to GDP per capita fell to 0.27 in 2024.

Articles.Title: The China Shock in the AI Era

stories.Headline: 82% of B2B buyers value thought leadership more as AI spreads, Edelman finds
stories.Summary:
Edelman and LinkedIn published the 2026 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report in November 2026, a 35-page survey of 1,135 business executives in seven countries. The survey was fielded from September 4 to September 21, 2026, through online questionnaires and computer-assisted telephone interviews. It covered the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, India, Australia and Singapore, with interviews in English except in Germany, where they were in German. The report is the eighth annual collaboration between the communications firm and the Microsoft-owned professional network. A commentary by Edelman's Annie Dunleavy introducing it is dated November 9.

The report defines thought leadership as content offering expertise, guidance or a unique point of view, made available free or in exchange for contact details. It excludes content primarily describing an organization's products or services and anything buyers pay for, such as client deliverables or subscription research. Managers made up 37% of respondents, directors 29%, vice presidents 7% and C-level executives 25%, with owners, founders and partners at 2%. Company size split 35% at 1 to 200 employees, 33% at 201 to 1,000 and 32% above 1,000. Most charts use a base of 1,063 B2B decision-makers, with final decision-makers at 317, C-suite executives at 310 and thought leadership suppliers at 495.

Edelman sells content strategy and business marketing services, and the commentary was written by its head of content strategy in the United States. LinkedIn sells advertising placements in its feed, including formats that promote posts by individual executives, and its B2B Institute promotes a framework it calls Buyability. Seven Edelman staff and three LinkedIn staff are credited as authors. The report names LinkedIn in one of its own questions as the example of a professional social media feed. The series has run since a combined 2017-2018 edition, with editions listed for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025 and no 2023 report.

Ginny Cartwright Ziegler, chief marketing officer of Pearson, is quoted saying thought leadership is most powerful when it helps people see what's possible and gives them confidence to act. Victoria Whitney, vice president of corporate communications and external affairs at Ecolab, is quoted saying that in an AI-driven world information is everywhere and credible insight grounded in real expertise carries greater weight. Social Media Today, reporting on the study on November 11, said through Andrew Hutchinson that AI cannot provide real, hands-on experience and insights and cannot summarize information that does not already exist. The report cites a 6sense study, the 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, for the statistic that 95% of contracts are won by companies already on a buyer's Day One List.

The report says 48% of final decision-makers and 46% of C-suite executives spend four or more hours each week reading or viewing thought leadership. Some 89% of decision-makers agreed high-quality thought leadership makes a company feel like a more viable long-term partner, and 78% said it had changed their view of a company from a vendor to a potential strategic partner. Some 48% said a vendor's thought leadership influenced a lot or a great deal whether that vendor made the initial consideration list. Asked which attribute most increases trust, 56% chose content demonstrating a clear understanding of challenges, priorities and constraints, 14% chose content showing product strength and 11% chose market leadership. A November 4 post covered by PPC Land cited B2B Institute buyer data in which a recommendation from similar companies was chosen by 58% against 39% for being the market leader.

Some 76% of decision-makers said thought leadership shared within the group helped assess whether a vendor understood the organization's needs, and 52% said it helped decide which vendor to select. Final decision-makers were asked whether poor or absent thought leadership contributed to a vendor being removed from consideration, and 59% said yes, around 187 people on a base of 317 by PPC Land's calculation. During vendor evaluation, 84% of decision-makers used an AI assistant or AI-powered search tool to summarize thought leadership, 72% to learn about a market or solution category and 67% to compare vendors or approaches. When an AI tool cited a company's thought leadership, 78% then researched the company, 70% read or viewed the cited content and 52% used the information in an internal discussion or business case. Some 82% said thought leadership is becoming somewhat or much more valuable as AI becomes a more common way to get answers, ideas and advice about business challenges.

Asked about its most important roles, 57% said providing original research, data or perspectives not found elsewhere and 51% said adding context, nuance and human judgment AI answers may lack. Among the 495 suppliers, 84% said distributing through professional social feeds such as LinkedIn was incorporated a lot or a great deal, 74% said the same of traditional search engines and only 46% said they optimize so content can be surfaced in AI-generated answers. Semrush's March analysis of 89,000 URLs found LinkedIn ranked second among domains cited in AI answers, and in June LinkedIn published guidance that posts of roughly 200 to 300 words earn the most AI search citations. The May launch framework cited a 6sense finding that 94% of buying groups consult large language models during research, and Demandbase reported in August that ChatGPT referrals to B2B websites grew 303% in a year. The report does not publish results by country, does not say whether averages are weighted by market and gives no margin of error.

Articles.Title: 82% of B2B buyers value thought leadership more as AI spreads, Edelman finds

stories.Headline: Google's AI glasses will have one surprising thing they're not allowed to see_id184820
stories.Summary:
Google introduced privacy features for its first Android XR smart glasses on November 14, 2026. Samsung developed these glasses in collaboration with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. The system prevents the devices from seeing human faces. This technology aims to solve privacy concerns regarding secret filming. It applies to all Android XR glasses, including Samsung Intelligent Eyewear.

The Samsung Intelligent Eyewear costs $395 and ships to South Korea and the United States on December 10, 2026. These glasses feature a 12MP ultrawide camera, built-in microphone, speakers, and nine hours of battery life. The system blurs faces before sending data to Google servers when Gemini translates signs or identifies objects. Users must agree not to record in sensitive places, record others without permission, or cover the indicator light. Play Store apps cannot use the camera for livestreaming or facial recognition.

Android XR Vice President and General Manager Shahram Izadi shared these details on Google's official blog on November 12, 2026. He stated that technology seeing the world has a responsibility to the people around the wearer. Izadi explained that Google listened to bystanders, wearers, and privacy experts during their research. He noted that bystanders expressed concerns about being filmed without their knowledge. He said wearers were constantly calculating their actions while out and about.

Some users may find the lack of livestreaming and action camera features a bummer for trips to Japan. Bystanders are affected by the recording capabilities, though the system blurs their faces. The glasses include a privacy LED indicator to alert others when the device is actively recording. This indicator prevents the camera from turning on if it is disabled or covered. The system also blurs the wearer's face if they look into a mirror.

Google designed these features because the original Google Glass failed due to privacy concerns. The company will not use visual data from Gemini queries for ad personalization or AI training. Gemini will not save images or videos from these queries in its history logs. These measures are intended to give people peace of mind while using the technology. The framework extends beyond Gemini to include third-party applications.

The Samsung Intelligent Eyewear is currently available for pre-order. The articles leave open whether the system is bulletproof or if some faces will slip through unblurred. They mention a Harvard student who turned Meta Ray-Ban glasses into a facial recognition device. Reports indicate government agencies have abused the recording capabilities of Ray-Ban glasses. It remains unclear if people will find sinister ways to use Android XR.

Articles.Title: Google's AI glasses will have one surprising thing they're not allowed to see

stories.Headline: AI CT analysis links myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Johns Hopkins University published a retrospective cohort study in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment showing that fully automated deep learning algorithms can quantify cardiometabolic biomarkers from routine abdominal CT scans in patients with high-risk invasive breast cancer. The study included 127 female patients diagnosed between 2016 and 2018. The work was reported on November 14, 2026, in an article by Nathaniel Bowman in Scienmag. The article appeared on bioengineer.org under the headline linking AI CT analysis of myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer. The study's subject was deep learning analysis of CT scans for cardiometabolic biomarkers in breast cancer.

The study was a retrospective cohort of patients with Stage I to IV breast cancer who newly presented to the Johns Hopkins Health System and had an abdominal CT scan within six months of diagnosis. Of the 127 female patients, 64.6 percent were postmenopausal, 57.5 percent were White and 26.8 percent were Black. The team excluded patients with insufficient medical records, missing BMI data or incomplete CT image data. Myosteatosis was defined quantitatively as a mean muscle density of 18.9 Hounsfield units or lower for females, a threshold previously established in the literature. The article was published in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, volume 220, issue 1, Article 38, with DOI 10.1007/s10549-026-08122-0.

The authors were Tsou, Yang, Wang, Qi, Blackford, Visvanathan, Summers and Sheng, and the authors noted several limitations. They said the observational design demonstrates important associations but does not independently indicate causation. They said the cohort was from a single institution and had few patients of Asian race or Hispanic ethnicity, which may limit generalizability to populations with different patterns of body adiposity. They said the sample size was small and did not provide sufficient power to study survival outcomes, leading them to analyze the Agatston plaque score dichotomously. They said the findings may only apply to patients with high-risk, invasive breast cancer who require CT scans as part of their routine care.

The results indicated that BMI was positively correlated with CT-derived adipose tissue area and muscle area and negatively correlated with liver intensity. Muscle intensity was significantly lower for patients in the overweight and obesity BMI groups than for those in the healthy weight group. The Agatston plaque score, measured as zero versus nonzero, did not significantly differ by BMI group. Postmenopausal women had significantly higher visceral fat area than premenopausal women, with a mean of 115.0 square centimeters versus 81.4 square centimeters. Of postmenopausal patients, 61.0 percent presented with aortic plaque compared to 15.6 percent of premenopausal patients, and 60.8 percent of patients with myosteatosis had a plaque score greater than zero compared to 34.2 percent of those without myosteatosis.

The research team aimed to address the limitations of body mass index in stratifying metabolic disease risk among cancer patients. The article states that BMI is the most accessible and commonly used surrogate for body adiposity, but previous scrutiny has highlighted its insensitivity to actual body fat distribution and its poor prediction of metabolic risk in certain demographics. Cardiometabolic diseases, including obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, are significant factors influencing breast cancer recurrence and survival. Obesity is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer recurrence and overall mortality, while excess body weight elevates the risk of cardiovascular disease, the second leading cause of death among breast cancer survivors. The deep learning algorithms performed quantification and segmentation of muscle and adipose tissues, liver fat and abdominal aortic calcification.

The findings suggest that CT-derived myosteatosis is a promising metric for assessing cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer patients. The article states that breast cancer treatments may increase the risk of developing diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, ischemic heart disease and stroke, so monitoring these biomarkers is essential. The authors suggest that integrating these CT-derived biomarkers into routine clinical practice could help medical oncologists better monitor breast cancer survivors' cardiometabolic risk after diagnosis. The article states this approach aims to minimize cardiovascular morbidity and mortality and the progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. The article leaves open how the single-institution, small-sample findings would generalize, and it states the observational design does not independently indicate causation.

Articles.Title: AI CT analysis links myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer

stories.Headline: Ceribell (CBLL) Stock Looks Stretched Despite New AI Monitoring Launch
stories.Summary:
Ceribell launched an AI driven delirium monitoring platform that has seen rapid adoption by hospitals. This medical technology company experienced a strong share price run over the past year. The stock price rose 102.6 percent during this twelve month period. These events were reported by Al Bentley on November 14, 2026.

The stock currently trades at a price to sales ratio of 9.3x, which is higher than the peer group level of 5.6x. This figure also exceeds the medical equipment sector average of 2.6x. The company plans to release a new hardware platform called Omni. These numbers suggest the shares are overvalued based on the Fair Ratio benchmark.

Analysts from Simply Wall St provided a consensus narrative regarding the company's value. They suggest the stock is 12 percent undervalued. These experts believe that adding AI algorithms for stroke and delirium transforms the tool into a multi indication system. This growth would justify the current market price.

The market is currently paying a premium because of optimism regarding future sales. Investors are focusing on revenue generation rather than immediate profits. There is less room for error if pricing power or adoption fails to meet expectations. The company must now convert its commercial momentum into durable expansion.

Articles.Title: Ceribell (CBLL) Stock Looks Stretched Despite New AI Monitoring Launch

stories.Headline: Adaptive AI System Models Student Learning Pathways Using Educational Proxy Data
stories.Summary:
Educational researchers Feibao Bao and Xiuliang Zhang introduced an adaptive intelligence framework called the Hybrid Transformer-Graph Reinforcement Adaptive Competency Engine, or HT-GRACE, on November 14, 2026. The framework is designed to model college students' educational outcomes and simulate personalized learning strategies. The research team developed a computational model that integrates structural relational modeling, sequential temporal tracking, and policy optimization. The model evaluates student engagement and simulates supportive interventions in higher education contexts. The framework operates on benchmark data from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, known as OULAD.

OULAD comprises records from 32,593 online students and does not include direct assessments, empirical records, or validated competency labels for real-world innovation or entrepreneurship skills. The researchers treated these unobserved attributes as latent educational constructs inferred from observable behavioral signals, including engagement intensity, assessment performance, learning consistency, and online interaction frequency. The architecture maps structural relationships using a competency-aware heterogeneous graph with 32,635 nodes and 148,420 edges, connecting students, 22 competency concepts, and 20 activity types. The system applies an exponential decay formulation for recency-based weighting and an uncertainty-aware fusion layer that computes dynamic attention weights across data modalities. HT-GRACE achieved an overall classification accuracy of 94.8 percent, an F1-score of 94.86 percent, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 94.95 percent, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.915.

The authors state that the resulting capability metrics represent model-defined educational proxies rather than direct, real-world measures of entrepreneurial ability. They emphasize that predicted scores and simulated policy actions cannot be interpreted as verified enhancements in human creativity, problem-solving, or entrepreneurship. They note that prospective recommendations generated by algorithmic policies have not undergone real-world trial deployment, where automated advising could introduce self-fulfilling feedback loops. They conclude that validation in operational university classrooms and prospective field trials remains necessary to ascertain whether simulated policy gains translate into meaningful educational improvements. The authors explain that OULAD contains no records of institutional intervention programs or subsequent outcomes, so outputs represent simulated policy recommendations rather than observed clinical or institutional interventions.

In comparative benchmarking against baseline models including Study-GNN and Transformer-based sequential predictors, the framework demonstrated consistent improvements in discriminative performance, with an error variance of 0.00007 and a normalized stability score of 0.91 in continuous regression evaluations. In reinforcement learning simulations, the agent attained a cumulative reward gain of 27.6 percent over baseline methods and demonstrated stable convergence across successive training iterations. Ablation experiments showed that removing the Graph Neural Network reduced classification accuracy to 90.7 percent, removing the Transformer temporal encoder dropped accuracy to 91.5 percent, and replacing the PPO module with a conventional policy mechanism decreased accuracy to 89.9 percent. Removing both the graph and transformer modules resulted in the lowest recorded accuracy of 87.6 percent. Learner outcomes were divided into three categories prior to training: low-outcome learners covering scores from 0.00 to 0.49, medium-outcome learners spanning 0.50 to 0.74, and high-outcome learners encompassing scores from 0.75 to 1.00, with medium-outcome learners registering an F1-score of 94.22.

The development of HT-GRACE was informed by architectural limitations identified across earlier intelligent education systems. Prior sequential models such as the Transformer-based Sequential Educational Prediction approach developed by Kusumawardani and colleagues modeled long-term behavioral dependencies but omitted structural relationships among students and competencies. Graph-focused frameworks like the Study-GNN architecture introduced by Li and collaborators and the relational network designed by Hakkal and co-authors modeled complex educational interactions yet lacked mechanisms for temporal tracking and reinforcement optimization. Adaptive systems proposed by Amin and collaborators or Yi and team incorporated reinforcement learning techniques such as Proximal Policy Optimization but either encountered reward sparsity constraints or omitted multi-head attention mechanisms required for extended behavioral trajectories. The authors describe a persistent gap in unified multi-modal modeling that their framework aims to address.

The experimental implementation was constructed in Python 3.10 and PyTorch 2.x, executed on hardware comprising an Intel Core i9 processor, 32 gigabytes of system memory, and an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card with 24 gigabytes of video memory. The Open University dataset contains more than 10 million virtual learning interaction logs alongside tables for student demographics, assessment scores, and course registrations, with interaction attributes including student identifiers, module codes, interaction dates, and click sums. Records were partitioned into 70 percent for training, 15 percent for validation, and 15 percent for testing, utilizing the Adam optimizer across identical configurations. Supervised predictive comparisons benchmarked HT-GRACE against specialized baseline architectures including T-SEP, GNN-PP, the Graph-Enhanced LSTM model, and Study-GNN. The Consistency Index tracked the stability of student representations by averaging cosine similarities between adjacent hidden state vectors across successive time steps, while a Participation Diversity Score applied an entropy calculation across distinct activity categories.

Evaluation of computational overhead indicated that HT-GRACE maintained manageable training durations, low inference latencies, and reduced floating-point operations relative to comparative baselines under identical laboratory hardware conditions. Cross-domain transfer tests evaluating concept drift across differing course module presentations showed consistent adaptation recovery metrics, suggesting the unified embeddings remain resilient when exposed to shifted interaction distributions. The authors emphasize several core methodological boundaries and scope limitations governing the interpretation of these findings. Validation in operational university classrooms and prospective field trials remains necessary, and the articles do not report any such deployment or trial results. The articles also leave open whether simulated policy gains would translate into meaningful educational improvements in real settings.

Articles.Title: Adaptive AI System Models Student Learning Pathways Using Educational Proxy Data

stories.Headline: New NAACP Report Warns AI Could Deepen Health Disparities in Black Communities
stories.Summary:
The NAACP and the pharmaceutical company Sanofi released a report during the AfroTech Conference 2026 in Houston, according to The Legacy Newspaper. The report is titled “AI Fluency is a Challenge on Both Sides of the Exam Room.” It is the third installment of the groups’ ACE Your Health StoryMap series, which looks at how AI, internet access, and healthcare inequities shape health in Black America. The findings draw on national datasets and input from nearly 23,000 community members across 47 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.

The report warns that new technology does not erase old gaps on its own. It says one in three Americans lives in a healthcare desert, and in the Mississippi Delta all 154,000 Black residents live more than 25 miles from a hospital rated four or five stars. About 3.8 million Black Americans live in homes without a broadband subscription, which limits access to digital health tools. Nineteen percent of people who use AI for health information say they did so because they could not afford to see a provider, and Black adults are significantly more likely than White adults to use AI for mental health advice.

Dr. Chris T. Pernell, Director of the NAACP Center for Health Equity, said too many Black communities face healthcare deserts, provider shortages, clinic closures, inadequate internet access, and concerns about racial bias. She said that if these gaps remain unaddressed, AI could widen existing disparities instead of helping close them. She said equity and fairness must be designed into healthcare AI from the beginning, not added as patchwork fixes. Tanisha M. Sullivan, Head of External Engagement & Health Equity Strategy at Sanofi, said innovation must be matched by efforts to expand access, build trust, and address barriers. She said pharmaceutical companies should partner with community organizations, healthcare providers, and policymakers so innovations reach the people who need them most.

The report says nearly two-thirds of Black adults believe racial bias remains a major problem in healthcare, and one-third expect AI to make that bias worse. It lays out steps communities can take, including expanding broadband adoption, building AI fluency and digital skills, strengthening community-based health education, and advocating for equitable technology policies. It also invites community members to add their voices to the StoryMap. The full report and other ACE Your Health resources are available at naacp.org.

Articles.Title: New NAACP Report Warns AI Could Deepen Health Disparities in Black Communities

stories.Headline: Fed report: AI valuations and data center debt
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published its November 2026 Financial Stability Report. The report says asset valuation pressures remain elevated and that equity valuations are partly driven by market enthusiasm for what it calls "super intelligence" (SI). It says debt issued to finance advanced computing infrastructure has grown rapidly. The report generally reflects information available as of October 28, 2026. The report is a financial-stability assessment and makes no statement about research funding, universities or grants.

The report says the ratio of equity prices to earnings for S&P 500 companies stayed well above its historical median. Section 1 says broad equity valuation metrics were partly driven by that enthusiasm, "though moderated by concerns over firms' capital expenditures and debt issuance plans." A boxed analysis, "Leverage in the Data Center Buildout," reports that debt issuance to finance advanced computing infrastructure has grown rapidly over the past year. The debt is shifting from mostly corporate bonds to a mix of public and private debt, structured credit and project finance. Advanced computing-related debt issuance rose to more than $680 billion by October 2026, about a fivefold increase from $130 billion in all of 2023.

Such borrowing rose from less than 6 percent of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate debt issuance in 2023 to about 31 percent in 2026. Outstanding public debt related to advanced computing is estimated at more than $1.1 trillion as of October 2026. The report notes that private credit transactions make the full magnitude harder to measure. Not-yet-commenced leases have undiscounted values above $1 trillion. Take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees are above $2 trillion.

The largest U.S. bank holding companies have close to $1 trillion of exposure to large technology firms, data center developers, advanced computing-related special purpose entities and private credit vehicles, and utility companies. The report says these exposures are evaluated in the annual supervisory stress test. The report describes a "circular financing" dynamic in which hyperscalers and GPU makers supplement debt financings with equity investments in smaller firms. It says the complex links among data center firms, public credit markets, private lenders and special purpose vehicles "create vulnerabilities that necessitate close monitoring." Box 5.1 summarizes a survey run by Federal Reserve Bank of New York staff, with responses from 23 contacts at broker-dealers, banks, investment funds and advisory firms in September and October.

The report notes the box does not represent the views of the Board or the New York Fed. AI was the top-cited risk. Respondents named three areas of concern: elevated equity valuations and the possibility of a market correction if earnings disappoint; cybersecurity risk, from sophisticated attackers or from damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and complex forms of AI-related financing. Mentions of AI, higher long-term rates and cyberattacks rose the most relative to the spring survey. In Section 5, the report says private fixed investment tied to new computing technologies has been a significant driver of U.S. economic growth this year.

The report says an unexpected downturn in corporate earnings could prompt lower asset valuations, tighter credit conditions and reduced capital expenditure. Research offices that depend on technology-sector gifts, sponsored agreements or endowment returns may find it useful as background on how regulators characterize AI-sector exposure, alongside their own institutional risk processes. The article points readers to CASRAI's grants management hub for funding-side practice. The article cites the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Financial Stability Report, November 2026 (PDF), released November 13, 2026. The article also cites the Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report publication page.

Articles.Title: Fed report: AI valuations and data center debt

stories.Headline: Teacher-Mediated AI Feedback Associated With Higher Undergraduate Piano Performance Scores
stories.Summary:
A 16-week quasi-experimental study by researchers Li Lin and Ping’an Zheng found that teacher-mediated artificial intelligence feedback in studio instruction was associated with greater performance score gains than conventional feedback alone. The study ran during the autumn semester of the 2025, 2026 academic year and followed 80 second- and third-year undergraduate piano students in two pre-existing instructional cohorts taught by the same instructor. Over a 12-week intervention period with six biweekly diagnostic cycles, students who received teacher-reviewed performance reports and targeted practice tasks showed a model-based growth advantage of 6.57 points over peers taught with traditional listening-based feedback and demonstrations. The contrast remained evident at a four-week follow-up assessment even after structured task assignments ceased. The findings were published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1733.

The evaluation framework relied on ScoreFeedback-Piano v1.2, an assessment pipeline incorporating a locally adapted MT3 encoder, decoder Transformer network for automatic note transcription. The system ran on Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.1, and torchaudio 2.1, sampled audio at 32 kHz, and generated 229-band log-Mel spectrograms with a 10-millisecond hop size. The MT3 checkpoint had been fine-tuned on the GiantMIDI-Piano dataset, with developmental training informed by MAESTRO v3.0.0 and HUPS-Piano-2021 collections, and the frozen checkpoint was fixed in June 2023. The pipeline aligned performed notes to reference events with cost weights of 1.0 per semitone for pitch, 0.5 per second for onset timing, and 0.5 per second for duration, within a local timing slack of plus or minus 15 percent and a 150-millisecond onset matching window. Four skill dimensions were scored on a 0 to 100 scale and weighted 30 percent for technical accuracy, 25 percent each for rhythmic stability and expressive control, and 20 percent for completeness.

The authors, Lin and Zheng, designed the framework on human-centered learning analytics and formative assessment theory, in which diagnostic reports serve as advisory tools for the instructor. They stated that teachers evaluate flagged acoustic passages alongside scores and recordings, translate acoustic deviations into passage-specific practice drills, and verify pedagogical progress in subsequent studio lessons. They noted that automated assessment can identify deviations from a musical score while teachers interpret their musical significance and choose an appropriate response. They warned that accepting automatic recommendations uncritically weakens independent judgment. They concluded that automated acoustic diagnostics offer the greatest educational utility when human teachers actively contextualize algorithmic findings into structured artistic goals.

Three independent external experts with at least 10 years of university piano teaching experience performed blind evaluations at baseline, posttest, and follow-up, achieving absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.974 at baseline, 0.978 at week 12, and 0.979 at week 16. Across 240 paired evaluation records, the automated platform composite scores achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.972 and an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.971, with a mean absolute error of 1.620 points and Bland, Altman limits from minus 3.976 to positive 4.067 points. Dimension-level scrutiny revealed a positive bias of 1.032 points for technical accuracy but a negative bias of 0.975 points for expressive control. The sample comprised 80 music majors aged 19 to 21 years, 50 female and 30 male, at repertoire difficulty Levels 4 through 6, with the 40 experimental students averaging 5.55 years of prior piano training and the 40 control students 5.71 years. Both groups completed weekly 45-minute individual lessons with the same instructor, totaling 9 hours during the 12-week intervention and 12 hours across the full 16-week study.

At the week 12 posttest, the experimental group achieved a model-based growth difference of 6.5667 points over the control group (95% CI [5.1926, 7.9408], p < 0.001). Observed blinded composite averages rose from 70.0650 to 80.5000 points in the experimental group, compared with 70.4667 to 74.3350 points in the control group, an unadjusted change effect size of Hedges g = 2.1297. Experimental students gained an additional 6.8475 points in technical accuracy, 6.7075 points in rhythmic stability, 5.1100 points in expressive control, and 5.7275 points in completeness, with all contrasts significant after Benjamini, Hochberg corrections. During the maintenance phase from week 13 to week 16, biweekly AI task assignments ceased while weekly private lessons continued and platform access remained available to experimental students. At week 16, blinded expert ratings registered composite scores of 79.2925 in the experimental group and 74.6425 in the control group, a sustained model-based growth difference of 5.0517 points (95% CI [3.6776, 6.4258], p < 0.001).

Practice logs between weeks 1 and 12 showed experimental students completed an average of 219.859 practice minutes per week compared to 192.205 minutes in the control group, an added 27.654 minutes weekly alongside 0.629 additional practice sessions per week. Exploratory parallel mediation modeling showed that bootstrap confidence intervals for practice minutes, error correction, and teacher-estimated feedback uptake all included zero, so these estimates do not establish the mechanisms underlying improvement. The authors emphasized that because the investigation relied on two intact institutional teaching groups assigned to a single instructor without randomized allocation, teaching group dynamics and instructional conditions remain statistically inseparable. They noted that expert evaluations assessed students within one specific institutional cohort performing intermediate repertoire, and that the week 16 assessment reflected continuous platform access rather than complete tool withdrawal. Robust sensitivity checks confirmed that varying composite dimension weights between 0.20 and 0.40 preserved the statistical direction and magnitude of the intervention effects.

Articles.Title: Teacher-Mediated AI Feedback Associated With Higher Undergraduate Piano Performance Scores

stories.Headline: ByteDance plans Meta Muse-like AI agent, boosts AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
ByteDance is preparing to launch a new artificial intelligence assistant in the coming weeks. This tool is designed to function similarly to Meta's Muse, which debuted in September. The move is part of a larger strategy to improve the company's overall AI capabilities. This development follows the June release of the Seed 2.1 language model.

The company plans to invest up to $70 billion to make Seedance the top video AI platform in China. Co-founder Zhang Yiming believes the firm can compete with Anthropic and OpenAI by 2029 or 2030. To achieve this, the Seed division employs about 1,000 researchers and engineers. This team is currently led by Wu Yonghui, who arrived from Google's DeepMind in 2025.

Zhang Yiming recently met with the AI team to discuss these goals. He noted that the datasets for Seed large language models are much smaller than those used by global rivals. Zhang stated that the company should prioritize long-term research and development. He specifically advised against using distillation, which uses larger models to train smaller ones.

ByteDance currently holds a strong position in video generation due to its vast pool of video data. However, the Seed team previously admitted that their models struggle with complex, open-ended tasks. The company is now expanding its workforce to address these weaknesses. They aim to strengthen their position through these massive financial investments and technical shifts.

Articles.Title: ByteDance plans Meta Muse-like AI agent, boosts AI ambitions

stories.Headline: Netweb is India's sole NVIDIA-certified GPU server builder
stories.Summary:
Netweb Technologies, an Indian company, says it is the only builder of NVIDIA-certified GPU servers in India, according to Swastik Chakrabarti, the company's Vice President of Technology. The company, which also offers an agent security framework and multi-tier GPU infrastructure solutions, was reported in TechGig's coverage published on November 13, 2026. Chakrabarti described Netweb as one of nine global manufacturers of NVIDIA GPU servers and the only one based in India. The company has a manufacturing partnership with NVIDIA, and its server designs are built on NVIDIA's Grace and Grace Hopper platforms. Netweb has also developed a power delivery design for NVIDIA's NVL72 architecture that NVIDIA approved.

The company is also widening its software range to help customers run AI infrastructure. Its offerings include Tyrone for cluster management, Kubyts for container management, and Skylus for private cloud and hyperconverged infrastructure, along with Skylus.ai for managing GPU-based AI systems. Netweb is building Agent Guard, a security framework that would require AI agents to obtain time-limited access tokens before reaching enterprise data. Under that design, an agent would request a fresh token for each access, which would be valid for five to ten minutes and usable only once, and every request would be logged. The company is also looking at post-quantum cryptography.

Chakrabarti said Indian government agencies account for 55 per cent of Netweb's clients, with enterprises making up the rest, and that enterprise demand for GPU servers is growing faster. Netweb serves banking, financial services and insurance, manufacturing, retail and healthcare customers. Government bodies use AI for document summarisation, procurement processing, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines and optical character recognition. Netweb is also developing a multi-tier token generation engine that would spread workloads across NVIDIA V100, A100, H100, H200 and B200 GPUs, so that older hardware can be used efficiently and the newest accelerators can be kept for latency-sensitive tasks. The company is further examining storage optimisation and CXL memory to improve AI inference performance.

Articles.Title: Netweb is India's sole NVIDIA-certified GPU server builder

stories.Headline: Leeroo open-sources Kapso for iterative enterprise data learning
stories.Summary:
Leeroo, an AI systems builder, has open-sourced Kapso, an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run, according to the company. The announcement was reported by TechGig on November 13, 2026. The system is meant to automate the repeated cycle of investigating a problem, forming hypotheses, testing them, and improving based on what the outcomes show. Its designers describe it as aimed at complex enterprise data environments where that cycle is slow to carry out by hand.

Kapso keeps a bank of lessons from past experiments, with each lesson carrying a credence score, the conditions under which it applies, and supporting evidence. For every new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas and ranks them by expected return against budget, then sends the top-ranked ideas to an implementor. A separate verifier module, which the experiments themselves cannot access, checks the results, which the company says prevents manipulation. The experimentation modules can also propose changes to the metrics and criteria the verifier uses, though those changes need the verifier's approval or rejection before they take effect.

The company reports strong results on public benchmarks. Kapso took first place on RelBench for predictive modeling on relational databases and ranked first on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, where it remains among the top open-source systems. In AI competitions, it performed ahead of agents reported by the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI and placed among the top three AI systems at the International Olympiad in AI 2026. The article does not give scores or details of those rankings beyond these placements. Kapso is described as model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic, with experience shared and updated through Git.

Articles.Title: Leeroo open-sources Kapso for iterative enterprise data learning

stories.Headline: Kiji Inspector uses Sparse Autoencoders for LLM agent explainability
stories.Summary:
Dataiku's 575 Lab has released Kiji Inspector, an open-source tool that uses sparse autoencoders to explain why large language model agents make the choices they do. The tool was presented by Hannes Hapke, Director of Engineering at Dataiku, and was reported on November 13, 2026. Rather than producing a plausible after-the-fact story, it aims to uncover the internal mechanisms behind an agent's decisions. It does this by looking at activation tokens instead of processing entire prompts.

The tool is built to explain how agents select tools. Its training method uses contrastive pairs, made of an anchor reply that is correct and an adversarial reply that is similar but wrong, so it can tell the different tool selections apart. Kiji Inspector is model-agnostic and works with open-source models such as Gemma 4 and Nemotron 3. It includes patches for inference software like vLLM so that activations can be retrieved for deeper analysis. The framework is distributed as a PyPI package and Docker containers, with trained models hosted on Hugging Face.

According to the report, Hapke presented the tool, and Dataiku's 575 Lab is behind it. The reporting describes the tool as open source, so it is available to others to use and examine. The articles do not describe any further statements from Dataiku about its plans beyond the tool itself. The tool's use cases include detecting agent misbehavior, supporting audit compliance, validating prompt engineering, and monitoring production drift.

The tool has clear limits, since it requires access to model weights and therefore cannot be used with closed-source models. The training process is also computationally intensive, especially when teams build custom datasets. Future work described in the report includes expanding support to more open-source models, running multi-layer experiments, and researching whether the approach transfers across models. The articles do not give dates or further details for those plans.

Articles.Title: Kiji Inspector uses Sparse Autoencoders for LLM agent explainability

stories.Headline: AI Roundup: Three Resources Related to AI and Advising
stories.Summary:
A recent report from the Clayton Christensen Institute examines how technology, and AI in particular, can be designed to be "prosocial," meaning it strengthens human connection rather than replacing it. The report reviews 10 career and college advising platforms that were funded to pilot such designs, with pilots spanning K-12 through workforce settings. It warns that in the age of AI, the relationships that help students get by and get ahead could disappear or never form at all. The authors include Julia Freeland Fisher, who discussed the work on NCAN's To a Degree podcast alongside Maurice McCaulley of the Gates Foundation.

The pilots produced measurable results. Uprooted Academy added an outreach feature that nudged students to identify and contact their support network, and 100% of students identified three or more contacts. Overgrad tested an alumni directory, and 75% of students said they preferred a counselor-brokered introduction over cold outreach on LinkedIn or email.
