Roadtrip Nation's career conversations tool, which included an AI simulation for practicing a professional conversation, produced a 6.7 percentage point increase in students' self-reported confidence in booking a career conversation.

Project Evident also released "Relational AI: From Principles to Practice in Empowering College Advisors," which includes a white paper, a technical quickstart guide, a tool for building chatbot "harnesses," and a half-day virtual convening. A harness is a set of instructions that sets parameters on a chatbot's output, and the tool lets users adjust settings for emotional support and guidance style, from informational to maximal support. The convening features much content from NCAN members, and the white paper's discussion of design principles is especially useful for anyone building tools that students will use. Those are the details the source gives for this release.

Separately, Education Strategy Group published a playbook for state education leaders, policymakers and funders on how states can shape AI use in postsecondary advising. Rather than urging states to build their own AI platforms, the playbook explains how they can set the context and conditions for responsible implementation by others. It also includes a landscape scan of current state practices and survey data on sentiments about AI and advising from professionals, parents and students. The resource is presented as a slide deck that state-level leaders may want to bookmark.

Articles.Title: AI Roundup: Three Resources Related to AI and Advising

stories.Headline: Enterprise AI agent observability with BigQuery and Looker
stories.Summary:
Google announced expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud on November 13, 2026, in a blog post by Kate Grinevskaja, Product Manager. The announcement covers first-party data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party agents built with frameworks such as Agent Development Kit or LangGraph. The post says enterprises are moving AI agents from experimental prototypes into production. It says deploying an agent is only half the battle, because teams also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. The capabilities give unified visibility into these agents, according to the post.

The framework captures telemetry from the agent, lands it in BigQuery tables the customer owns, and lets teams analyze it where they already work. Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent workflows, now generally available, send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs into the agent's project. Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation. Managed first-party conversation logging, now generally available, writes to BigQuery tables the customer owns.

The Conversational Analytics API, now generally available, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs. It supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys, and regional and multi-regional data residency. Agent monitoring in BigQuery, now generally available, provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency. System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics are now generally available in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), tracking engagement and token usage. User ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab are in preview.

Admins can enable Cloud Monitoring for aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage, and Cloud Trace for step-by-step spans, at the project or organization level. Cloud Trace observability scopes consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. Operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL. When conversation logging is enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table called agent_events via the BigQuery Storage Write API. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn, skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking.

Developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin called BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin. With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads into BigQuery. Because conversation logs land natively in the agent_events table, teams can run BigQuery AI functions such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring issues. They can also use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis.

Each turn in BigQuery conversation logs records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency. Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across business intelligence workloads. Teams can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps, called big_query_max_billed_bytes, on an agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, daily input and output token quotas, in preview, can be enforced per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.

The open-source evaluation tool Prism lets teams test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP. Prism can stream completed evaluation runs into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in the customer's project. First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery, built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support, are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Enterprise AI agent observability with BigQuery and Looker

stories.Headline: AI slop papers published under academics' names
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, investigations reported that a coordinated ring of predatory open-access journals had published low-quality, AI-generated “slop” papers falsely attributed to established academics without their knowledge, submission, or consent. The scheme was discovered when automated indexing alerts flagged bogus manuscripts to senior researchers at institutions including the University of Gothenburg, Stanford University, and the University of California, Berkeley. Alan Said, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Gothenburg, received an automated Google Scholar notification alerting him to a newly indexed paper bearing his name as author. The paper, titled “Intelligence Systems Supporting Sustainable Global Development,” appeared in the American International Journal of Research and Innovation (AIJRI). Said had never written, reviewed, or submitted the work.

Upon examining the text, Said found vacuous, computer-generated prose supported by irrelevant and hallucinated citations, describing the article as having no substantive content and reading “like slop.” Subsequent investigations uncovered dozens of similar papers falsely listing Stanford University professors Fei-Fei Li and Christopher Manning, as well as UC Berkeley faculty Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell. None of the listed scholars had any relationship with the publications or the publishing entities. Cross-journal investigations linked the fraudulent papers to a cluster of closely affiliated titles, including AIJRI, the American Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Innovation (AJAMRI), and the American Journal For Multidisciplinary Research (AJFMR). All three domains were newly registered in 2026 while hosting fabricated back-archives with dates predating their registration.

The websites shared identical page layouts, graphic templates, a common United States WhatsApp contact number, and overlapping editorial boards featuring faculty primarily from Indian institutions without verifiable affiliations. Multiple titles listed a common editor-in-chief under the name Denish Brown. The network operates on an open-access author-fee model, charging article processing charges (APCs) of approximately $200 for international authors. This operational model mirrors patterns documented in analyses of paper-mill red flags and predatory indexing rings cataloged in Cabells Predatory Reports. When Said contacted the hosting provider and domain registrar to report the impersonation and demand removal, the journal did not retract or delete the paper.

Instead, the site operators merely swapped Said’s name with another author’s name, cycling through several different credited scholars over subsequent days across identical AI-generated text. The case underscores how predatory publishing networks exploit automated discovery infrastructure to bootstrap illicit credibility. Search engines and bibliographic scrapers ingest newly posted web pages rapidly, automatically attaching unvetted articles to researchers’ public bibliographies. Because indexing happens within hours while formal investigation and removal take weeks or months, deceptive journals gain a window of apparent legitimacy. The primary danger extends beyond reputational damage to senior researchers.

By presenting mastheads and author lists populated by renowned scientists, these operations create a deceptive facade of prestige designed to trap early-career researchers, graduate students, and authors under institutional publication mandates. Unsuspecting scholars who submit genuine manuscripts to these venues lose both their publication fees and their work to unindexed, unpreserved repositories that fail minimum standards of scholarly archiving. The emergence of AI-generated identity-theft publishing requires coordinated countermeasures from both individual researchers and institutional research offices. Scholars should review their ORCID record permissions, disabling open third-party write access and configuring trusted-organization controls so that unauthorized entities cannot automatically assert works or affiliations on their persistent records. Researchers should change their Google Scholar profile configuration from automatic article additions to manual review, auditing attributed papers regularly to remove mistakenly linked slop manuscripts.

University research offices, research integrity officers, and scholarly communication librarians should establish rapid-intake channels for faculty reporting unauthorized bylines. Institutions can apply standard COPE flowcharts to structure formal complaints and collaborate across international networks using NISO CREC communication practices. When predatory journals refuse retraction or cycle author names, institutional legal and library teams should issue formal copyright and impersonation complaints directly to domain registrars, hosting infrastructure providers, and indexers to remove fraudulent records at the root. The CASRAI article was published on 14 Nov 2026 and is licensed under CC-BY 4.0. Inside Higher Ed published “AI-Generated Slop Papers Published Under Prominent Academics’ Names” on 2026-11-13, checked 2026-11-14.

Times Higher Education published “Predatory journals publish AI slop under top academics’ names” on 2026-11-13, checked 2026-11-14. The CASRAI article states that everything CASRAI publishes stays free to read, with no account and no card. The article offers an AI assistant that cites the sources behind every answer, labels web answers and says when it can’t answer. Answers draw on CASRAI’s guides and dictionary plus the federal and funder documents CASRAI indexes: Federal Register, Grants.gov, Regulations.gov and UKRI. The assistant works on the CASRAI site and inside Claude, Cursor and the AI tools users already use.

Articles.Title: AI slop papers published under academics' names

stories.Headline: Leading AI safety advocate likely to run for president
stories.Summary:
Brad Carson, a former Oklahoma congressman and a leading AI safety advocate, is likely to run for president, according to two people directly familiar with his plans, as reported by Politico on November 13, 2026. The Democrat, who served as a "blue dog" lawmaker, is reportedly considering the bid. Those close to him say a push from like-minded donor groups has also encouraged the idea. The report describes Carson as someone who helped build the political infrastructure of the AI safety movement.

The timing is tied to the midterm elections, in which many Democrats won while campaigning on backlash against data centers and skepticism toward big tech. The article says this has left AI safety advocates feeling emboldened. Carson has become a central voice in the debate over how far the companies developing AI should be restrained. The report presents his interest as part of a broader political shift rather than a formal policy change.

The article also makes clear the run would be a major long shot. Carson has a military background as an Iraq War veteran and once served as undersecretary of the Army, which the report says could sound presidential. However, he has not served in Congress since 2005 or in government since 2016. One person familiar with his plans called it a "keyhole shot," while stressing that no final decision has been made.

Politico's Decoded newsletter carried the report, which is based on people with direct knowledge of Carson's thinking. The article does not describe any formal announcement or filing. It offers no timeline for a decision. Readers should expect further reporting on whether Carson moves forward with a campaign.

Articles.Title: Leading AI safety advocate likely to run for president

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Survey Finds Widespread AI Adoption Amid Veterinary Training Deficits
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey evaluated artificial intelligence adoption among veterinary professionals in Hong Kong. Researchers gathered responses between December 2023 and March 2024 from four different cohorts. The participants included undergraduate students, doctoral researchers, university faculty, and practicing clinical veterinarians. Findings revealed widespread engagement with digital tools alongside acute deficits in formal training. Nearly half of the respondents reported being unfamiliar with fundamental conceptual frameworks.

The study used a thirty-seven-item online questionnaire for students at City University of Hong Kong. It also included licensed practitioners registered with the Hong Kong Veterinary Association. Practitioners must hold qualifications from the American Veterinary Medical Association or other recognized bodies. The sampling frame included 146 undergraduates, 34 doctoral students, 28 faculty, and 956 registered individuals. The final analytical dataset comprised 79 complete submissions from these specific professional groups.

The authors stated that there is an urgent requirement for formalized curricular updates. They noted that academic institutions face pressure to embed computational literacy into professional syllabi. The researchers said continuing education bodies must address the lack of readiness among veterinarians. They suggested using practical, clinically focused modules to help licensed professionals. The authors also emphasized that their modest sample size necessitates a cautious interpretation.

Practicing veterinarians registered the highest trepidation, with 66.7 percent feeling unprepared for algorithmic integration. Undergraduate students and faculty members reported higher rates of using tools than clinicians. Many participants expressed concerns regarding professional accountability, diagnostic reliability, and systemic rigidity. Those affected include students who lack formal instruction despite having a strong interest. Only 46.8 percent of respondents agreed that current technology aligns with veterinary ethics.

The research compared Hong Kong findings against similar studies from Australia, the United States, and the Iberian Peninsula. These international inquiries also documented high student interest and limited curricular implementation. Most respondents used ChatGPT for language editing, proofreading, and literature reviews rather than diagnostics. Only 17.7 percent of the surveyed population reported receiving formal instruction in these applications. Most participants viewed educational enhancements with more confidence than direct therapeutic interventions.

Future directions require the creation of regulatory frameworks and context-specific model validation. Institutions must decide how to integrate these tools into the tertiary veterinary schooling process. The articles leave open how to objectively test competency rather than relying on self-reporting. It remains unclear how to resolve the divergence between exploratory use and safe integration. The study does not specify the exact timeline for implementing these suggested curricular changes.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong Survey Finds Widespread AI Adoption Amid Veterinary Training Deficits

stories.Headline: ITU announces funding for educational AI research
stories.Summary:
The IT University of Copenhagen announced on 9 November 2026 that it has received DKK 7.1 million from Independent Research Fund Denmark for a five-year educational AI project. The project is led by Jichen Zhu and is titled Friction by Ambiguity: Improving Engagement and Critical Thinking in LLM-Supported Learning. The research will investigate ambiguity in learning supported by large language models. A planned chatbot called Diffrakt is a research output to be developed.

Diffrakt will use guided questions and deliberately open responses in AI ethics teaching. The team will also research how to calibrate ambiguity to model uncertainty. Christian Hardmeier is co-principal investigator, and Pawel Grabarczyk contributes ethics expertise. Initial testing is planned with ITU students, alongside work with educators.

Zhu's institutional profile identifies Zhu as a professor in Human-Computer Interaction and Design and head of the Human-AI Interaction Lab. The lab's description connects interaction design and critical technical practice with research on how people interpret and live with AI. Independent Research Fund Denmark describes its remit as supporting researcher-initiated, high-risk research within and across disciplines, alongside thematic funding. The announcement does not establish that Diffrakt improves learning.

The article draws a distinction between a funded research question, a planned tool and evidence of educational benefit. It says 9 November marks ITU's announcement and should not be treated as the funder's grant decision date. An institutional assessment can track the proposed technology separately from evidence about students' reasoning and engagement. Funding and a chatbot development plan alone cannot establish that the educational approach works.

Articles.Title: ITU announces funding for educational AI research

stories.Headline: Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley executives have turned against Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, according to a New York Times report published on November 13, 2026. The article, written by Kalley Huang, Mike Isaac and Cecilia Kang, says the company has grown into a rival that peers increasingly view as a nuisance. Anthropic and OpenAI had been lobbying the White House to keep some advanced A.I. models from being developed and widely shared, arguing they were too dangerous. Companies such as Nvidia and Microsoft, however, saw those models as a major business opportunity.

At the end of July, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Jensen Huang, then the chief executive of Nvidia, moved against that effort. According to four people familiar with the discussions, they exchanged drafts of a letter calling for those models to stay open. Two dozen companies agreed to sign before the letter became public, and over the following week about 200 more joined, including OpenAI. The article also says Amodei has spent years frustrating rivals with warnings about extreme A.I. risks, even as his company builds some of the most powerful systems available. Frustration grew as Anthropic moved into the lead in A.I. development and reported rapid revenue growth.

The article describes Anthropic as a company that has cultivated an image of doing the right thing while also gaining a reputation for playing hardball. It reports that Anthropic has cut some customers off from its service and lobbied against free alternatives offered by other companies. More than 20 people in the technology industry told the newspaper that competitors and investors have organized to push back over the past year. Many of those sources spoke on condition of anonymity to protect their relationships with Anthropic. The report notes that the company is moving toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever, expected later in the month.

Articles.Title: Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic

stories.Headline: Is GDS Holdings (NasdaqGM:GDS) Undervalued Given Its AI Data Center Scale?
stories.Summary:
Al Bentley wrote an analysis of GDS Holdings on November 14, 2026. The report examines if the company is currently undervalued by the market. It focuses on the scale of its artificial intelligence data centers. The author looks at the relationship between share price and earnings. This analysis was produced with the help of AI automation.

The company operates DayOne campuses, which are among the largest AI data centers globally. A planned build program for these assets requires RMB 30 to 50 billion. The stock trades at a P/E ratio of about 7.2x. This figure is below the IT sector average of roughly 23.2x. It is also under the peer group average of about 25.8x.

Analysts provided a consensus narrative that compiles price targets and forecasts. They suggest the share price does not fully reflect multi year contracted capacity. This bullish stance implies the stock is 59 percent undervalued. The analysts believe the current price ignores the planned build program. Their view is based on revenue momentum and margin structure.

Investors are affected by swings in sentiment regarding AI infrastructure. The market may not be pricing in earnings from the DayOne campuses. Some see the stock as a laggard despite rising compute demand. Others must weigh the headline metrics against two major internal warning signs. These concerns could change how investors view the valuation picture.

The share price of GDS Holdings has gained about 71.5 percent over three years. The company has experienced a turbulent few years in the market. Its value recovery depends on whether the earnings profile is sustainable. The business is tied to AI infrastructure with substantial capital needs. Earnings power is a key factor for the current stock trade.

Future value depends on utilization, pricing, and the intensity of future expansion. The market must decide if earnings can support the current share price. New information may change the views on revenue and key risks. The report leaves open how internal warning signs affect the valuation. It does not state the specific nature of those two warnings.

Articles.Title: Is GDS Holdings (NasdaqGM:GDS) Undervalued Given Its AI Data Center Scale?

stories.Headline: Changes to Greek life, AI integration, potential city-wide changes, campus support systems and more
stories.Summary:
WSU Provost Chris Riley-Tillman outlined several institution-wide changes meant to support students as they progress through college. Greek life is among those subject to change, alongside finances, support systems and general education revision. The Student Belonging and Success Initiative will move forward despite Greek row's public protest, and is expected to take effect some time next year. The initiative could delay rush week by a semester for first-year students. It aims to give students more time to explore campus life without the pressure of committing to anything.

The initiative is still in development and subject to change, with many aspects modifiable in the future. Stronger accountability and recognition standards will also be implemented for fraternities and sororities. As of fall 2023, Greek life housing does not fulfill the first-year on-campus residence requirement. Students can also expect changes to advising, AI integration, general education reform, bus system changes and possible changes to first-year classes. The General Education Reform Committee has been leading many of these revisions.

Discussions have involved optional grading in general education courses not related to a student's major and restructuring or removal of U-core, global and late-start classes. Late-start classes currently exist in a smaller capacity and are specific to differing colleges on campus. An expansion could bring interchangeable courses, more course options and a stronger support system. How many late-start classes students can take a semester is still under review, and eight-week courses are also available. WSU uses AI to improve recruitment and recognize when students may need academic help.

With the launch of Google Gemini, students have another university-sanctioned resource, and Microsoft Co-pilot remains available for students, faculty and staff. The Office of the Provost is reconstituting the AI Council. Riley-Tillman acknowledged the current lack of a movie theater, limited bar availability and transportation downtown as factors affecting the college experience. Fulmer Hall is currently being rebuilt, alongside revisions across all six campuses. A proposed change would remove the need to apply formally to transfer between campuses.

Another proposed change would carry over discounted tuition and other credentials between campuses. A partnership with The National Institute for Student Success found that universities overcommunicate, causing most students to overlook or ignore most forms of communicative media. Southside Dining Hall's soon-to-be all-you-can-eat meal plan is meant to support food security by providing students with more meals. $17 million was enacted through the 2025-2027 operating budget for retention and compensation. Retention has increased 1.1% this year, while enrollment has gone down 3.7%.

Across the six campuses, enrollment has been on a steady decline since 2019. Riley-Tillman cited rising tuition, economic challenges, after effects of COVID-19, the disbanding of Pac-12 and less of the U.S. population participating in college. Seventy percent of WSU students change majors at least once. Nearly eighty-two percent of current WSU students are Washington residents, which may be influencing the strategy to pursue out-of-state students. Changes to out-of-state residency awards are likely as restructuring continues.

Articles.Title: Changes to Greek life, AI integration, potential city-wide changes, campus support systems and more

stories.Headline: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data
stories.Summary:
A customer message containing a name, a card ending 4111 and a phone number was wrapped in a prompt, sent to a model and logged in plain text by a Java service, in an article by TechPanda published on sitepoint.com on November 14, 2026. The article said this happens more often than people admit and that prompts and responses are some of the most personal text an application touches. It said AI calls are messier to log than regular web requests because output changes from run to run. It said prompts are built from a template, retrieved document chunks, chat history and the user's message stitched together. It said cost is paid by the token, so without per-call records you cannot say which feature is burning money.

The article said the first three sensitive groups follow patterns and are easy to catch, while the last two do not. It said metadata includes a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. It said a sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call. It said metadata can be kept for a year and masked content for a couple of weeks, and that the request ID should go into the logging framework's MDC.

The article said one small component should be the chokepoint every AI log call passes through, and nothing else should write raw prompts. It gave regex rules for emails and bearer tokens, with patterns compiled once and a fixed order because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. It said replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable for whoever debugs it later. It said regex will not catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence.

The article said named-entity recognition can tag people, places and organisations and mask anything above a confidence threshold. It said exact replacement can swap values already known, such as the customer's name from the current session, and that masking at the field level while building the prompt is best of all. It said consistent pseudonyms turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. It said an HMAC with a secret from a secrets manager should be used because a plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes.

The article said one JSON record per AI call should be written with clearly separate fields so dashboards for cost and latency never touch the text fields. It said streaming tokens arrive in tiny pieces and a card number can be split across two chunks, so the full response should be collected in a buffer, masked once the stream ends and logged. It said tool arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the exchange, so the tool name, duration and outcome should be logged by default and arguments only after masking. It said masking lowers risk but never removes it, so content fields should get a short retention period, AI log readers should be limited, log storage and its pipeline should be encrypted, and the hashed user ID should be logged so one person's records can be found and deleted.

The article said a masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none because everyone assumes the logs are clean. It said a small set of messy, realistic samples should be built and run in the CI pipeline, with a new case added every time a leak turns up. It said a scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net. It said mistakes to watch for include logging raw text at debug level, masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results, letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs, leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, and treating masking as finished once it ships.

Articles.Title: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

stories.Headline: Patient comfort with AI’s clinical decisions tied to provider oversight: Gallup
stories.Summary:
A new Gallup survey found that over half of U.S. adults would be fine with AI tools making clinical decisions about their care, but only if their healthcare provider can review and override those decisions. The survey polled more than 5,000 American adults in August, and Healthcare Dive published its report on Nov. 13, 2026. The finding indicates that having human oversight of AI is still important to patients. Providers severely underestimate how comfortable patients are with AI making clinical decisions even with their oversight. Only about a third of providers said patients would be on board with this use of AI.

People are most comfortable with AI diagnosing them and making treatment decisions, with the majority wanting providers to sign off. Over a third also said they are fine with AI assisting providers in making decisions. When it comes to selecting medications and reviewing images, patients also prefer provider oversight, and their comfort with AI drops sharply if a provider is not involved in the decision-making at all. A separate Gallup poll of over 1,000 practicing primary care physicians shows a major gap between what they think patients are comfortable with and what patients actually deem acceptable. There is a 20-percentage-point gap between how comfortable patients are with AI making diagnostic and treatment decisions and how comfortable providers think patients are.

According to the report authors, providers should ask patients their preference about how AI is used in their care. Healthcare providers being able to review AI’s decisions emerged as the most critical factor in boosting patient comfort with the technology in clinical care. Nearly half of adults in the consumer survey said that provider review made them more comfortable with AI-led decisions on diagnosis and treatment and imaging review, more so than other factors, including privacy protections, safety and efficacy studies and lower healthcare costs. Having strong privacy protections was the next most important factor increasing patient comfort with AI, with a third of patients saying it would make them more comfortable with AI taking the reins, even without provider review.

More patients are comfortable with AI making medication decisions and performing imaging reviews than providers assume. Research has shown that patients support AI use for low-risk administrative tasks like appointment scheduling but prefer that AI not make diagnoses, even when a human reviews the output. Tracking patient comfort with AI is especially important as the healthcare industry allows AI to act more autonomously, even in work that directly impacts patient care. Just last month, Utah approved a slate of new healthcare pilots that would eventually allow prescriptions to be issued and refilled without clinician review. A growing number of healthcare organizations are piloting or conducting proof-of-concept projects with agentic AI tools, which can make complex decisions and complete multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention.

Articles.Title: Patient comfort with AI’s clinical decisions tied to provider oversight: Gallup

stories.Headline: Hybrid AI Model Flags Maternal Mental Health Risk With Uncertainty
stories.Summary:
A study published in Discover Artificial Intelligence evaluated a hybrid ensemble model combining Support Vector Machine and Gaussian Process algorithms against standard machine learning benchmarks, bioengineer.org reported on 14 November 2026. The primary objective was to determine whether combining the nonlinear discrimination of SVMs with the probabilistic inference of GPs could provide more reliable risk assessments. The model was tested on a pooled dataset of 14,008 retrospective maternal health records. The records came from Kawempe National Referral Hospital and Mukono General Hospital in Uganda and the publicly available PERI_DEP dataset. The Ugandan records were collected between May 2016 and October 2025.

The PERI_DEP data accounted for 10,786 records, or 77% of the total. The researchers ran a full-feature sensitivity analysis that included individual items from the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and closely related depression-symptom variables. They also ran a primary leakage-free analysis that excluded these outcome-defining variables. In the full-feature analysis, Random Forest achieved an accuracy of 97.75% and a ROC-AUC of 0.996. The proposed Hybrid SVM-GP framework achieved an accuracy of 93.54% and a ROC-AUC of 0.982.

The Hybrid SVM-GP framework achieved the lowest Expected Calibration Error of 0.015. In the leakage-free analysis, the Classical SVM achieved the highest performance with an accuracy of 0.9487 and a ROC-AUC of 0.9763. Random Forest accuracy dropped to 0.8971 and its ROC-AUC to 0.9461 in that setting. The model calculates a normalised predictive entropy for each final fused probability, where values approaching zero indicate confident classifications. The Gaussian Process component provides a posterior variance representing uncertainty in the latent function underlying the prediction.

SHAP was used to examine the contribution of individual predictors to model outputs. Influential predictors in the leakage-free analysis included the relationship with the mother-in-law, current appearance acceptance, sufficient money for basic needs, male-child preference, family system, previous miscarriage history, and perceived social support. The authors emphasize that SHAP values should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships. The authors stress that the framework is intended to support, rather than replace, professional clinical judgement. The uncertainty-guided applications remain hypothetical because the study did not prospectively evaluate whether uncertainty-informed decisions improve clinical outcomes.

Postpartum depression is estimated to affect between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide. Conventional clinical screening has traditionally depended upon self-report instruments such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale administered during postpartum checkups. The research team constructed a unified data dictionary matching 51 demographic, socioeconomic, obstetric, and psychosocial features. Missing continuous measurements were addressed through median imputation, while missing categorical values were replaced using the most frequent category. The hybrid architecture was implemented in Python with Scikit-learn and CatBoost in Google Colaboratory.

DeLong's tests and McNemar's comparisons showed Random Forest correctly identified 1,779 non-risk cases and 960 risk cases with only 37 false positives and 26 false negatives. The hybrid model correctly categorized 1,723 non-risk cases and 898 risk cases, recording 93 false positives and 88 false negatives. The hybrid model attained a statistically significant reduction in Expected Calibration Error by 0.0651 compared to Random Forest. Prospective external validation and clinical-utility assessment are required before the framework can be recommended for routine maternal healthcare deployment. Future studies should follow TRIPOD+AI reporting recommendations and apply PROBAST+AI to systematically assess risk of bias and applicability.

Articles.Title: Hybrid AI Model Flags Maternal Mental Health Risk With Uncertainty

stories.Headline: AI’s Productivity Boom Needs a Worker Dividend
stories.Summary:
Qantas Airways announced it will cut 850 jobs and outsource work to Accenture to overhaul its IT systems and prepare for further artificial intelligence disruption of the travel industry. The cuts came as Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was promising technology guardrails, and the announcement was reported in a column by Paul Karp of POLITICO dated November 13, 2026. Many affected workers reportedly fear they will be next, and the column says the airline's move is a massive blow to them. The column does not say when the cuts take effect or how the outsourcing contract is structured.

The column argues that AI's productivity gains need to reach workers, not just shareholders, if voters are to accept the technology. It points to a snap review into an OpenAI data breach, whose recommendations were released to draw a line between Australian Labor's approach and a more laissez-faire U.S. stance. It also cites a call by workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth for businesses to consult staff on AI rollouts, which the Greens answered by demanding better pay and shorter hours written into law. The author suggests public sector workers could be offered higher pay in return for efficiency gains. The piece frames this as a response to voters who distrust AI and are experiencing stagnant wages and rising costs.

Paul Karp, the Canberra Playbook editor at POLITICO, wrote the column and is its author. He describes Albanese's remarks that AI cannot be switched off and that its benefits include boosting productivity and revolutionizing health care. The column quotes Albanese noting that social licence had slipped in places without guardrails, and it notes that protests have grown in his home state of New South Wales, which votes in March 2027. Karp also draws on a 2013 article by Adam Creighton about intensified work in journalism to illustrate how productivity pressure leads to burnout. He concludes that the government must give voters a reason to embrace the technology rather than simply asserting that it is inevitable.

Articles.Title: AI’s Productivity Boom Needs a Worker Dividend

stories.Headline: Can AI Make Smaller Mortgage Loans Profitable?
stories.Summary:
Pavan Agarwal, CEO and creator of Angel AI and head of Sun West Mortgage Co., said his company has reduced core mortgage processing costs from approximately $5,000 per loan to $125 or less through AI and blockchain technology. He spoke during NMP's recent webinar, AI & Digital Assets Are Here: Is Your Mortgage Business Ready?, alongside leaders from Angel AI and the National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals. The webinar was presented by Sun West Mortgage and Angel AI. Agarwal said Angel AI's income analysis technology can evaluate tax returns, K-1s, 1099s, and other financial documents in approximately five or six minutes. He cited an Angel AI analysis of Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data suggesting that an additional 1.1 million borrowers could have qualified for mortgages in 2025 if its underwriting technology had been used nationwide.

Agarwal said that when costs are high and a low- and moderate-income family is doing a $150,000 loan, two or three points are spent just on manufacturing costs. He said those borrowers get left behind, with rates getting higher or borrowers simply not being marketed and approached. He said that if a borrower has multiple K-1s, different deductions and income complications but is buying a $5 million house, most bankers are happy to put in the effort. He said that if the borrower is buying a $150,000 house, it can take multiple days of an underwriter's time to get through all of it. Agarwal began his mortgage career serving lower-income communities around Los Angeles.

Jason Riveros, senior advisor to NAHREP's CEO, said those capabilities could be particularly valuable for first-time buyers, self-employed borrowers, and multigenerational households. He said family dynamics are very important, with multigenerational households potentially purchasing together and multiple signers potentially involved. He noted that entrepreneurs and borrowers with multiple income streams often face more complicated underwriting requirements. Riveros said he thinks AI is one of those tools that will allow people to eliminate the complexity of those files. Riveros said NAHREP wants its members to use AI to become more efficient while preserving the relationships that drive their businesses.

Riveros said NAHREP is still very firm in believing that whether you are an LO or real estate broker, you need to be at the center of that transaction, and AI will be a facilitator of that. He added that the ability to have someone you can connect with if something goes wrong is very valuable. Angel Sumlin, managing director of organizational development at Angel AI, said most of the people in these transactions have never even seen each other's name before. She said buyers, sellers, agents, and lenders depend on documents and information passed between multiple parties, often without a reliable way to independently verify each step. Sumlin demonstrated Angel AI's digital wallet, showing how mortgage professionals can begin using blockchain-based tools without extensive technical knowledge.

Sumlin said everything you're doing in Angel AI is just a chat, and users can create an account, establish a digital wallet, and ask the platform questions throughout the process. She said Angel AI's approach is designed to remove the technical barriers that have historically made blockchain wallets difficult for everyday users, and she said it makes it easy and accessible to everyone. Sumlin said originators can earn points through everyday activities and potentially use those rewards to provide additional value to borrowers and referral partners. She said you earn these points and can then share them directly, offset costs of the loan like the credit pull and the appraisal, and continue to add value to your clients and referral partners. Agarwal described how an AI-generated mortgage approval could be recorded on a blockchain, allowing sellers to verify the lender's financing commitment.

Agarwal said a blockchain-based smart contract could then track the purchase agreement, earnest money, and outstanding closing conditions. He said that from the seller's perspective, the money is already there once that blockchain transaction happens. He said the combination could eventually make financed offers more competitive with cash transactions, and he said it basically makes every real estate transaction as powerful as a cash transaction. Agarwal said the approach would still account for traditional closing requirements, including title and appraisal conditions, but could make the process more transparent and predictable.

He said the technology could be particularly beneficial for FHA and VA borrowers, including buyers with lower credit scores who might otherwise struggle to compete against cash offers. Riveros said NAHREP is working with Angel AI on a digital token initiative designed to introduce its members to blockchain technology while creating additional professional benefits. He said the association plans to introduce its Avance token, which members could use to access educational resources, VIP event opportunities, and rewards from participating partners. Riveros said to think of it more like a frequent flyer club type of benefits, not something that grows with value or from a dollar standpoint, but things you can redeem within the organization.

He said the initiative is intended to introduce real estate professionals to digital wallets and tokenization through practical applications rather than cryptocurrency speculation. Riveros said NAHREP expects to share additional details about the program in the coming weeks, and he said the association wants its members to be familiar with what's happening in the marketplace in terms of tokenization, but also with wallets and digital wallets and their ability to use those. Agarwal said the company's broader vision is to connect loan officers, real estate professionals, and consumers through a digital marketplace where AI handles increasingly complex tasks. He said stronger financing commitments could become a valuable advantage for LOs and their real estate partners in winning purchase business.

The articles do not say when the Avance token will launch or what specific educational resources, VIP event opportunities, and partner rewards it will include. The articles do not give the date of the webinar or the full names of the NAHREP CEO and the participating leaders beyond those named. The articles do not say how Angel AI's underwriting assessments are warranted or what the warranty covers. The articles do not give the modeling details behind the estimate that 1.1 million additional borrowers could have qualified in 2025.

Articles.Title: Can AI Make Smaller Mortgage Loans Profitable?

stories.Headline: Bracco, Avicenna.AI announce US FDA clearance for new brain aneurysm detection and assessment software
stories.Summary:
Bracco and Avicenna.AI announced that the US Food and Drug Administration has granted 510(k) clearance for UPTUNITY-Aneurysm, the first product in Bracco's new UPTUNITY portfolio and a result of their collaboration. The announcement was published on November 13, 2026. The software is designed to help medical specialists detect and assess brain aneurysms on computed tomography angiography images of cerebral arteries by building artificial intelligence assistance into a radiologist's existing reading workflow. Bracco presents it as a complement to its AiMIFY software, which was developed with Subtle Medical to enhance contrast on brain MRI.

According to the companies, the detection tool, a computer-assisted detection and diagnosis program, is meant to be used as a concurrent reading aid by appropriately trained specialists. It flags suspected saccular brain aneurysms larger than 3mm on head CTA images and reports their presence, location and size. For aneurysms already known, a follow-up component provides quantitative measurements and compares examinations to show changes over time. The software is said to give information to be reviewed alongside the CTA images, and the companies state that it does not replace a full patient evaluation or a physician's review and should not be relied on alone to make or confirm a diagnosis.

Bracco executives framed the product in terms of supporting radiologists, with Cosimo DePinto, executive vice president of marketing and commercial operations at Bracco Americas, saying the clinical decision remains with the radiologist. Fabio Tedoldi, head of global research and development at Bracco Imaging, said the tool supports physicians from first detection through monitoring. Cyril Di Grandi, chief executive officer and co-founder of Avicenna.AI, said the product combines the two companies' strengths. Avicenna.AI is set to lead promotion and commercial distribution in the United States, and the product will be showcased at the upcoming Radiological Society of North America annual meeting from November 29 to December 3 in Chicago.

The launch builds on a strategic partnership the two companies announced in March 2026, when Bracco also launched AiMIFY commercially in the European Union. The articles describe the partnership as aimed at advancing AI applications in contrast-enhanced CT imaging. Bracco says the UPTUNITY line reflects its wider push into digital health technologies beyond contrast agents. The articles do not say when UPTUNITY-Aneurysm will reach US clinical sites or report any pricing.

Articles.Title: Bracco, Avicenna.AI announce US FDA clearance for new brain aneurysm detection and assessment software

stories.Headline: AI Ambition Outpaces Data Readiness in Tax and Finance Functions, EY Study Finds
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, EY published its 2026 Tax and Finance Operations Survey, which polled 1,600 CFOs and senior finance and tax leaders across 30 jurisdictions. The study finds that tax and finance functions are moving from AI experimentation toward expectations of measurable value. Geopolitical pressure and increasingly digital, real-time tax administration are raising the stakes, and nearly two-thirds of organizations, 64%, say they are not fully prepared for real-time tax demands. Most organizations are adapting their operations in response.

Despite strong ambition to scale AI, the survey identifies weak data foundations and legacy operating models as the main barriers. Insufficient AI-ready data was named the greatest obstacle to advancing AI initiatives by 64% of respondents. Only 16% consider their tax function highly effective at accessing, organizing, using and reusing data, and among those who do not, 61% cite data silos and 52% cite poor data quality. Forty-three percent say their inability to execute a sustainable data, AI and technology strategy is the biggest challenge to their function's purpose. Meanwhile, 77% now expect AI agents to benefit the tax function, up from 21% a year ago, yet 71% remain at a nascent or exploratory stage of maturity.

EY's leaders say the gap lies in transforming data, governance and talent, not in enthusiasm. Marna Ricker, EY Global vice chair for tax, said that many organizations have already invested in AI, but that ambition alone will not produce returns, and that tax leaders must be deliberate about how their function creates value for the wider business. Stuart Lang, EY Global tax and finance operate leader, argued that the future tax function will not separate compliance from insight, and that trusted data from filings and reconciliations can become tax intelligence when combined with AI and human judgment. He said realizing that potential requires investment in people skills and culture as well as technology.

The survey also shows workforce plans shifting. More than four in five respondents, 83%, say building an agentic workforce is important, and 81% emphasize hiring professionals with AI-related skills. Leaders nonetheless stress that AI will augment rather than replace human expertise, with 60% ranking strategic thinking and problem-solving among the five most critical future skills. Organizations are also turning to outside help: among those using co-sourcing, 86% report greater ability to focus on higher-value work, 78% report improved tax risk management, and 77% report better success navigating legislative and regulatory change. The findings point to a growing need to connect tax strategy with broader finance and business decisions.

Articles.Title: AI Ambition Outpaces Data Readiness in Tax and Finance Functions, EY Study Finds

stories.Headline: Opinion: Telcos can be a broker for AI workloads
stories.Summary:
The articles do not report a discrete news event; they carry an opinion column published November 13, 2026, by Joe Madden, principal analyst at Mobile Experts, arguing that telecom operators could act as brokers for AI workloads. Madden begins by describing the current AI market as a contest among large companies investing heavily in frontier models, with customers paying developers for subscriptions. He then observes that specialty models and AI agents are making that choice harder, and he expects the number of options to grow sharply over the next decade. The columnist frames the coming phase as one in which users will need help choosing the right model for each task.

Madden argues that operators are well placed to fill that role, since a connectivity provider can identify and authenticate each AI agent, confirm that each workflow is authorized, and govern how many tokens it may consume. He adds that operators could set guardrails on sovereignty, cost and latency so that results are delivered in the way the customer intends. He points to South Korea, where SK Telecom and KT have deployed substantial computing resources across a distributed network and in centralized data centers, and he expects similar moves in markets including Japan, France, Germany and India. He also describes an edge AI path and a way for operators to earn revenue from authentication and governance services.

Madden acknowledges that the American situation is harder, because U.S. mobile operators lack the sovereign protection that Korean operators receive from their government. He argues, however, that operators hold advantages no one else has, namely detailed information about each customer's location, identity and billing tier, and a secure core network that already manages hundreds of millions of SIM cards. He says extending that management to what he projects as 100 billion AI agents is the natural next step. He warns that operators must move quickly, and he expects Google, Microsoft and Anthropic to offer comparable agent services well before 6G reaches the market. He concludes that the operator's position and its ability to assure network performance, including a guaranteed wireless link under specified conditions, give it an edge that hyperscalers cannot match.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Telcos can be a broker for AI workloads

stories.Headline: Self-efficacy links AI enthusiasm to perceived learning success
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey study published in Discover Artificial Intelligence in November 2026 found that self-efficacy significantly mediates the link between learners' positive attitudes toward technology and their perceived effectiveness of AI-supported English language learning. Amr M. Mohamed and Fawaz Al Mahmud conducted the research with 234 students enrolled in English-language courses at a private college of health sciences in Saudi Arabia. The study examined whether self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to manage prospective situations, explains the relationship between technophilia and positive emotional experience on one hand and perceived learning effectiveness on the other. The findings indicate that confidence in managing AI-supported tasks is a central cognitive mechanism linking affective dispositions to learners' appraisals of educational utility. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional correlational design to examine associations among the constructs without manipulating variables.

The sample of 234 students had a mean age of 20.85 years and a standard deviation of 4.06, and was 77.8% male and 22.2% female. Academic levels included 128 undergraduates and 106 foundation-year students, and 41.5% reported daily AI tool use for English learning, 29.9% weekly, 10.3% monthly, 13.2% rarely and 5.1% no use. Technophilia was measured with four items adapted from Martínez-Córcoles et al. with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87, and positive emotional experience with four items adapted from Bieleke et al. with an alpha of 0.91. Self-efficacy was evaluated with three context-specific items based on Bandura's framework with an alpha of 0.82, and perceived learning effectiveness with a scale adapted from Ashfaq et al. whose final three-item version had an alpha of 0.927. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping using 5,000 resamples showed a chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio of 1.75, a Comparative Fit Index of 0.941 and a Root Mean Square Error of Approximation of 0.057.

The authors interpret the findings through Social Cognitive Theory, which posits that self-efficacy regulates effort allocation, persistence and strategic action. They state that in AI-mediated learning environments perceived ability is decisive when learners must interpret automated responses, select appropriate tools and organize learning activities with agency. They say learners with high self-efficacy are more likely to apply feedback strategically and sustain performance under higher task demands. The study suggests self-efficacy functions as a proximal cognitive mechanism through which AI affordances become usable learning opportunities rather than merely a motivational belief. The authors say this perspective highlights the importance of confidence in managing the complexities of AI-supported language learning.

The researchers acknowledged limitations including the cross-sectional design, which prevents causal inference and restricts interpretation to associational rather than directional relationships. They noted that reliance on self-report measures increases the likelihood of common-method bias, although statistical checks using the common latent factor approach suggested this was not a significant issue. They said the study focused on perceived learning effectiveness, a subjective evaluation, rather than objective performance outcomes, which limits generalizability to actual language proficiency gains. They added that the single-institution convenience sampling and the gender imbalance in the nursing student population further constrain applicability to broader EFL contexts. The authors noted the demographic imbalance may limit generalizability of the findings to female-majority nursing populations.

The theoretical model drew on the Technology Acceptance Model, Control-Value Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, which collectively suggest that stable technological dispositions and dynamic emotional experiences influence perceived learning effectiveness through proximal cognitive beliefs, specifically self-efficacy. The structural model explained 52% of the variance in perceived learning effectiveness and 48% of the variance in self-efficacy. Preliminary analyses confirmed that measurement invariance was supported across gender groups, and multicollinearity diagnostics indicated tolerance and variance inflation factor values were within acceptable ranges. The study contributes to computer-assisted language learning research by clarifying how positive orientation toward AI-supported technologies, emotional experience and efficacy beliefs jointly relate to learners' perceptions of effective AI-supported language learning. The findings suggest pedagogical strategies should focus on progressively scaffolded practice and mastery-oriented AI tasks to strengthen self-efficacy.

Future research should prioritize experimental and longitudinal designs that manipulate or track self-efficacy and examine its influence on objective AI-supported language-learning outcomes. Qualitative or mixed-methods research could also investigate how learners develop, maintain or lose confidence over time during authentic interactions with different AI tools. The authors say these approaches would clarify the temporal and potentially causal processes underlying the relationships identified in the study. The current findings provide a foundational understanding of the psychological dynamics at play in AI-supported EFL education, highlighting the pivotal role of self-efficacy in shaping learners' experiences and evaluations. The article was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1737, with the DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02712-z.

Articles.Title: Self-efficacy links AI enthusiasm to perceived learning success

stories.Headline: Neurosymbolic AI and Peer Networks Reshape Mexican Healthcare
stories.Summary:
Healthcare institutions, pharmaceutical companies, and enterprises in Mexico are struggling to turn artificial intelligence investment into measurable financial returns while medical training adapts to automated tools. At the Entre Pares forum organized by IntraMed in Mexico City, technology and healthcare executives described how deterministic neurosymbolic AI models and credentialed peer networks could address regulatory compliance, operational bottlenecks, and the loss of clinical experience among junior physicians. The forum drew on figures showing a wide gap between corporate AI spending and results. Among the points raised, only 8 percent of companies saw bottom-line benefits, and 47 percent of corporate AI initiatives were canceled during the year.

Teresa Gutiérrez, Head of Mexico and LATAM at Growth Protocol, argued that generative tools based on probability compound errors when the same question is asked repeatedly, producing variability of 20 to 30 percent in results. She proposed neurosymbolic AI, which pairs neural language understanding with a deterministic reasoning layer that works directly on legacy systems, spreadsheets, and emails without prior data cleansing. According to her presentation, this design runs on central processing units rather than graphics processing units, cutting energy use and computing costs by 94 times while producing auditable decision trails. Her case rests on auditability, which carries regulatory weight in the sector. The articles report that in August 2026 U.S. insurance regulators restricted black-box probabilistic AI agents in claims, underwriting, and pricing.

Gutiérrez also said Mexican enterprises score at 30 percent of global standards for AI readiness, with 28 percent in strategic preparedness and 12 percent in talent readiness, compared with 90 percent among U.S. peers. She noted that Mexico has one of the strictest data protection frameworks in the world and lacks universal electronic health records or electronic prescriptions, which she warned could widen the competitiveness gap with Argentina, Colombia, and Chile if AI regulation becomes restrictive. Gastón Valverde, CEO of IntraMed, described junior doctors using AI applications to answer diagnostic questions faster than senior physicians, bypassing the experiential learning that builds clinical judgment. He said medical practice depends on shared experience and mentorship among colleagues rather than isolated algorithmic outputs. Nicolás Vega Olmos, Country Manager of IntraMed Mexico, said the forum was designed for direct interaction among stakeholders rather than passive panels.

IntraMed, founded 29 years ago as a medical education platform, now serves more than 1.1 million verified healthcare practitioners across Latin America, including over 200,000 in Mexico, according to a September 2026 interview with Mexico Business News. Gutiérrez urged early-career professionals in medicine, law, and business to develop critical judgment and communication skills to avoid displacement by automation, and she urged executives to diagnose specific operational bottlenecks before adopting AI tools. The articles also note that the clinical intelligence platform Telepatía entered Mexico in November 2026, a sign of expanding digital infrastructure in healthcare. The articles suggest that combining deterministic reasoning with peer-to-peer medical networks will shape competitiveness in the sector.

Articles.Title: Neurosymbolic AI and Peer Networks Reshape Mexican Healthcare

stories.Headline: Most Cardiovascular AI Systems Lack External Validation, Systematic Review Finds
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of 35 peer-reviewed studies, published in Artificial Intelligence Review by Alam, Bulbul, Hossen, Azad, Khan and Moni in 2026, examined artificial intelligence software systems for detecting cardiovascular disease from physiological signals. The review followed PRISMA guidelines across Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase and IEEE Xplore, and assessed quality and risk of bias with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework. The studies reported an average accuracy of 93.7 percent, and the 21 studies that reported diagnostic performance documented accuracies from 70.5 to 99.9 percent. Electrocardiogram data was the dominant signal source, used by 71.4 percent of the systems, and developers mostly applied deep learning, relying heavily on convolutional and recurrent neural networks.

The review found several gaps. Only 23 percent of the studies carried out external validation, and only 14 percent reached clinical-scale deployment. None of the 35 studies used a principled multi-signal fusion strategy combining electrocardiogram, photophlethysmogram and phonocardiogram signals, and only one system, or 2.9 percent, had a conversational interface designed for patients. The authors said inconsistent reporting of metrics and a pronounced absence of rigorous evaluation severely limit confidence in the high accuracy figures. They outlined a three-directional framework prioritizing multi-signal models for generalisability, large language model clinical narratives for interpretability, and edge-cloud deployment for accessibility.

The authors framed the work around a global crisis, noting that cardiovascular disease claims more than 17.9 million lives each year, nearly one-third of all global deaths, and that diagnostic delays are a particular concern in resource-limited environments. They said the evidence base has remained fragmented and difficult to translate into practical healthcare settings. The review recommends the three directions as the path toward clinical use. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that framework.

Articles.Title: Most Cardiovascular AI Systems Lack External Validation, Systematic Review Finds

stories.Headline: Corewell Health's ambient AI cuts nursing documentation time by 52%
stories.Summary:
Corewell Health, a system headquartered in Grand Rapids, Michigan, ran a 90-day pilot of ambient AI for nursing documentation on two medical-surgical units. The pilot, reported by Healthcare IT News on November 13, 2026, involved 101 registered nurses and 81 nursing support staff. Nurses narrated care on Corewell-provided mobile devices, and the technology drafted structured flowsheet and narrative content in Epic. The article says the pilot eliminated more than 277,000 clicks and averaged about 754 recordings per week.

The pilot's results were encouraging but limited. In the pilot, 44% of nurses reported time savings and reduced charting burden, and when nurses used ambient documentation for about 60% of a shift they saved an average of 28 minutes per shift. Top users averaged a 52% reduction in flowsheet documentation time, and Epic data showed a 15-minute, or 9%, improvement in flowsheet documentation latency. The article notes that 41% of nurses reported better patient interactions, while patient-experience results were mixed across the two units and effects on length of stay still need validation.

Jill Sheipline, RN, vice president and chief nursing informatics officer at Corewell Health, is the main voice in the article. She said the aim is to make documentation a byproduct of care instead of a separate, retrospective task, and that the goal is more time for nurses to be present with patients. She also said the nurse must stay in the loop, reviewing, editing and signing every entry, and that patients should receive a clear verbal explanation and be able to decline. Sheipline added that Corewell must validate every in-scope template, test notifications and corrections under real conditions, and invest in change management before expanding the technology.

The article places the pilot against a documentation burden that is well documented across the field. Acute care nurses spend about two hours per shift in EHR documentation activities, and KLAS data cited in the article indicates that 79% experience time lost to unproductive or duplicative charting. At Corewell, 38% of acute care nurses surveyed in 2025 reported symptoms of burnout. Sheipline advised other health systems to begin narrowly and not scale until the workflow consistently reduces burden. The article does not say when or whether Corewell will expand the pilot beyond the two units.

Articles.Title: Corewell Health's ambient AI cuts nursing documentation time by 52%

stories.Headline: Nvidia's Huang Forced Out, Shaking AI Circular-Deal Ecosystem
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang would immediately resign as president, CEO, and board member. Major financial outlets reported that Huang was effectively ousted from the company over workplace affairs. He faced three infidelity allegations, including a relationship with a woman suspected of Chinese espionage. Huang apologized on November 8, stating his actions hurt his wife and children. The company began the process of selecting a permanent CEO following his departure.

Colette Kress, the CFO since September 2013, became interim CEO while keeping her existing roles. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, was appointed as the first board chairman. Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore based Megaspeed. He also dated Kimberly Powell, a vice president who joined Nvidia in 2008. Reuters reported a third affair with an unidentified female employee on November 12.

Interim CEO Colette Kress told employees in an email that this was an extraordinarily difficult time. She announced a company wide meeting for November 18, following the November 17 earnings release. Jensen Huang apologized for his actions but did not name the women involved in the affairs. Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Tim Cook should replace the departing legend. Mandeep Singh said Nvidia's aggressiveness in beating targets will now be gone.

Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons expressed grave concerns about national security and technology controls. They requested that officials preserve all documents regarding Chinese intelligence and communications between Trump and Huang. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast summoned Huang to testify before congressional committees next week. Chinese spokeswoman Mao Ning said the United States should stop fabricating espionage narratives for blockades. Shareholders and memory chip suppliers like SK hynix and Micron saw their values fall.

Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, co-founded Shanghai Hexi, which held stakes in Huawei linked data centers. Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore revenue in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, after earning $10.2 billion. The U.S. Commerce Department may block AI companies from accessing chips in seven additional countries. Huang previously funded AI developers like OpenAI and Anthropic to create a circular trading ecosystem. This system allowed recipients to use investments to buy more Nvidia chips.

Nvidia shares fell 13.08 percent at the open before closing down 4.34 percent on November 12. Citigroup and Bernstein lowered their price targets for the company to $225 and $200 respectively. Rivals including AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet, and Samsung Electronics may benefit from a diversified supply chain. Huang has tentatively agreed to testify behind closed doors, though Brian Mast may issue subpoenas. The articles leave open how the AI ecosystem will reshape without Huang's central link.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's Huang Forced Out, Shaking AI Circular-Deal Ecosystem - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Customer-Facing Artificial Intelligence Strongly Correlates With Brand Bonds in Hospitality
stories.Summary:
A meta-analysis published on 14 November 2026 in bioengineer.org found a strong positive association between customer-facing artificial intelligence and customer-brand relationships in tourism and hospitality. The study pooled twenty-three independent empirical samples covering 9,875 respondents. It reported a random-effects pooled zero-order correlation of 0.62. The authors said this figure is an upper bound rather than an absolute baseline for commercial practice.

The review searched Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection in May 2026 and found 792 unique records published between 2016 and 2026. Screening fifty-six full-text reports retained twenty-nine eligible studies, and citation searching added one more. A re-extraction phase removed six studies lacking correlation matrices or suitable exposure metrics and merged two companion reports on one cohort. The final database held twenty-three samples from twenty-four published articles across global travel, tourism and lodging settings.

The authors said every included primary study used cross-sectional, single-source self-report questionnaires, so shared method variance inflates the observed alignment. They reported a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.54 to 0.68 and an I-squared value of 96.4 percent. They described the 95 percent prediction interval of 0.18 to 0.85 as excluding zero but wide. They cautioned that subgroup power was limited, indicating a failure to detect differences rather than proven equivalence.

Primary studies reported correlations from 0.22 to 0.81. Conversational chatbots pooled 0.71 across four samples, embodied service robots 0.64 across four, generative tools 0.64 across six and general platforms 0.53 across nine, with a non-significant Q-between of 4.09 and p of 0.25. Anthropomorphic predictors reached 0.71 across three samples against 0.60 across twenty for functional attributes, with p of 0.21. Trust registered 0.71, behavioral intention 0.69, satisfaction 0.65, engagement 0.54 and co-creation 0.41.

The theoretical foundation rests on the stimulus-organism-response framework with the computers-are-social-actors paradigm and anthropomorphism theory. The authors said prior work was mostly narrative overviews or models of initial technology acceptance. They said the review adds trust, engagement, attachment and brand loyalty and integrates studies from the generative artificial intelligence period. They said the synthesis resolves contradictions and provides a unified benchmark for service research.

Hotels yielded 0.63 across nine samples against 0.61 across ten for travel destination platforms, with p of 0.75. Asian samples averaged 0.61 across ten studies, European samples 0.59 across four and other regions 0.64 across nine, with p of 0.85. Correlation source gave p of 0.42 and publication year p of 0.78. Five pre-specified sensitivity analyses affirmed the stability of the pooled findings.

Articles.Title: Customer-Facing Artificial Intelligence Strongly Correlates With Brand Bonds in Hospitality

stories.Headline: Forescout Research: Standard AI Finds 66 Bugs in 90 Hours
stories.Summary:
Forescout Technologies, a cybersecurity firm, published a report on 13 November 2026 showing that generally available AI models can find serious software flaws quickly and cheaply. The study, titled "Finding Critical Infrastructure Bugs with Off-the-Shelf AI," was conducted by Forescout Research, Vedere Labs. Researchers tested whether defenders and attackers could both use standard AI tools on a limited budget. The work was carried out against foundational networking software in real-world scenarios.

The research team built a vulnerability research harness and deployed it across 10 popular TCP/IP stacks, seven of which Vedere Labs had examined before and three newly analysed. The total analysis time fell from roughly nine months of manual effort to 90 hours, combining about 10 hours of autonomous AI evaluation with roughly 80 hours of human validation. The AI uncovered 99 distinct vulnerabilities, including 66 previously unknown flaws, and 52% of the new ones were rated high or critical. Of the new vulnerabilities, 54 were reported to vendors and maintainers, while responsible disclosure continues for the others. Automated static analysis across all 10 stacks cost approximately US$935, averaging US$2.58 per finding, and the AI rediscovered 40% of previously known vulnerabilities.

The report also found that AI can hunt bugs in proprietary firmware without source code, though binary analysis took twice as long and cost about six times as much as source-code analysis. Forescout states that 29% of the vulnerabilities affect core components of the TCP/IP stacks rather than application-level or other protocols. Daniel dos Santos, VP of Research at Forescout, said AI did not eliminate the need for expert vulnerability researchers but dramatically compressed the work. Barry Mainz, CEO of Forescout, said the speed of vulnerability discovery is increasing with AI, but the situation for asset owners and operators has not changed.

Mainz argued that organisations still have legacy systems, operational requirements and devices that cannot easily be patched or taken offline, so containing risk must be the priority over patching. Forescout's guidance is that enterprise defenders should prioritise risk by reachability, exploitability and operational impact, and disable non-essential services such as FTP, Telnet, IPv6 and web administration interfaces.
