It also advises isolating end-of-life and unsupported devices within controlled network segments, accelerating patching where fixes exist, and building security into procurement. Software vendors are urged to adopt AI-assisted security analysis and prepare their teams for growing volumes of AI-generated reports.

The research says identical networking software is embedded in products across operational technology, Internet of Things, medical devices, network equipment and other cyber-physical systems, so a single flaw creates cascading risk across the supply chain. Based on previous Vedere Labs research, flaws in these core components are likely to affect hundreds of downstream products built by dozens of manufacturers. Vulnerable networking software often resides in legacy hardware designed to operate for decades, and even when an upstream developer releases a fix, it must pass through firmware creators and hardware manufacturers before reaching operators. For discontinued equipment, a patch may never arrive at all, leaving operators exposed.

Forescout's platform, Vistaro, is described as delivering a Universal Zero Trust Network Access architecture that integrates with more than 180 security and IT products. Forescout collaborates with partners including Microsoft, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, Netskope, ABB and Keysight Technologies. The articles do not say how many organisations are affected by the flaws, which specific stacks or products contain them, or when the remaining disclosures will be made. They also do not state whether any of the 99 vulnerabilities has been exploited in the wild. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Forescout Research: Standard AI Finds 66 Bugs in 90 Hours

stories.Headline: AI helps digital humans move more naturally as they speak
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Tohoku University and the University of Hong Kong have developed DynaConTalk, an artificial intelligence system that turns speech into coordinated movements of the body, hands and face. The work was published in ACM Transactions on Graphics and is scheduled for presentation at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, from December 1 to 4. Unlike earlier approaches that generate only isolated gestures, the system coordinates several parts of the body while keeping movement smooth over longer speeches. Users can also steer the output by specifying poses or supplying reference examples.

The system addresses two common problems in generating realistic movement from speech. Large shifts in posture can overshadow small motions such as finger gestures and facial expressions, which leads to repetitive or unnatural shaking. Joining separately generated segments can also create noticeable changes in speed or rhythm. To handle this, DynaConTalk splits movement into slower and faster components, much as sound is split into low and high frequencies, and learns them together so they stay synchronized.

It also adjusts how much it relies on speech features such as rhythm, voice characteristics and spoken words, and it uses previously generated movement to guide the next segment. The researchers tested the system on two publicly available data sets of speech and human movement, BEAT2 and SHOW. In a study, 30 participants compared videos made by three systems across 15 speech examples. DynaConTalk received the highest average ratings for naturalness, correspondence with spoken content, synchronization and movement diversity.

Automated evaluations also found that its generated movements more closely matched the distribution of recorded human movement. The article says the technology could be used in video game and film character animation, virtual presenters, online education and remote communication, where a creator might set a character's starting pose and let the AI produce the surrounding gestures. The team hopes to extend the approach to whole-body movement such as walking, but notes that existing data sets contain limited examples of large-scale movement and that speech alone does not determine how a person should move through space. The researchers plan to explore larger motion data sets and additional guidance about movement paths to address these limits.

Articles.Title: AI helps digital humans move more naturally as they speak

stories.Headline: British Racing Uses AI and Wearables for Horses
stories.Summary:
The Horse Welfare Board launched a new welfare strategy on Tuesday at a reception in Westminster. This plan focuses on using artificial intelligence and wearable technology to identify injury risks before they occur. The initiative aims to improve the safety and health of Thoroughbreds throughout their entire lives. It represents a shift toward using data to prevent falls and fatalities.

The British Horseracing Horse Welfare Strategy 2027-2031 establishes 20 priorities for horses from birth through retirement. It requires tracking every British racing horse through the Retraining of Racehorses program to ensure lifetime responsibility. The plan utilizes gait analysis software, heart monitors, and equine data to create better risk models. This effort builds upon the first industry-wide strategy, A Life Well Lived, which was published in 2020.

The independently chaired Horse Welfare Board, which was created in 2019, is responsible for the strategy. Independent board member Fred Barrelet stated that the industry is starting a technology revolution in horse management and training. The board's independent chair, Minette Batters, told reporters that fatalities will never be accepted. They believe that transparency and accountability are essential for building trust.

The industry faces significant public scrutiny when horses die during major racing events. Maintaining a social license depends on the sport showing clear progress in animal welfare. The Retraining of Racehorses charity also released a five-year plan on the same day to support aftercare. Future efforts will focus on using these modern technologies to identify risks earlier.

Articles.Title: British Racing Uses AI and Wearables for Horses

stories.Headline: New AI 'copilot' lets engineers guide structural designs as algorithms create them
stories.Summary:
MIT researchers developed an AI copilot system that lets engineers give feedback as an algorithm generates a structural design, according to an open-access paper in Communications Engineering. The system presents regions of the evolving structure to the human designer for feedback while the algorithm is still generating it. The researchers showed the approach led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads. It added only 15 seconds to the total design time compared with all-algorithmic approaches. The paper is titled "AI-guided human-in-the-loop inverse design of high performance engineering structures."

The system uses topology optimization, a technique that iteratively fills in the space given for a design to maximally achieve stated goals. In demonstrations, the human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39% while only modestly increasing total design time. The approach currently only allows users to make structures within identified regions thicker or thinner. The researchers trained a machine-learning model on a synthetic data set of probable human feedback to thousands of designs critiquing aesthetics, performance criteria and manufacturability. The paper's DOI is 10.1038/s44172-026-00818-x.

Lead author Dat Ha, Ph.D. '26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student now a structural designer at LeMessurier, said the human currently has no agency or control over the design process as it plays out. Ha said the researchers wanted to tap into the brain, the most complex machine there is, to solve design problems more practically for industry. Ha said engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give very weird-looking or unexpected designs. Ha said topology optimization is really powerful on paper but its black-box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry. Ha said the researchers thought that if they could create a record of where humans have made changes to these programs, perhaps there is a pattern to those choices.

Senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering, said a big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves. Carstensen said the lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use. Carstensen said the idea is to tap into the brains of the designers and get them to infuse their domain knowledge as the design evolves. Carstensen said the hope is that by addressing these hurdles, they open up topology optimization to a much wider audience, not only in industry but also to researchers and students in academia. Carstensen said they are arguing there is room for both approaches, and that if you really need the human input, you can use this collaborative approach.

Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and Carstensen. Carstensen said in some settings humans need to make the final decisions before advancing the final design. Carstensen said that by involving humans, higher-performing designs can get to the real world to create higher-performing structures. Carstensen said it is not just about designing good artifacts but about creating good artifacts that humans will actually accept and make.

Carstensen compared the approach to having a design copilot. Algorithmic design has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas and F1 racing cars. The best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time, and users only see the final design after it is complete. Users often must start the design process all over again to make changes, which also makes it harder to trust that final designs are structurally sound.

Some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world. Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries but has been used less to design buildings or bridges. The researchers hope to add other options for modification in future versions of the system. The researchers see their approach complementing AI-only approaches to design.

The story was republished courtesy of MIT News. The article was published on 13 November 2026. The article states that this document is subject to copyright. The article states that apart from fair dealing for private study or research, no part may be reproduced without written permission.

Articles.Title: New AI 'copilot' lets engineers guide structural designs as algorithms create them

stories.Headline: CVS Health (CVS) Wins Seven Stevie Awards For AI And Technology
stories.Summary:
CVS Health received seven Stevie Awards recognizing its use of artificial intelligence and technology in healthcare, Yahoo Finance reported on November 13, 2026. The honors cover CVS Health projects in emergency response, virtual care delivery, and tools that support workforce training and development. The awards highlight how CVS Health is applying AI to practical, operational problems across its healthcare and pharmacy ecosystem. The article was written by Sasha Jovanovic and published at 11:12 PM CST. CVS Health trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker CVS.

The awards center on tools including multilingual translation, an automation engine for prior authorizations, and CVS Air Response for emergency supply delivery. CVS Health has more than US$1 billion of operating expense reductions tied to automation and a long term tech spend plan above US$20 billion. The article cites a $114 fair value for CVS Health. The article mentions events like the Wolfe Research Healthcare Conference as a setting where hard numbers on AI programs could be attached. The article also references 53 AI infrastructure stocks and a warning sign it says its analysis turns up for CVS Health.

The article says the key test is whether future earnings calls and CVS Health presentations start attaching hard numbers to AI programs, such as annual run rate savings, cycle time reductions in prior authorization, or measurable productivity gains in pharmacy operations. It says the awards act as proof points that AI is moving from PowerPoint to production inside claims, prior authorization and care delivery workflows. It says recognition for the AI and technology work highlights how digital tools are being embedded into day-to-day services rather than sitting in a separate technology silo. It says the awards line up directly with how CVS Health earns money, through insurance and fee based services where faster decisions and fewer manual steps can lower operating costs and improve customer experience. It says the Narrative already leans on technology and AI driven cost savings.

The article says CVS Health runs a large US healthcare operation that spans pharmacies, insurance plans, and care delivery. It says the seven Stevie Awards are one chapter in the broader CVS Health story that investors are assessing. It says most holders track CVS Health through headlines, earnings releases, and product news, yet rarely stop to ask who sets the priorities and how their pay packets are structured to do it. It says the article is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

The article says it provides commentary based on historical data and analyst forecasts only using an unbiased methodology and its articles are not intended to be financial advice. It says the article does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock and does not take account of objectives or financial situation. It says the analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It says readers can get in touch with the outlet directly or email editorial-team@simplywallst.com. It says the companies discussed in the article include CVS.

The article leaves open whether future earnings calls and CVS Health presentations will attach hard numbers to AI programs. It leaves open what annual run rate savings, cycle time reductions in prior authorization, or measurable productivity gains in pharmacy operations will be reported. It points readers to a separate look at who is steering CVS Health and how they are paid. It points readers to a path to a $114 fair value and to 53 AI infrastructure stocks. It says the analysis turns up one warning sign for CVS Health.

Articles.Title: CVS Health (CVS) Wins Seven Stevie Awards For AI And Technology

stories.Headline: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters.
stories.Summary:
A study of native ads on news sites found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising, and in a Contently survey two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand. According to an impact.com survey, 47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure question so far is the citation link, since launching ChatGPT search it has included links to sources in answers so users can check them for themselves. One study found that about a quarter of the pages cited by ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure, and 86% of answers cited at least one such page.

In the impact.com survey, 24% of shoppers said they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads, and Pew found people clicked a link inside an AI summary on just 1% of visits. According to impact.com’s survey, Gen Z is split between those who never click through at 11% and those who always do at 21%. In a University of Michigan study, people rarely noticed when a chatbot wove ads into its responses, many preferred those answers, and even when the ads were labeled about half the participants did not spot them. Early research from the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management found shoppers who clicked ChatGPT ads bought at a rate of 0.37%, versus 2.21% for those who arrived through ChatGPT’s regular answers.

OpenAI’s ad principles promise that “ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you,” and ads only appear in ChatGPT’s free and Go tiers, always separate from the answer itself. Perplexity made similar promises when advertising was part of its business model, though it walked away from ads earlier this year, with one executive saying “A user needs to believe this is the best possible answer.” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on Meta’s October earnings call that the company will “build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate.” In the writer’s tests with Meta’s Muse, when asked which robot vacuum was best, it recommended a model that could be checked out right there but was not the top model on the review it cited.

Consumer Reports’ work on AI agents uses the phrase “loyalty by design,” the idea that agents should always put the needs and desires of the user first and make transparent any other considerations or conflicts. Sen. Mark Warner has floated draft legislation that would write a similar duty of loyalty into law for some AI agents. The SPJ code says to “distinguish news from advertising and shun hybrids that blur the lines,” and recommendation sites like Wirecutter or The Strategist make their business model clear on every page. The writer argues that an agent that knows your email, your calendar and what you bought last month is a lot harder to fire than a search engine.

The writer notes that legitimate sites monetizing via affiliate disclose that fact on any page with affiliate links, and FTC guidelines require that they do so. The writer says almost none of those disclosures survive the journey into an AI answer, and that if they carried over they would be in almost every shopping answer. The writer pictures a world where AI users have the option of seeing labels or not, perhaps via something like a “flag paid sources” toggle. The writer concludes that labels protect readers from sketchy sources, but what protects us from sketchy agents has not been invented yet.

Articles.Title: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s S-1 Says Natural Gas, Not Chips, Is AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. Here’s the Stock That Sells the Engines.
stories.Summary:
Anthropic revealed in its S-1 filing that power is a major bottleneck for artificial intelligence companies. The company mentioned natural gas five times in one paragraph of the filing. This disclosure occurred around November 14, 2026, according to the provided reports. The filing highlights the critical need for energy to support data center operations. This shift suggests that fuel, not chips, is now a primary constraint.

Certain planned data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation. This exposes Anthropic to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions outside its control. These facilities face constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation for natural gas. Failure to secure gas supply could cause a planned site to be delayed or abandoned. Energy Transfer operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines across 44 states.

Anthropic stated that it bears the costs of fuel volatility on a pass-through basis. Micron executives called DRAM the principal constraint versus logic or power to the data center. Micron management said over 75 percent of fiscal 2027 shipments are already committed. They have 26 Strategic Customer Agreements running through 2030 to support their growth. Micron is also co-designing HBM4E with NVIDIA to improve memory performance.

Energy Transfer is affected by AI adoption, which grew to 26.8 percent of U.S. businesses by October 2026. Oracle is affected through an agreement for natural gas at three of its United States data centers. Nexus Data Center and Entergy Louisiana also have agreements to receive natural gas from Energy Transfer. Meta Platforms is connected because it partners with Entergy Louisiana to power a data center facility. Micron is affected by a 30 percent weekly plunge in its stock price.

Energy Transfer has long-term debt at 68.8 billion dollars from expanding its energy pipeline network. Its adjusted EBITDA grew 31 percent in the third quarter of 2026 to 5 billion dollars. Micron finished a fiscal year with 133.19 billion dollars in revenue and 75.52 in non-GAAP EPS. Micron's fiscal 2026 capex reached 30.71 billion dollars, while free cash flow was 62.31 billion dollars. SanDisk revenue grew 377.95 percent, while NVIDIA revenue growth was 105.85 percent.

OpenAI may go public in 2027 and will compete by creating the best AI models. Micron guided fiscal Q1 revenue to 61.5 billion dollars plus or minus 1.5 billion dollars. Analysts set a median one-year price target of 25 dollars for Energy Transfer stock. The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Micron is 913.86 dollars over the next year. Articles leave open if pipeline returns will be lower than expected or if DRAM pricing rolls over.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s S-1 Says Natural Gas, Not Chips, Is AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. Here’s the Stock That Sells the Engines.

stories.Headline: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
stories.Summary:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel published his two incompleteness theorems in 1931, transforming mathematics and paving the way for the digital age. Since 2017 the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand 16 notebooks Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. In September von Plato enlisted the AI model Claude, which within a couple of days provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material. Claude revealed that Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. The most famous logician of modern times had discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

The material, called the workbooks, is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic, much of it in the German shorthand Gabelsberger. Von Plato received a €2.5m grant from the European Research Council and taught himself the shorthand, saying he is one of only six people in the world who can read it. Claude produced a 650-page explanation of the workbooks, which had to be controlled page for page. Claude found 663 theorems for which Gödel had a proof, a sketched proof or an idea for a proof. When these were put into the proof assistant Coq, about 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired and about 50 were false.

Von Plato said he was flabbergasted, that the workbooks contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, and that they contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. He said Gödel was far ahead of his time, and that humans read one page at a time and take a year to read about 50 pages. He said the AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages and see all of Gödel's writings as one piece. He said the first task he set Claude was to discover if the workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice. The answer came back yes, almost, and von Plato said Gödel was just one step away, with one definition wrong but the right definition two years earlier.

Von Plato ran Claude's reconstructed proof through Coq and it passed, and he believes Gödel would have won the 1940 Fields medal had he published his work on the axiom of choice. Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude's reconstruction but said that if it stood up it is remarkable and historically interesting, though how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians. Hamkins said the fact that there are things in there that resemble Cohen's proof does not mean Gödel had it, and that you don't get credit for work you don't tell anyone about. He said Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising his notebooks are full of exciting things. Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis in 1940 and settled in Princeton, New Jersey, where he became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow, about a page a week, until September. In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested he co-opt Claude, and on his return to Helsinki he showed Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks and six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature. Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved nor disproved, and his work inspired Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation. In 1966 the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal for showing the independence of the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice, and Gödel reacted by saying he had already proved the result in the 1940s but was unable to reconstruct a proof when pushed by his peers. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, Gödel refused to eat food not cooked by his wife and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he is sure continued study of Gödel's manuscripts will reveal further treasures, and that Claude says the workbooks contain more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics not found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. He said Gödel's physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory he plans to start exploring once he is finished with his present logic projects. Von Plato started the project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. The articles do not say what became of the 14 unpursued themes or the more than a dozen further themes beyond von Plato's stated intention to explore them. The articles also do not say whether the reconstructed proof will be published or how historians will separate Claude's contribution from Gödel's.

Articles.Title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

stories.Headline: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association, the nation's largest physicians group, has called for federal and state legislation that would shield doctors from liability when AI products injure patients, even when physicians use those tools as intended. The announcement came this week, according to Axios, which reported it on November 13, 2026. The push reflects growing concern that AI systems are taking on more consequential medical tasks, such as deciding whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug, with less direct oversight. The question of who is responsible when something goes wrong has become more pressing as a result.

The AMA policy also asks lawmakers to require AI companies to carry adequate liability insurance and to disclose product limitations and performance data. It states that hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should bear responsibility if the required use of a specific AI product leads to harmful errors. The group points to particular risks, including triage errors in which an AI system misjudges how severe a case is without the attending doctor knowing. It also warns that a physician may be unable to verify inputs such as incomplete laboratory results or outdated diagnoses. In such cases, the AMA argues, liability should fall on manufacturers and vendors, and possibly on health systems that require the tools, rather than on physicians through malpractice claims.

The AMA's position is shaped by earlier lawsuits over algorithm-driven medical decisions. Axios cited a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities, where the software developer was not held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors. Martin Hilbert, a professor at the University of California, Davis who studies digital information and algorithms, told Axios that courts around the country are concluding that companies designing, training and deploying AI systems bear responsibility for what those systems do. He said different parties are responsible for different cases and that the end user cannot simply be held responsible for everything. Hospitals have generally supported placing monitoring duties on developers and vendors, citing the "black box" nature of many systems.

The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices, though its authority covers only software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all AI used in health care. AdvaMed, the trade group for device makers, has urged the FDA to keep its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled devices and to avoid post-market monitoring burdens unrelated to a product's actual risk. Axios reported that the AMA's proposals are aimed at situations where use of an AI system is mandatory. The article did not report whether any legislation has been introduced or what action lawmakers have taken so far.

Articles.Title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes

stories.Headline: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise
stories.Summary:
Leidos, the defense contractor, has been reporting gains from its 2025 purchase of Kudu Dynamics, a cyber company it bought for $300 million. In October, Leidos won two contracts from U.S. Cyber Command: a $160 million operations support contract and a $99 million other transaction authority contract to keep developing a cyber mission planning platform that Kudu brought over from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Together these amount to nearly $260 million in new business over the next several years. Leidos Intelligence president Jason O'Connor said the customers are ones the company had not really worked with before.

The acquisition was announced in May 2025, when CEO Tom Bell said it moved Leidos into offensive cyber by 18 months compared with building those capabilities internally. Kudu brought roughly 170 employees, and much of its earlier work was in research. O'Connor said the company's artificial intelligence work has also benefited, pointing to Parcata, an AI-driven tool that finds and ranks software vulnerabilities so teams can fix the most serious ones first. Leidos introduced Parcata in August, and it grew out of Kudu's work on DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge. O'Connor said Leidos is testing it on its own software before a commercial release, and Bell discussed it on a November 5 earnings call as part of a cyber product business the company hopes to launch later this year.

O'Connor credited Kudu with a broader effect he called a "halo," in which its offensive background lets Leidos view the systems it builds the way an attacker would, which he said has improved the company's chances on engineering, software development and analytics bids as well. He said Leidos has worked to protect Kudu's culture, which had a 47,000-employee parent to worry about, and that Kudu engineers are now being placed on traditional Leidos contracts to coach and mentor staff. O'Connor linked the shift to fixed-price, outcome-based contracts and to rapidly changing technology, saying customers now expect solutions that are ready to go. He described the Leidos Intelligence cyber business, which sits in one of five sectors the company formed on January 1, and said the company is "just getting started," with possible wins in weapon system and communications cyber.

Articles.Title: Kudu has given Leidos a cyber boost and an AI surprise

stories.Headline: Nigeria: Can the influence of AI in the upcoming elections be mitigated?
stories.Summary:
The Independent National Electoral Commission found AI generated images in its preliminary voter register. This discovery happened just over two months before the 2027 general elections in Nigeria. Incumbent President Bola Tinubu is running against Peter Obi and former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. Tinubu focuses his campaign on resolving the economic crisis and combating raging insecurity. The commission is now investigating discrepancies that were potentially created by the use of AI.

The register contains duplicate names and identities of people who died since the previous election. AI usage was indicated by inconsistencies and exaggerated facial features in the voter images. The commission must now monitor AI threats and detect deepfakes through a new dedicated unit. This effort aims to protect the integrity of the vote for 103 million registered Nigerians. The commission faces criticism for not making its procedures more transparent during this process.

Chairman Joash Amupitan said the body is investigating the development and focusing on AI discrepancies. He warned that the credibility of the upcoming elections could be under attack without monitoring. Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace urged journalists to avoid believing reports that AI might have manipulated. He stressed the importance of due diligence and protection measures within the news media. Ndace noted that public institutions like the commission struggle to provide impartial information.

Lois Ugbede of DUBAWA said AI driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace. She noted that parties use inflated crowds to show large followership or support. Akintunde Babatunde of CJID warned that people may begin to doubt authentic information. He cited a lawmaker who claimed inflammatory campaign rally clips were manipulated. Chibuike Mgbeahuruike said AI intrusion into the portal could undermine the institutional credibility.

Nigeria previously dealt with fabricated images, doctored audio, and fake videos during the 2023 elections. Deepfakes then falsely linked candidates to terror activities to influence public perception. Electronic assistance began in 2011 with Direct Data Capture Machines for biometrics and facial recognition. The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System was introduced ten years later to combine fingerprints and faces. However, poor cell signals caused system failures during the general elections of 2023.

Voter apathy is a concern, as 2023 saw the lowest turnout since democratic rule began in 1999. Only 27 percent of registered voters went to the polls during that previous election. Mgbeahuruike stated that the real threat is the absence of effective accountability for tech deployment. He argued that technology must be transparent, accountable, and subject to human and institutional oversight. The articles leave open whether the influence of AI can be mitigated before the vote.

Articles.Title: Nigeria: Can the influence of AI in the upcoming elections be mitigated?
