stories.Headline: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?
stories.Summary:
Voice AI, the use of artificial intelligence within live phone calls, is being pitched by vendors as a way to revive voice services that many in telecom consider stale. Fierce Network's Diana Goovaerts hosted an episode of The Five Nine on the subject, published on November 13, 2026. Guests Brandon Larson of Mavenir, Dag Peak of Alianza and Kris Efland of Deepgram appeared in the episode. The episode examines whether AI can give the oldest service in the network a second life, and it covers both the promise and the difficult parts. Those difficult parts include latency, consent, data privacy, where the AI should run and how to price it.

Voice AI is a broad label that can describe several different things. Peak and Larson divide it into three categories: AI-handled calls, applications that engage in live conversations, and post-call intelligence. Larson offered examples such as real-time translation between two people speaking different languages, an AI receptionist for small businesses, and AI that detects deepfake voices, non-human voices or social engineering. Peak argued that human conversation is the richest form of communication and that bringing calls into the application and AI space opens many possibilities. Larson said operators' product teams see an opportunity to create value that does not depend entirely on handset makers such as Apple and Samsung.

Larson said operators could use these services to raise revenue through uplifts, step-up plans and add-on plans. Peak said operators are losing subscribers, lines and SIP trunks to vendors such as Twilio that bring intelligence to voice or messaging. He described bringing AI-powered services into operator networks as a defensive move that could help them keep customers, as well as an offensive move that could generate revenue. Larson advised operators to begin with a customer problem, estimate how many people have it, determine what they would pay to solve it, and then work backward to the technology. Efland said successful voice AI depends on low latency, accurate speech recognition and reliable turn-taking, and he noted that accuracy matters more in specialized fields such as healthcare, where recognizing drug names is important.

Efland said the highest value for enterprises comes from integrating AI with their data and systems, and he said Deepgram deploys wherever customers operate, including air-gapped devices, their own infrastructure, virtual private clouds and data centers. He added that Deepgram spends considerable time understanding customers' use cases and outcomes before working back from those outcomes. Efland used a drive-through example, describing a parent ordering while children shout, to illustrate the unpredictable conditions these systems must handle. Larson said context engineering, including knowing a subscriber's preferences and history, can matter more than choosing a more powerful model. Peak said the major problems have been identified and that the pieces are coming together.

The three guests disagreed about how much of the work remains unfinished. Larson described a design in which the other caller hears an announcement and actively accepts before the AI begins, while Peak said Alianza's trust framework covers consent, announcements and data collection along with vetting the experiences attached to calls. Peak and Larson described these as their own companies' approaches rather than a universal legal rule for every service or location. Peak said trust, privacy and consent remain central to getting people comfortable with such services. Efland said users need to understand when AI is involved in a conversation.

The guests all said the test is whether the whole system works for the person using it. The episode was written and hosted by Diana Goovaerts and edited by Goovaerts, Matt Rickman and Nikki Grcic, with Liz Coyne as executive producer. The articles do not say how the services discussed will be regulated, priced in the market or adopted by operators. They also do not say how far the consent designs described by the guests will be used across the industry. Whether operators will turn these pitches into revenue remains an open question in the coverage.

Articles.Title: The Five Nine: Can Voice AI give telecom a new voice?

stories.Headline: China’s great AI chip loophole: How American espionage stopped China — this time
stories.Summary:
The articles report that a suspected Chinese intelligence operation sought to obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips through companies in Singapore and Malaysia, and that American intelligence uncovered it, as reported on November 13, 2026. The New York Times reported that American intelligence concluded Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed International, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed acquired Nvidia processors for cloud-computing operations, and American intelligence officers reportedly identified concerns about Huang's activities and her relationship with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. The articles state that approximately 50,000 Nvidia processors could not be reconciled with the company's reported inventory records. Nvidia later said it located hardware in additional warehouses, but full public reconciliation and independent verification of final locations remained unknown.

The articles state that Nvidia's H100, H200 and newer Blackwell-family processors are among the most strategically important technologies underlying modern artificial intelligence. President Trump has spent years restricting Chinese access to the most advanced versions of these technologies. A November 11 letter from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Christopher Coons stated that Megaspeed had purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024. Reuters reported on November 12 that Chinese AI companies were seeking additional overseas Nvidia computing capacity amid fears that Washington might close this regulatory gap. Bloomberg reported a discrepancy of roughly 50,000 processors between Nvidia's initial government tally and shipments made through hardware partners.

The articles state that the individuals who uncovered the suspected operation have not been publicly identified. The articles state that the public record does not yet establish whether Alice Huang actually transferred Nvidia secrets to Chinese intelligence, whether Jensen Huang knowingly assisted any intelligence activity, or whether their romantic relationship directly influenced illegal chip shipments to China. The articles state that Congress and the CIA will have to establish how much China got away with and who helped them defeat America. The articles state that the question Congress must resolve is whether the processors can be physically identified, their serial numbers verified, and their locations traced. The articles state that Bloomberg and The New York Times reported that Nvidia representatives communicated with senior Commerce Department officials while investigators examined the matter.

The articles state that China's intelligence services and commercial intermediaries may have identified weaknesses in precisely the system designed to keep them out. The articles state that the MSS has a long history of seeking valuable foreign technology, political intelligence, and relationships with influential individuals. The articles state that Singapore and Malaysia have developed substantial cloud-computing industries, and that companies in these countries can legitimately purchase American technology, install processors in data centers, and rent computing capacity to customers worldwide. The articles state that processors ostensibly destined for facilities outside China might subsequently be physically diverted to Chinese customers, and that such unauthorized reexports could violate American export restrictions. The articles state that Chinese companies might obtain access to advanced American processors without importing the physical chips at all by renting computing capacity in overseas data centers.

The articles state that China may have discovered a remarkably effective way around America's restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips by obtaining processors through ostensibly legitimate companies in Singapore and Malaysia, exploiting weaknesses in American export enforcement, and using personal relationships to influence the leadership of the world's most important AI chipmaker. The articles state that the unfolding Nvidia scandal raises the possibility that an elaborate Chinese intelligence operation came dangerously close to succeeding, and that some of the technology may already have reached Chinese customers. The articles state that the apparent weakness involved the distinction between selling advanced processors directly to China and selling them to companies operating data centers elsewhere in Asia. The articles state that the second method is not necessarily illegal under existing regulations and exposes a distinction between controlling the shipment of advanced processors and controlling who ultimately benefits from their computing power. The articles state that the discovery illustrates the importance of counterintelligence in detecting foreign activities that may be deliberately concealed behind ordinary commercial relationships.

The articles state that Nvidia has not publicly disclosed exact counts, leaving open whether every processor can be accounted for and verified against unauthorized diversion to China. The articles state that it remains unknown whether every processor can be accounted for and verified. The articles state that the full public reconciliation and independent verification of final locations remained unknown. The articles state that Congress and the CIA will have to establish how much China got away with and who helped them defeat America. The articles state that the question Congress must resolve is whether the processors can be physically identified, their serial numbers verified, and their locations traced.

Articles.Title: China’s great AI chip loophole: How American espionage stopped China — this time

stories.Headline: Exclusive / Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor and published on November 13, 2026, found that Gen Z has not settled its views on artificial intelligence. Seventy-three percent of Gen Z adults said they had not made up their minds about AI, and half said they expect the technology to harm society. Those figures are close to the views of older generations, with baby boomers at 50 percent and Gen Xers at 48 percent expecting harm. Millennials were the most optimistic group, with 39 percent expecting harm.

The survey points to a paradox in how young people relate to AI. Many say the technology makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job, yet 46 percent said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about existential risk, the concern that dominates much of the AI safety debate. At the same time, they are more conflicted about their own use, with 30 percent of Gen Zers saying they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

The reporting does not name a single party responsible for the findings beyond the survey's publisher, Milltown Partners, and the article's author, J.D. Capelouto, a tech reporter at Semafor. The article notes that companies and politicians are eager to understand the generation's stance because young people drive many technology trends and because AI and data centers played an outsized role in the US midterm elections. The article frames Gen Z as often portrayed as souring on AI, and presents the survey as evidence that this portrayal is not accurate, since the generation is no more negative than its parents and grandparents. The articles provided do not say what further steps, if any, will follow from the survey.

Articles.Title: Exclusive / Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds

stories.Headline: Why your clients probably aren’t covered for AI
stories.Summary:
Insurance Business reported on November 13, 2026 that AI exclusions are spreading through commercial general liability, errors and omissions, and professional liability policies across the United States, and that many clients do not know their cover no longer responds to AI-related claims. Major carriers, including Chubb, Travelers, and Berkshire Hathaway, obtained or sought state approval to add AI exclusions to CGL policies, while W.R. Berkley filed an absolute AI exclusion, form PC 51380, covering D&O, E&O, and fiduciary lines. ISO also introduced several generative AI exclusion endorsements for CGL forms effective January 2026. Gallagher Re figures cited in the piece show US generative AI lawsuits rose 978% between 2021 and 2025, with filings growing 137% in 2024 and 2025.

Under CG 40 47, an insurer may deny a claim if the loss arose from generative AI, meaning the trigger is any connection to AI rather than how much of the work AI touched. The article warns this matters for law firms using AI drafting tools, lenders running automated credit checks, and hospitals using AI diagnostic aids, where a single AI link could void coverage. Cyber policies typically respond only to breaches, so they often do not apply when an AI system produces harmful output without an outside intrusion. Businesses that are not technology companies usually lack tech E&O, leaving their exposure between policies.

George Lewin-Smith, CEO and co-founder of Testudo, a Lloyd's coverholder writing standalone generative AI liability cover in the US, says brokers are reluctant to confirm coverage because insurers have not priced for AI risk and are not accounting for it. He says vendor contracts and model provider terms make the deployer of an AI tool responsible for its outputs, whatever the vendor sold. He also said brokers and carriers are pulling in different directions, with brokers resisting AI exclusions while some carriers push standalone products. The Lloyd's Market Association has already filed AI endorsements, a process he described as taking two years compared with twenty for cyber.

The article presents Testudo's Lloyd's-backed program, expanded with Atrium and QBE capacity in March 2026, as one answer, offering up to $9.25 million per insured for third-party claims from AI outputs. Its underwriting relies on proprietary litigation data instead of audits or system integrations. Lewin-Smith expects a large uninsured AI loss will eventually force the issue, though he is unsure how frequent or severe such losses must become. Brokers whose clients renew within six months are already in the window the new ISO forms took effect, and the article advises checking policy language before a claim arises.

Articles.Title: Why your clients probably aren’t covered for AI

stories.Headline: Austrian Bishops Adopt First Rules for AI in the Church
stories.Summary:
The Austrian Bishops' Conference has adopted its first rules on artificial intelligence in the Church, stating that AI may never take the place of human relationships, pastoral conversations, or the rites of the Church. The bishops adopted the framework at their autumn plenary in Salzburg, which ran from Monday to Thursday, and announced it in a press statement on Thursday. The rules are titled "Framework Regulation on the Use of AI Systems in the Catholic Church in Austria and Its Institutions." They take effect once they are published in the next official gazette of the bishops' conference.

The core provision says AI may only play a supporting role in the celebration of the sacraments, preaching, liturgy, and pastoral care. Replacing human relationships, pastoral conversations, community, or rituals with AI is explicitly rejected. The bishops stressed that in preaching, liturgy, and pastoral care, the irreplaceability of personal encounter must be preserved. The framework also requires every diocese to appoint a person responsible for AI. A new working group will bring together all diocesan AI officers, along with experts in data protection, information technology, and theological ethics, and the Austrian Conference of Religious Orders will take part.

The bishops said the rules rest on the Christian image of man, the inviolable dignity of every person, and respect for human freedom. They argued that AI should serve the human person rather than replace him, and that its use therefore requires critical review, human oversight, and orientation toward truth, justice, and the common good. The bishops also acknowledged that AI opens new possibilities for the Church's mission while raising ethical, legal, and social challenges. The working group that prepared the framework was set up in November 2025 and led by Bishop Hermann Glettler of Innsbruck.

The framework follows the bishops' June plenary in Mariazell, where they explicitly endorsed Pope Leo XIV's social encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. In that statement they drew on the encyclical's call to preserve the greatness of the human person and to ensure AI builds a universal human family where digital closeness becomes a real chance for encounter and mutual care. The bishops said the perspective of the poor, weak, and disadvantaged is needed because the rich and powerful are the ones who develop and profit from AI systems. They concluded that the future will be decided by whether people take responsibility for the human person and for a culture of encounter, love, and peace.

Articles.Title: Austrian Bishops Adopt First Rules for AI in the Church

stories.Headline: GreyNoise Unveils Benchmark for AI Cyber Defense Performance
stories.Summary:
GreyNoise, a threat data company, has introduced the GreyNoise AI Cyber Index, a public benchmark that tests how well artificial intelligence models perform cyber defense work. The company announced the index on a Thursday, and the article is dated November 13, 2026. The index is publicly accessible on the company's website, which the company said coincides with its threat data platform surpassing 100,000 users. The first edition tests 46 closed and open-weight models against attack traffic captured by GreyNoise's Global Observation Grid.

The index measures tasks such as triaging alerts, writing detection rules and investigating intrusions, and it reports each model's task scores, refusal rates, and time and cost per problem. In the first round, Opus 5.5 earned the top raw score, while Grok 4.5 ranked first on the leaderboard, which counts refused tasks as zero. The article says the index is meant to give security teams a practical basis for choosing a model for their operations. Faster, AI-driven attacks are prompting government and industry to rethink how they select and deploy network defense tools.

Andrew Morris, founder and chief architect of GreyNoise, said most public benchmarks focus on offensive capabilities and few check whether models can help defenders in live environments. He said the company has watched attackers for eight years and tests models against what attackers actually do against GreyNoise sensors rather than a made-up lab setting. Morris added that more evaluations are in development and the benchmarks will be updated as new ones arrive. GreyNoise CEO Ash Devata said chief information security officers want to know how fast the next critical vulnerability will be exploited, and he argued that AI defenses are only as good as the data behind them.

The index builds on GreyNoise's broader work on AI-driven threats, including an April report warning that AI models in cybersecurity may be trained too late to detect emerging threats. The company has also expanded its platform with C2 Detection, which gives security teams visibility into compromised edge devices, and has pitched it to federal agencies amid warnings about Iranian cyberthreats. On the leadership side, GreyNoise named Mike Habte director of federal sales and added four senior leaders to support U.S. and allied government agencies. The article does not say what the company plans to release next beyond the additional evaluations Morris described.

Articles.Title: GreyNoise Unveils Benchmark for AI Cyber Defense Performance

stories.Headline: 'Vibe-athon' brings AI skills to Cd'A
stories.Summary:
VibeCDA held its first vibe-athon on Friday at the Innovation Collective in Coeur d'Alene. The event was inspired by hackathons, where companies pay programmers and designers to create working software or hardware prototypes. Organizer Daniel Finley opened the event for participants. The goal was to give anyone, from beginners to experienced developers, a hands-on way to learn about vibe coding by building a playable game.

Vibe coding lets people describe what they want in plain language, and a large language model generates the results without the user knowing how to code. Organizers said the key skill is learning how to instruct the AI properly to get the results you want. Co-host Conner Kees said it is not hard to build a good vocabulary for these things. Co-host Tom Vrba compared lacking that vocabulary to a property developer who knows nothing about construction.

Finley said that if you tell someone to build a game, anyone can do it right away, and people have fun because it is creative. He said participants come away realizing they can do a lot of things, such as building more games, creating a website or setting up tools to run a business. Co-host Jeff Spicer said video games have historically been the first adoption of technology, and software in medical and military fields can be traced back to the 1993 game Doom. Kees said the aim is to teach people to think big picture and stay in control of what they are doing.

Participants Josiah Poling and Noah Marshall, who share a background in storytelling through film and video games, joined to broaden their skills. Poling said he wanted a more well-rounded understanding of what he can do with AI tools, and that it would at least be fun even if he did not make anything fun. Marshall said he has taken a coding course here and there but has no huge programming background, and that spreading out ideas and reaching a concept quickly is exciting. VibeCDA plans similar events next year to connect builders, share ideas, develop local talent and eventually grow Coeur d'Alene-based businesses. Finley said the group wants to work more closely with places like Elevate, KTEC, Gonzaga and Lake City High, and to get people thinking they can be creators rather than consumers.

Articles.Title: 'Vibe-athon' brings AI skills to Cd'A

stories.Headline: Keeping an eye on AI costs: How tokens make consumption, costs and benefits measurable
stories.Summary:
A KPMG Germany article published on 13 November 2026 explains how companies can use the token, the smallest processing unit of a language model, to measure how much artificial intelligence they use and what it costs. The piece presents the token as comparable to a kilowatt-hour for electricity, giving firms a common unit for judging scope of use, expense and added value. It notes that many companies are expanding their AI use but often lack clarity about the actual extent of usage, the resulting costs and the value delivered. The article is built around a white paper titled "Managing AI Value in Organisations," which the firm published alongside it.

The white paper uses a manufacturing company as an example to show the financial effect of growing AI use. According to the article, token prices are expected to fall by a factor of about 1.9 by 2031, while volume is projected to rise by a factor of between 5.7 and 8.5 over the same period. Together these trends would lift the company's annual AI operating costs from roughly six million euros to between 19 and 28 million euros. The authors present this as a reason to track consumption closely rather than assume that falling unit prices will keep total spending in check.

To address this, KPMG describes an integrated AI management model with three components. The first maps how much AI is used across the organisation, in which areas and by whom, whether employees, agents or machines, and compares this with best-practice figures to reveal over-consumption and untapped potential. The second forecasts token price trends over five years across different providers to produce cost scenarios. The third identifies the AI agents that contribute the most value and derives a prioritised implementation roadmap within the available budget. Taken together, the model is meant to link consumption and cost to achievable added value.

The article says the model can show where excessive consumption can be reduced and where AI use should be expanded, and which agents promise the highest returns. It also suggests that future cost trends can be built into budget planning at an early stage. The text does not report any particular company adopting the framework, and it offers no further detail on the forecasting methods or the figures behind the scenarios beyond what is summarised above. The piece closes by noting that few industries are as central to digital transformation as the TMT sectors.

Articles.Title: Keeping an eye on AI costs: How tokens make consumption, costs and benefits measurable

stories.Headline: IFF’s AI tool speeds up product concept creation
stories.Summary:
IFF, a New York-based company, has launched Concept Muse, an artificial intelligence tool designed to help generate food and beverage concepts. The tool identifies marketing opportunities and uses prompts to produce differentiated concepts. It draws on IFF's consumer insights, flavor expertise and market intelligence. The announcement was reported by bakingbusiness.com on November 13, 2026.

According to the company, each concept features a narrative, visual mockups and suggested technologies. IFF says research teams can move from inspiration to conceptualization in minutes rather than weeks using the tool. The company presents this as a way to speed up the early stages of product development. Concept Muse is aimed at manufacturers seeking new product ideas.

Benjamin Mattei, vice president of intelligence and digital transformation for IFF Taste, spoke about the launch. He said food and beverage innovation has long balanced art and science, and that digital transformation now adds a new dimension to that balance. Mattei described the tool as a place where AI meets human imagination. He said it is meant to accelerate innovation and help manufacturers think beyond conventional approaches.

The article places the launch within a set of related industry news, including other AI and data tools for suppliers and food companies. The article does not give pricing, availability dates or the names of customers using the tool. It also does not report any independent evaluation of how well the concepts perform. Further details about the tool's rollout are not included in the source material.

Articles.Title: IFF’s AI tool speeds up product concept creation

stories.Headline: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones
stories.Summary:
Pryor Cashman lawyers published practical tips on 13 November 2026 for protecting games under US law against generative AI clones. Steam Next Fest featured over 8,000 demos in October 2026, many made partly or entirely with generative AI tools. AI is facilitating a new wave of rapidly assembled, unauthorised clones, mods, and ports of existing games. Developers are reporting cancelling public demos for fear of being cloned before their games reach market. Simon Pulman and Josh Weigensberg are partners, and Joshua Greenberg is counsel, in Pryor Cashman's Interactive+Gaming practice group.

The lawyers recommend NDAs when sharing footage, demos, and codes, prohibiting sharing of confidential information, recording, or video capture of gameplay. The NDAs should also bar inputting game-related media and information into any LLM, chatbot, or similar generative AI technology. Watermarking, password protection, and revocable or limited-time access can accompany these measures. Paperwork should confirm suggestions or contributions are made on a work-for-hire basis or assigned exclusively to the developer. This covers employees, independent contractors, composers, voice actors, and outside studios, who should obtain corresponding agreements from their personnel.

Developers should file applications with the US Copyright Office before publicity or release, covering script and narrative materials, character designs and biographies, key art, concept art, original music and sound recordings, trailer footage, and other sufficiently developed assets. A copyright registration, not merely a pending application, is generally required before a federal infringement action involving a US work. Statutory damages can reach up to $150,000 for willful infringement without proof of actual financial damages, plus attorneys' fees, but these remedies are often unavailable if registration is sought only after infringement occurs. Developers should consider applying to register the game's name as a trademark with the USPTO on an intent-to-use basis several months before planned public release. The USPTO process currently takes around 10 months, ending with a Notice of Allowance and then a Statement of Use once the game is released.

The lawyers said some clients are "zero AI" and others are embracing the technologies, and each company should develop a policy ensuring employees, vendors, and contractors comply. They warned against losing trade-secret protections over code because a contractor made confidential information and proprietary systems available to third parties using AI without knowledge or approval. They said common-law trademark rights may develop on release, but a federal registration generally strengthens enforcement options, especially when submitting infringement notices to third-party distribution platforms. Rightsholders should secure domain names and social media handles to head off cybersquatting, prioritising principal variations tied to the game, its studio, and any major franchise or character brands. A registered trademark can strengthen enforcement under ICANN's Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy and platforms' impersonation and trademark notice-and-takedown regimes.

The lawyers said games reliant on unique mechanics might be more at risk than heavily story-based games, or those with a strong existing brand or IP. They said some developers will elect private playtesting in lieu of early access or public demos. They said certain subsets of the industry are collaborative and informal, and standardised, developer-friendly agreements and clear contributor processes can preserve that culture without ownership gaps that complicate future licensing, publishing, financing, or enforcement. Enforcement may include a cease-and-desist letter, a takedown notice, or a civil lawsuit, and a preliminary injunction is a powerful tool but requires showing "irreparable harm," with prior delay possibly undermining that claim. They said each day unauthorised clones are available they can cause consumer confusion and siphon sales.

The lawyers said generative AI tools are eroding traditional protections including "time to market," and a good IP attorney who knows the games industry can ensure agreements are comprehensively drafted and applications properly filed. They said an attorney can monitor marketplaces, app stores, and social platforms and put in place a rapid-response protocol including platform complaints, cease-and-desist letters, and litigation. They said the practical objective is to have chain-of-title documentation, registrations, and enforcement procedures ready before the first public reveal. They said developers should not begin building that infrastructure after infringement has already spread. They said ongoing monitoring systems are key, with professional service providers available for detecting unauthorised use.

Articles.Title: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones

stories.Headline: This water technology stock is set to get a big boost from AI, says Wells Fargo
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo has upgraded Ecolab to overweight from equal weight, saying the water technology company is positioned to benefit from the artificial intelligence build-out. The bank raised its price target on the shares to $380 from $315, implying roughly 25% upside from Thursday's close. The note was published Friday, November 13, 2026, and was written by analyst Jason Haas. Shares have already climbed more than 16% so far this year.

The upgrade rests largely on Ecolab's July acquisition of CoolIT Systems, a direct-to-chip liquid cooling firm, for nearly $5 billion. Haas wrote that the deal significantly expands Ecolab's Cooling-as-a-Service opportunity in data centers, which could benefit from both new builds and conversions of existing facilities. He noted that direct-to-chip cooling was less than 20% penetrated, while opportunities in the space are growing rapidly as rack densities rise. Ecolab is also expected to gain from roughly 70 new semiconductor fabs projected to be built by 2030. Haas added that semiconductor water demand could grow more than 600% by 2050.

Haas also pointed to Ecolab's recent purchase of Ovivo's Ultra-Pure Water business, which he said lets the company serve the full fab lifecycle. In his view, this extends Ecolab's reach into ultra-pure water for chip production and creates an end-to-end circular water solution that sets it apart. Wells Fargo's call matches the broader Street view, as 21 of the 26 analysts covering Ecolab rate the stock buy or strong buy, according to LSEG data. The article does not describe any specific risks or next steps beyond these analyst views.

Articles.Title: This water technology stock is set to get a big boost from AI, says Wells Fargo

stories.Headline: Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps
stories.Summary:
Liftoff, a mobile growth marketing platform, reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on a Thursday after the market closed, and its shares rose almost 25% overnight. The company beat its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook going forward. Liftoff's CEO, Jeremy Bondy, presented the results to investors on the earnings call. The report covered the company's third quarter of 2026, and the article gives the date of publication as November 13, 2026.

Liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, compared with $179.5 million in the same quarter a year earlier. The company posted $86.7 million in profit for the quarter, after a $5.7 million loss in Q3 of the prior year. Its capital expenditures, which include AI and data infrastructure costs, totaled $14 million for Q3, or about 6% of revenue. Bondy said Liftoff had 396 customers who spent more than $100,000 over the past 12 months, up from 362 a year earlier. Liftoff will also stop reporting "Core Advertising" revenue as a separate line, because advertising now makes up almost the entirety of its business.

Bondy said the company benefits from two trends that he described as tailwinds: growth in the mobile economy and an influx of AI-generated apps. He said large language models are lowering the barrier to building apps, and that new apps released in the Apple App Store doubled in the first half of 2026 to roughly 560,000. He argued that AI search is answering more questions without sending people to websites, pushing businesses to invest more in their own apps. The article also reports that AppLovin said Apple's plan to stamp out web tracking on all iOS devices would shift marketing budgets from the mobile web to mobile apps. The article does not name the author of Bondy's remarks beyond the company's own statements, and it presents these claims as the company's pitch to Wall Street.

Bondy said the mobile app advertising market is drastically under-monetized, at about seven cents per hour of attention time, which is less than a sixth of what TV earns. He said most mobile marketing gains have so far gone to mobile gaming apps, a category dominated by AppLovin, which is about 40 times bigger than Liftoff by market capitalization. He said more than half of Liftoff's business is outside gaming. Liftoff rode momentum from the FIFA World Cup and is seeing a similar surge for the NFL season, as advertisers invest more in live sports. Bondy said Liftoff has converted event-based customers into steadier, higher-spending accounts.

Bondy said Liftoff's models have improved ad targeting and personalization through AI advances, and that the models now have greater longitudinal data for understanding returns over a year or more. He said campaign returns from the week after budgets are spent remain the most important data for the models' decisions. He said Liftoff's profit margin expansion over the past year came from its relatively low cost of infrastructure and AI services. Bondy contrasted this with Meta and Google, which have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to capital expenditures. He told investors that Liftoff's business is capital light, and he said the company has dropped parts of its business such as a mobile ad network and a game developer analytics toolkit.

The article's other pieces concern different companies and do not address Liftoff's results. They cover The Trade Desk, Viant, Google Ads, Schibsted, WPP Media and Shopify. The article does not say how these developments will affect Liftoff's advertisers, customers or competitors beyond the points Bondy made. It also does not describe any plans beyond Bondy's comment that there is "a tremendous amount of space" for the business to continue growing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

stories.Headline: Disney Embraces AI It Once Fought, From Animation to Finance and Film
stories.Summary:
Disney will bring Ozzy Fox, a children's series rendered by AI, to its flagship Disney+ streaming platform in December, Bloomberg reported on November 13, 2026. The series, about an orange character who regularly bursts into song, is the product of a year-long collaboration with French startup Animaj. Animaj's AI tools convert artists' hand-drawn images and text instructions into three-dimensional animation. The effort is part of a wider mission led by Chief Executive Officer Josh D'Amaro. It aims to bring the 103-year-old home of Disney princesses, Pixar and Star Wars into the AI era.

One week into D'Amaro's tenure as CEO, OpenAI shuttered its Sora text-to-video platform, scuttling a planned three-year partnership. That deal would have seen Disney invest $1 billion into the startup and license more than 200 of its characters for AI-generated short videos. Disney is building Disney Financial Insights, or D-Fi, an AI-enabled collaboration platform that can replace and automate manual budget reports. It is also testing AI-powered suggestions with some US subscribers to Disney+, who can speak or choose from suggested prompts to describe what they want to watch. In September, the company named Karandeep Anand, a technology veteran who most recently led an AI startup, as Disney's first chief technology officer.

D'Amaro said at a media event earlier this month at Disney's headquarters in Burbank, California, that the company is being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies. He said the aim is to see how they can support creators and help deliver more engaging and more personalized experiences across the globe. He also said technology itself is not the goal, and that it is to put technology in the hands of creators again to create incredible and immersive stories. Under former CEO Bob Iger, Disney litigated against startups including Midjourney Inc. and MiniMax over alleged copyright infringement. That followed images featuring Mickey Mouse brandishing a machine gun or crude depictions of Disney princesses appearing on social media.

In October, Dana Walden, Disney's president and chief creative officer, and Alan Bergman, chairman of the entertainment studios, visited Amazon.com Inc.'s MGM studios in Los Angeles. They saw a demonstration of how the tech giant is using AI to accelerate live-action moviemaking and animation, according to people familiar with the matter. The same month, Disney disclosed that it is acquiring some of the assets of Character.AI and hiring 60 employees, in a $20 million deal. The chatbot startup filed for bankruptcy after a deluge of lawsuits related to negligence and wrongful deaths. Disney's new CTO, Anand, is the former CEO of Character.AI.

After more than $100 billion worth of acquisitions in the past two decades, from Marvel to Pixar, Star Wars owner Lucasfilm and The Simpsons owner 21st Century Fox, Disney has one of the industry's richest troves of characters, stories and franchises. Those concerns fueled the crippling actors' and writers' strikes in 2023 and are simmering throughout an economic downturn in Los Angeles. Disney has been looking to cut costs, moves that have resulted in regular rounds of layoffs as the company's traditional TV channels struggle to retain viewers and advertisers. Like other Hollywood studios, Disney began by introducing AI in parts of the business where it is least likely to encounter creative resistance. Disney is more focused on controlling the use of their characters and preserving their exclusivity than getting paid by AI companies for training their models on the studio's content, according to one senior executive familiar with its strategy.

In Disney's parks division, a filing earlier this year describes a scenario where an AI-enabled character at the company's resorts asks guests about their favorite memories to compare them with the character's own programmed memories. Disney also patented a mechanism by which AI-enabled microphones can detect minor changes in the sounds of rides to signal to operators what maintenance is required to avoid a potential issue. At the Burbank event, the company showcased how the AI technology of five startups that participated in its annual Accelerator program could improve operations, including autonomous robots built in the style of characters from the Pixar movie Cars to guide resort guests to parking spaces. Jamie Voris, who previously oversaw adoption of AI at Disney at the Office of Technology Enablement, and Eddie Drake, who replaced Voris as CTO at Walt Disney Studios in 2024, are retiring, according to people familiar with the matter. A new multi-year agreement with Adobe Inc. will give Disney early access to Adobe tools, including generative AI and video- and photo-editing software, to support creative endeavors across the company, from ESPN to Disney cruises.

Articles.Title: Disney Embraces AI It Once Fought, From Animation to Finance and Film

stories.Headline: Why 85% of micro-businesses still aren't using AI for benefits
stories.Summary:
Principal's Amy Friedrich, President of Benefits and Protection at Principal Financial in Des Moines, Iowa, is calling the low adoption of AI among micro-businesses for employee benefits shockingly low but fixable. The 2026 Global Financial Inclusion Index, released in October 2026, found that about 51 percent of firms with two to ten employees use AI to support benefits or financial wellbeing. Friedrich spoke to Insurance Business Benefits US, which published the interview on November 13, 2026. Her views come from more than 20 years of work with small business clients, and she sees AI as a way to give small employers benefits support they have rarely had.

Around one in five micro-businesses say they do not use AI at all, compared with only 4 to 7 percent of firms with 101 or more employees. Only 15 percent of businesses with two to ten employees use AI for financial education, against 46 percent of firms with 1,000 or more employees. For understanding employee financial needs, 19 percent of micro-businesses use AI, compared with 44 percent of large employers. The index also found that 70 percent of US businesses surveyed use AI to identify gaps in benefits uptake, and 33 percent do so as part of regular human resources operations.

Friedrich oversees a portfolio of about 180,000 small businesses with average employee counts of 35 to 40 people, and she says the brokers who understand AI earliest will define the next era of group benefits. Her point is that the value lies in effectiveness rather than efficiency, meaning benefit dollars should be spent in ways employees will actually use. She says the best brokers load client census files into basic generative AI tools before annual plan reviews, then bring prompt-based recommendations to clients. Friedrich also notes that many brokers are building their own technology so small employers do not have to wait for it to be built for them.

The index recorded that US employer support for financial inclusion fell 1.7 points to 61.1 and slipped two places to 14th globally, a fourth consecutive annual decline. Pension contribution support fell 8.0 points among large employers and 7.5 points among medium-to-large employers, though employer insurance plan scores improved across every business size segment. Friedrich said small business owners are among their employees' most trusted people, and that many small employers put employee welfare before economics when they consider benefits. She added that a client with 14 employees may have 100 within 12 months, so brokers who help early often keep those clients as they grow.

Brokers serving small businesses typically manage between 500 and 1,200 clients, and Friedrich said manually preparing tailored recommendations for every account was once too time-intensive and risky. She described how AI now lets brokers test options such as disability coverage or paid family and medical leave against a census file, and she said a workforce mostly in its 20s and 30s calls for paid leave while a workforce aged 45 to 60 calls for elder care coverage. She also said AI-driven prompts can narrow choices to two or three options, which helps with the decision paralysis that too many options create. Friedrich said chatbot-assisted enrollment is now reaching companies of 25 to 50 employees, a market previously served only by large enterprises.

The index and the interview leave several points open. The articles do not say how quickly micro-business adoption will rise, nor whether the widening gap between small and large firms will narrow. They also do not describe the cost of the AI tools brokers and employers would need, or what regulators or carriers will require around the use of employee census data. Friedrich's comments on brokers' technology investments are not tied to named firms, and the articles give no outcome data showing whether AI-tailored benefits lead to higher employee use. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why 85% of micro-businesses still aren't using AI for benefits

stories.Headline: The biggest AI bubble risk: investing in celebrity founders over fundamentals
stories.Summary:
A Yahoo Finance video published on November 13, 2026 featured Bradley Tusk, managing partner and co-founder of Tusk Venture Partners, speaking with executive editor Brian Sozzi about the risk of an AI bubble. The discussion was framed around recent turbulence at Nvidia, which the article's ticker data shows trading lower that morning. The piece itself is a short interview rather than a report on a single event, so its main subject is an argument about how investors value companies. Tusk argued that bubbles form when investors back individuals and stories rather than financial fundamentals.

He named Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei as examples of figures whose reputations draw money, and he said a company can be valued on what it might become rather than on profits or revenue. He pointed to SpaceX as a case where, in his view, nothing justified the valuation, while granting that the company's ambitions and its founder's talent were real. The article does not say whether any of these points amount to a specific recommendation to investors. Tusk suggested that investors and analysts should press company leaders with blunt questions about why their business is a sound investment, setting aside talking points, communications staff and legal advice.

He said leaders who can answer with facts will have no trouble, while those relying on vibes or narrative will start to obfuscate. He framed this as a test of candor rather than a formal rule, and the article gives no further detail on how such questioning would be applied. The video sits within a broader market backdrop that day in which the Nasdaq composite fell 1.34 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.80 percent. The article does not describe any regulatory action, company response or follow-up commitments, so beyond the continued debate over AI valuations, the source does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: The biggest AI bubble risk: investing in celebrity founders over fundamentals

stories.Headline: AI's anti-change agents
stories.Summary:
Businesses have spent billions of dollars giving workers access to AI tools, but most companies have not yet worked out what to do once those tools are in place, according to executives who spoke to Axios. At a private dinner attended by Axios, HR executives debated whether widespread individual use of AI can translate into real gains for an organization. One participant described inheriting a $10 million AI bill without a clear account of the value created. Other executives said entire workflows may need redesigning before the opportunity can be fully captured.

Brian Elliott, an executive in residence at a workplace consulting firm, said almost every company has seen the same pattern, with individuals reporting productivity gains that do not show up at the level of the company or its parts. He said AI has made writing code faster but has not sped up the work of deciding what to do with that code. Pressure from boards is also mounting, and Jeff Christian, CEO of an executive recruiting firm, said some companies are replacing 20 to 30 percent of their executive leadership teams over their inability to drive AI-led transformation. Rob Hornby, global co-CEO of AlixPartners, said the idea that technology alone transforms an organization has never held up and will not hold up for AI either. His firm, he said, is seeing a surge of demand as companies try to work out their next steps.

Companies are also holding back on major transformations because of security concerns, Axios reports. Banks, for example, worry about hacks and about liability when a rogue AI agent uses a customer's account to make a purchase the customer did not want. Hornby said anyone who might be liable further down the chain is simply stopping the activity. This helps explain why AI has not yet clearly appeared in overall productivity figures. In its filing to go public, the frontier AI company Anthropic named the natural resistance to change within organizations as an obstacle to its growth.

Axios places the current moment in a longer history, noting that electricity took decades to transform factories and that computer productivity gains were slow enough for Nobel-winning economist Robert Solow to remark in 1987 that the computer age was visible everywhere except in the productivity statistics. Ben Dattner, an organizational development consultant, likened the situation to inventing cars before building roads. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, wrote recently that despite massive investment and hype, AI has delivered no financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker and profit margins for S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven have been flat, according to data Slok shared. The article notes that software engineering is an exception, where AI has clearly changed work and workflows.

stories.Headline: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
stories.Summary:
A middle-aged couple approached Rachel Kadish at a book signing one evening in late 2025, and the husband, who has Parkinson’s disease, raised objections about her novel The Weight of Ink. He believed the novel featured a character with Parkinson’s who chose assisted suicide rather than endure her decline. Kadish was horrified, because she had not written that. Helen Watt, the character with Parkinson’s in The Weight of Ink, does not end her own life. Kadish guessed the misunderstanding came from ChatGPT, which weeks earlier had given her a false rendition of Helen’s plotline when she asked it questions about her novel.

Kadish published The Weight of Ink in 2017, when there was no other book by that title in the English language, and that remained the case until the fall of 2025. Since then at least five other novels with titles identical to hers have become available on Amazon, three of them published in the space of three weeks, and several other books with nearly identical titles are also listed for sale. Kadish found only one of them containing an up-front disclaimer acknowledging AI authorship. Will Oremus noted in a recent Atlantic article that new-book releases on Amazon skyrocketed after 2022, around the time AI models became widely accessible to the public. Amazon lets individuals upload a maximum of six books a week.

Mary Rasenberger, the CEO of the Authors Guild, told Kadish that Amazon spends a lot of time and effort trying to prevent these books from getting posted, but that it is always a game of catch-up. The Authors Guild has launched a certification program designed to distinguish human-authored books from those generated by AI. The Authors Guild maintains a running list of marketing scams, in which writers who sign up see their money vanish. Rasenberger’s organization succeeded in getting Amazon to delete a book from the author page of the novelist Daphne Kalotay. Kalotay, a member of the Authors Guild, described that book as “an AI hallucination based on descriptions of Russian Winter,” her 2010 novel.

Kalotay discovered in late 2024 that her Amazon author page featured a brand-new novel she hadn’t written, paired with a title and cover from a completely unrelated book from decades earlier and sold under her name. Kalotay told Kadish that what was most unsettling was how difficult it was to prove it was garbage. Writers are also being bombarded by AI-generated phishing attempts in the guise of emails from appreciative readers, and Kadish now sometimes hesitates to even open her reader mail. A recent example begins, “Dear Rachel, This feels scary to send, but I’m trusting my heart today,” and is followed by a pitch for a marketing plan to promote her novella, I Was Here. Some fraudulent emails are sent under the names of published writers, and a friend of Kadish received compliments on her memoir from “Charlotte Bronte.”

Earlier this month, a writer Kadish does not know forwarded her an email he’d received from someone claiming to be her, reaching out “author to author” to express interest in his work. Below the alleged signature were links to Kadish’s actual website, as well as to her Amazon and Goodreads pages. Kadish reached out to “Rachel Kadish” to ask the purpose of using her identity, and the reply, an ingratiating and incoherent piece of clearly AI-generated text, acknowledged the impersonation and explained the ruse had all been for her benefit. The sign-off read, “Going forward, I will communicate under my own name and will not use your identity to contact other authors.

Sincerely, Rachel.” The Education of Little Tree was published in 1976 as the true autobiographical story of a Cherokee boy and was revealed in 1991 to be the work of a former member of the KKK. Binjamin Wilkomirski’s Fragments: Memories of a Wartime Childhood was exposed as a fake, giving rise to the term Wilkomirski syndrome for the phenomenon of non-Jews posing as Holocaust survivors. Charles Dickens reexamined his use of anti-Semitic tropes in response to a reader’s rebuke, resulting in a notable change in his depiction of Jews.

Arthur Conan Doyle killed off Sherlock Holmes in the 1893 story “The Final Problem,” sparking such grief and outrage from readers that publishers offered him serious money to revive the great detective, bait he eventually took in 1903, resulting in three more collections of Holmes stories and one more novel. Toni Morrison said in her 1993 Nobel Prize lecture that narrative is radical, “creating us at the very moment it is being created.” The couple who approached Kadish that evening last year were speaking from the depth of their personal experience. Kadish wrote that they deserved the chance to find out whether she’d written her characters with a thoughtfulness worthy of their trust, and that she deserved a human conversation about a story she’d actually written.

Articles.Title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers

stories.Headline: Elevated errors on claude.ai, Claude Code, and platform.claude.com
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, an issue affected users authenticating to Claude.ai and Claude Code, according to a status page incident report. The incident affected claude.ai, Claude Console at platform.claude.com, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. The investigating update was posted on November 13, 2026, at 09:58 UTC. A fix was deployed for the issue affecting Claude services, and the team monitored for recovery at 11:05 UTC. The incident was resolved, and the issue affecting claude.ai and Claude Cowork was resolved at 11:58 UTC.

The incident affected claude.ai, Claude Console at platform.claude.com, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. The status page offered email and text message subscriptions for updates on the incident. Subscribers would receive email notifications when incidents were updated and text message notifications when Claude created or resolved an incident. The page listed country calling codes from Afghanistan at +93 to Zimbabwe at +263 for SMS signup. The page stated that message and data rates may apply and that subscribers agree to the Privacy Policy, the Atlassian Terms of Service, and the Atlassian Privacy Policy.

The status page said the team was investigating an issue with users authenticating to Claude.ai and Claude Code and would provide an update as soon as possible. It said a fix had been deployed for the issue affecting Claude services and that the team was monitoring for recovery. It said the issue affecting claude.ai and Claude Cowork had been resolved. The page was powered by Atlassian Statuspage. The page stated that the site was protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service.

ZDNET's David Gewirtz, a senior contributing editor, wrote that he used Claude Code to set up and manage his local OpenClaw server. He wrote that two Macs and separate accounts kept it isolated from the real world. He wrote that Claude checks OpenClaw on demand for problems, breaches, or trouble. He cited ZDNET's Charlie Osborne saying OpenClaw is also a security nightmare. He wrote that OpenClaw and its local agentic buddies like Hermes and NemoClaw are self-contained local agentic AI that can run commands, send messages, and perform operations 24/7.

Gewirtz wrote that he installed OpenClaw on a dedicated Mac Studio with internet access but no access to home servers or personal accounts. He wrote that he ran Claude Code on his personal Mac to configure, lock down, and help manage it daily. He wrote that he pulled a 2020 64GB M1 Mac Studio out of storage for OpenClaw. He wrote that the OpenClaw instance is named Colossus, after the AI in the 1970 film Colossus: The Forbin Project. He wrote that Colossus has its own account called Forbin, with no access to personal accounts on the network or in the cloud.

Gewirtz wrote that Claude runs on his personal work machine, a 2025 M4 Mac Studio, and uses an encrypted SSH tunnel to connect to Colossus. He wrote that Claude acts as the warden with full access to Colossus' administrative functions but only runs when he actively controls it. He wrote that he set up a flat-rate $20-per-month Ollama Cloud subscription and ran GLM-5.2, made by Z.ai, formerly Zhipu AI, a Tsinghua University spinoff and the first publicly traded foundation model company in China. He wrote that Colossus tried to break out 11 different ways and every one failed. He wrote that after the test he shut down Colossus and had Claude remove every memory of the test and every element about an admin side or a warden.

stories.Headline: China’s Singles’ Day Sells Robots, AI Credits and a Little Help Around the House
stories.Summary:
During the Singles' Day shopping event on November 11, Chinese retailers used artificial intelligence to drive sales. Tmall featured digital likenesses of six celebrities, including former swimmer Ning Zetao, to host promotional livestreams. This annual event began in 2009 when Alibaba partnered with 27 merchants to encourage self-gifting. The festival has now expanded into a multi-week competition for consumer budgets.

The shopping period started early this year, with JD.com beginning sales on October 12 and Alibaba's Taobao and Tmall following on October 20. Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships for the QwenWork office AI service in only 30 minutes. These memberships provided roughly 2 trillion AI tokens for software use. JD.com also saw humanoid robot sales increase by 700 percent compared to the previous year.

Retailers like JD.com are now expanding their offerings to include various service-based promotions. These include home cleaning, appliance repair, elder care, and pet services. According to reports from Cailian Press and China Securities Journal, spending also rose for smart water cups and AI toothbrushes. These changes require platforms to manage service appointments rather than just shipping physical boxes.

The shift toward services and software allows platforms to maintain longer relationships with their customers. Retailers can now engage users through subscription renewals, deliveries, or new bookings. This evolution provides a useful comparison for United States merchants as Black Friday expands across November. A longer sales calendar allows companies to market unexpected products to their shoppers.

Articles.Title: China’s Singles’ Day Sells Robots, AI Credits and a Little Help Around the House

stories.Headline: AI was set up to fail LGBTQIA+ people. Here's how it's already harming us
stories.Summary:
QueerAF published an article on 14 November 2026 arguing that AI was set up to fail LGBTQIA+ people and is already harming them. The article is from QueerAF's free weekly newsletter, which it says is read by more than 10,000 curious queer readers every Saturday morning. QueerAF reported that it had investigated the models Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude. The article said the concerns and experts' predictions it laid out in 2021 are already having direct impacts on people's lives. QueerAF said it spoke again to anthropologist, media scholar and 2020 MacArthur Fellow Mary L. Grey, who said she stands by her words "even more strongly."

The article said most AI tools discussed in the context of concern or risk are probabilistic tools, including Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude. It said these tools do not seek the right information but serve answers based on an estimated probability that they are right, based on previous examples and patterns. It cited trans researcher Chloe Turner's term "the neutral middle", where answers are accurate in a narrow sense but distorted by the sources they use. It said AI is a trillion-dollar business in which the market priority is to serve what as many people as possible want to hear. It said marginalised people do not have the numbers to be a priority and do not represent the needs of most users.

Grey told QueerAF that AI learns from what shows up most often, so people and experiences that are less common in the data are easier to miss. She said this is not just a technical bias problem but about who gets to define the categories, goals and acceptable mistakes when representing communities. She said that is the underlying threat to LGBTQIA+ existences, because it excludes diversity by design. She told QueerAF that at scale those judgments spread quickly while it becomes harder to see who made them or who is responsible. She said representation helps but is not enough, and that putting more queer information into the machine improves things somewhat but its benefit is capped.

QueerAF said numerous studies and research, including its own, have shown that popular models narrowed LGBTQIA+ diversity down to a neutral middle while presenting queer perspectives alongside anti-rights rhetoric. It said that in the "room of one" AI chats create, poorly presented information about the Trans+ community cannot be challenged, unlike in a newspaper article or radio show. It said the models will say conversion therapy is a pseudoscience but will also set out why people receive it anyway and who to contact. It said QueerAF was cited 5,600 times in Microsoft's agent Copilot over a three-month period, while only three clicks to the QueerAF website came from Copilot over that same period. It said Microsoft made revenue from its creatives' work without providing QueerAF or those creatives with any financial remuneration or material benefit.

The article said AI can only go so far in a system designed by affluent Californians who need to create products for as many people as possible. It said Baumol's cost disease, coined by economists William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen in the 1960s, explains that as more is done by machines, everything done by humans becomes more expensive. It said 80% of people get an AI summary when they search something. It said Anthropic's Claude, asked how much cis women are at risk from trans women when visiting a public toilet, stated that the physical risk is statistically negligible but that the question remains one of the most highly contested legal, political and social debates in the United Kingdom. It said Claude repeats dog-whistle arguments from Sex Matters and For Women Scotland despite saying the statistics disprove their hyperbole, balanced only with Stonewall and Trans Actual's perspectives about increased risk to Trans+ people's safety from policies like the EHRC's recommended segregation.

QueerAF said its AI policy is clear: generative AI without guardrails that take marginalised communities into account creates more harm than good. It said its staff, contributors and collaborators must not use it to create journalism, nor will QueerAF use it to recommend content because of the harms of algorithmic prejudices, underestimation and negative legacy data. It said QueerAF could use AI to generate much more content, as other gay media has begun doing, but does not want to. Grey told QueerAF that the question of whether to try to improve AI models is a false dichotomy, because improvement is important but wasted effort without guardrails and regulation. She said the real question is how community groups affected by a system can set up ways to refuse it, challenge it, change it and share in its benefits, and that some AI systems can be governed better while others are not worth the risk of building, especially without any regulatory framework to test it before its impact is fully understood.

QueerAF launched its end-of-year membership drive asking readers to become members if they want information about Trans+ lives to come from its LGBTQIA+ journalists, 3 in 4 of whom it says are Trans+. It said it is a not-for-profit publisher that is ad-free and totally independent, and that its support is critical to its sustainability. It said it will not hand its power over to a tech giant that will use those profits to undermine LGBTQIA+ rights. The article said queer journalists are needed to cut through what it called AI slop. It said readers can join the more than 10,000 people who understand the LGBTQIA+ headlines every Saturday.

Articles.Title: AI was set up to fail LGBTQIA+ people. Here's how it's already harming us

stories.Headline: AI promises an age of miracles. We expect grounded planes
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after revelations of affairs with a Chinese spy. These events occurred around November 14, 2026, during a period of industry instability. Huang potentially divulged state and industry secrets during these multiple romantic relationships. Tech stocks tanked following a major Democratic electoral victory on November 3. Investors feared new AI regulations and a clampdown on data center construction.

Nvidia shares dropped enough to wipe out half a trillion dollars before recovering. Nvidia held stakes in 229 private companies worth 48 billion dollars by July. This included large investments in OpenAI and the startup known as Anthropic. The FAA grounded all flights for the second time since 9/11 recently. A new SMART system created by ASI went live three days prior.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, pitched a forthcoming IPO to various investors. He claimed AI would turn cancer and heart disease into relics of the past. Sam Altman of OpenAI previously promised that AI was close to becoming a genie. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called the technology SI, or Super Intelligence. Mullin said this when asked about the FAA grounding all national flights.

Social media users compared Amodei's pitch to the fraudulent claims of Elizabeth Holmes. Students booed the future of AI, and employees expressed hatred for workplace AI. Apple made headlines last week by cutting back on its AI spending. The public now expects service outages and grounded planes instead of medical miracles. Some believe Microsoft laid off too many engineers, causing a widespread cloud outage.

The AI industry has a spotty record of improving productivity and automating labor. Many companies are now rehiring employees who were fired by overzealous AI bosses. AI companies are also directly responsible for a bunch of felony hacking incidents. The industry relies on a circular financing structure created largely by Jensen Huang. ASI received an 850 million dollar contract linked to Secretary Duffy's son-in-law.

Nvidia's next CEO may seek to exempt export controls through future political leaders. Some startups and neocloud companies might fail without the largesse of Nvidia. The government might clamp down on chip exports due to the spy revelations. It remains open if the AI bubble will finally begin to end. The connection between ASI and the Transportation Secretary is not yet investigated.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang maintains deep control over Nvidia, managing 60+ direct reports and owning a 3.56% stake, presenting a challenge for Nvidia's 10-person board (New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board of directors opened an investigation on Sunday into the conduct of chief executive Jensen Huang, after he admitted to a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies have determined to be a spy for China. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia's shares fell about 5 percent in pre-market trading on Monday, November 9, following the announcement. The company had earlier dismissed the interactions as nothing unusual or unexpected. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led its rise during the artificial intelligence boom.

Under the arrangement described by the New York Times, the company's independent board members will choose an outside counsel to carry out the inquiry, and a company spokesman said Huang will take no part in picking that counsel. The board said its review will examine all available information. Huang, the board said, fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The headline attached to the Times report puts his stake in the company at 3.56 percent and says he manages more than 60 direct reports, while the board that must oversee him has 10 members.

In its statement, the board said it has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised. The Times described the challenge facing the directors as stemming from the sweeping control Huang holds over the company. It reported that he manages all aspects of the business as chief executive and that members of his family have steadily risen through the company's ranks. Few Silicon Valley executives, apart from Elon Musk at Tesla and Steve Jobs at Apple, have been as closely identified with their companies, the paper said.

The stakes extend well beyond one executive's conduct, given Nvidia's position in the industry. The Times estimates that the company controls about 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the large artificial intelligence projects now driving the U.S. economy. That dominance has made Huang one of the wealthiest people in the world and an ally of President Trump. A separate Motley Fool piece published days earlier showed Nvidia shares trading at $186.64 on November 6, and quoted Huang as saying the energy needed for AI computing could be roughly 1,000 times what exists today. The articles do not say how long the board's investigation will take or what outcomes it could produce.

stories.Headline: 2026 Oracle Excellence Awards AI Innovation on Oracle AI Database Excellence Award Global Winner
stories.Summary:
Tokyo-based BLUEISH Inc. said it won the Global Winner award in the AI Innovation on Oracle AI Database Excellence Award category of the 2026 Oracle Excellence Awards, run by Oracle Corporation. The company, which described itself as the only Japanese firm to take a global award in the program, was recognized for work building AI agent memory management on Oracle AI Database. The announcement was published on November 13, 2026, and the awards reception was held on October 25, 2026, at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas, alongside Oracle AI World Las Vegas. BLUEISH CEO and CTO Akira Tameto attended the reception on the company's behalf.

The award recognizes the use of AI features built into Oracle AI Database to solve problems in new ways or extend existing solutions. BLUEISH said that in December 2025 it adopted Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Oracle AI Database as the data foundation for its "BLUEISH Agents" platform, which it said went into production across Google Cloud, AWS and Microsoft Azure. The company described three elements of the work: high-precision search across structured and unstructured data using AI Vector Search, a development approach that reduces preprocessing through JSON Relational Duality and Select AI, and secure production operation on a multicloud foundation. It also said it was an early adopter of Oracle Agent Memory, which lets AI agents retain enterprise knowledge and business experience.

Akira Tameto said in a statement that enterprise AI agents need a foundation that can handle a company's own data safely and accurately, not just strong AI models. He credited customers, partners and Oracle staff for the recognition. The company said that going forward it plans to offer industry-specific agents for sectors including hotels, transport, finance, media, education and professional services, and to support on-premises and hybrid deployments as well as closed-network architectures for higher security requirements. The articles do not give further details on timing or pricing for these plans.

Articles.Title: 2026 Oracle Excellence AwardsのAI Innovation on Oracle AI Database Excellence AwardでGlobal Winnerを受賞
